findings.finding_value: The primary M01-A terms and their root meanings: (1) **ya.re (H3372G, H3372H, H3373)** — root meaning: to fear, to be afraid, to stand in awe. The same root generates the stative verb (to be in a state of fear/reverence), nominal form, and adjective. Stative root significance: the characteristic is a state of being, not primarily an act — it is what the person is, not only what the person does. (2) **yir.ah (H3374)** — nominal form of the ya.re root: "the fear" as a possessed quality, a stable disposition. (3) **pa.chad (H6343)** — root meaning: to dread, to tremble in dread. Derived from a root suggesting the quaking that accompanies overwhelming encounter. (4) **pach.dah (H6345)** — a feminine noun from the pa.chad root — "dread" as a named inner state. (5) **mo.rah / mo.ra (H4172A, H4172B)** — from the ya.re root: "that which causes fear/awe" — the fear-inspiring quality of God or his instruments. (6) **fobeō (G5399)** — root meaning: to flee from, to be put to flight; by extension, to fear (what one flees from). The Greek root's flight-connotation is significant: fear-as-flight is the underlying image. (7) **fobos (G5401)** — the noun form, spanning fear, reverence, and awe. (8) **deos (G6015, Heb 12:28)** — a more refined Greek term for reverential fear distinct from the fobos family — awe in the presence of the sacred.

M01-B's distinctive primary terms: (1) **de.chal (H1763, Aramaic)** — dread, terror in visionary contexts (Dan 2:31 anchor). (2) **za.chal (H2119B)** — to shrink back, crawl in fear (Mic 7:17 anchor — nations crawling out in fearful retreat). (3) **ya.gor (H3016)** — to be afraid of a specific object, anticipatory object-directed dread. (4) **ra.hah (H7297)** — to be afraid, in a specific Isaianic context. (5) **ekthambeo (G1568), ekthambos (G1569)** — to be greatly amazed/alarmed; the ek- prefix intensifies the thambeo root (amazement/astonishment) — extreme awe-shock. (6) **ekfobos (G1630)** — frightened out of one's senses; extreme terror. (7) **emfobos (G1719)** — in a state of fear; afraid, trembling within. (8) **ptoeō (G4422), ptoēsis (G4423), pturomai (G4426)** — roots meaning to be put to sudden flight, startled, alarmed — the image is of startled birds or sudden fright.

M01-C's distinctive terms: (1) **e.mah (H0367)** — terror as an overwhelming force; derived from a root suggesting the effect of dread rather than the feeling itself. (2) **bal.la.hah (H1091)** — sudden terror, consternation; from a root of hasty, overwhelming onset. (3) **chit.tah (H2847)** — terror that paralyzes; related to cha.tat (dismay). (4) **chit.tit (H2851)** — the terror projected by military power; a technical term for the radiating dread of empire. (5) **ma.gor (H4032)** — from a root meaning to sojourn as a stranger, hence the terror of the homeless/unsafe — encircling dread with no refuge. (6) **me.chit.tah (H4288)** — terror/ruin as an instrument of destruction.

M01-D's distinctive terms: (1) **ba.hal (H0926)** — to dismay, alarm, agitate; root meaning sudden, overwhelming disruption — the term uniquely covers both inner shock and the hasty rashness that follows. (2) **be.hal (H0927, Aramaic)** — the Aramaic cognate, dominant in Daniel. (3) **cha.tat (H2865)** — to be dismayed, shattered; from a root of breaking, shattering — the image is of an inner vessel broken. (4) **tim.ma.hon (H8541)** — bewilderment, confusion of mind; from a root of astonishment leading to cognitive disorientation.

M01-E's distinctive terms: (1) **cha.rad (H2729)** — to tremble, quake; a bodily root. (2) **cha.red (H2730)** — the trembling one/trembling posture — a qualitative adjective describing the person defined by trembling reverence. (3) **cha.ra.dah (H2731)** — trembling as a noun — "the great trembling." (4) **ra.gaz (H7264)** — to tremble, quake, be agitated — a broader term covering both inner agitation and outward trembling. (5) **ra.ad (H7460, H7461A, H7461B)** — to tremble, shudder — specifically the shaking motion. (6) **sa.ar (H8175A, H8178A)** — to shudder, to bristle (as in hair standing on end) — a visceral somatic reaction. (7) **pal.la.tsut (H6427)** — shuddering, horror-trembling. (8) **entromos (G1790)** — trembling, in a state of trembling; compound of en- (in) + tromos (trembling). (9) **tromos (G5156)** — trembling; from the root treo (to tremble). The Greek distinguishes tromos (sustained trembling) from entromos (being in a state of trembling).

M01-F's distinctive terms: (1) **de.a.gah (H1674)** — anxiety, worry; from a root suggesting cognitive engagement with something painful — the worry/anxiety that circles around a concern. (2) **ya.gor (H3025)** — to fear, dread in an anticipatory mode; distinct from the M01-B ya.gor (H3016) by a different root grouping — here the anticipatory-dread sense is primary. (3) **me.go.rah (H4034), me.gu.rah (H4035)** — fear as something harboured within the person — an inner terror lodged and held. (4) **foberos (G5398)** — fearful, dreadful; specifically the fearful expectation of judgment (Heb 10:27 anchor) — the adjective form used to describe divine judgment as the object of dread.

M01-G's distinctive terms: (1) **deilia (G1167)** — timidity, cowardice; a Greek moral-ethical term with evaluative weight — the opposite of andreia (courage/manliness in Greek ethics). (2) **deiliaō (G1168)** — to be timid, to be cowardly. (3) **deilos (G1169)** — cowardly, fainthearted — the adjective used in Jesus's evaluation of the disciples' storm-fear (Mat 8:26; Mar 4:40) and in Rev 21:8.

The cluster's primary Hebrew terms are: ya.re / yir.ah (the broadest fear root, spanning reverential to acute), pa.chad / pach.dah (dread with intensity), mo.rah / mo.ra (the fear-inspiring quality), ba.hal / cha.tat (dismay/shattering), cha.rad / ra.gaz (trembling), and de.a.gah (anxiety/worry). The primary Greek terms are: fobeō / fobos (the dominant NT fear vocabulary), the ek-/em- intensifier compounds (extreme encounter fear), tromos / entromos (trembling), deilia / deilos (evaluated timidity), and foberos (fearful as an objective quality of the object). The term inventory confirms the cluster's broad semantic range across the fear-spectrum.

Primary Hebrew: *cha.rah* (H2734) — root meaning to burn/kindle; reveals anger as inner heat that ignites. *che.mah* (H2534) — related to heat; the noun of the burning interior state. *cha.ron* (H2740) — burning as intensifying quality, the most thermally explicit term. *za.am* (H2194/2195) — indignation; possibly related to a root of denunciation, revealing anger as moral verdict declared. *qin.ah* (H7068) — jealousy/zeal; root of passionate attachment, revealing anger arising from violated exclusive claim. *qa.na* (H7065) — to be jealous; the verb of jealous response. Primary Greek: *orgē* (G3709) — from a root meaning to reach for, to swell; reveals anger as a swelling inner impulse that presses toward expression. *orgizō* (G3710) — the verb of the anger-event. *paroxunō* (G3947) — to sharpen/stimulate alongside; reveals anger as something that is sharpened by external stimulus. The root meanings collectively reveal anger as: (1) thermally grounded (heat/burning/kindling); (2) a swelling inner pressure pressing toward expression; (3) a response to a stimulus that sharpens or ignites it.

Primary Hebrew: ba.khah (H1058) — the primary OT weeping verb, used 99 times in M03-A-VCG-01/02/03/04 corpus, root meaning: to weep, cry. sa.phad (H5594) — the primary OT mourning verb (29 verses — M03-B-VCG-01/02/03/04), root: to wail, lament. tsa.rah (H6869B) — primary distress noun (62 verses — M03-D), root: constriction, narrowness, the pressed-in experience. tsar (H6862B) — closely related distress noun (28 verses — M03-D), root: narrow, tight, enemy (the one who presses). ya.gon (H3015) — sorrow (14 verses — M03-C-VCG-01), root: grief as physical and inner toil/pain. makh.ov (H4341) — pain/sorrow (15 verses — M03-F-VCG-01), root: pain, bodily and emotional suffering. a.nach (H0584) — to sigh/groan (11 verses — M03-E-VCG-01), root: the sigh or groan itself. Primary Greek: lupeō (G3076) — to grieve (21 verses — M03-C), root: pain, sorrow; perilupos (G4036) — deeply sorrowful, soul-deep grief (5 verses — M03-C-VCG-03); klauthmos (G2805) — weeping/wailing (9 verses — M03-A-VCG-05); sunochē (G4928) — anguish, constriction, "pressed together" (2 verses — M03-D-VCG-02/05); odunaō/odunē (G3600/3601) — anguish, inner pain (6 verses — M03-D-VCG-02/05).

Root analysis summary: the Hebrew root vocabulary consistently moves between the physical and the inner — the root of constriction (tsar/tsa.rah) names the physical sensation of being pressed in as a metaphor for the inner experience; the root of the sigh (a.nach) names the bodily expression as the characteristic's primary form. The Greek vocabulary is more explicitly inner-located: lupeō/perilupos name states of the inner being; sunochē names the constriction as an inner experience.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Primary terms and root meanings: (1) **gil_verb / gil** (H1523 / H1524A) — root associated with spinning or circular movement, capturing the kinetic energy of rejoicing; used in 36 of 83 verses in this corpus; (2) **su.s** (H7797) — to rejoice, exult, take delight; used in 22 instances; strong affective-volitional force; used of both God's and human exultation; (3) **re.na.nah** (H7445) — triumphing, ringing cry of joy; the sonic-expressive form of exultation (5 instances); (4) **cha.dah** (H2302) — to rejoice, be glad; less frequent (3 instances: Exo 18:9, Job 3:6, Psa 21:6); (5) **te.ev** (H2868, Aramaic) — to be glad (1 instance, Dan 6:23). No primary Greek terms in this corpus — M04-A is exclusively OT. The roots consistently emphasise physical movement (gil — spinning), intensity (su.s), and sonic expression (re.na.nah), revealing exultation as a characteristically kinetic and expressive inner state.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primary terms with root meanings: (1) **sa.mach** (H8055) — to rejoice, be glad; the verbal form used 147 times in M04-B; root meaning connotes brightness and happiness; the causative (hiphil) form frequently shows God as the one who makes people joyful; (2) **sim.chah** (H8057) — joy, gladness, mirth; nominal form, 89 instances in M04-B; the noun names the state that sa.mach produces; (3) **sa.me.ach** (H8056) — joyful, glad; adjectival form; the person characterised by the state; (4) **ma.s.vo.s** (H4885) — joy, exultation, rejoicing; nominal form; associated with festive, communal, bodily-expressive joy; (5) **sa.s.von** (H8342) — gladness, joy, exultation; 22 instances in M04-E; strongly restoration-linked; (6) **chairo** (G5463) — to rejoice, be glad; the primary NT rejoicing verb; 58 instances in M04-C; (7) **chara** (G5479) — joy; noun; 57 instances in M04-C; (8) **agalliao** (G0021) — to exult, rejoice greatly; 11 instances in M04-E-VCG-02; roots carry the sense of leaping or bounding exultation; (9) **sunchairo** (G4796) — to rejoice with, co-rejoice; M04-D; the syn- prefix makes shared participation constitutive; (10) **eufrosune** (G2167) — gladness, good cheer; 2 instances in M04-C.

Root-level summary: The Hebrew roots consistently connote brightness, inner gladness, and outward expression; the Greek roots connote active rejoicing (chairo), the resulting state (chara), and intensified leaping-joy (agalliao). The shared thread across all terms is an active, positive, inner-being brightening that moves outward.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Primary terms: (1) **agalliao** (G0021) — to exult, leap for joy, rejoice greatly; root: agan (very much) + hallesthai (to leap); the root's leaping-intensity quality captures the paradox: this is not mild comfort but intense, outward-moving exultation; 11 instances in M04-E-VCG-02; (2) **ba.lag** (H1082) — to smile, gleam, be cheerful; root: a gleaming or brightening; 3 instances in M04-F-VCG-01 (Job 9:27; 10:20; Psa 39:13) — the root's connotation is fragile, momentary brightening, the exact opposite of agalliao's intensity; (3) **mav.li.git** (H4010) — consolation, comfort; 1 instance (Jer 8:18) — root related to comfort and solace; used here negatively ("my joy/comfort is gone"); (4) **agalliasis** (G0020) — the noun form of agalliao; appears in Luk 1:14 (agalliasis = gladness alongside chairo); Luk 1:44 (the baby leaping in agalliasis); Heb 1:9 (oil of gladness — agalliasis). At definitional level: the agalliao/agalliasis root names an intense, superlative, leaping-quality exultation; ba.lag names its fragile, barely-attainable opposite in the human struggle.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary terms: (1) **tov** (H2896A) — noun, adjective, and evaluative particle; the core goodness-root. Root meaning: pleasant, good, beautiful, beneficial; in its evaluative use it names the quality of what satisfies a standard of genuine excellence. 133 instances across M04-L (83) and M04-O (50). The root generates the noun tov (goodness, good thing), the adjective tov (good, better, best), and the verbal idiom "ki-tov" (for he is good) that forms the liturgical refrain; (2) **makarismos** (G3108) — blessing, blessedness; 3 NT instances in M04-O-VCG-04 (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15). Root: makarios (blessed, happy in divine favour); makarismos names the state of being declared blessed by divine pronouncement; (3) **sa.s.von** (H8342) — gladness, exultation, joy (22 instances in the overlapping M04-E-VCG-01 corpus that serves both Characteristics 2 and 3). Root related to the concept of brightness and joyful gladness; (4) The **ki-tov formula** — not a single term but a liturgical construction ("for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever") functioning as a fixed doxological expression whose repetition across Psalms 100, 106, 107, 118, 135, 136 makes it a structural feature of Gladness's primary register.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Primary terms: (1) **sha.a.shu.im** (H8191) — plural of intensity from sha.a root; root meaning: to delight, play, caress; the plural intensification names not a single act of pleasure but accumulated, multiple-faceted cherishing — the richness of God's treasuring of Ephraim (Jer 31:20), Wisdom's treasuring of humanity (Pro 8:31), the psalmist's treasuring of God's testimonies (Psa 119:24); (2) **sha.a** (H8173B) — verb: to delight, play, sport; root: carefree enjoyment, playing without threat; the nursing-child-over-cobra (Isa 11:8) and bounced-on-knees (Isa 66:12) images bring out the playful-carefree quality; (3) **a.nog** (H6026) — to be delicate, to luxuriate, to delight oneself; root: delicateness, soft/luxurious quality; the most physically-textured of the Delight terms — Deu 28:56's delicate woman, Isa 55:2's rich food, Isa 66:11's deep drinking from abundance; (4) **cha.phets** (H2654A) — to take delight in, to desire, to be pleased; root: to bend down/bow toward; the most volitionally-oriented verbal root — the bending of the will toward its object; (5) **che.phets** (H2656) — delight, desire, matter, affair; the nominal form of H2654A; (6) **cha.phets adj** (H2655) — delighting in (1Ki 13:33; 21:6 — "any who would"); (7) **eudokeo** (G2106) — to think it good, to be well pleased; from eu (well) + dokeo (think/seem); the NT equivalent that carries both the affective-approval quality and the cognitive-positive assessment; the Father's eudokeo in the Son is the deepest NT deployment; (8) **sunēdomai** (G4913) — to rejoice/delight together with; compound: sun (together with) + hēdomai (to be pleased/enjoy); the co-delight register of Rom 7:22 — the inner being delighting in God's law in solidarity with it; (9) **arestos** (G0701) — pleasing, acceptable; from areskō (to please); the compliance/acceptability register of M04-M; (10) **ni.cho.ach** (H5207) — soothing, pleasing (as an aroma); root: to rest/settle; the aroma that settles or soothes — used for the inner-being condition of correctness in worship (or its corruption).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Primary terms: (1) **na.im** (H5273A) — pleasant, agreeable; root na.em — to be pleasant, comfortable, agreeable; the quality of what is fitting and agreeable to the inner sense; the root carries gentleness and ease without harshness; (2) **na.em** (H5276) — to be/experience pleasant; the verbal experience of pleasantness; (3) **no.am** (H5278) — pleasantness, beauty, graciousness; the noun naming the quality: God's own beauty (Psa 27:4), wisdom's character (Pro 3:17); (4) **na.a.man** (H5282) — pleasant (adj): Isa 17:10's "pleasant plants"; (5) **ni.cho.ach** (H5207) — soothing, pleasing (aroma); root nuach — to rest, settle, give rest; the quality of what causes to settle, calm, and rest; the soothing quality of the worship-aroma that causes God's regard to settle into receptive acceptance; (6) **a.nog** (H6026) — to be tender, delicate, to luxuriate; (7) **a.nog adj** (H6028) — tender, delicate; (8) **a.las** (H5965) — to exult, delight (in pleasure); (9) **ta.a.nug** (H8588) — daintiness, luxury; (10) **ed.nah** (H5730B) — pleasure, luxury, delight; (11) **tov** (H2896A) in the comparative register; (12) **thambeō** (G2284) — to be amazed (Mar 10:24). Root synthesis: the na.em root names gentle agreeableness; the nuach root of ni.cho.ach names settling/rest as the mechanism of worship-Pleasure; a.nog/ta.a.nug name delicate, luxuriant ease; a.las names exultant pleasure.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Primary terms: (1) **pa.la** (H6381) — verb: to be extraordinary, surpass, be too difficult; root meaning: to be separated out, set apart from the ordinary; the fundamental semantic: Wonder arises at what is categorically distinct from normal reality; 47 instances; (2) **pe.le** (H6382) — noun: wonder, marvel; 7 instances; Exo 15:11; Isa 9:6 ("Wonderful Counselor"); Psa 77:11; 88:10, 12; 89:5; Isa 25:1; 28:29; 29:14; Lam 1:9; Dan 12:6; (3) **miph.la.ah** (H4652) — wondrous work, noun: Job 37:16; (4) **thambeō** (G2284) — to be seized with astonishment; root: thamb- — to seize, arrest; the bodily and inner arrest quality of Wonder; Mar 1:27; 10:24 (cross-assigned); 10:32; (5) **thauma** (G2295) — wonder, marvel (noun); 2Cor 11:14; Rev 17:6; (6) **thaumazō** (G2296) — to marvel, be astonished; Gal 1:6; Rev 17:6, 7 (also cross-assigned in M04-N-VCG-02). Root synthesis: pa.la/pe.le names Wonder as arising from what is categorically set apart from ordinary reality; thambeō names the inner seizure-quality of Wonder; thaumazō names the sustained state of marvelling.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The comparative root-meaning analysis across the seven characteristics reveals three semantic families: (1) **The movement roots**: gil (H1523 — spinning/circular movement; Exultation); agalliao (G0021 — leaping intensification; Joy/Suffering-Joy); su.s (H7797 — energised surging; Exultation/Delight). These movement-roots name characteristics whose inner experience is characterised by kinetic energy — the inner being in motion toward its object; (2) **The settling/resting roots**: no.am/nuach (H5278/5207 — pleasantness/rest; Pleasure); sha.a (H8173B — carefree resting; Delight); a.nog (H6026 — luxuriating ease; Delight/Pleasure). These settling-roots name characteristics whose inner experience is characterised by resting-in-the-good rather than active movement; (3) **The evaluative/perceptive roots**: tov (H2896A — genuine goodness; Gladness); pa.la (H6381 — set apart from ordinary categories; Wonder). These roots name characteristics whose inner experience is characterised by the inner being correctly assessing or perceiving what is genuinely extraordinary or genuinely good. The cluster's vocabulary thus reflects its phenomenological architecture: the seven characteristics are distributed across motion (Exultation, Joy, Suffering-Joy), rest (Pleasure, Delight), and assessment/perception (Gladness, Wonder).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Primary Hebrew: *bosh* (H0954) — root meaning: to be ashamed, to become pale/confounded, to dry up (the withered-grass image of 2Ki 19:26 echoes this); the root suggests inner collapse/paling. *Ke.lim.mah* (H3639) — from *ka.lam* (to be wounded, humiliated); root suggests a cutting, wounding inner state of disgrace. *Bo.shet* (H1322) — the nominal form of *bosh*, naming shame as a condition or state. *Cha.pher* (H2659) — to be disappointed, disgraced, confounded; root related to searching/digging (seeking what is not found, then becoming ashamed of the failed seeking). **[CHAR-1]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398)** — a verb whose root meaning is "to miss (a target), to go wrong, to offend, to incur guilt." The primary NT term is **hamartanō (G0264)** — from hamartia, likewise meaning "to miss, to err, to sin." The semantic convergence of Hebrew and Greek roots around the "missing the mark" image is analytically significant: both Testaments anchor wilful sinning in the concept of a directional failure — not a neutral act but one that misses what was aimed at. Paraptōma (G3900, once in VCG-05: Gal 6:1) means "a false step, a trespass" — accidental entanglement rather than directed missing.

**[CHAR-15]** E — The sole primary term across all 8 verses is **cha.ta (H2398)** — the verb "to miss the mark, to sin, to incur guilt." The root meaning (missing the mark) reveals that generational sin is not conceptually separated from ordinary sinning at the lexical level: the inherited condition is transmitted through and as the same sinning acts that cha.ta names in its individual-act register. CHAR-15 has no specialised vocabulary for its distinctive feature (the generational inheritance mechanism); the inherited condition is named through the same verb as individual wilful sinning, applied to ancestors ("your first father sinned" — Isa 43:27) and to successive generations ("they sinned still more" — Psa 78:17). No NT Greek vocabulary appears in the 8-verse corpus.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Two primary terms. (1) **chat.ta (H2400)** — OT agent-noun from the cha.ta root ("miss the mark"). The agent-noun form (*qattāl* pattern in Hebrew) indicates habitual or intensive action: chat.ta names not one who has sinned once but one whose character is constitutively defined by sinning. Gen 13:13 — "great sinners" (*chat.ta.im gĕdōlîm*) — the plural agent-noun names a class of persons constituted by extreme habitual sinning. (2) **hamartōlos (G0268)** — NT noun/adjective from hamartanō ("to sin, to miss the mark"). Hamartōlos functions both as a noun ("the sinner" — Luk 7:37) and as an adjective ("sinful man" — Luk 5:8; "sinful generation" — Mar 8:38). The root reveals: the sinner-identity is defined by the same "missing the mark" as ordinary sinning but at the level of constituted character rather than discrete acts.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Five primary term-groups. (1) **a.sham (H0816)** — verb "to be guilty, to become guilty, to realize one's guilt" — dominant in VCG-01's guilt-recognition sequences (Lev 4:13/22/27; 5:2/3/4/5/17/19; Num 5:6; Hos 5:15). The root (*ʾāšam*) means to offend, to incur guilt — the verb form names the becoming-guilty moment and the realising-of-guilt moment. (2) **a.shem (H0818)** — noun "guilty one" — Gen 42:21; Ezr 10:19. (3) **ash.mah (H0819)** — noun "guilt, guiltiness" — dominant in VCG-02's accumulation passages (Ezr 9:6/7/13/15; 2Ch 24:18/28:10/13/33:23). The noun form names the guilt-condition as an accumulated state. (4) **a.von (H5771H)** — "iniquity, guilt, liability" — VCG-03's transferable-burden register (Gen 44:16; Exo 28:38; 2Sa 14:9; Jer 33:8). (5) **a.von (H5771I)** — "punishment, punitive consequence" — VCG-04's punitive register (Gen 4:13; Eze 4:4/5/6). (6) **pu.qah (H6330)** — "staggering, stumbling" — 1Sa 25:31 — the single-term expression of conscience-stagger under guilt. No NT Greek appears in this corpus.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Single primary term throughout: **a.von (H5771G)** — the crime/moral-wrong sub-entry. The root (*ʿāwôn*) derives from a verbal root meaning "to be bent, crooked, twisted" — naming sin as moral deviance from the straight path. In its H5771G crime-sense, the noun names the accumulated moral wrongdoing itself — the twisted inner reality — not merely the act or the punishment. The root's "crookedness" metaphor is significant: iniquity is the constitutive moral distortion of the person's inner orientation, not merely an external act. The "crime" register distinguishes H5771G from the guilt-register (H5771H — the moral liability arising from the crime) and the punishment-register (H5771I — the penal consequence). No NT Greek appears in this 162-verse corpus.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Four primary term-families. (1) **pe.sha (H6588)** / **pa.sha (H6586)** — noun/verb "transgression/to transgress, to rebel, to break away" — OT dominant (115 verses); root *pāšaʿ* means "to break away from, to revolt, to rebel" — naming the act as a relational-political breaking-away from authority. The root is the vocabulary of political rebellion applied to the moral-theological sphere; (2) **sa.rah (H5627)** — "revolt, turning aside, apostasy" — 7 verses in VCG-02; root *sārar* — to turn aside, to rebel — names the inner defiance as an orientation-reversal; (3) **parabasis (G3847) / parabatēs (G3848) / parabainō (G3845)** — NT "transgression/transgressor/to transgress" — 15 verses; Greek compound *para* (beside/past) + *bainō* (to go, to step) — literally "stepping past/beside" — the boundary-crossing spatial metaphor made explicit; (4) **paraptōma (G3900)** — "trespass, false step, lapse" — 5 verses (VCG-05 Adam-paradigm); Greek *para* + *piptō* (to fall beside) — a stumbling aside from the right path.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The primary Hebrew construction is **cha.ta (H2398) + bishgagah** — the verb (sin, miss the mark) combined with the adverb derived from the root *shagah* (to err, to wander, to go astray without intending to). The root *shagah* carries the sense of *unintentional wandering from the path* — the person who strays not through rebellion but through inadvertence. Num 15:27 — "ki tekheta bishgagah" — "when he sins in error/inadvertence." The *shagah* root (with its derivatives *shegagah* H7684 — inadvertent sin, and *shegag* H7683 — to err unintentionally) is the vocabulary that specifically names the unintentional quality, absent from CHAR-1's corpus. The VCG-02 cultic-purification use of cha.ta in the Piel stem (to de-sin, purify) does not carry the *bishgagah* qualifier — it is cha.ta as a denominative process-verb rather than an act-of-sinning description.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Two primary term-families, exclusively OT Hebrew (no NT vocabulary). (1) **ma.al (H4603/H4604)** — verb and noun "to commit a breach of faith, to act unfaithfully, to trespass against sacred things"; from a root meaning "to cover up, to conceal, to act covertly" — naming faithlessness as a concealed inner breach; the ma.al-faithlessness is the hidden betrayal of what was owed; used primarily for unfaithfulness toward God and sacred things (VCG-01 dominant); 1Ch 10:13 — "breach of faith with the Lord." (2) **ba.gad (H0898)** — verb "to act treacherously, to be faithless, to deal deceitfully"; root meaning relates to garment-covering (clothing that covers while hiding) or to dealing deceitfully; the ba.gad-treachery is the betrayal that wears a friendly face; used more for interpersonal treachery (VCG-02 dominant) and constitutional character (VCG-03). The two roots together reveal: ma.al names the sacred-covenantal breach; ba.gad names the relational-interpersonal betrayal.

Together the terms reveal: perversion as the overturning of the proper order (tah.pu.khah/sa.laph), the mixing of what should be kept separate (te.vel), the twisting of what should be straight (a.vah/sur), and the decay/ruin of what was good (cha.val/ftheirō/fthora).

**[CHAR-22]** E — Five primary term-families. (1) **a.vel (H5766A)** / **av.lah (H5766B)** — noun/verb "injustice, wrong, violence, wickedness" — root *ʿāwal* meaning "to act unjustly, to be crooked in dealings"; names the act and condition of moral-conduct wrongness; (2) **av.val (H5767)** — "the unjust one, the unrighteous person" — agent-noun from *ʿāwal*; (3) **a.vil (H5760)** — "ungodly, morally lawless" — from a root denoting moral worthlessness; (4) **adikos (G0094)** — NT "unjust, unrighteous" — Greek compound *a-* (not) + *dikē* (justice, right); literally "not-right/not-just"; the alpha-privative construction names injustice as the negation of justice; (5) **adikēma (G0092)** — NT "wrongdoing, crime, injustice" — the act-noun; the specific deed of injustice. Together the terms reveal: injustice as crookedness in dealings (*ʿāwal*), as person-type (*av.val/adikos*), and as specific legal-moral crime (*adikēma*) — three levels of the same moral failure.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398) in its first-person perfect confessional form**: *chatati* ("I have sinned") and *chatanu* ("we have sinned"). The root (miss the mark, offend, incur guilt) applied in the first-person perfect creates the confessional form: the act of sinning (marked by the root) is now named as completed by the speaker themselves. This is not a distinct confession-vocabulary but the sinning-vocabulary deployed self-referentially. A secondary Hebrew term appears in the corpus through the confession-formula: *yadat* (to know) in 2Sa 19:20 — "your servant *knows* that I have sinned" — the cognitive-knowledge basis of confession. The NT primary term is **hamartanō (G0264) in its aorist/perfect self-application**: Mat 27:4 — *hēmarton* ("I sinned"), Luk 15:18/21 — *hēmarton* ("I have sinned"). No dedicated confession-term appears; the sinning vocabulary is self-applied.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398)** in three forms: (1) the *negated first-person perfect* (Jer 2:35 — "I have not sinned" — *lo chatati*), the direct inversion of the confessional form; (2) the *participle/sinner-type* (Ecc 2:26; 8:12 — "the sinner" — *hachotet/lehachotet*), naming the person constituted by the characteristic; (3) the *question-form* (Jer 16:10 — "what is the sin that we have committed?" — using the noun form alongside the verb). The NT primary terms are **hamartanō (G0264)** in the present continuous (1Cor 15:34 — "do not go on sinning" — ongoing action) and the adjectival/participial **hamartōlos-equivalent** in Tit 3:11 ("sinful"). The root meaning — "to miss the mark" — deployed in the negated/suppressed mode reveals: the characteristic is the refusal to acknowledge what the root reveals — that the mark has been missed.

**[CHAR-5]** E — No single dedicated Hebrew or Greek term names refusal to repent; the characteristic is expressed through *compound constructions*. The primary OT construction is: **lo sar min** ("did not turn aside from") or **lo sur min** ("did not depart from") + **chat.tat** (the sins of Jeroboam). Sur (H5493) means to turn aside, depart, remove; its negated form (*lo sur*) names the refusal-direction explicitly. The complementary construction is **davaq** (H1692 — 2Ki 3:3: "clung to") meaning to cling, adhere, be joined — revealing the active dimension of the refusal. The OT bodily-metaphor construction is **qashu et-orpam** (Neh 9:29 — "stiffened their neck" — H7185 qasha: to be hard, stiff) + **natan kateph sorerah** ("gave a stubborn shoulder" — H5637 sarar: to be stubborn/rebellious). The primary NT construction is **hekousiōs hamartanontōn** (Heb 10:26: sinning willingly/deliberately) and **hamartanontōn** in the present continuous (1Ti 5:20: those persisting in sin).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The primary Hebrew term is **cha.ta (H2398)** in three CHAR-6-distinctive configurations: (1) *Person-type participial*: *hachotet* ("the sinner" — Ecc 7:26; 9:2/18; Pro 11:31/13:22) — the participial used as a substantive naming the constituted sinner-type; (2) *Iterative verb*: "sinned yet again" (Exo 9:34) — the verb used with temporal repetition markers; (3) *Pattern-continuation*: "you have sinned... there they have continued" (Hos 10:9) — sinning as an unbroken temporal pattern. The root meaning ("to miss the mark, to incur guilt") deployed in these configurations reveals: habitual defection is the root action (*miss the mark*) stabilised into a person-type and a continuing pattern rather than an episodic act. The NT primary terms are: **hamartanō (G0264)** in the present continuous (*hamartanōn* — 1Jo 3:6: "keeps on sinning") and the constative aorist (*hēmarton* — Heb 3:17: "those who sinned" naming the historical pattern). The continuous present of 1Jo 3:6 is the NT's most precise formal marker of habitual defection.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The defining term is the **Hiphil stem of cha.ta (H2398)**: *heheti* / *wayaḥṭē* — "caused to sin," "made to sin." The H2398 root means to miss the mark, to incur guilt — when placed in the Hiphil causative stem, it means: *to cause another to miss the mark, to make another incur guilt*. The root meaning in its causative form reveals the essential nature of CHAR-7: the leader does not merely sin themselves (the Qal personal action) but makes others sin (the Hiphil causative action). The Hiphil of cha.ta uniquely encodes the transmission mechanism — the leader's action is the cause; the community's sinning is the effect. No Greek vocabulary appears in the 19-verse corpus; the characteristic is entirely Hebrew in its primary vocabulary. The Hiphil causative form is CHAR-7's exclusive grammatical marker — no other sinning characteristic in the corpus uses the Hiphil.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The primary and exclusive term is **pa.sha (H6586)** in its political-revolt register. The root means *to break away from, to transgress, to revolt* — specifically naming the wilful decisive breaking of a binding relationship. In CHAR-8 the binding relationship is always political-governing (Moab under Israel; Edom under Judah; Israel under the house of David). The root meaning reveals: political revolt is not passive non-compliance but an *active breaking-away* — the pa.sha act has the moral weight of transgression embedded in the root. Pa.sha in the political register confirms that breaking political submission carries the same moral character as transgressing moral-covenantal boundaries — it is wilful, decisive, and morally accountable. No NT Greek vocabulary appears in the 9-verse corpus; the characteristic is entirely OT Hebrew.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The primary and exclusive terms are **blasfēmia (G0988)** — noun — and **blasfēmos (G0989)** — adjective. The root combines *blapto* (to harm, to damage) and *phēmi* (to speak, to say — related to *phōnē*, voice). The compound root meaning: *harmful speech, speech that damages*. The root reveals that sinful speech is defined not by its doctrinal content alone (a claim about God) but by its *effect*: it harms. Both the slander register (VCG-01 — person-directed harmful speech) and the blasphemy register (VCG-02/03 — God-directed presumptuous speech) are subsumed under this single root, revealing that the Greek term covers a unified semantic field: speech that damages, whether the target is God or persons. No OT Hebrew vocabulary appears in the 22-verse corpus — the characteristic is exclusively NT Greek, confirming that CHAR-9 as a distinct named characteristic is a NT conceptual configuration.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Primary Hebrew terms: ra.sha (H7563, 179V) — the adjective/noun for the wicked person; re.sha (H7562, 9V) — abstract noun, wickedness as condition; mir.sha.at (H4849, 1V) — collective noun, wicked-woman-type. Secondary: ro.a (H7455, 1V — 1Sa 17:28). The RSH root (resh-shin-ayin) is the generative root. RSH connotes a fundamental moral wrongness or badness — it is not primarily a legal term in its root but a character-quality term designating the person whose inner moral orientation is bad, wrong, or wicked. The root generates ra.sha (the wicked person), re.sha (wickedness as abstract condition), and rasha' (the verb "to act wickedly" — the root's verbal form, as in Dan 12:10: "the wicked shall act wickedly"). At the root level, RSH is a moral-character assessment: the person defined by what is fundamentally wrong in their inner orientation. No Greek term is primary for CHAR-1 — this characteristic is predominantly a Hebrew-OT phenomenon; the Greek evidence base for M10b belongs primarily to Characteristics 2 (ponēros, kakia) and 6 (blasfēmeō, kakopoios) rather than to CHAR-1.

**[CHAR-2]** E — This characteristic is exclusively NT Greek in its evidence base (90V — no Hebrew OT verses assigned; this is the key vocabulary distinction from CHAR-1). Primary terms: ponēros (G4190, 63V) — from the root ponos (toil, hardship, pain) — originally naming what is laborious or painful, which developed into a moral-quality term for what is evil in its character, harmful in its effects, and wicked in its inner orientation. kakia (G2549, 11V) — from kakos (bad, evil as a quality) — naming settled inner badness, malice, and ill-will as a character trait. adikia (G0093, 8V) — from a- (not) + dikē (justice, right) — naming the structural condition of not-rightness; unrighteousness as the constitutional state of being at odds with the right order. ponēria (G4189, 7V) — from the same root as ponēros but a feminine abstract noun naming wickedness, villainy, active malice as a condition. faulos (G5337, 1V) — from an alternative root meaning cheap, worthless, bad — applied to morally deficient deeds. Root meanings reveal: the characteristic is named from both the painful quality of evil (ponos root) and the structural wrongness (a-dikē) — it is evil as what is constitutionally deficient and wrong.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary Hebrew: to.e.vah (H8441, ~35V) — the primary abomination term covering both moral-character (M10b-C = CHAR-3) and idolatrous (M10b-D = CHAR-4) registers. The root etymology of to.e.vah is uncertain — possibly connected to a verb meaning to loathe or turn away from with revulsion. At root level, to.e.vah names that which provokes active turning-away in revulsion — the opposite of what attracts or draws near. Primary Greek: bdelugma (G0946, 4V — Luk 16:15; Rev 17:4; 17:5; 21:27) — from bdeo (to stink); names what is repugnant through its stench-quality, the morally-putrid. bdeluktos (G0947, 1V — Tit 1:16) — the adjectival form: the detestable, the stench-bearing person. The root revelation: Hebrew to.e.vah emphasises the relational dimension (what prompts revulsion and turning-away); Greek bdeo root emphasises the sensory-disgust dimension (what stinks, what is putrid). Together they name abomination as both relationally rejecting and sensory-revolting.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Primary Hebrew: to.e.vah (H8441, ~72V idolatrous sub-corpus) — see CHAR-3 T7.1.1 for root analysis. Applied to the idolatrous register, to.e.vah names the divine revulsion at idolatrous practices (Deu 12:31 — VCG-02: "every abominable thing that the Lord hates they have done for their gods"). shiq.quts (H8251, 25V) — from the root sh-q-ts (to loathe, abhor). The shiq.quts root generates: shiq.quts (noun — the detestable idol-thing), shaqats (verbal — to abhor, to make/regard as unclean). Root meaning: that which is loathed, the object of abhorrence. Applied to idols, shiq.quts names the foreign deity or idol-object specifically as an abhorrent thing — not merely wrong but inherently disgusting. 1Ki 11:5 (vc=65898 — VCG-03): "Milcom the abomination (shiq.quts) of the Ammonites" — the foreign deity is named by its quality of being loathsome. Primary Greek: bdelugma (G0946, 2V — Mat 24:15; Mar 13:14 — VCG-06) — from bdeo (to stink) — the sacrilegious desolation event as what stinks in the moral-spiritual register.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Two primary Hebrew terms; no NT Greek terms in this corpus. a.ven (H0205G, 66V) — the root a-w-n denotes emptiness, nothingness, and trouble. At root level, a.ven names that which is morally empty-yet-harmful: the scheming of the wicked is empty of genuine moral substance (futile, hollow — the "worthless" quality of the evildoer in Pro 6:12 — VCG-03: "a worthless person, a wicked man") while simultaneously generating genuine trouble and harm. The root reveals a dual quality: inner moral vacuity paired with outward harmful productivity. ro.a (H7455, 13V evil-deeds sub-corpus) — from the root r-'-' (ra.a — to be evil, bad, harmful). The root names what is intrinsically bad in quality — not merely wrong by rule but harmful in essence. Applied to deeds (VCG-05), ro.a names the moral quality of acts whose inner source is wickedness: Jer 25:5 (vc=38445 — VCG-05): "evil way and evil deeds" — the way and the deeds both carry the ra.a quality. Root revelations: a.ven = empty-and-troubling; ro.a = intrinsically bad in quality.

**[CHAR-6]** E — No OT Hebrew terms appear in the 17-verse corpus (exclusively NT Greek). Three Greek terms carry the characteristic. blasfēmeō (G0987, 11V) — from blapto (to harm, injure) + phēmē (speech, reputation). Root revelation: blasfēmeō names injurious speech — speech that harms a person's or God's standing/reputation. The root combines the harm-concept (blapto) with the speech-concept (phēmē) — the compound names exactly what the characteristic is: speech that harms. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): "utter blasphemies against God" — the verbal harm directed at the divine. kakopoios (G2555, 5V) — from kakos (evil/bad) + poieo (do/make): the evil-doer; the one whose actions are morally bad. Root revelation: the term names a person by the moral quality of their acts — the one who "makes bad." atopos (G0824, 1V — Act 25:5 — VCG-03) — from a (not) + topos (place): "out of place," irregular, improper. Root revelation: wrongdoing as that which is "out of place" in the moral-social order — a spatial-order metaphor for moral irregularity.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's full vocabulary array spans four Hebrew roots and three Greek roots. OT Hebrew: (1) RSH root — ra.sha (H7563, Char 1), re.sha (H7562, Char 1), rasha' verbal — the moral-wrongness root naming the wicked person as a type and wickedness as their condition; (2) a-w-n root — a.ven (H0205G, Char 5) — the emptiness-and-trouble root naming iniquity as moral vacuity that generates harm; (3) r-'-' root — ro.a (H7455, Chars 1 minor and 5 secondary) — the intrinsic-badness root naming the quality of evil deeds; (4) sh-q-ts root — shiq.quts (H8251, Char 4) — the loathing-abhorrence root naming the detestable idol-objects; (5) to.e.vah (H8441, Chars 3 and 4) — the revulsion-and-turning-away root naming what provokes divine active turning-away. NT Greek: (1) ponē- root — ponēros (G4190, Char 2), ponēria (G4189, Char 2) — the hardship/pain-and-moral-evil root; (2) ka- root — kakos, kakia (G2549, Char 2), kakopoios (G2555, Char 6) — the inherent-badness root generating constitutional malice (Char 2) and the evildoer person-type (Char 6); (3) blasphē- root — blasfēmeō (G0987, Char 6) — the harmful-speech root. At cluster scope, the root analysis reveals two dominant root-meanings across the vocabulary: (a) inherent moral badness/wrongness (RSH, r-'-', ka- roots) and (b) abhorrence and turning-away (sh-q-ts, to.e.vah, bdelugma roots). The cluster's vocabulary is built from these two root-meaning domains.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Three terms carry Characteristic 1. H2930A (ta.me, verb, root ṭ-m-ʾ): "to be unclean, to defile" — the root conveys contamination, the condition of being ritually or morally impure, with the basic sense of a thing made unfit through contact or condition. H2931 (ta.me, adjective, same root): "unclean" — the stative form naming the condition as a property of the person. H5079 (nid.dah, from nādad — "to flee, to wander"): "impurity, menstrual impurity, uncleanness" — the root meaning of separation/withdrawal may encode the social dynamic of the defilement-state (the defiled person is one who is separated from). G0169 (akathartos, alpha-privative + katharos — "clean, pure"): "unclean, impure" — the Greek term is simply the negative of the clean/pure term; it names the condition by the absence of what it lacks. The root meanings confirm the characteristic as a condition of unfitness/contamination (Hebrew) and the absence of the positive state (Greek).

**[CHAR-2]** E — Five terms carry Characteristic 2 (see §2). H2931 (ta.me adj, root ṭ-m-ʾ): "unclean" — in this characteristic's Hebrew metaphorical register (Job 14:4, Isa 6:5, Isa 64:6, Hag 2:14), the root meaning of contamination/unfitness is applied to the inner person's constitutional moral condition rather than to a ritual-bodily state. G0167 (akatharsia, alpha-privative + katharos — "clean/pure"): "impurity" — the noun naming the absence of moral purity in the inner person; the root reveals it as the negative of the clean/pure state. G3435 (molunō, from the same root as "smear, stain, soil"): "to defile, soil" — the active verb of the defiling act on the inner person or garment; the root suggests physical smearing applied metaphorically to the moral inner person. G3436 (molusmos, from molunō): "defilement" — the noun form of the soiling act. G3394 (miasmos, from miainō — "to stain, pollute"): "defilement" — the staining/pollution image applied to the inner person's defiled condition.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three terms carry Characteristic 3, all Hebrew (no NT Greek terms appear in the 83-verse corpus). H2930A (ta.me verb, 63V, root ṭ-m-ʾ): "to be/become unclean, to defile" — the dominant term, operating here primarily in the hiphil (causative) and qal forms: the community defiles the land (Jer 2:7: "you defiled my land"), the sanctuary (Eze 5:11), the divine name (Eze 43:7/8), and themselves (Eze 20:7: "do not defile yourselves"). The root conveys contamination — something has been rendered unfit, rendered repugnant, rendered incompatible with holiness. H2931 (ta.me adj, 11V): "unclean" — the stative form describing the resulting condition of persons, places, and names (Eze 22:5: "your name is defiled"; Lam 4:15: "Unclean!"). H5079 (nid.dah, 9V, from nādad — "to flee, to wander"): "impurity/menstrual impurity" — used metaphorically in this characteristic's register for the community's corporate moral repugnance before God (Eze 36:17: "like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity"; Lam 1:17: "a filthy thing").

**[CHAR-4]** E — One Greek term carries this characteristic exclusively: G0169 akathartos (21V, alpha-privative + katharos — "not clean/pure"), always appearing as the modifier of pneuma ("unclean spirit" — pneuma akatharton). The root katharos conveys cleanness, purity, freedom from contamination. The alpha-privative negation names the absence of that cleanness. In Characteristic 4, akathartos operates exclusively as the modifier of pneuma: the spirit is fundamentally characterised by the absence of holiness. The term names the agent's character (unclean) rather than the condition it produces in the person — a definitional feature unique to Characteristic 4 within the M10c cluster.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's primary vocabulary reveals a unified lexical domain built on two root systems. The Hebrew ta.me root (ṭ-m-ʾ) generates: H2930A (ta.me verb — to defile/become unclean) and H2931 (ta.me adj — unclean) across Characteristics 1, 2, and 3; H5079 nid.dah ("impurity of separation" — from nādad, to flee/wander) operating in both Characteristic 1's bodily-physiological register and Characteristic 3's corporate-prophetic metaphorical register. The Greek katharos/akathartos root generates: G0169 akathartos (unclean — adjective) across Characteristics 1, 2, and 4; G0167 akatharsia (impurity — noun; Characteristic 2's primary NT term); G3435 molunō (to defile/soil — verb; Characteristic 2); G3436 molusmos (defilement — noun; Characteristic 2). Characteristic 4 alone has no Hebrew vocabulary — it is entirely NT Greek (pneuma akatharton as the technical compound). The root meanings reveal: the ta.me root conveys contamination and unfitness (the condition of being rendered incompatible with holiness); the akathartos/katharos root conveys the absence of the clean/pure state (the negative of cleanness); the nid.dah root's "separation/fleeing" dimension encodes the social dynamic of the defilement-state (the defiled person is one who is separated from the community). Characteristic 4's vocabulary uniquely describes the agent's character (unclean spirit) rather than the person's condition — the only register where the primary term names the producer rather than the produced condition.

- **Verb (sa.lach, afiēmi):** The act — something done. God forgives; the human forgives. The event in time.
- **Noun (se.li.chah, afesis):** The condition/possession — something held or received. Forgiveness as a state, as a divine attribute, as the condition the recipient occupies.
- **Adjective (sal.lach):** The disposition — something characterising a person constitutively. God is "forgiving" as a settled character description, not only as a description of specific acts.
- **Participle (implied in multiple group descriptions):** The ongoing process — the act as continuous or habitual operation.

**What the range reveals:** Forgiveness operates as all four simultaneously — it is an **act** (verb), produces a **state** (noun), reflects a **character** (adjective), and operates **continuously** (participial aspect). This grammatical completeness is analytically significant: very few characteristics in the programme have a vocabulary that simultaneously names the act, the resultant condition, the dispositional character, and the ongoing operation. The grammatical range confirms that forgiveness is not a simple single-mode characteristic but a constitutionally rich one.

findings.session_b_note:
The vocabulary covers the full grammatical range, and each grammatical form reveals a distinct operational mode:

**Verbal forms (ra.cham, splanchnizō, sumpatheō, sumpaschō, chus):** Name compassion as an event — something that happens. The verb form captures the moment of inner movement, the act of being moved, the event of gut-stirring. Compassion as verb is compassion in its most dynamic and event-specific form.

**Noun forms (ra.cha.mim, splanchnon, chesed, eleēmosunē, ni.chum):** Name compassion as a reality, a substance, a quality that exists and can be quantified, accumulated, or given. The plural noun (ra.cha.mim — compassions/mercies) is particularly revealing: it names compassion as multiple and inexhaustible rather than singular and bounded. Chesed as noun names it as a relational substance — something that holds and can be appealed to.

**Adjectival forms (ra.chum, ra.cha.ma.ni, channum, sumpathēs, eusplanchnos):** Name compassion as a character quality — what kind of person one is. The adjective form is the most constitutional: it describes the inner being rather than an act or a reality. Ra.chum (compassionate) and sumpathēs (sympathetic) name the person whose inner being is constituted by this quality.

**Compound forms (polusplanchnos, sumpatheō, sumpaschō, eusplanchnos):** Name compassion in its intensified, combined, or modified expressions. Compounds reveal: the characteristic can be intensified (polusplanchnos — deeply compassionate); it can be combined with participation (sumpaschō — suffering-with); it can be grounded in inner constitution (eusplanchnos — of good/tender entrails).

**What the range reveals:** Compassion is a constitutional quality (adjective), an inner event (verb), an existing reality (noun), and an intensifiable experience (compound). The full grammatical range confirms that compassion is not reducible to any single operational mode — it is simultaneously a character disposition, an event-movement, a relational substance, and a constitutional quality.

findings.session_b_note:
The grammatical range of H1792 da.kha (the lexical anchor):
- **Niphal** (passive/reflexive): "to be crushed," "to be contrite (figuratively)" — the inner-being meaning emerges specifically from the passive form
- **Piel** (active intensive): "to crush" actively — used of the Servant being crushed (Isa 53:5) and of God crushing enemies
- **Hithpael** (reflexive/permissive): "to allow oneself to be crushed" — the volitional-receptive dimension
- **Adjectival forms**: H1793A/B dak.ka (contrite/dust) and H1795 dak.kah — describe the settled condition

The grammatical range reveals: contrition is most precisely a **state arising from passive reception** (Niphal) but involves a **volitional element of consent** (Hithpael). The adjectival forms establish it as a **settled condition** rather than a momentary event. The Piel shows that the crushing action can be performed by God or by an agent on another. The range as a whole confirms: contrition is the condition of the one who has been crushed (passive), who may have either permitted (Hithpael) or resisted the crushing, and whose condition has become a settled posture (adjective).

findings.session_b_note:
**koinōnia (G2842):** Primarily nominal (noun). The noun form means that koinōnia names a *reality* or *state* — fellowship is something that exists, that one participates in, not primarily something one does. The nominal dominance suggests fellowship is conceptualised as a condition or state rather than primarily as an action.

**koinōnos (G2844):** Nominal, but personal — the participant-person. This is the agentive form: the one who is characterised by koinōnia.

**cha.var (H2266):** Primarily verbal. The verbal form means that in the Hebrew, the primary conceptualisation is of fellowship as *action* — joining is something that happens, is done, or is undergone. The verbal Hebrew contrasts with the nominal Greek: Hebrew fellowship foregrounds the act; Greek fellowship foregrounds the state.

**Gap:** Without completed word analysis, the full grammatical range (participles, infinitives, specific forms) of each term is not available.

findings.session_b_note: H2896A (tov) operates primarily as an adjective — modifying persons, things, words, actions, and states. Its adjectival nature means it names a quality of its subject rather than an action performed. However, H2895 (tov verbal — be pleasing) shows the root also generates a stative verb — describing the state of being good/pleasing. The grammatical range (adjective + stative verb + verbal noun in related forms) reveals that goodness in Hebrew is primarily characterological (it names what something is) and secondarily experiential (it names the state of being good/pleasing to someone). G0019 (agathōsunē) is exclusively an abstract noun — naming goodness as a substantive virtue. G5544 (chrēstotēs) is also exclusively an abstract noun. The NT's grammatical form (abstract nouns only) reveals a shift from the Hebrew's adjectival breadth (goodness applied across contexts) to a specialised inner-being virtue-noun. (OBS-067-OBS-007, OBS-067-OBS-008, SBF-067-Q088)

findings.session_b_note: Taking agapaō/agapē as the primary NT term: **agapaō** (verb, 344 occurrences) — love as an action, exercisable and commandable; the verbal form affirms love's volitional dimension. **agapē** (noun, 133 occurrences) — love as an entity, a reality that can be 'poured into hearts' (Rom 5:5), that 'never fails' (1Cor 13:8), that is the greatest (1Cor 13:13). **agapētos** (adjective/participle, 79 occurrences) — beloved, the passive recipient of love; love as constituting an identity-state in the object. Together: verb + noun + adjective-participle spans the full grammatical range: love as act (verb), love as reality/quality (noun), and love as identity-constitutive state (adjective). This three-part grammatical range confirms Q&A-016's finding that love is simultaneously act, disposition, and condition. For chesed: primarily noun (covenant-quality) with verbal cognate (chasad — to act with chesed) — the noun-primary form confirms love as a stable quality before it is an act.

findings.finding_value: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-covenantal (chesed), Spirit-produced self-giving (agapē), somatic-compassionate (racham), intense-erotic (ahavah/dod), and naturally affective (phileō). The vocabulary structure itself distinguishes disposition/act/condition, received/given, and quality/person-type — making it architecturally precise. The semantic range of the primary terms spans from divine ontology (God is love) to moral inversion (love of darkness) — the widest semantic arc in the programme. The primary anchor is Lam 3:22 — love's most definitive affirmation precisely at the moment of maximum empirical falsification: a theological confession rather than an empirical observation. The LXX connection is partially evidenced (agapē as chesed-translated); full LXX analysis is limited by NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags. The human science frameworks identified (attachment theory, virtue ethics) are named as Session D pointers but not elaborated — the instruction prohibits importing framework content not grounded in the data.

findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispositional), racham (somatic-compassionate), ahavah/dod (intense-erotic), phileō/agapē (affective-natural and willed-unconditional). The grammatical range analysis confirms the tripartite definition (Q&A-123): verb (act) + noun (disposition) + adjective-passive (condition). The semantic range analysis confirms the vocabulary arc (Q&A-124, Q&A-131). The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136, Q&A-137) confirms the definition's most counterintuitive feature: love at its most definitional is not evidenced by love's presence but confessed against its apparent absence. The definition says love is permanent, unwavering, faithful — and the evidential ground for this claim is a verse written in the context of Jerusalem's destruction. The evidential foundation is thus not primarily experiential but confessional — the definition's permanence-claim is a theological assertion, grounded in the character of God rather than in the consistency of human experience.

Each constitutional level identified in T2 has specific vocabulary evidence in T7: Spirit-level origin — Gal 5:22 (fruit of the Spirit), Rom 5:5 (poured into hearts through the Spirit); soul-level — Song 5:6 (soul failing), Mat 22:37 (all your soul), Joh 15:13 (lay down the soul); heart-level — Pro 3:3 (heart inscription), Rom 5:5 (into our hearts); mind-level — Mat 22:37 (all your mind), Joh 15:15 (knowledge disclosure); body-level — kiss/embrace/tears/inner-organ-movement vocabulary across multiple groups. The lexical range of the primary terms (Q&A-122 — chesed, racham, agapē, dod, phileō) corresponds precisely to the five constitutional levels: each term carries a different constitutional register as its primary habitat. The evidential foundation thus not only confirms the constitutional claims but shows them to be lexically grounded in the vocabulary's own structure.

findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation grounds the formation claims at the lexical level. The growth-capacity finding (Q&A-092) is grounded in the verbal form agapaō and the noun-verb movement: chesed as noun (stable quality) requires formation before it functions as such; the transition from occasional loving acts (verb) to stable covenantal character (noun-quality) is the formation process in lexical form. The reversibility asymmetry (divine love irreversible; human love redirectable — Q&A-094) is grounded in the vocabulary's own structure: the divine forms of chesed and agapē carry permanence qualifiers (olam — everlasting; Lam 3:22 — never ceasing) that the human love forms do not. The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136) is itself a formation text: the confession of love's permanence in extremity is a formation of the inner person toward trust in what cannot be seen. The formation process produces the person capable of making the Lam 3:22 confession — the developmental trajectory toward love's perfection includes the formation of the inner person's capacity to confess love against empirical evidence.

The primary anchor verses (Isa 57:15, Psa 51:17) are architecturally complementary: Isa 57:15 provides the complete relational frame (divine character → divine dwelling → divine reviving); Psa 51:17 provides the inner-being substance (broken spirit, contrite heart as the acceptable sacrifice). The cross-testament gap (T7.1.8–9) is the methodological limitation — without LXX analysis the vocabulary arc from OT to NT cannot be closed from this registry's data. Human science frameworks confirm rather than challenge the biblical account, with the theocentric causality as the point of genuine divergence.

findings.finding_value: The constitutional tier (T2) establishes spirit and heart as primary loci, bones as somatic expression; the evidential tier (T7) shows that these same loci are explicitly named in the primary anchor verses. The spirit/heart pairing in the verse evidence (Psa 34:18, Psa 51:17, Isa 57:15) and the bone imagery in Psa 51:8 are the exegetical ground for T2's constitutional account. T7 provides the textual evidence base from which T2 draws its constitutional conclusions. The two tiers are evidence-to-interpretation: T7 is the verse evidence; T2 is the constitutional interpretation of that evidence. Isa 57:15 as the primary anchor verse (T7) is also the verse that most completely names the constitutional event (T2): "contrite and lowly spirit... revive the spirit... revive the heart."

findings.finding_value: T7 reveals that the fellowship vocabulary has the widest semantic arc of any characteristic in the programme: from tabernacle seam (physical construction) through wound (somatic joining) through companionship (relational) through moral complicity (evaluative) through ontological divine nature participation. This breadth is encoded in the root-level architecture (chavar — the joining logic applied universally). The two primary anchor verses (2Pe 1:4 and 1Jo 1:3) are complementary in perspective: 2Pe 1:4 is the vertical-ontological statement (human participating in divine nature); 1Jo 1:3 is the relational-structural statement (horizontal derived from vertical). The LSJ gap (T7.1.8) is an acknowledged data limitation — the classical background of koinōnia is unavailable from this registry's data, which means the NT's transformation of a Hellenistic civic-philosophical term into a theological term cannot be traced from this evidence base.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-007: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structura…
findings.finding_value: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structural theological claim. The cross-testament vocabulary development (LXX applying aphiēmi to render salach; NT extending aphiēmi to commanded human forgiveness) carries the programme's clearest lexical theological claim: human forgiveness is structurally shaped by divine forgiveness, named by the same vocabulary. The grammatical analysis (Niphal passive — "they shall be forgiven"; active Qal — God forgives) precisely encodes the act-structure: divine act → creaturely received status. The primary anchor trio (Jer 31:34, Psa 86:5, Luk 7:47) spans three literary forms (prophetic-eschatological, wisdom/psalm, Synoptic narrative) and three analytical registers (eschatological promise, divine character-statement, inner-being consequence). T7 synthesis: the forgiveness vocabulary is the most theologically structured in the current review set — its cross-testament development carries an explicit structural claim visible at the lexical level.

Cognition-locus (Jer 31:34) is carried by the H5545 Niphal passive (the worshipper as receiver) and the se.li.chah noun (forgiveness as the quality God has, which enables the cognitive-relational access). Somatic-compassion locus (Mat 18:27 — splagchnizomai) is outside the registry's own vocabulary but is confirmed as the constitutional origin point of the horizontal forgiving act. T7 provides the grammatical evidence base for T2's constitutional account.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-007: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: …
findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the v…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-018: T2's constitutional levels are each carried by specific vocabulary families in T7. The somatic-body level (T2.6 — gut, womb) is carried by the RACHAM/SPLANCHN root families — the body's interior as th…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional levels are each carried by specific vocabulary families in T7. The somatic-body level (T2.6 — gut, womb) is carried by the RACHAM/SPLANCHN root families — the body's interior as the etymological ground of both. The soul-character level (T2.2) is carried by the CHASAD family — chesed as the settled covenantal character disposition. The heart-deliberative level (T2.3) is evidenced most richly in Hos 11:8 (T7's primary anchor for divine compassion). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) traverses exactly the constitutional range T2 maps: from the most interior somatic level (womb) through the character-soul level to the externalised action level. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T2's constitutional depth: Hos 11:8 evidences constitutional depth (heart-level deliberation of compassion over judgment); Luke 10:33 evidences constitutional breadth (the full four-stage movement from sight to action).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-018: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The spirit-reception level (T2.1) is carried by the perfect passive form of charitoō (kecharitōmenē — the completed act of b…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The spirit-reception level (T2.1) is carried by the perfect passive form of charitoō (kecharitōmenē — the completed act of being-made-the-object-of-grace, with continuing state) — the most precise grammatical encoding of a constitutional arrival that has permanently changed the person's standing. The soul-standing level (T2.2) is carried by charis as noun (the inhabited state of favour) and chen as the relational standing-in-favour term. The character-expression level is carried by chen in its conduct/speech register (889-003) and charizō in its human-forgiving mode. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō invented to carry the standing-in-favour concept) is the lexical evidence that T2's spirit-level reception was conceptually unprecedented — no prior vocabulary could name what happened constitutionally when grace-as-standing arrived.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-025: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-le…
findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. This is unique in the programme's vocabulary data: no other characteristic has the giving-side and receiving-side vocabulary built from the same root. T4's relational architecture and T7's lexical analysis are the relational and lexical descriptions of the same structural reality — that grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit whose two sides are inseparable at the root level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: H1285 (berit): noun only — covenant is primarily a noun-reality, a state/bond rather than an action. The verb for covenant-making is a separate term (karat — to cut). This grammatical fact reveals that covenant is the standing relational reality (a state), not primarily the act of making it (an action). The act of making is expressed through the verb (karat berit = cut a covenant), but the covenant itself is a noun — it is what exists after the act. H7650 (shava): verb — swearing/oath-taking is an action, not primarily a state. This confirms that the oath is the performative act that constitutes the covenant. G1242 (diathēkē): noun — same as Hebrew; the covenant/testament is a standing reality. The noun-dominance of the primary covenant terms reveals that covenant is constituted through acts (cutting, swearing) but exists as a standing reality (the bond, the testament, the disposition). This noun-reality structure confirms the T1 finding (Q&A-016) that covenant is, in its sustained mode, a relational disposition rather than a repeated act.

findings.session_b_note: Sha.lom (H7965G) functions as: (1) Noun (primary): the condition of peace — "in peace I will lie down" (Psa 4:8), "covenant of peace" (Isa 54:10); (2) Noun used as greeting formula: "Peace be to you" (1Sa 25:6, H7965K); (3) Noun functioning as an identity statement: "I am for peace" (Psa 120:7 — ani sha.lom, where sha.lom is the predicate nominative); (4) Noun used adverbially (H7965L): "wholly" (Jer 13:19 — all-verses-fail, no inner-being); (5) Noun in construct chain as descriptor: "covenant of peace" (brit sha.lom), "man of peace" (ish sha.lom, Psa 37:37), "Prince of Peace" (sar sha.lom, Isa 9:6). The identity-statement form (ani sha.lom — "I am peace") is analytically distinctive: sha.lom becomes a predicate nominative, identifying the person with the characteristic. This grammatical form is unique in the registry and is the most concentrated expression of the moral-character dimension.

The mind location (T2.4 — Isa 26:3 yetser, Rom 8:6 phronema, Phili 4:7 noema) uses three distinct vocabulary terms for different aspects of the mind's engagement — T7.1.4 confirms that the vocabulary distinguishes state/disposition/act. The constitutional analysis is lexically grounded at every point.

findings.session_b_note: H5414G na.tan is a verb — it has no primary nominal or adjectival form in this registry's OWNER terms. Grammatical range: Qal (active — the subject gives), Niphal (passive — something is given/permitted), Hophal (passive causative — something is made to be given). The exclusively verbal character of the OWNER term is analytically significant: this characteristic, as accessed through na.tan, is known only through action — not through a noun naming a quality or an adjective describing a person. It is grammatically actional at its core. This contrasts with the XREF vocabulary: emunah, emet, hesed are all nominals — they name the quality itself. The grammatical gap between OWNER (verb) and XREF (nouns) mirrors the analytical gap between enacted faithfulness (na.tan) and named faithfulness (emunah/emet/hesed). The characteristic is grammatically event-shaped: it happens, it is given, it occurs — it is not primarily described as a state one possesses.
