findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-007: T7 as a whole reveals the evidential and methodological shape of this registry's analysis. The vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) is the governing finding: two poles — na.tan (enacted) and emunah/hesed/pistis (…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals the evidential and methodological shape of this registry's analysis. The vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) is the governing finding: two poles — na.tan (enacted) and emunah/hesed/pistis (constituted) — are both necessary and neither alone is sufficient. The grammatical gap (verb vs. nominal) maps directly onto the analytical distinction between the two poles. The literary diversity of the anchor corpus (narrative, prophecy, wisdom, liturgy) means no single interpretive lens covers the full evidence base. The primary analytical anchor (Hos 11:8) is identified for its unique revelation of the divine inner-being decision structure. The human science frameworks (virtue ethics, attachment theory) illuminate the characteristic while also diverging at critical points — the divergences are themselves analytically productive: biblical faithfulness requires both a virtue-ethical foundation (the character basis of giving) and something that virtue ethics cannot supply (the constitutive primacy of received divine giving as the ground of human virtue). What T7 reveals as a whole: the evidential base of this characteristic is rich, methodologically complex, and internally consistent. The two main methodological challenges — the registry label/OWNER term gap, and the legacy-VC status of all classified verses — are acknowledged and do not undermine the analysis but do qualify its certainty.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-006: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) is confirmed and grounded by the vocabulary arc (T7). The grammatical structure of na.tan (exclusively verbal) is precisely the lexical form of the dispositio…
findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) is confirmed and grounded by the vocabulary arc (T7). The grammatical structure of na.tan (exclusively verbal) is precisely the lexical form of the disposition-in-action structure: a verb cannot be possessed without being enacted. The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10) — enacted pole (na.tan) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) — maps directly onto the T1 finding that the registry captures the enacted dimension while the XREF vocabulary carries the dispositional. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) confirms the T1 finding that the characteristic's most analytically revealing expression is the one that shows the inner-being decision mechanism — precisely because that is where disposition and act are most visibly integrated. What this pair reveals: the lexical evidence independently confirms the definitional analysis. The characteristic is verbally grounded because faithfulness as enacted commitment is inherently event-shaped — it happens at a moment, from an inner state, toward a recipient. It cannot be abstracted from this event structure.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-011: The constitutional evidence (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body all engaged) and the lexical/literary evidence (T7 — na.tan as exclusively verbal, Hos 11:8 as primary anchor) mutually …
findings.finding_value: The constitutional evidence (T2 — spirit, heart, soul, hidden inner parts, body all engaged) and the lexical/literary evidence (T7 — na.tan as exclusively verbal, Hos 11:8 as primary anchor) mutually confirm. The lexical finding that na.tan is grammatically a verb (T7, Q&A-171) is the lexical expression of the constitutional finding that the characteristic moves across constitutional levels through distinct movement patterns (T2.10) — a verb in motion describes constitutional movement in language. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) identifies precisely the verse that shows the deepest constitutional engagement: leb (heart) and rahamim (visceral inner parts) both named in a single verse showing inner-being movement. The verse evidence and constitutional analysis converge on the same verse for the same reason: it is the verse where constitutional depth and inner-being movement are most explicitly disclosed. What this pair reveals: the lexical and constitutional evidence are independently converging on the same structural reality.

findings.finding_value: The structural landscape analysis (T6 — hub position, aman root architecture entangling R059/R044/R060, distinction of kind from nearest neighbours) and the vocabulary/methodological analysis (T7 — full vocabulary arc, grammatically actional, primary anchor Hos 11:8) produce the final convergent finding. The aman root architecture (T6.4.2, Q&A-157) and the vocabulary arc (T7.1.10, Q&A-179) are describing the same reality: the programme's separation of registries by word is an analytical convenience that cuts across a root-level unity. The vocabulary arc — enacted pole (na.tan/verb) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis/nouns) — names the same reality that the root architecture identifies: the aman root generates both the dispositional terms and the contextual terms, while na.tan provides the enacted verbal expression. The grammatically actional character of na.tan (T7.1.2, Q&A-171) is the structural reason for its distinction-of-kind from the nominal faithfulness vocabulary (T6.5.3, Q&A-162). What this pair reveals as the final synthesis: the vocabulary evidence and the structural landscape evidence independently converge on the same conclusion — this characteristic is the enacted form of what the faithfulness vocabulary names dispositionally, and this distinction is fundamental to understanding both the characteristic itself and its position in the inner-being landscape.

findings.finding_value: The primary M01-A term ya.re functions as: **verb** (ya.re — to fear/revere, stative; the ongoing state of being in fear/reverence), **noun** (yir.ah — the fear as a possessed quality), and **adjective / participle** (ya.re — the one who fears; Job 1:1: "a man who feared God" — the present participle as a character-defining description). This grammatical range reveals that the characteristic operates as: a state of being (stative verb), a stable possession of the person (noun), and a defining character quality (participle). The stative verbal form is especially significant: ya.re describes an ongoing state rather than a completed action, confirming that M01-A is dispositional rather than episodic.

M01-B's Greek terms: fobeō functions as a verb (episodic — "feared, was afraid") and fobos as a noun. The verb form in M01-B contexts is predominantly aorist or imperfect (completed past or ongoing past event) rather than the present participle (defining quality). This grammatical pattern confirms M01-B as episodic rather than dispositional.

M01-D's ba.hal functions as a Piel verb (intensive action stem in Hebrew — the characteristic is intensive, not gentle), and cha.tat functions as a Niphal (passive — "to be dismayed, to be shattered") — confirming that dismay is something that happens to the person rather than something they do.

M01-E's cha.rad functions as a Qal verb (basic stem, often reflexive in context — the body naturally trembles), cha.red as a Qal participle / adjective (the trembling one — character description), and cha.ra.dah as a noun (the trembling as an event). The participle form cha.red (Isa 66:2 anchor: "the one who trembles at my word") functions as a character-defining description, confirming that the trembling-at-word tradition (E-VCG-02) is dispositional like M01-A.

M01-G's Greek terms (deilia, deiliaō, deilos) are predominantly: noun (deilia — the quality of timidity), verb (deiliaō — to be timid), and adjective (deilos — the cowardly one). The adjective deilos is used in evaluative character-judgments (Mat 8:26; Rev 21:8) — it describes what the person is, not merely what they experience.

The grammatical range across M01 reveals: stative verbs and nouns cluster in the dispositional sub-groups (M01-A, G); aorist and event verbs cluster in the episodic sub-groups (M01-B, C); passive Niphal forms cluster in the experience-of-imposition sub-groups (M01-D: "to be dismayed/shattered"). The participle as character-defining form appears in M01-A (ya.re — the God-fearer) and M01-E-VCG-02 (cha.red — the one who trembles at God's word) and M01-G (deilos — the cowardly one). Grammar confirms the dispositional vs. episodic distinction structurally.

The cluster shows a comprehensive grammatical range. *Cha.rah* (H2734) and *qa.tsaph* (H7107) and *qa.na* (H7065) are verbs — naming the anger-event as an active occurrence. *Che.mah* (H2534) and *qin.ah* (H7068) and *orgē* (G3709) are nouns — naming the anger-state as a substantial reality. *Cha.ron* (H2740) and *cho.ri* (H2750) are nouns with intensifying force — naming the quality of the anger. *Orgilos* (G3711) is an adjective — naming the anger-susceptible person (the quick-tempered character). *Orgizō* (G3710) is a verb. The full grammatical range (verb / noun / adjective) confirms that anger is evidenced as an event (verb), a state (noun), an intensifying quality (intensive noun), and a character disposition (adjective). This range reveals a characteristic that operates across all grammatical modes — event, state, quality, and character.

The grammatical range of M03's vocabulary spans: verbs (ba.khah — to weep; sa.phad — to mourn; a.nach — to sigh; lupeō — to grieve; pen.the.o — to mourn; odunaō — to be anguished); nouns of state (tsa.rah — distress; tsar — distress; ya.gon — sorrow; makh.ov — pain; klauthmos — weeping); nouns of substance (dim.ah — tears; be.khi — weeping; a.na.chah — sighing); adjectives (perilupos — sorrowful; a.vel — mourning adj). The verbal form of the characteristic (weeping, mourning, groaning) emphasises that grief is an act — something the person does. The noun forms (sorrow, anguish, tears) emphasise that grief is a condition — something the person is in or has. The grammatical range reveals that grief spans the act/condition distinction — it is both something that happens to the person (condition) and something the person does (act).

**[CHAR-1]** E — **gil** functions as both a verbal root (H1523, gil_verb — 36 instances: the act of rejoicing as a dynamic event) and a noun (H1524A — 7 instances: joy/rejoicing as a state or quality). This grammatical dual-functioning reveals exultation operating as both an **act** (something done, commanded, chosen) and a **condition** (something present as an ongoing state). The verbal form's frequency over the nominal form confirms that exultation is primarily experienced as an active dynamic event rather than a passive condition.

**[CHAR-2]** E — **sa.mach** (H8055) is exclusively verbal — it always names an act of rejoicing, not a condition or quality. Its dominance (147 verbal instances) over sim.chah (89 nominal) reveals that Joy is fundamentally an act before it is a condition — the grammar of the Hebrew primary term names the characteristic as a dynamic event (something happens) rather than a static state (something is). **chairo** (G5463, 58 instances) is similarly verbal. **chara** (G5479, 57 instances) is the corresponding nominal form — the state that chairo produces. The near-equal frequency of verbal and nominal forms in the NT (58 vs. 57) suggests that Joy operates equally as act and state in the NT register. **sa.me.ach** (H8056, 21 adjectival instances) names the person defined by the state — the one who habitually is glad. Together the three grammatical forms (verb + noun + adjective) show Joy as: an event (sa.mach/chairo), a state (sim.chah/chara), and a character quality (sa.me.ach) — a fully developed inner-being characteristic across all grammatical registers.

**[CHAR-7]** E — **agalliao** (G0021) functions primarily as a **verb** — naming an event of exultation rather than a stable state. The 11 verbal instances in M04-E-VCG-02 show Suffering-Joy as primarily an act or event: Luk 1:47 ("my spirit rejoices"); Luk 10:21 ("he rejoiced"); Joh 8:56 ("Abraham rejoiced"); Act 16:34 ("he rejoiced"); 1Pe 1:6 ("in this you rejoice"); 4:13 ("rejoice insofar as"); Rev 19:7 ("let us rejoice"). **agalliasis** (G0020, noun) appears adjacent (Heb 1:9 — "oil of gladness") — naming the quality of the state. The verbal predominance reveals Suffering-Joy as primarily an event/act rather than a stable condition — consistent with its paradoxical character (genuine joy arising in and through the suffering event, not a settled state independent of the suffering context).

**[CHAR-3]** E — **tov** operates across three grammatical registers in this corpus: (1) **Adjectival / predicative** — "God saw that it was good" (Gen 1:4–31); "the Lord is good" (Psa 25:8; 100:5; Nah 1:7) — predicate adjective naming a stable quality; (2) **Comparative** — "better than" forms (Rut 4:15; 2Sa 18:3; Pro 8:11; 16:16; 17:1 — various) — the comparative form "tov min" (good from) names surpassing worth; (3) **Negated / substantive** — "not good" (Exo 18:17; 1Sa 2:24; Neh 5:9; Pro 17:26; Eze 18:18) — tov negated to name moral deficiency. The grammatical range reveals: Gladness is not primarily a verbal action (unlike Joy's dominant sa.mach verb) but a quality-assertion — it predicates goodness of persons, actions, circumstances, and God's character. The predicate form is the primary grammatical mode, confirming Gladness's status as a quality/condition rather than an act.

**[CHAR-4]** E — **cha.phets** (H2654A) functions across all grammatical modes: (1) **Verbal** — Gen 34:19 (Shechem delighted in Dinah); Psa 40:8 (I delight to do your will); Isa 53:10 (it was the will of the Lord to crush him) — active volitional acts; (2) **Adjectival** (H2655) — 1Ki 13:33 ("any who would") — predicate adjective of willingness; (3) **Nominal** (H2656) — Psa 1:2 ("his delight is in the law"); 1Sa 15:22 ("has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings") — stable nominal state or orientation; 2Sa 23:5 ("all my help and my desire"). The tri-form grammatical spread (verb/adjective/noun) reveals Delight as a characteristic that operates simultaneously as act (verbal), disposition (adjectival), and condition (nominal). This grammatical completeness distinguishes Delight from characteristics that operate primarily in one grammatical mode.

**[CHAR-5]** E — **na.im** (H5273A) functions primarily as an **adjective** — it attributes the quality of pleasantness to persons, places, and circumstances (Psa 133:1 — "pleasant it is"; Job 36:11 — "years in pleasantness"; Song 1:16 — "truly delightful"). **na.em** (H5276) functions as a **verb** (2Sa 1:26 — "you have been pleasant to me"; Pro 2:10 — "knowledge will be pleasant"; Pro 9:17 — "bread eaten in secret is pleasant"). **no.am** (H5278) functions as a **noun** (Psa 27:4 — "the beauty of the Lord"; Pro 3:17 — "ways of pleasantness"). The adjectival-verbal-nominal spread of the na.em root covers: the quality itself (no.am), the attribution of that quality to something (na.im), and the experience of that quality by a person (na.em). This grammatical completeness reveals Pleasure as both an objective quality of what is pleasant and a subjective experience of pleasantness felt by the inner person.

**[CHAR-6]** E — **pa.la** (H6381) functions across four modes: (1) **Verb** — "God thunders wondrously" (Job 37:5); "who does great things and unsearchable, marvellous things" (Job 5:9); "the Lord will do wonders" (Exo 3:20; Jos 3:5); (2) **Niphal reflexive/passive** — "it is marvellous in our eyes" (Psa 118:23); "things too wonderful for me" (Job 42:3); "too difficult for you" (Deu 17:8; 30:11); (3) **Piel intensive** — "you have wondrously shown your steadfast love" (Psa 31:21); "God deals wondrously with you" (Joel 2:26); (4) **Nominal derivative pe.le** — used as a noun and as a component of the name "Wonderful Counselor" (Isa 9:6). The grammatical spread reveals pa.la as active in divine agent contexts (God does wonders), reflexive in human perceptive contexts (it is marvellous to us), and intensive in contexts of surpassing action (wondrously showing love). This grammatical range confirms Wonder as simultaneously a quality of divine acts (active pa.la) and a perceptive response by humans (niphal pa.la).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The grammatical distributions across the seven characteristics reveal their primary phenomenological mode: (1) **Verbal-dominant**: Joy (sa.mach — 147 verbal instances vs. 89 nominal; chairo — 58 verbal vs. 57 nominal) — Joy is primarily an act; (2) **Nominal-balanced**: Gladness (tov as predicate adjective/noun, not primarily verbal) — Gladness is primarily a condition asserted; Pleasure (na.im primarily adjectival; na.em secondarily verbal) — Pleasure is primarily a quality attributed; (3) **Verbal-plus-nominal**: Delight (cha.phets verbal + che.phets nominal + cha.phets adjectival) — Delight spans all three modes; (4) **Verbal-dominant-in-primary-term**: Wonder (pa.la verbal dominant — 47 instances) — Wonder is primarily an event; (5) **Verbal-primary**: Suffering-Joy (agalliao verbal — 11 instances — dominant) — Suffering-Joy is primarily an act/event. The pattern reveals: Joy, Wonder, and Suffering-Joy are primarily acts; Gladness and Pleasure are primarily qualities/conditions; Delight spans all modes. Exultation (gil verbal + nominal) is both act and condition. This grammatical differentiation confirms that the cluster's characteristics are not synonyms but genuinely distinct inner-being phenomena with different primary modes of existence.

**[CHAR-1]** E — *Bosh* functions as both verb (to be ashamed — the most common usage) and noun (via *bo.shet* and *bu.shah*). The verbal usage dominates in the CHAR-1 corpus: "they are ashamed," "they were put to shame," "you shall not be ashamed" — the stative/passive verb is the primary grammatical form. This reveals that shame as experienced inner state is primarily *received* or *arrived at* rather than *active* — the person does not do shameing to themselves; shame happens to them or in them. The passive construction confirms the condition-character of CHAR-1 (T1.2.1): it is undergone rather than performed.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Ka.lam operates primarily as a verb (being humiliated). Sha.phel operates as verb (Hiphil — causing to be brought low) and adjective (sha.phel nefesh — lowly of spirit). The verbal dominance confirms CHAR-2's action-character: it is something done, not merely something possessed. Semantic range covers bodily-social, national-political, and cosmic dimensions (moon and sun ashamed, Isa 24:23) — CHAR-2 applies wherever pride-structures or elevated standing exists.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary terms: Atimazō (G0818): to dishonour, treat as without honour — active verb, the dishonoring act. Atimia (G0819): dishonour as a state — the condition of assigned or received diminished worth. Entrepō (G1788) in its absence register: the failure of the regard-faculty. Paradeigmatizō (G3856): to expose publicly, hold up to contempt. Roots: a-timē — without honour, without worth — the alpha-privative of honour. **[CHAR-20]** E — Wide across both terms. (1) *Ma.al (H4603)*: verb form — "acted faithlessly" (*māʿal*) — Eze 14:13; 2Ch 26:16/36:14; noun form H4604 (*māʿal*) — "breach of faith" — 1Ch 10:13 — "died for his breach of faith"; "faithlessness" — Ezr 9:2/4; 2Ch 33:19. Both verb and noun cover the same semantic range; (2) *Ba.gad (H0898)*: Qal active — "dealt treacherously" (*bāgad*) — Jer 3:20; Mal 2:14; Hos 6:7; agent-noun — "the treacherous" (*bōgĕdîm*) — Psa 119:158 — "I look at the faithless"; Isa 24:16 — "the traitors have betrayed"; "treacherous" (*bāgĕdāh*) — Jer 3:8; Psa 25:3 — "those who are wantonly treacherous." The grammatical range — verb (act), noun (event/condition), and agent-noun (person) — covers the act, the condition, and the person constituted by the act.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Wide across all term-families. (1) *A.vah (H5753A/B)*: Qal active verb — "acted wickedly/perversely" (1Ki 8:47; Dan 9:5); participle — "one who commits iniquity" (Psa 106:6); noun form — "twisted mind" (Pro 12:8); (2) *Tah.pu.khah (H8419)*: noun — "perverseness" (Pro 2:12/14; Pro 6:14/8:13/16:28/23:33); (3) *Sa.laph (H5557)*: verb — "subverts/perverts" (Exo 23:8; Pro 21:12/22:12); (4) *Ftheirō (G5351)*: active verb — "corrupts" (1Cor 15:33; 2Cor 7:2; Rev 19:2); passive — "is being corrupted" (Eph 4:22 — *phtheiromenos*); (5) *Fthora (G5356)*: noun — "corruption/decay" (Rom 8:21; Gal 6:8; 2Pe 1:4/2:12/19; 1Cor 15:42/50). The grammatical range covers the act (verb — "perverts"), the condition (passive — "is being corrupted"), the noun-state (tah.pu.khah — "perverseness"), and the noun-consequence (fthora — "corruption/decay").

**[CHAR-22]** E — Wide across OT and NT. (1) *A.vel (H5766A)*: noun — "injustice/wrong" (Lev 19:15 — "do no injustice in court"; Job 34:10 — "far be it from God that he should do wrong"); (2) *Av.lah (H5766B)*: noun — "wickedness/injustice" (Psa 58:2 — "devise wrongs"; 2Ch 19:7 — "no injustice with the Lord"); (3) *Av.val (H5767)*: agent-noun — "the unrighteous" (Job 27:7 — "be as the unrighteous"; Job 29:17 — "broke the fangs of the unrighteous"); (4) *Adikos (G0094)*: adjective/noun — "unjust/unrighteous" (Mat 5:45 — "on the just and on the unjust"; Luk 16:10 — "dishonest in a very little"; 1Cor 6:9 — "the unrighteous will not inherit"); (5) *Adikēma (G0092)*: act-noun — "wrongdoing/crime" (Act 18:14 — "a matter of wrongdoing"; Rev 18:5 — "her iniquities"). The grammatical range covers the condition (a.vel — wrong-state), the act (adikēma — wrong-deed), and the person (av.val/adikos — wrong-person).

**[CHAR-3]** E — In the confession-mode, cha.ta operates almost exclusively as a **first-person perfect verb**: *chatati* (I have sinned) or *chatanu* (we have sinned). This grammatical configuration reveals two things: (1) *Self-application*: the first person makes the speaker the agent of the named sin — "I" not "they" or "he" sinned. (2) *Past-completion*: the perfect aspect names the act as completed — it is already done; confession names a fait accompli, not a future intention or a general principle. The grammatical precision of the confessional form thus encodes the moral precision of genuine confession: it names a specific completed act by a specific identified person. No other grammatical configuration carries this confessional weight.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The grammatical range within the CHAR-4 corpus: (1) *Negated perfect* (Jer 2:35 — *lo chatati*): the completed act of sinning denied; (2) *Participial/nominal* (Ecc 2:26; 8:12 — *hachotet*): the sinning person as constituted type; (3) *Interrogative noun* (Jer 16:10 — the sin unrecognised and questioned); (4) *NT present infinitive/participle* (1Cor 15:34 — ongoing sinning in a state of suppression); (5) *NT adjective/participial* (Tit 3:11 — the person as "sinful" — a settled character description). The grammatical range reveals that conscience suppression can be expressed at every grammatical level: the denial of a completed act, the constituted type, the unrecognised noun, the ongoing present action, and the settled character description.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The grammatical range of the primary construction: (1) *Negated movement verb + preposition + sin-noun* (lo sur min + chat.tat): this is a predicate negation construction — it names what did not happen (turning/departing) relative to a specified object (the sins). (2) *Perfect/imperfect verb* of clinging (davaq — 2Ki 3:3): the perfect aspect of "clung to" names a completed act of attachment with ongoing effect. (3) *Hiphil stem* of the hardening verbs (Neh 9:29 — qasha, sarar): the Hiphil makes these causative — they actively caused their neck to stiffen, their shoulder to be stubborn. (4) *NT present participle* (hamartanontōn — 1Ti 5:20; Heb 10:26): ongoing action, active voice — sinning that continues. The grammatical range reveals: refusal to repent is expressed as both *completed adherence* (perfect davaq) and *continued ongoing action* (present participle hamartanō) — the will's past commitment to non-departure and its present continuation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The grammatical range covers all major categories: (1) *Noun/participial person-type*: hachotet (Ecc 7:26; 9:2/18; Pro 11:31/13:22) — the most characteristic CHAR-6 form, naming the constituted sinner; (2) *Qal perfect verb with iterative modifier*: "sinned yet again" (Exo 9:34) — completed acts accumulated through repetition; (3) *Qal perfect with continuative*: "you have sinned... there they have continued" (Hos 10:9) — completed act + continuation; (4) *NT present continuous participle*: hamartanōn (1Jo 3:6) — the ongoing continuous state as the characteristic's definitive NT form; (5) *NT constative aorist*: hēmarton (Heb 3:17) — viewing the extended historical sinning pattern as a single unit. The grammatical range reveals that habitual defection is expressed through the *person-type*, *iterative/continuous*, and *pattern-viewing* grammatical configurations — all of which distinguish settled pattern from single act.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The Hiphil of cha.ta appears across the corpus in three forms: (1) *Hiphil perfect*: *heheti* — "he made to sin" (completed action — 1Ki 14:16); (2) *Hiphil imperfect/wayyiqtol*: *wayaḥṭē* — narrative past: "and he made to sin" (the ongoing narrative sequence — repeated across Kings); (3) *Hiphil infinitive construct*: *lehaḥṭi* — "to cause to sin" (Jer 32:35 — "to cause Judah to sin"). These grammatical forms cover the completed past (the historical act), the narrative past (the sequence of kings), and the purposive infinitive (the intentional causative — built the high places for the purpose of causing Judah to sin). The range reveals that contagious sin is expressed as: completed historical acts, recurring narrative patterns, and deliberate purposive construction.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Pa.sha appears in three forms across the corpus: (1) *Qal perfect*: "has been in rebellion" (1Ki 12:19; 2Ch 10:19 — the state of ongoing revolt as a completed and persisting condition); (2) *Qal wayyiqtol (narrative past)*: "rebelled" (2Ki 1:1; 3:5 — the sequential narrative past: Moab rebelled at a specific historical moment); (3) *Qal perfect / compound verb*: "revolted from the rule of... and set up a king of their own" (2Ki 8:20; 2Ch 21:8 — the act plus its positive constructive consequence). The grammatical range covers: completed ongoing state (perfect), narrative past event (wayyiqtol), and compound act with consequence. This range reveals that political revolt can be: an established ongoing condition (Israel's rebellion — "to this day"), a specific historical event (Moab's rebellion — "after the death of Ahab"), or an act with positive constructive consequence (Edom setting up its own king).

**[CHAR-9]** E — The grammatical range covers: (1) *Noun (blasfēmia)*: "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" (Mat 12:31 — the act named as a noun); "slander" (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8 — the act in community context); "blasphemous names" (Rev 13:1 — the noun used attributively); (2) *Adjective (blasfēmos)*: "blasphemous words" (Act 6:11 — qualifying the words); "a blasphemous judgment" (Jude 9; 2Pe 2:11 — qualifying the speech-act); "abusive" (2Ti 3:2 — the dispositional adjective naming the person); (3) *Verb (blasfēmeō — implied in the nominal form)*: "He is blaspheming!" (Mar 2:7 — verb form); "to utter blasphemies against God" (Rev 13:6 — verbal phrase). The range covers act (noun), quality (adjective), and ongoing action (verb), showing the characteristic operates as event, property, and continuous practice.

**[CHAR-1]** E — ra.sha (H7563) functions grammatically as both adjective ("wicked" — attributive to person) and noun ("the wicked [person]"). The verbal root rasha' appears in Dan 12:10 ("the wicked shall act wickedly" — vc=42664). This grammatical range reveals that the RSH root describes both what the person is (nominal/adjectival: the wicked man, the wicked as a class) and what they do (verbal: to act wickedly). The co-presence of adjectival/nominal and verbal forms confirms that wickedness in this tradition is both a person-type (what they are) and an activity (what they do) — though the nominal/adjectival usage is dominant in the corpus (179V of ra.sha and 9V of re.sha vs. the single verbal instance), confirming that the characteristic's primary reference is the person-identity rather than the act.

**[CHAR-2]** E — ponēros (G4190) functions as: (1) adjective — "evil persons" (Mat 5:45 — VCG-04), "evil thoughts" (Mat 9:4 — VCG-03), "evil generation" (Mat 12:39 — VCG-02), "evil eye" (Mat 6:23 — VCG-03), "evil conscience" (Heb 10:22 — VCG-06); (2) substantive noun — "the evil one" (Mat 6:13 — VCG-01), "the evil" (Rom 12:9 — VCG-06), "evil people" (2Ti 3:13 — VCG-06); (3) neuter substantive — "evil things" (Luk 6:45 — VCG-03). This grammatical range reveals that ponēros operates across all the major grammatical categories of attribution (adjective describing a faculty/person/generation), hypostatisation (substantive noun naming the evil one or evil as a force), and abstract reference (naming evil things). The range confirms that ponēros is the most flexible and comprehensive of the characteristic's terms — naming the quality, the person, the cosmic force, and the abstraction.

**[CHAR-3]** E — to.e.vah (H8441) functions exclusively as a noun in the 40-verse corpus — it names the category of abomination as a substantive ("an abomination to the Lord," "abominations"). There is no verbal form used in this corpus. The noun-only function reveals that the characteristic is primarily a categorical designation — it names a type of violation, not an action-verb. In contrast, the Greek bdelugma (G0946) is a noun (abomination as a thing/category), while bdeluktos (G0947) is an adjective applied to persons (Tit 1:16 — "they are detestable"). The grammatical range thus spans: noun (naming the category — to.e.vah, bdelugma) and adjective (naming the person-type who embodies the category — bdeluktos). The absence of a verbal form in the primary Hebrew term suggests abomination is conceived as a state or category rather than an act — the verdict that something is abominable, not the act of making it so.

**[CHAR-4]** E — to.e.vah (H8441): noun-only in the corpus — the abomination as a category or quality. shiq.quts (H8251): noun-only in the corpus — the detestable idol-object as a substantive thing. The verbal root sh-q-ts does not appear in the CHAR-4 corpus, though it generates the nominal shiq.quts. This noun-only pattern across both primary Hebrew terms reveals that the characteristic is conceived as naming things (categories, objects, practices) rather than as naming actions. To.e.vah names the category of divine revulsion; shiq.quts names the specific detestable objects that provoke it. The absence of verbal forms in the corpus (no "to abominate" verb in use here) confirms that the characteristic names states and objects, not the act of performing abomination — the act belongs to M10c/M10.

**[CHAR-5]** E — a.ven (H0205G) functions in the corpus primarily as a noun — naming iniquity as a substantive condition, object, or quality. The phrase po.al a.ven ("workers/doers of iniquity") treats a.ven as the object of the verb "to work" — showing iniquity as something that can be actively worked/produced. This noun-as-object-of-activity grammatical pattern confirms the characteristic's generative mode: iniquity is what is actively produced by the po.al ("workers"). The plural "abominations" (a.vanim) and compound constructions (Isa 59:7: "thoughts of iniquity") extend the range. ro.a (H7455) functions exclusively as a noun naming the quality-of-evil in the deeds, always in construct state: "evil of your deeds" (Deu 28:20 — VCG-05), "evil of their deeds" (Jer 23:2 — VCG-05) — a genitive construction naming the evil quality as a property of the deeds. The noun-quality range confirms ro.a as naming the moral character of expressed acts rather than an inner state or process.

**[CHAR-6]** E — blasfēmeō (G0987) appears as a verb in all its occurrences in this corpus. The verbal form is significant: blasphemy is an act, not merely a state or quality — the verb names the speech event as an ongoing, enacted process. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): "opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name" — both the infinitive and participial forms of the verb appear, showing sustained blasphemous action. The verb-only occurrence confirms the characteristic as constitutively an enacted speech-event rather than a static condition. kakopoios (G2555) appears as a noun (person-type term) in all five VCG-03 occurrences — the evildoer-person-type as a substantive category. atopos (G0824) appears as an adjective in Act 25:5 — "anything wrong (atopos) about the man" — modifying the act as "out-of-place."

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's primary terms span noun, adjective, verb, and participle forms, revealing the grammatical range of inner evil's expression. Char 1 (ra.sha — primarily adjective/noun used as person-type substantive, rarely verbal): inner evil as a stable person-type category. Char 2 (ponēros — primarily adjective used substantively and predicatively; kakia — noun; adikia — noun): inner evil as a quality-designation and condition-noun. Chars 3/4 (to.e.vah — noun, shiq.quts — noun): inner evil as a category-label and object-designator. Char 5 (a.ven — noun; po.al a.ven — verb+noun construction): inner evil as a productive activity (verb) producing a person-type (noun). Char 6 (blasfēmeō — verb; kakopoios — noun): inner evil as an enacted speech-event (verb) and charged identity (noun). The grammatical range reveals: the cluster addresses inner evil primarily as a noun-condition and adjective-quality (Chars 1-4), with Char 5 introducing the verb-dimension (active scheming process) and Char 6 introducing the speech-verb dimension (enacted blasphemy). The shift from noun to verb across the cluster is analytically significant — it corresponds to the movement from settled identity (noun) to active process (verb) to expressive speech-act (verb).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The ta.me root operates as both verb (H2930A: "to become unclean, to defile") and adjective (H2931: "unclean"). This verb/adjective pairing reveals the characteristic as having both a dynamic and a static dimension: the verb captures the event of acquisition (the person becomes unclean), while the adjective captures the condition as a property (the person is unclean). The verb form also appears in causative constructions (hiphil: "to make/render unclean"), showing that the condition can be produced in another through one's own actions. G0169 akathartos in the 133-verse corpus operates predominantly as an adjective (describing the person or thing as unclean) — consistent with the characteristic's status as a condition. The full grammatical range shows the characteristic as a condition (adjective) that is dynamically acquired (verb) and potentially transmitted (causative).

**[CHAR-2]** E — G0167 akatharsia (primary NT noun) operates exclusively as a noun throughout the 26-verse corpus, naming the condition as a state. G3435 molunō operates as a verb (1Cor 8:7 — "is defiled"; Rev 3:4 — "have not soiled") — capturing the act of defiling or the condition of being defiled. G3436 molusmos is a noun (2Cor 7:1 — "every defilement"). H2931 operates as an adjective (ta.me adj — "unclean" as a predicate or attributive). The range across noun (state/condition), verb (act of defiling or incurring defilement), and adjective (property of the person) reveals the characteristic as a condition (noun/adjective) that is dynamically acquired or maintained through specific acts (verb) — the same grammatical range as Characteristic 1, confirming the shared lexical architecture.

**[CHAR-3]** E — H2930A ta.me operates in both qal (intransitive: "become unclean" — Lev 18:20: "make yourself unclean with her") and piel/hiphil forms (causative: "defile/render unclean" — Jer 7:30: "they have set... to defile it"; Eze 5:11: "you have defiled my sanctuary"). This verbal range reveals the characteristic as operating in both directions: the community undergoes defilement (qal — passive reception of the condition) and actively defiles sacred objects and spaces (piel/hiphil — causative action directed outward). The community is both subject (defiling themselves) and agent (defiling land, sanctuary, name). This bidirectional verbal grammar is the linguistic foundation of the characteristic's centrifugal movement: the community's inner moral corruption goes outward to contaminate the sacred environment.

**[CHAR-4]** E — G0169 akathartos operates exclusively as an adjective throughout the 21-verse corpus — never as a noun, verb, or participle. It modifies pneuma in every verse: "unclean spirit" (pneuma akatharton — nominative, accusative, dative, genitive forms). The exclusive adjectival range reveals the characteristic as defined by the character of the defiling agent: the term describes what the spirit is (unclean), not what the person does or is. This grammatical range is distinctive within the M10c cluster: Characteristics 1-3 use the ta.me verb (H2930A) as their primary term capturing the act of defiling or becoming defiled; Characteristic 4 uses akathartos as a purely adjectival descriptor of the external agent's character.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The grammatical range across the cluster reveals a pattern that maps onto the cluster's internal structure. Characteristics 1-3 all use the ta.me root in both verb (H2930A — to defile, to become defiled) and adjective (H2931 — unclean) forms, with Characteristic 3's verb appearing in causative constructions (hiphil/piel — the community defiles the land, the sanctuary, the name). This bidirectional verbal grammar (intransitive — becoming defiled; causative — defiling sacred objects) is the linguistic foundation of Characteristic 3's centrifugal movement: the community is both subject (defiling themselves) and agent (defiling their environment). Characteristic 2 additionally deploys the NT verb G3435 molunō (to soil/defile) — capturing the act of defiling the inner person. Characteristic 4's primary term (G0169 akathartos) operates exclusively as an adjective — never as a verb — confirming the characteristic as defined entirely by the character of the external agent (what the spirit is) rather than by any act or process of acquisition. The grammatical range cluster-level pattern: Characteristics 1-3 use verb+adjective grammar (dynamic acquisition + static condition); Characteristic 4 uses adjective-only grammar (character of the agent). The grammatical structure maps onto the defilement mechanism: where defilement is acquired through process or act (Chars 1-3), the vocabulary is dynamic (verb); where defilement is constituted by the character of an external agent (Char 4), the vocabulary is purely descriptive (adjective).

findings.session_b_note:
The semantic range of the primary NT term (G0863 — afiēmi) is unusually broad — the three sub-variants within this registry alone demonstrate:

- **Forgive (G0863H):** Releasing moral debt — the primary forgiveness sense. 64 occurrences.
- **Leave/forsake (G0863G):** Releasing relational or material bonds — discipleship-leaving, abandonment of first love, leaving a gift at the altar. 236 occurrences (broader NT use).
- **Permit (G0863I):** Releasing access — granting or withholding entry. 32 occurrences.

The semantic range therefore covers: moral release (forgiveness), relational release (leaving), and access release (permitting). All three share the core act-structure of intentional release but apply it in different domains.

**The Hebrew range:** H5545 (sa.lach) is semantically narrower — exclusively divine forgiveness of sin. The Hebrew vocabulary is more specialised; the Greek is broader.

**Semantic range significance:** The breadth of the Greek afiēmi reveals that forgiveness in the NT is not an isolated act but an instance of a broader human (and divine) capacity for intentional release. The act-structure that generates forgiveness is the same structure that generates discipleship, hospitality, and the granting of access. Forgiveness is the morally-directed instance of a larger act-category.

findings.session_b_note:
The SEMANTIC_RANGE_BREADTH flag is raised for the primary active term G4697 splanchnizō. Pass 1 identifies four semantic domains for splanchnizō:

1. Compassion toward physical suffering or need — healing miracles (Matt 20:34; Mark 1:41; Luke 7:13)
2. Compassion toward spiritual destitution — "sheep without a shepherd" (Matt 9:36; Mark 6:34)
3. Compassion toward physical hunger — crowds without food (Matt 15:32; Mark 8:2)
4. Compassion in relational/moral context — parable of prodigal (Luke 15:20), unforgiving servant (Matt 18:27), Good Samaritan (Luke 10:33)

The four-domain breadth of splanchnizō across physical, spiritual, material, and relational-moral contexts is the primary semantic range evidence. The flag is confirmed fully warranted (Pass 1).

For the chesed vocabulary, the semantic range spans: divine constitutive character (Exod 34:6), covenant loyalty (sustained through time and violation), steadfast love (Lam 3:22 — inexhaustible), human character quality (Prov 19:22; Hos 6:6; Mic 6:8), and covenantal faithfulness (2 Sam 22:26). The chesed range is wider than any single English term can capture — hence the programme retaining it under "compassion" alongside "kindness" (R99) and "love" (R103) in multiple registries.

findings.session_b_note:
H1792 da.kha operates across:
- Physical crushing of persons, enemies, or objects (literal)
- Inner anguish produced by external crushing (enemy-produced suffering — group 7552-001)
- Penitential contrition of the spirit before God (the inner-being meaning — groups 7552-003, 7553-001)
- Substitutionary crushing of the Servant (theologically distinctive — group 7552-002)
- Crushing as divine chastisement (God as the subject crushing the psalmist — Psa 51:8)

The semantic range moves from physical to inner-being across a metaphorical bridge that is intrinsic to the vocabulary. The breadth is: outer physical destruction → inner-being anguish → penitential posture before God → vicarious redemptive suffering. This is a remarkably wide range anchored in a single root.

findings.session_b_note:
**koinōnia (G2842):** The STEP search gloss "participation" reflects the NT use. The registry evidence shows the term operating across: vertical fellowship with God (873-001), horizontal fellowship among believers (873-002), and by extension in the NT, fellowship of suffering (Phili 3:10), fellowship in the Spirit, and fellowship at the Lord's Supper. The semantic range spans from participatory communion to practical sharing and generosity (a dimension present in the Pauline epistles beyond the anchor verses, but within the programme's active verse count of 17).

**cha.var (H2266):** The STEP search gloss "to unite." The registry evidence shows the term operating across: idolatrous joining (Hos 4:17), occult charming (Psa 58:5), rhetorical word-joining (Job 16:4), communal participation as hope-ground (Ecc 9:4), and divine joining of divided communities (Eze 37:19). The semantic range spans from physical binding, to moral alignment, to speech-act construction, to eschatological restoration.

**The breadth is significant:** Both primary terms span a very wide semantic range — from the physical to the spiritual, from the mundane to the eschatological. Fellowship vocabulary is semantically broad, which is consistent with the six modes of operation identified in finding 062-OPER-001.

**Gap:** Full semantic range determination requires completed lexical analysis (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag limits this).

**koinōnia (G2842):** The STEP search gloss "participation" reflects the NT use. The registry evidence shows the term operating across: vertical fellowship with God (873-001), horizontal fellowship among believers (873-002), and by extension in the NT, fellowship of suffering (Phili 3:10), fellowship in the Spirit, and fellowship at the Lord's Supper. The semantic range spans from participatory communion to practical sharing and generosity (a dimension present in the Pauline epistles beyond the anchor verses, but within the programme's active verse count of 17).

**cha.var (H2266):** The STEP search gloss "to unite." The registry evidence shows the term operating across: idolatrous joining (Hos 4:17), occult charming (Psa 58:5), rhetorical word-joining (Job 16:4), communal participation as hope-ground (Ecc 9:4), and divine joining of divided communities (Eze 37:19). The semantic range spans from physical binding, to moral alignment, to speech-act construction, to eschatological restoration.

**The breadth is significant:** Both primary terms span a very wide semantic range — from the physical to the spiritual, from the mundane to the eschatological. Fellowship vocabulary is semantically broad, which is consistent with the six modes of operation identified in finding 062-OPER-001.

**Gap:** Full semantic range determination requires completed lexical analysis (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag limits this).

findings.session_b_note: H2896A (tov) has the widest semantic range of any OWNER term in this registry: aesthetic pleasantness, moral rightness, covenantal reliability, comparative excellence, experiential benefit, evaluative good, ontological goodness (Gen 1 creation pronouncement), volitional preference, and inner well-being. The 12 distinct modes identified at Q&A-022 correspond to 12 distinct positions within this range. The breadth is confirmed by the 10 sub-senses of the TOV root and the 9 distinct H2896A groups. G0019 (agathōsunē): narrow range — goodness as Spirit-produced inner virtue/resolve (4 NT occurrences, all Pauline, all pneumatological). G5544 (chrēstotēs): medium range — kindness/goodness/gentleness as inner character quality and divine attribute (7 occurrences). The semantic range across the three OWNER terms covers breadth (H2896A's 12 modes) and precision (G0019 and G5544's specialised NT meanings). (OBS-067-OBS-007, OBS-067-OBS-008, OBS-067-OBS-009, OBS-067-OBS-048)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-007: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two language…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two languages with distinct semantic ranges, a full root-family analysis, a NT coinage (agathōsunē), and a comprehensive vocabulary arc from phenomenological breadth (H2896A) to virtuous precision (agathōsunē) to relational precision (chrēstotēs — Q&A-177). The lexical evidence is rich. Literary: the primary anchor (Mic 6:8) uniquely combines revelatory and covenantal-obligation frames with an internal tri-fold structure that no other verse replicates (Q&A-183); the anchor corpus spans prophetic, wisdom, psalmic, and epistolary forms across multiple contextual settings (Q&A-181). Human science: virtue ethics is the closest parallel framework, with the critical divergence at the source of goodness (divine gift vs natural achievement — Q&A-186). Constraints: NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms limit the LXX analysis (Q&A-175); LSJ data is absent. The evidential foundation is strong at the lexical-semantic and verse-literary levels; it is constrained at the LXX-continuity and human-science elaboration levels. This asymmetry is itself an analytic finding — it identifies where future investigation would most strengthen the registry's evidential base.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-013: T1 identified that goodness is complex in structure — the name "goodness" does not capture the semantic breadth of the vocabulary (Q&A-013). T7 confirms and explains this complexity through the vocabu…
findings.finding_value: T1 identified that goodness is complex in structure — the name "goodness" does not capture the semantic breadth of the vocabulary (Q&A-013). T7 confirms and explains this complexity through the vocabulary arc (Q&A-177): the three-stage development (H2896A's phenomenological breadth → agathōsunē's virtuous precision → chrēstotēs's relational precision) corresponds precisely to T1's finding that goodness operates across quality, disposition, condition, and evaluative act (Q&A-016). Each stage of the vocabulary arc covers a different aspect of T1's definitional complexity: H2896A covers quality, condition, and evaluative act; agathōsunē covers the character-quality and virtuous-resolve aspect; chrēstotēs covers the dispositional-relational aspect. T7 thus provides the lexical grounding for T1's multi-modal portrait — the vocabulary complexity matches the definitional complexity.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-022: T3's finding that goodness has an inherently perceptual character — it must be encountered and tasted, not merely inferred (Q&A-068) — is confirmed and grounded by T7's lexical and literary analysis. …
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that goodness has an inherently perceptual character — it must be encountered and tasted, not merely inferred (Q&A-068) — is confirmed and grounded by T7's lexical and literary analysis. The Psa 34:8 primary verse functions literarily as an invitation to perceptual encounter (Q&A-178) — "taste and see" is the literary form that corresponds to the T3 perceptual faculty engagement. The phenomenological root of H2896A (Q&A-168 — begins with concrete experience of what is agreeable and beneficial, rises to moral categories) explains why T3's perceptive faculty is so prominently engaged: the Hebrew root of goodness is itself experiential-perceptual before it is ethical-conceptual. T7's etymological grounding explains the T3 perceptual finding: the vocabulary encodes the experiential mode of knowing goodness that T3's faculty analysis confirms.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-028: T6 confirmed that goodness has the most extensive vocabulary-sharing and cross-registry connection pattern of any characteristic analysed so far in the programme. T7 confirms through the vocabulary ar…
findings.finding_value: T6 confirmed that goodness has the most extensive vocabulary-sharing and cross-registry connection pattern of any characteristic analysed so far in the programme. T7 confirms through the vocabulary arc (Q&A-177) that this extensiveness is a lexical reality, not a programme classification artefact: the three root families (TOV, AGATHO, CHRESTO) each generate multiple terms distributed across multiple registries because the semantic ranges genuinely overlap. The vocabulary sharing (T6.4) is not the result of how the programme has drawn its boundaries — it reflects the actual lexical distribution of the Hebrew and Greek goodness vocabulary, which crosses conceptual boundaries that English vocabulary maintains more distinctly. The three-stage vocabulary arc (H2896A breadth → agathōsunē precision → chrēstotēs precision) tracks the same movement as the cross-registry distribution pattern: H2896A generates the widest distribution (TOV root to R103, to R42, to multiple other registries); the NT precision terms (G0019, G5544) generate narrower distributions (R65 and R99 respectively). As the vocabulary narrows to precision, the cross-registry connections narrow correspondingly. T6's structural pattern and T7's lexical arc describe the same underlying phenomenon: goodness vocabulary begins broad and specialises, and its cross-registry connections follow the same trajectory.

findings.session_b_note: Agapē's semantic range in the NT evidence: (a) divine love for humanity (Joh 3:16); (b) human love for God (Mat 22:37); (c) mutual love in community (Joh 13:34); (d) love of enemy (Mat 5:44); (e) disordered love (love of darkness — Joh 3:19; love of the world — 2Ti 4:10; love of the pre-eminent position — 3Jo 9). The semantic range spans divine, human-covenantal, communal, and misdirected forms. Chesed's range: divine faithfulness, human loyalty, the person-type (chasid), the failure of chesed (withdrawal, demand). The combined semantic range of the primary terms covers the full moral landscape — from the highest (God's love as his being) to the lowest (love misdirected toward darkness). This breadth is unique in the programme — no other characteristic has primary terms whose semantic range spans from the ontologically highest (divine nature) to the morally inverted (love of darkness).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-007: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-cove…
findings.finding_value: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-covenantal (chesed), Spirit-produced self-giving (agapē), somatic-compassionate (racham), intense-erotic (ahavah/dod), and naturally affective (phileō). The vocabulary structure itself distinguishes disposition/act/condition, received/given, and quality/person-type — making it architecturally precise. The semantic range of the primary terms spans from divine ontology (God is love) to moral inversion (love of darkness) — the widest semantic arc in the programme. The primary anchor is Lam 3:22 — love's most definitive affirmation precisely at the moment of maximum empirical falsification: a theological confession rather than an empirical observation. The LXX connection is partially evidenced (agapē as chesed-translated); full LXX analysis is limited by NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags. The human science frameworks identified (attachment theory, virtue ethics) are named as Session D pointers but not elaborated — the instruction prohibits importing framework content not grounded in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-006: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispos…
findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispositional), racham (somatic-compassionate), ahavah/dod (intense-erotic), phileō/agapē (affective-natural and willed-unconditional). The grammatical range analysis confirms the tripartite definition (Q&A-123): verb (act) + noun (disposition) + adjective-passive (condition). The semantic range analysis confirms the vocabulary arc (Q&A-124, Q&A-131). The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136, Q&A-137) confirms the definition's most counterintuitive feature: love at its most definitional is not evidenced by love's presence but confessed against its apparent absence. The definition says love is permanent, unwavering, faithful — and the evidential ground for this claim is a verse written in the context of Jerusalem's destruction. The evidential foundation is thus not primarily experiential but confessional — the definition's permanence-claim is a theological assertion, grounded in the character of God rather than in the consistency of human experience.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-111-007: Reading T7 as a whole reveals the evidential foundation as both rich and gapped. The lexical foundation is comprehensive: mercy has terms for all grammatical roles (noun, verb, adjective, person-type)…
findings.finding_value: Reading T7 as a whole reveals the evidential foundation as both rich and gapped. The lexical foundation is comprehensive: mercy has terms for all grammatical roles (noun, verb, adjective, person-type), all operational aspects (disposition, act, seeking, structural opposite), and all major dimensions (compassion, covering, grace, propitiation, supplication). The vocabulary arc is itself a theological narrative (Q&A-180). The primary anchor verse is Psa 78:38 — the verse that most fully encodes the complete mercy-event structure (Q&A-185). The gaps are structural: LXX analysis and NT coinage data are unavailable (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag, 67 terms). Human science engagement identifies three relevant frameworks (moral psychology, attachment theory, shame theory) with the key divergence that the biblical model grounds mercy in prior reception rather than autonomous moral development (Q&A-189). The T7 synthesis: mercy's evidential base is wide and cross-genre (liturgical, prophetic, sapiential, narrative, epistolary) — this breadth confirms that mercy is not a sectional or contextual biblical theme but a structural reality appearing in every major literary context.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-030-007: T7 as a whole reveals that the contrition vocabulary has a high degree of internal coherence and a sophisticated grammatical apparatus (distinguishing process, settled state, active/passive/volitional…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals that the contrition vocabulary has a high degree of internal coherence and a sophisticated grammatical apparatus (distinguishing process, settled state, active/passive/volitional voice) that the English word "contrition" cannot render. The primary anchor verses (Isa 57:15, Psa 51:17) are architecturally complementary: Isa 57:15 provides the complete relational frame (divine character → divine dwelling → divine reviving); Psa 51:17 provides the inner-being substance (broken spirit, contrite heart as the acceptable sacrifice). The literary context (psalm and prophecy) requires reading the same characteristic in two modes: as human address to God (penitential psalm) and as divine address to the community (prophetic promise). The cross-testament gap (T7.1.8–9) is the methodological limitation — without LXX analysis the vocabulary arc from OT to NT cannot be closed from this registry's data. Human science frameworks confirm rather than challenge the biblical account, with the theocentric causality as the point of genuine divergence.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-030-013: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the …
findings.finding_value: The definition tier (T1) establishes the three-mode structure (penitential, anguish, substitutionary); the evidential tier (T7) reveals that this three-mode structure is encoded in the grammar of the primary vocabulary. The Pual passive at Isa 53:5 (most intensive form of received crushing) corresponds to the substitutionary mode; the Niphal (received crushing) corresponds to the anguish mode; the adjectival settled states (dak.ka, na.kheh) correspond to the penitential condition. The vocabulary's grammatical range (T7) is not incidental — it encodes the definitional complexity (T1) at the lexical level. The two tiers are mutually explanatory: T7 explains why T1's definitional complexity is textually grounded; T1 explains why T7's grammatical range is analytically significant.

findings.finding_value: T7 reveals that the fellowship vocabulary has the widest semantic arc of any characteristic in the programme: from tabernacle seam (physical construction) through wound (somatic joining) through companionship (relational) through moral complicity (evaluative) through ontological divine nature participation. This breadth is encoded in the root-level architecture (chavar — the joining logic applied universally). The two primary anchor verses (2Pe 1:4 and 1Jo 1:3) are complementary in perspective: 2Pe 1:4 is the vertical-ontological statement (human participating in divine nature); 1Jo 1:3 is the relational-structural statement (horizontal derived from vertical). The LSJ gap (T7.1.8) is an acknowledged data limitation — the classical background of koinōnia is unavailable from this registry's data, which means the NT's transformation of a Hellenistic civic-philosophical term into a theological term cannot be traced from this evidence base.

findings.finding_value: T1's five-mode structure is encoded in the vocabulary's semantic arc (T7): existential → companionship → moral complicity → suffering → ontological maps precisely onto the semantic range (Ecc 9:4 → Psa 119:63 → Mat 23:30 → Phili 3:10 → 2Pe 1:4). The vocabulary is not a loose collection but a precisely structured arc corresponding to the definitional five modes. T7's grammatical analysis confirms T1's dispositional/act/constitutional distinction: the Hithpael (self-joining act) corresponds to T1's active dimension; the Pual (being-joined condition — Hos 4:17) corresponds to T1's constitutional dimension; the adjectival terms (H2270 companion, H2278 consort) correspond to T1's dispositional dimension.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-007: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structura…
findings.finding_value: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structural theological claim. The cross-testament vocabulary development (LXX applying aphiēmi to render salach; NT extending aphiēmi to commanded human forgiveness) carries the programme's clearest lexical theological claim: human forgiveness is structurally shaped by divine forgiveness, named by the same vocabulary. The grammatical analysis (Niphal passive — "they shall be forgiven"; active Qal — God forgives) precisely encodes the act-structure: divine act → creaturely received status. The primary anchor trio (Jer 31:34, Psa 86:5, Luk 7:47) spans three literary forms (prophetic-eschatological, wisdom/psalm, Synoptic narrative) and three analytical registers (eschatological promise, divine character-statement, inner-being consequence). T7 synthesis: the forgiveness vocabulary is the most theologically structured in the current review set — its cross-testament development carries an explicit structural claim visible at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-013: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebr…
findings.finding_value: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebrew terms (H5545 verb, H5546 adjective, H5547 noun). T1's four modes map onto the vocabulary's grammatical range (Niphal passive = covenantal-objective received status; Qal active = divine forgiving act; human commanded = G0863H in imperative/hortatory forms; seeking = H5545 imperative in intercessory prayer). T7's cross-testament development finding (NT applies divine-forgiveness vocabulary to commanded human forgiveness) is the lexical expression of T1's structural claim about the human horizontal mode being shaped by the divine model. T1 and T7 are mutually encoded — the vocabulary is structured to carry the definition.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-028: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis confirm and explain each other. The salach root's lexical isolation (T6.4 — no root-sharing with other programme registries; T7.1.1 — no XREF t…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis confirm and explain each other. The salach root's lexical isolation (T6.4 — no root-sharing with other programme registries; T7.1.1 — no XREF terms) reveals that forgiveness maintains a lexically distinct divine-exclusive domain — the strongest co-occurrence registry (guilt-073 at 51 shared verses) operates in the same semantic territory but at the verse level, not at the root-sharing level. This means the structural partnership between forgiveness and guilt is relational-definitional, not lexical-etymological. The Jer 31:34 multi-registry convergence (T6.6 — shared with guilt, love, thought) is also T7's most analytically rich verse (T7.2.5 — the primary anchor trio includes Jer 31:34): the verse that carries the most structural connections is the verse that is exegetically richest, confirmed from both directions.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-007: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: …
findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the v…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-018: T2's constitutional levels are each carried by specific vocabulary families in T7. The somatic-body level (T2.6 — gut, womb) is carried by the RACHAM/SPLANCHN root families — the body's interior as th…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional levels are each carried by specific vocabulary families in T7. The somatic-body level (T2.6 — gut, womb) is carried by the RACHAM/SPLANCHN root families — the body's interior as the etymological ground of both. The soul-character level (T2.2) is carried by the CHASAD family — chesed as the settled covenantal character disposition. The heart-deliberative level (T2.3) is evidenced most richly in Hos 11:8 (T7's primary anchor for divine compassion). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) traverses exactly the constitutional range T2 maps: from the most interior somatic level (womb) through the character-soul level to the externalised action level. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T2's constitutional depth: Hos 11:8 evidences constitutional depth (heart-level deliberation of compassion over judgment); Luke 10:33 evidences constitutional breadth (the full four-stage movement from sight to action).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-018: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The spirit-reception level (T2.1) is carried by the perfect passive form of charitoō (kecharitōmenē — the completed act of b…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The spirit-reception level (T2.1) is carried by the perfect passive form of charitoō (kecharitōmenē — the completed act of being-made-the-object-of-grace, with continuing state) — the most precise grammatical encoding of a constitutional arrival that has permanently changed the person's standing. The soul-standing level (T2.2) is carried by charis as noun (the inhabited state of favour) and chen as the relational standing-in-favour term. The character-expression level is carried by chen in its conduct/speech register (889-003) and charizō in its human-forgiving mode. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō invented to carry the standing-in-favour concept) is the lexical evidence that T2's spirit-level reception was conceptually unprecedented — no prior vocabulary could name what happened constitutionally when grace-as-standing arrived.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-025: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-le…
findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. This is unique in the programme's vocabulary data: no other characteristic has the giving-side and receiving-side vocabulary built from the same root. T4's relational architecture and T7's lexical analysis are the relational and lexical descriptions of the same structural reality — that grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit whose two sides are inseparable at the root level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-117-007: T7 establishes that the peace vocabulary is structurally complete — covering state, disposition, act, and person-type — with a single root (SHA.L = completeness-wholeness-settlement) generating all He…
findings.finding_value:
T7 establishes that the peace vocabulary is structurally complete — covering state, disposition, act, and person-type — with a single root (SHA.L = completeness-wholeness-settlement) generating all Hebrew peace vocabulary. The vocabulary arc culminates in two primary anchors that jointly constitute the definitive biblical statement: Isa 26:3 (perfect peace for the trust-directed mind — experiential) and Eph 2:14 (he himself IS our peace — ontological). The most fundamental divergence from human science (attachment theory being the closest framework): biblical peace has a Person as its substance; no psychological framework contains the concept of a person being a condition. The NT coinage of eirēnopoieō (G1517) names what no OT term could name — the unique once-for-all act of making peace through the cross.

findings.finding_value: T1's central finding (peace as structured four-dimensional reality culminating in a Person who IS peace) is lexically grounded in T7's root analysis: SHA.L (completeness-wholeness-settlement) names the essence at the root level; the sub-forms (G/H/I/J/K/L) map onto T1's four dimensions; and the two primary anchor verses (Isa 26:3 and Eph 2:14) name the experiential and ontological dimensions respectively. The lexical arc (root → state → act → person-type → NT coinage) maps precisely onto T1's four-dimensional sequence: the root names the ground (completeness), the person-type terms name the formed character, and eirēnopoieō (G1517) names the unique act that accomplishes the eschatological dimension. Word and meaning are structurally aligned.

findings.finding_value:
T6's structural relationships and T7's lexical foundation are the most directly complementary tiers in the analysis. T6's root-level finding (SHA.L shared with R34 covenant, T6.4.2) is validated and grounded by T7's etymology (T7.1.1 — SHA.L root meaning completeness-wholeness-settlement; sha.lam = to pay in full). The root-level semantic bond between peace and covenant (T6) is not lexical coincidence but semantic identity: they share the same root because they name the same underlying reality from different angles — the covenant is the relational structure of completeness; shalom is the experiential condition of completeness. T6's shared anchor network (59 relationships, T6.6) is confirmed as structurally grounded by T7's lexical richness (10 vocabulary dimensions, person-type terms, supplication terms, antonym vocabulary) — the wide vocabulary arc (T7) generates the wide structural network (T6).

findings.finding_value: Charis range: grace as sovereign soteriological disposition (Eph 2:8), relational favour (Luk 1:30), apostolic commissioning (Gal 1:15), the sphere of the believer's standing (Rom 5:2), gratitude/credit (Luk 17:9), and political favour (Act 24:27). The range spans theological register (salvation) through social register (political favour). The grace-characteristic accommodates all these uses because its root structure (joyful giving from the greater to the lesser) is flexible across contexts.

findings.finding_value: Tov range: aesthetic (Num 24:5 — "how lovely are your tents"), moral (1Ki 8:18 — goodness in the heart), material (Deu 5:33 — going well), relational (2Ki 25:24 — it shall be well with you), volitional-preference (2Sa 15:26 — "what seems good to him"), and comparative (Song 4:10 — "much better than wine"). The semantic breadth is among the widest of any term in the programme.
