findings.session_b_note:
The vocabulary includes one person-type term in the adjective form: **H5546 (sal.lach)** — "forgiving" — applied exclusively to God in Psa 86:5 as a character description. This is the closest the vocabulary comes to a person-type term — naming the subject as constitutively characterised by forgiveness.

However, H5546 is a divine-exclusive person-type term — it describes what God is, not what a human habitually is. There is no equivalent human person-type term in the vocabulary ("the forgiver" as a character type for a human person). The NT commands the human to forgive habitually (Mar 11:25; Luk 17:4) but does not coin a lexical label for the person who does so.

*Partial:* The person-type term exists for the divine subject (H5546 — sal.lach); it is absent for the human subject. This asymmetry is itself analytically significant — the language reserves the character-description of "forgiver" for God.

The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-covenantal (chesed), Spirit-produced self-giving (agapē), somatic-compassionate (racham), intense-erotic (ahavah/dod), and naturally affective (phileō). The primary anchor is Lam 3:22 — love's most definitive affirmation precisely at the moment of maximum empirical falsification: a theological confession rather than an empirical observation. The LXX connection is partially evidenced (agapē as chesed-translated); full LXX analysis is limited by NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags. findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient for the depth of compassion at the point of maximum permitted suffering) is the lexical expression of T5's most profound formation claim: suffering in the context of compassion-formation produces a depth of compassion that transcends ordinary vocabulary. findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-028: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural f…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is confirmed and extended by T7's vocabulary analysis: the CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the root itself (T7.1 P5), not as an external antonym. This means the cluster-crossing T6 identifies is not an external structural anomaly but an internal semantic feature: the compassion vocabulary contains its own opposite at the root level. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (T6.6 — 6 registries) is also T7's most evidentially rich single text — the verse that carries the most structural connections is the same verse that is most analytically central to the vocabulary analysis. The love co-occurrence dominance (T6.1 — 196/351 verses) is confirmed by T7's vocabulary arc: the vocabulary's fullest range (womb to almsgiving) overlaps extensively with the love vocabulary's range, which is why they co-occur across more than half of all active verses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-025: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-le…
findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. This is unique in the programme's vocabulary data: no other characteristic has the giving-side and receiving-side vocabulary built from the same root. T4's relational architecture and T7's lexical analysis are the relational and lexical descriptions of the same structural reality — that grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit whose two sides are inseparable at the root level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-117-018: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational scope findings (peace given to Israel → expanding to nations → universal in Christ) are lexically grounded in T7's vocabulary arc. The greeting-blessing (H7965K, T4.3 — human giving of peace) has its person-type lexical ground in T7.1.6 (ish sha.lom — the man of peace as person-type). The absence of a dedicated antonym term (T7.1.5) confirms T4's finding that peace is primarily defined by its presence and relational giving, not by its absence — the vocabulary is positive-directional, matching the God-to-human direction of peace's primary flow (T4.1). The NT coinage eirēnopoieō (T7.1.9) names what T4.1.2 describes as the basis of God's peace-giving through Christ — the cross-accomplishment has its own unique verbal form precisely because it is a unique relational act.

**[CLUSTER]** E. Yes — tsad.diq (H6662) is the dominant person-type term: the righteous one, the righteous person. This is one of the most widely used person-type designations in the entire Hebrew Bible. In the Psalms and Proverbs, tsad.diq functions as a recognised social-moral category — the type of person who is righteous, in contrast to ra.sha (the wicked person). The person-type term is the evidence that righteousness in Hebrew is primarily a governing state of the person, not merely a description of specific acts.

In Greek, dikaios (G1342) serves the same function — the just/righteous one. The designation is used of God, of Christ (the Righteous One, Act 3:14), and of persons who walk in righteousness.

findings.finding_value: Yes, and prominently. The participial form **ya.re (H3373)** — "the one who fears (God)" — functions as a person-type term across M01-A-VCG-03 and VCG-06 extensively. Job 1:1 ("a man who feared God"), 1Ki 18:3 ("Obadiah feared the Lord greatly"), Neh 7:2, Mal 3:16 (those who feared the Lord), Act 10:2 (Cornelius "feared God"). The person-type term is formally "the God-fearer" (ya.re elohim / ya.re YHWH) — a recognised biblical category of person defined by this characteristic. In the NT, the "God-fearer" (foboumenos ton theon) is a recognised community category (Act 10:2, 22, 35; Act 13:16, 26).

M01-G has an implicit person-type: **deilos (G1169)** — the cowardly one. Used as a character-description in Mat 8:26 (Jesus calling the disciples timid) and Rev 21:8 (the cowardly as a person-category heading the list of the condemned).

The cluster has a well-developed person-type vocabulary for M01-A (the God-fearer: ya.re / foboumenos) and a negative person-type for M01-G (deilos — the cowardly one). The existence of a recognised person-type category confirms that reverential fear is understood in Scripture as a defining character quality, not merely an episodic experience.

Yes. *Orgilos* (G3711 / Tit 1:7 / M02-C-VCG-02) is a person-type adjective naming the quick-tempered person. *Filoneikos* (G5380 / 1Cor 11:16 / M02-F-VCG-01) names the dispute-loving person. In Hebrew, the wisdom corpus uses the construct "a man of great rage" (Pro 19:19; 22:24 / M02-B-VCG-05) as a person-type descriptor. These terms name persons characterised by the anger-disposition rather than naming the anger-event itself.

Yes, minimally. a.vel (H0057 — M03-B-VCG-01 anchor Gen 37:35: Jacob's "mourning") functions as a mourning-participant noun in some instances (Est 6:12 — "mourning with his head covered"; Job 29:25 — "among mourners"). mis.ped and sa.phad similarly name the one who mourns as a participant in the act (Ecc 12:5 — mourners going through the streets — M03-B-VCG-01). The mourner as a person-type is implicit in the mourning vocabulary rather than a dedicated person-type noun. There is no dedicated Hebrew or Greek term for "the person who habitually grieves" analogous to "the wise" in wisdom vocabulary.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Not a distinct person-type term in this corpus. The closest is the characterisation of the one who exults "all the day" (Psa 89:16) and the one who "joyfully works righteousness" (Isa 64:5 — su.s) — these describe a person-type by their characteristic activity rather than by a specific noun designation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes: **sa.me.ach** (H8056, 21 instances) — the adjectival form naming the joyful/glad person as a type: 1Ki 4:20 ("Judah and Israel were… sa.me.ach"); 1Ki 1:40 ("rejoicing with great joy"); Pro 15:13 ("glad heart"); Isa 24:7 ("merry-hearted"). The NT equivalent is the one who "rejoices in the Lord" as a standing posture (Phili 4:4's commanded "rejoice always" produces a person-type: the one who habitually rejoices in the Lord).

**[CHAR-7]** S — No dedicated person-type term for the one who habitually possesses Suffering-Joy appears in this corpus. The "blessed are those who are persecuted" (Mat 5:10 — makarismos, adjacent to Mat 5:12) is the closest: the persecuted person who rejoices is implicitly typed as blessed. But no single-word person-type term is evidenced.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes: **tov** used substantivally to name the person — "a good man" (ish-tov / ha-tov: Pro 12:2; 13:22; 14:14; 14:19; 15:3). The person-type is the "good man" — one in whom the evaluative-gladness faculty correctly operates and who lives accordingly. This is the person-type most directly generated by Gladness's moral-evaluative face.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Partially: (1) **The man who greatly delights in God's commandments** — Psa 112:1 (cha.phets adj — "greatly delights in his commandments") — this is a person-type: the blessed man who greatly delights; (2) **The eunuchs who choose the things that please Me** — Isa 56:4 (cha.phets) — persons defined by their volitional Delight-orientation; (3) **Those who delight in my righteousness** — Psa 35:27 (cha.phets adj) — a person-type defined by what their Delight is directed toward. These are descriptive person-type references rather than a single dedicated person-type term, but they constitute a functional person-type vocabulary.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Partially: (1) **The man of tender/refined living** (a.nog adj, H6028) — Deu 28:54 ("the man who is the most tender and refined among you") — a person defined by their orientation toward pampered ease; (2) **The cheerful of heart** — Pro 15:15 ("the cheerful of heart has a continual feast") — a functional person-type term; (3) **The one who gazes upon God's beauty** — Psa 27:4 — a functional person-type (the seeker of divine beauty) rather than a dedicated vocabulary term.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Not a dedicated person-type term, but functional person-types: (1) **The one who considers/meditates on wondrous works** — Job 37:14; Psa 119:27; 145:5 — a functional person-type defined by their Wonder-contemplative practice; (2) **The one who proclaims wonders** — Psa 71:17 ("I still proclaim your wondrous deeds") — the lifelong wonder-proclaimer as a person-type; (3) **The humble person** — Psa 131:1 ("I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvellous for me") — a functional person-type defined by their epistemic humility toward Wonder.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Person-type terms are evidenced for five of the seven: Joy (sa.me.ach — the joyful person, 21 instances), Gladness (ish-tov — the good man, throughout Proverbs), Delight (cha.phets adj — the one who greatly delights), Pleasure (a.nog adj — the delicate/refined person), Wonder (functional person-types: the one who meditates on wonders, the humble person). Exultation (Char 1) and Suffering-Joy (Char 7) do not have dedicated person-type terms. The most established person-type: **the good man** (Gladness, Char 3) — the evaluative-gladness faculty at its fullest produces a characterised person recognisable throughout Proverbs and the Psalms as the "good man" (ish-tov). This confirms Gladness's distinctive cognitive-formative role: it is the characteristic most directly named by a person-type in the wisdom literature.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The CHAR-1 corpus does not include a specific person-type term naming "the one who characteristically experiences shame" in the way that "the humble" or "the proud" are person-type terms. The closest are descriptive: "a son who acts shamefully" (Pro 17:2), "the shameful" — but these name conduct rather than a person-type defined by shame as an inner characteristic. The evidence is silent on a person-type term for CHAR-1.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The evidence does not include a person-type term for the one who characteristically undergoes CHAR-2. The "proud" is the person-type who invites CHAR-2, not the person-type defined by it.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary terms: Atimazō (G0818): to dishonour, treat as without honour — active verb, the dishonoring act. Atimia (G0819): dishonour as a state — the condition of assigned or received diminished worth. Entrepō (G1788) in its absence register: the failure of the regard-faculty. Paradeigmatizō (G3856): to expose publicly, hold up to contempt. Roots: a-timē — without honour, without worth — the alpha-privative of honour. Structural opposite: timaō (to honour, to assign worth) and timē (honour as assigned worth-recognition). The evidence pairs these explicitly in Joh 8:49. The CHAR-3 corpus is entirely NT — the OT vocabulary for relational worth-denial (qa.lah, H7034; entrepō in its absence register) is thinner. The NT's christological context gives CHAR-3 its sharpest definition: dishonour as what is directed at Jesus personally and at God through human hypocrisy. Person-type: the "unjust judge" (Luk 18:2) is the closest person-type but is not a technical term. Supplication: the widow's persistent coming to the judge (Luk 18:3) is a supplication for the reversal of CHAR-3 — the only supplication-context in the corpus.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Person-type: "false teachers" (Tit 1:11) and "those who glory in their shame" (Phili 3:19) are the VCG-01 and VCG-03 person-types respectively — but these are descriptive rather than technical terms.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The CHAR-5 corpus does not include a specific person-type term for the one who characteristically receives contempt-produced shame. Bartimaeus functions as a narrative person-type (the despised beggar) but is not a technical term. Silent.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The 8-verse corpus does not include a specific person-type term for the one who characteristically possesses CHAR-6. The psalmist of Psa 26 functions as a narrative person-type (the innocent one who approaches God's altar) but is not a technical term. Silent.

**[CLUSTER]** S — The cluster does not produce consistent person-type terms across the six characteristics. Individual characteristics identify person-types (the unjust judge — Char 3; the self-righteous one — Char 5; the false teachers — Char 4) but no cluster-wide person-type vocabulary emerges. The absence of a general "shame-bearer" or "dishonoured-one" technical person-type term reflects that M07's characteristics describe situations and conditions rather than constitutive character types.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, explicitly. Ge.eh (H1343): the proud person as a type — Job 40:11 (vc=33949, M08-A4-VCG-02): "everyone who is proud [ge.eh]"; Job 40:12 (vc=33951): "look on everyone who is proud [ge.eh]"; Psa 94:2 (vc=33952, M08-A4-VCG-02): "repay to the proud [ge.eh] what they deserve"; Pro 15:25 (vc=33955, M08-A4-VCG-02): "the proud [ge.eh] person's house." **[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Chat.ta (H2400) is the person-type term — "sinner" — naming the one who habitually possesses or embodies the sinning characteristic. However, this term belongs primarily to CHAR-16 (Sinner as moral character) rather than to CHAR-1 directly. Within the CHAR-1 corpus, person-type language is present but secondary: "sinful nation" (Isa 1:4 — cha.ta.im, plural of chat.ta) names the people-type constituted by sinning. The person-type term confirms the connection between the act (CHAR-1) and the character (CHAR-16): repeated wilful sinning constitutes the sinner as a moral type.

**[CHAR-10]** S — The corpus contains no dedicated person-type terms for the habitual practitioner of these mechanisms. The enticers of 2Pe 2:14/18 are described adjectivally and verbally ("hearts trained in greed... they entice") rather than through a nominal person-type term. Apostasia (G0646) is a noun but names the condition/practice rather than the person-type.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Yes. *Hamartōlos* (G0268 — sinner) appears in the broader Gospel context (Luk 7:37/39 — the sinful woman; Luk 18:13 — "God, be merciful to me, a sinner" — outside the 112-verse corpus but structurally implied as the person-type named by the universal condition). Within the 112-verse corpus: Gal 2:17 — "found to be sinners" — the person-type of the sinner is invoked as the charge that might be brought. The sinner-person-type (CHAR-16) is the person-level expression of CHAR-11's universal condition.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Yes, implicitly. Joh 8:34 — "everyone who practices sin" (*pas ho poiōn tēn hamartian*) — the present-participle construction names a person-type: "the one who makes sin" (i.e. the habitual sinner). 1Jo 3:8 — "whoever makes a practice of sinning" (*ho poiōn tēn hamartian*) — the same construction names the person-type whose identity marker is the enslaving practice. These constructions function as person-type identifiers: the type is constituted by the ongoing practice.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Yes — through the bearer-of-sin language. Num 9:13 — "that man shall bear his sin" (*nāśāʾ ḥeṭʾô* — "shall carry his chet"); Deu 24:16 — "each one shall be put to death for his own sin" (*ḥeṭʾô*). These constructions identify the person-type as "the one who bears sin" — the individual moral subject who carries a personal record. Isa 53:12 — "he bore the sin of many" — the servant's person-type is the sin-bearer, creating a positive person-type in contrast to the negative.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Implicitly. Luk 7:47 — "he who is forgiven little" (*hō oligon aphietai*) and "she loved much" — the contrast names two person-types: the much-forgiven and the little-forgiven. These are person-types defined by the magnitude of their forgiveness-reception. The priest (Lev 10:17 — "given to you that you may bear the iniquity") is the person-type of the forgiveness-mediator — the one through whom others seek and receive.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes. Isa 65:20 — "the sinner (*hachôṭeʾ*) a hundred years old shall be accursed" — the participial form *hachôṭeʾ* (the sinning-one, the sinner) is the person-type term: it names the person whose characteristic is the ongoing sinning-pattern that results in curse. The participle form (present active — "the one who is sinning") names the person-type as constituted by ongoing sinning rather than a single act. Within the generational context, this sinner-person-type is the individual who perpetuates the inherited sinning-pattern to the end of their days.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Chat.ta (H2400) and hamartōlos (G0268) are themselves the person-type terms: they are agent-nouns naming the person whose character is constituted by sinning. The *qattāl* pattern of chat.ta is the Hebrew grammatical form specifically for intensive/habitual agents. 1Ti 1:15 — "of whom I am the foremost" (*prōtos* — first/foremost) names Paul as the paradigmatic worst-case person-type within the sinner category. Isa 65:20 — "the sinner (*hachôṭeʾ*) a hundred years old shall be accursed" — the participial form names the person-type by their ongoing sinning character.

**[CHAR-17]** E — A.shem (H0818) — Gen 42:21 — "we are guilty" — functions as the person-type description (though not a dedicated agent-noun like chat.ta). The participial form of a.sham used in Judg 21:22 (*ʾāšēm*) and Hab 1:11 (*ʾāšēm* — "guilty men") approaches a person-type term: it names the person constituted by the guilt-state. Amo 8:14 — "the Guilt of Samaria" (*ʾašmat Šōmĕrôn*) uses ash.mah as a personalised title for the idol — an ironic inversion where the guilt-condition name becomes an idol-name.

**[CHAR-18]** E — No dedicated person-type term within the a.von H5771G corpus; the characteristic is content-focused (the crime-reality) rather than person-type-focused (compare CHAR-16's chat.ta/hamartōlos agent-noun). The nearest person-type usage: Isa 1:4 — "a people laden with iniquity (*ʿăwōn*)" — describing the person/community by their iniquity-burden. The person-type dimension is expressed through the adjective or participial: Eze 33:8 — "you shall surely die" addressed to *rāšāʿ* (the wicked) who "shall die in his iniquity" — the wicked person is named separately from the iniquity they carry.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — multiple person-type terms. (1) *Pa.sha (H6586) as agent*: Isa 46:8 — "you transgressors" — direct person-type address; Isa 53:12 — "numbered with the transgressors"; (2) *Parabatēs (G3848)*: "transgressor" as agent-noun — Rom 2:25/27; Gal 2:18; Jam 2:9/11; (3) *Sa.rah (H5627)*: Deu 13:5 — "that prophet... taught rebellion" — the revolt-teacher as person-type; (4) *Psa 51:13* — "transgressors" as a class the forgiven person will teach — the person-type as a reachable group. CHAR-19 is the richest person-type vocabulary in M10.

**[CHAR-2]** S — No person-type term appears in the 18-verse corpus for the characteristic of unintentional sinning. There is no Hebrew or Greek term for "the unintentional sinner" as a constituted moral type — because unintentional sinning does not constitute a person's moral character in the way that CHAR-16 (sinner as moral character) does. The inadvertent sinner is a normal person who sinned without knowing; they are not a constituted type. The absence of a person-type term for CHAR-2 is analytically significant: the characteristic does not generate a moral identity but describes a moral episode.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — ba.gad generates the person-type. Isa 24:16 — "the traitors (*bōgĕdîm*) have betrayed" — the plural agent-noun names the person-class of traitors; Psa 119:158 — "I look at the faithless (*bōgĕdîm*) with disgust" — the faithless as a recognisable class; Pro 2:22 — "the treacherous (*bōgĕdîm*) will be rooted out of it." The *bōgĕd* (participle/agent-noun form of ba.gad) is CHAR-20's person-type term — the one whose inner character is constituted by treachery.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — multiple person-type terms. Tah.pu.khah produces the person-type "the man of perverted speech" (Pro 2:12 — *ʾîš tahpukôt*); "the perverse tongue" (Pro 10:31/32) names the person-type by their organ; 1Ti 6:5 — "people who are depraved in mind" names the person-type by their faculty; 2Pe 2:12 — "like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed" — the ultimate perverted person-type named as the animal-instinctual creature.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — two distinct person-type terms. (1) *Av.val (H5767)*: OT agent-noun — "the unrighteous one" (Job 27:7; 29:17; 31:3; Zep 3:5) — the OT person-type characterised by injustice as a defining moral identity; (2) *Adikos (G0094)*: NT adjective-as-noun — "the unjust" (Mat 5:45; Luk 18:11; Act 24:15; Rom 3:5; 1Cor 6:1/9; Heb 6:10; 1Pe 3:18; 2Pe 2:9) — the NT person-type; used in eight NT verses, making it the most frequently deployed person-type term across the Phase 9 characteristics.

**[CHAR-3]** S — No person-type term for "the habitual confessor" appears in the 34-verse corpus. Confession is presented as an episodic moral event rather than as a constituted character-type. The absence is consistent with confession's responsive nature: it is what the person does in response to sin, not what they are.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — more prominently than in any other characteristic in the corpus so far. Ecc 2:26 — *lechotet* ("to the sinner"); Ecc 8:12 — *hachotet* ("the sinner") — the person-type term for the one who exists in the conscience-suppressed orientation is the *sinner* (chat.ta / hachotet). This is the same root as CHAR-16 (Sinner as moral character): the sinner-type term in Ecclesiastes defines a person by their fundamental orientation (not-God-pleasing, not-fear-of-God) rather than by a specific act. The person-type is the constituted character of the conscience-absent person.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Limited person-type evidence. 1Ti 5:20 — "those who persist in sin" (*hamartanontōn* — present participle used substantively) names the person-type as "the ones sinning [continuously]." This is not a dedicated person-type term but the participial construction used to name the type. The Kings corpus does not produce a dedicated person-type term for "the one who refuses to repent" — the characteristic is always expressed through the predicate (did not depart from) rather than as a substantive type-name.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes — more prominently than in any other characteristic in the M10 corpus. The participial *hachotet* ("the sinner" — Ecc 7:26; 9:2/18; Pro 11:31/13:22) appears across 5 verses, making CHAR-6 the characteristic most thoroughly expressed through person-type vocabulary. This reflects the definition's emphasis: habitual defection is the will's *settled direction* — a formed character, a constituted type — rather than an episodic act. The person-type vocabulary is the natural form for this because the characteristic is constitutively about what the person *is* rather than what they *do* at a given moment.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The primary person-type is named by the role rather than a dedicated moral-type term: the *leader who made Israel to sin* — the Jeroboam-pattern leader — is the person-type of CHAR-7. Jeroboam's name itself functions as the person-type within the Kings corpus: "the sins of Jeroboam... who made Israel to sin" — Jeroboam is the eponymous contagious-sin leader, the canonical instance of the type. No dedicated Hebrew term equivalent to *hachotet* (the sinner — CHAR-6/16) exists for the contagious-sin leader.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The corpus contains no dedicated person-type term for the habitual practitioner of political revolt. The revolting parties are named by their political-ethnic identity (Moab, Edom, Libnah, Israel) rather than by a moral-type term. The characteristic does not produce a person-type vocabulary in this corpus.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes. 1Ti 1:13 — "I was a *blasphemer*" (blasfēmos used as a substantive person-type noun) — the adjective functioning as a person-type term naming the one whose character is defined by sinful speech. 2Ti 3:2 — "abusive" (blasfēmos) — the adjective as a person-type marker in the end-times character list. Both instances use blasfēmos to name the constituted person-type, confirming that sinful speech can form a settled character identity.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes — this is the definitional feature of ra.sha (H7563). Ra.sha is itself the person-type term: "the wicked [person]" as a recognized moral-anthropological category. The person-type vocabulary is unusually rich in this characteristic: ra.sha (the wicked individual), the plural resh'im (the wicked as a class — present throughout Psalms and Proverbs), re.sha (the abstract condition naming the class), and mir.sha.at (H4849 — the wicked woman collective). The person-type vocabulary is the dominant form of the characteristic's lexical expression — it is first and foremost a person-type vocabulary, which is the primary evidence that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity is the correct analytical category for this characteristic.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. ponēros functions as a person-type term across multiple contexts: "evil persons" (Mat 5:45 — VCG-04), "evil people" (2Ti 3:13 — VCG-06), "the evil one" as a cosmic person-type (Mat 6:13 — VCG-01), "wicked and evil men" (2Th 3:2 — VCG-06), "wicked servant" (Mat 18:32 — VCG-06; Mat 25:26 — VCG-06). 1Cor 5:13 (vc=14465 — VCG-04): "purge the evil person from among you" — person-type term used for community action. The person-type function of ponēros confirms that the characteristic, like CHAR-1, has a person-identity dimension — the evil person is a recognisable type. The distinction from CHAR-1: ponēros person-type is primarily NT and constitutional; ra.sha person-type is primarily OT and volitional-directional.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. bdeluktos (G0947, Tit 1:16) is specifically the person-type term: "they are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work" — the term designates the abominable person as a type. In the Hebrew corpus, the person-type is constructed through the predicate structure rather than a dedicated term: "the devious person is an abomination" (Pro 3:32 — VCG-02), "the scoffer is an abomination" (Pro 24:9 — VCG-01). The equivalent of a person-type term is embedded in the abomination statement itself. Rev 17:5 (vc=65878 — VCG-05) creates the person-type at cosmic scale: "the mother of prostitutes and of earth's abominations" — the identity constituted entirely by generating abomination.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The shiq.quts vocabulary partially generates a person-type: Deu 18:12 (vc=1685 — VCG-02): "whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord" — the person who practises divination and occult arts becomes personally abominable, not merely the practice. The to.e.vah predicate structure names the person-type through the "is an abomination to the Lord" construction. No dedicated person-type noun is coined for the habitual idolater within this corpus — the person-type is constructed through the predicate abomination-verdict applied to the person. The closest person-type evidence is Hos 9:10 (vc=1632 — VCG-04): "they became detestable like the thing they loved" — the community collectively becomes the person-type of the abominable through sustained idolatrous devotion.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The evildoer vocabulary is one of the richest person-type terminations in the programme. po.al a.ven (H6466 + H0205G — "workers/doers of iniquity") is a person-type construction appearing throughout VCG-03: Psa 6:8 (vc=38243 — VCG-03): "workers of evil"; Psa 59:2 (vc=38241 — VCG-03): "those who work evil." Pro 6:12 (vc=38223 — VCG-03): "a worthless person, a wicked man" — ish beliyya.al + ish a.ven as person-type designation. Isa 31:2 (vc=38199 — VCG-03): "evildoers" and "workers of iniquity" as named classes. The person-type vocabulary is unusually developed in this characteristic, comprising VCG-03's full 24-verse corpus — the evildoer-as-person-type is constitutive of the characteristic's presentation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. kakopoios (G2555, 5V — VCG-03) is the person-type term: "evil-doer" or "one who does evil" — the person defined by the moral quality of their acts. In VCG-03, kakopoios functions as the identity attributed through hostile accusation: 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): "when they speak against you as evildoers (kakopoious)" — the kakopoios is the specific person-type identity that the accusing speech imposes on the falsely accused. The person-type term reveals the social-identity dimension of CHAR-6: evil expressed through speech can attribute a person-type identity to the innocent, making the false accusation an identity-creating speech act with serious social consequences.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics include person-type vocabulary, with Chars 1 and 5 having the most developed person-type suites. Char 1: ra.sha (H7563) as the primary OT wicked-person term — the dominant person-type in the cluster. Char 2: ponēros used substantively ("the evil one / evil person" — Mat 12:35; 1Jo 2:13); the evil-hearted person of Heb 3:12. Char 5: po.al a.ven (the worker/doer of iniquity — VCG-03 24V) as the evildoer person-type. Char 6: kakopoios (G2555 — the evil-doer as charged identity — VCG-03 5V). Chars 3 and 4 address person-types through their person-level VCGs (the devious person, the arrogant person — Chars 3; those whose heart goes after idols — Char 4) without distinct person-type terms. The cluster's richest person-type vocabulary is in Chars 1 and 5 — both of which have extensive evildoer/wicked-person vocabulary suites encompassing multiple Hebrew constructions (ra.sha, re.sha, mir.sha.at, po.al a.ven).

**[CHAR-1]** S — The 133-verse corpus does not include a distinct person-type term for the habitual bearer of the ritual defilement-state. The vocabulary uses the condition-descriptors ("the one who is unclean," "the one with the discharge," "the leprous person") but not a fixed noun naming a type of person defined by the characteristic. The disease registers come closest: "the leprous man" (Lev 13:44-45, M10c-B-VCG-02/03) is a quasi-person-type, but it is a contextual description, not a vocabulary term.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, partially. Eph 5:5 (VCG-04): "everyone who is... impure" (akathartos) — this is a person-type designation: the impure person defined by their identity in the characteristic. 2Pe 2:10 (VCG-03): those who "indulge in the lust of defiling passion" — a person-type characterised by their pattern of practice. Mat 23:27 (VCG-04): "scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites" — a named person-type whose defining inner character is moral-inner defilement masked by outward purity. The vocabulary includes contextual person-type designations without a fixed noun-term for the habitually morally impure person.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Partially. Lam 4:15 (VCG-05) — "Unclean! Away!" — names the exiles as a collective person-type: those publicly declared unclean and expelled. The ta.me adjective functions as a quasi-person-type descriptor: "everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead" (Num 5:2, Characteristic 1 register, but analogous in form to the characteristic's corporate designation). Within the 83-verse corpus, the nearest person-type is the corporate Israel as "the house of Israel" in a state of defilement (Eze 14:11: "the house of Israel may no more go astray from me, nor defile themselves"). No fixed noun-term for the habitually corporately defiling community exists in the corpus.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Partially. Act 5:16 (VCG-02): "those afflicted with unclean spirits" (ochleoumenoi — present participle of ochleō — to be troubled/afflicted) — names a class of persons defined by their affliction. Luk 6:18 (VCG-02): "those troubled with unclean spirits" (same verb in participial form) — a person-type of the afflicted. These participial forms are the closest the vocabulary comes to person-type terms. There is no fixed noun-term for the habitually possessed person in the 21-verse corpus.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's person-type vocabulary is partial across all four characteristics — no characteristic has a fixed noun-term for the habitually defiled person. The closest approximations: Characteristic 1 — "the leprous man" (ha-metsora — the one with the disease, Lev 13:44-45) as a contextual quasi-person-type for the disease register; Characteristic 2 — Eph 5:5 ("everyone who is... impure" — akathartos as a predicate designation) and Mat 23:27 ("scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites" — a named person-type defined by concealed moral-inner defilement); Characteristic 3 — Lam 4:15's "Unclean!" as a collective person-type designation for the exilic community; Characteristic 4 — Act 5:16's "those afflicted with unclean spirits" (ochleoumenoi — present participle as a person-type). The cluster's uniform partial person-type evidence reveals that the M10c domain is primarily a condition domain (what the person is in) rather than an identity domain (what type of person they are). findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the intercessory vocabulary (group 5379-002) functions as the supplication register. Dan 9:19 — "O Lord, forgive" — uses the imperative of H5545 (sa.lach) as a direct supplication: the human person commanding/appealing to God to perform the divine act of forgiving. The imperative of the divine-exclusive verb functions as the supplication term — the human uses the vocabulary of divine action in the mode of urgent appeal.

Additionally, the prayer context of Mar 11:25 — "whenever you stand praying, forgive" — embeds the forgiveness act within the supplication posture, suggesting the intercessory and the horizontal-giving acts are structurally linked in prayer.

**What the supplication term reveals:** Using the imperative of the divine-exclusive verb (sa.lach) as a supplication term is theologically and linguistically remarkable. The human person calls on God to perform the act that only God can perform — the supplication term acknowledges the divine exclusivity while urgently invoking it. The inner posture encoded: radical dependence on divine action, not a claim of human agency.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the supplication vocabulary is a substantive and structurally significant XREF set in the data:

**H8467 techinah** (XREF, 24 occurrences): "supplication/plea for favour" — the earnest appeal for divine compassion and grace. Derived from the CHANAN root.

**H8469 tahanun** (XREF, 18 occurrences): "entreaty/supplication" — closely related; names the act of earnest pleading for divine mercy.

**H2603A chanan** (XREF, 72 occurrences): "be gracious" — the verbal form often rendered "have mercy" in contexts of prayer. The imperative form (chonneni — "be gracious to me") is the prayer-appeal for divine compassion.

**H5165 nech.amah / H5164 no.cham** (XREF, 2/1 occurrences): seeking comfort/compassion from God in the context of grief.

The supplication vocabulary establishes that compassion has a well-developed seeking-language — the human person's acts of appeal to God for compassion are named and differentiated in the vocabulary. This is not merely incidental: the existence of a supplication sub-vocabulary confirms that compassion is understood as something that can be sought, approached, and appealed for — it is not merely received passively but actively sought in earnest petition.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-007: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: …
findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-027: T5's finding that suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion is grounded in T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was …
findings.finding_value: T5's finding that suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion is grounded in T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient for the depth of compassion at the point of maximum permitted suffering) is the lexical expression of T5's most profound formation claim: suffering in the context of compassion-formation produces a depth of compassion that transcends ordinary vocabulary. T7's framework divergence at purposive suffering (Jas 5:11 — teleological frame required) is the analytical expression of T5.4's finding that suffering in the biblical frame produces compassion (as a formative outcome) rather than merely accompanying it. The dual primary anchor (Hos 11:8 and Luke 10:33) maps onto T5's dual-role finding: Hos 11:8 evidences compassion as the character being formed in God (which the human images); Luke 10:33 evidences compassion as the formed character in the human person (the moral norm).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-028: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural f…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is confirmed and extended by T7's vocabulary analysis: the CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the root itself (T7.1 P5), not as an external antonym. This means the cluster-crossing T6 identifies is not an external structural anomaly but an internal semantic feature: the compassion vocabulary contains its own opposite at the root level. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (T6.6 — 6 registries) is also T7's most evidentially rich single text — the verse that carries the most structural connections is the same verse that is most analytically central to the vocabulary analysis. The love co-occurrence dominance (T6.1 — 196/351 verses) is confirmed by T7's vocabulary arc: the vocabulary's fullest range (womb to almsgiving) overlaps extensively with the love vocabulary's range, which is why they co-occur across more than half of all active verses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-025: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-le…
findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. This is unique in the programme's vocabulary data: no other characteristic has the giving-side and receiving-side vocabulary built from the same root. T4's relational architecture and T7's lexical analysis are the relational and lexical descriptions of the same structural reality — that grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit whose two sides are inseparable at the root level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.
