findings.finding_value: M01-A does not include a dedicated seeking term for reverential fear of God. The seeking pattern is indirect: Psa 34:11 (the psalmist offering to teach fear — the implied seeking is through receptive formation); Pro 2:5 (fear as the fruit of earnest seeking after wisdom — the seeking is of wisdom, the fruit of which is fear). No direct petitionary vocabulary for seeking the characteristic from God or another person is identified.

The M01 vocabulary does not include a dedicated supplication or seeking term. The characteristic is formed through encounter, formation, and divine implantation rather than through explicit seeking-petition directed at the characteristic itself.

The vocabulary does not include a dedicated supplication-for-anger term (anger is not typically sought by the person experiencing it, unlike characteristics such as mercy or peace). However, petitions for God's anger are evidenced: Psa 79:6 (M02-B-VCG-06) — "pour your wrath on nations" — is a petition invoking God's anger against enemies. Jer 10:25 (M02-B-VCG-06) — petitioning God to pour wrath as a weapon of justice. The petition-form for anger is a request for its enactment against enemies, not for its personal reception.

Not as a dedicated seeking term, but the vocabulary's distress-drives-prayer pattern (M03-D-VCG-01) effectively encodes supplication within the grief register. The act of crying out in distress (tsa.rah producing prayer — Psa 18:6; Psa 50:15) is the grief vocabulary's built-in supplication movement. The penitential weeping vocabulary (ba.khah toward God — 1Sa 1:10 M03-A-VCG-02; Joe 2:12 M03-A-VCG-02) encodes seeking as weeping before God. The characteristic itself functions as a supplication mode rather than having a separate seeking term.

Not as a dedicated seeking term, but the vocabulary's distress-drives-prayer pattern (M03-D-VCG-01) effectively encodes supplication within the grief register. The act of crying out in distress (tsa.rah producing prayer — Psa 18:6; Psa 50:15) is the grief vocabulary's built-in supplication movement. The penitential weeping vocabulary (ba.khah toward God — 1Sa 1:10 M03-A-VCG-02; Joe 2:12 M03-A-VCG-02) encodes seeking as weeping before God. The characteristic itself functions as a supplication mode rather than having a separate seeking term.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Psa 51:8 ("let the bones that you have broken rejoice") is the closest to a seeking or supplicatory form — the psalmist asks that his broken exultation-capacity be restored. Psa 9:14 ("that I may rejoice in your salvation") frames future rejoicing as the hoped-for outcome of divine rescue. These are supplicatory uses of the exultation vocabulary — seeking the characteristic from God as gift.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes: Psa 51:12 ("restore to me the joy of your salvation") — the petitionary use of sim.chah (requesting the restoration of lost Joy); Psa 86:4 ("gladden the soul of your servant") — a direct petition for God to produce Joy; Psa 90:14–15 ("that we may rejoice and be glad all our days… make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us") — intercession for Joy. These confirm Joy is something that can be sought from God as a gift.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, in M04-F: Job 10:20 ("leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer") — a plea for the condition of ba.lag-cheerfulness; Psa 39:13 ("look away from me, that I may smile again") — the psalmist's petition for a brief brightening before death. These are seeking/supplication forms of ba.lag — seeking the comfort/cheer from God as a temporary respite.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Partially. Psa 86:5 ("for you, O Lord, are good and forgiving… abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you") — "all who call upon you" frames seeking as the means of access to divine goodness. Lam 3:25 ("the Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him") names seeking as the required orientation. These are not a dedicated seeking-term but the functional seeking-orientation that enables reception of Gladness.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Partially. The M04-H-VCG-03 "if it pleases the king" / "if it seems good to you" formulas function as seeking-Delight language: they are the verbal acts of seeking the other person's inner pleasure as the condition for a request. Psa 37:4's "delight yourself in the Lord" functions as an implicit seeking command — orient yourself toward him as your object. Job 9:3 ("if one wished to contend with him") and Job 13:3 ("I desire to argue my case with God") express the desire to seek an encounter with God. These are functional seeking-expressions rather than a single dedicated seeking term.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes: (1) **Psa 27:4** ("one thing have I asked of the Lord… that I may gaze upon the beauty of the Lord") — seeking divine Pleasure explicitly through petition; (2) **Psa 90:17** ("let the favor/pleasantness of the Lord our God be upon us") — communal supplication for divine no.am to rest on them; (3) **The cultic instruction** — Num 28:2 ("be careful to offer to me at its appointed time") — the Levitical instruction as the form of seeking to produce the pleasing-aroma relationship.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes: (1) **Psa 119:18** ("open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law") — the explicit petition for God to enable Wonder-perception; (2) **Jer 21:2** ("perhaps the Lord will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw") — the petition invoking God's wonder-works as the basis of request; (3) **Jeremiah's prayer** (Jer 32:17 — "nothing is too hard for you") — the confession-as-petition establishing the basis for God's wonder-acts.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Supplication forms are evidenced for most characteristics: Joy (Psa 51:12 — "restore to me the joy of your salvation"), Pleasure (Psa 27:4 — seeking to gaze on God's beauty; Psa 90:17 — "let your pleasantness be upon us"), Wonder (Psa 119:18 — "open my eyes"), Suffering-Joy (Job 10:20; Psa 39:13 — seeking ba.lag before death). The most distinctive supplication: **Wonder's petitionary seeking** (Psa 119:18 — "open my eyes that I may behold wondrous things out of your law") is the only instance in the cluster where the perceptive capacity itself is sought from God as a gift — the ability to perceive wonders must be divinely opened. This uniquely confirms Wonder as the characteristic most dependent on divine enabling of the perceptive faculty itself.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, indirectly. The repeated Psalm petitions "let me not be put to shame" (Psa 25:2; 31:1; 71:1; 119:31) constitute a supplication pattern — the person seeking from God the protection from shame. The supplication is the negative request: "shield me from shame." This is not a specific lexical term but a grammatical-formulaic pattern within the bosh corpus that constitutes a distinctive mode of seeking.
**[CHAR-2]** S — Not evidenced. CHAR-2 is not typically the object of supplication in the corpus.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary terms: Atimazō (G0818): to dishonour, treat as without honour — active verb, the dishonoring act. Atimia (G0819): dishonour as a state — the condition of assigned or received diminished worth. Entrepō (G1788) in its absence register: the failure of the regard-faculty. Paradeigmatizō (G3856): to expose publicly, hold up to contempt. Roots: a-timē — without honour, without worth — the alpha-privative of honour. Structural opposite: timaō (to honour, to assign worth) and timē (honour as assigned worth-recognition). The evidence pairs these explicitly in Joh 8:49. The CHAR-3 corpus is entirely NT — the OT vocabulary for relational worth-denial (qa.lah, H7034; entrepō in its absence register) is thinner. The NT's christological context gives CHAR-3 its sharpest definition: dishonour as what is directed at Jesus personally and at God through human hypocrisy. Person-type: the "unjust judge" (Luk 18:2) is the closest person-type but is not a technical term. Supplication: the widow's persistent coming to the judge (Luk 18:3) is a supplication for the reversal of CHAR-3 — the only supplication-context in the corpus.

---
**[CHAR-4]** S — Supplication is not evidenced — CHAR-4 is not the object of supplication. Silent.
**[CHAR-5]** S — Not evidenced in a formal sense. Psa 14:6's "shame the plans of the poor" implies a supplication context but does not constitute a formal supplication term. Silent.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Psa 26:6's "I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar" constitutes a seeking term in the cultic sense: the hand-washing is the preparatory act for seeking access to God's presence at the altar. The seeking is not a verbal supplication but a ritual act of approach — and CHAR-6 is the inner condition that this approach-act requires and declares.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The supplication register is concentrated in Char 1's M07-C VCG-02: the repeated Psalm formula "let me not be put to shame" (Psa 25:2; 31:1; 71:1; 119:31) is the cluster's distinctive supplication pattern. This negative request — protecting the person from shame's inner collapse — is the primary supplication form across the entire cluster. No other characteristic produces an equivalent supplication vocabulary. This concentration in Char 1 confirms that the felt experience of shame is the M07 characteristic whose resolution is primarily sought through direct supplication to God.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The verse evidence is silent on a supplication or seeking term within CHAR-1's vocabulary. CHAR-1 is characterised by its refusal to seek — Psa 10:4 (vc=34074, M08-A2-VCG-02): "does not seek him" — rather than by any term for seeking CHAR-1 from another. CHAR-1 generates itself internally (Mar 7:22, vc=33928: "flows out of a person") rather than being received through seeking from an external source. No seeking/supplication term for CHAR-1 is evidenced in §3.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes — uniquely within M08. Psa 19:13 (vc=34095, M08-B-VCG-02): "keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me" — the psalmist's prayer against CHAR-2 is a seeking/supplication term of resistance. This is not a term for seeking CHAR-2 from another but for seeking deliverance from CHAR-2's internal dominion-seeking impulses. The prayer against CHAR-2 is itself a finding: it confirms that CHAR-2 is understood as an internal impulse that requires divine restraint, not merely an external behaviour to be regulated.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The verse evidence in §3.B does not include a supplication or seeking term directed toward CHAR-3. Unlike CHAR-2 (which has Psa 19:13's prayer against presumptuous sins), CHAR-3 lacks a direct prayer-against formulation in its 70-verse corpus. The closest is 1Cor 1:29 (vc=33877): God's elective design is described as specifically aimed at eliminating human boasting — but this is descriptive of God's purpose, not a human supplication against CHAR-3.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The verse evidence is silent on a supplication or seeking term for CHAR-4 in §3.C. No prayer-against-CHAR-4 formulation appears in the corpus, unlike CHAR-2's Psa 19:13 prayer against presumptuous sins.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The verse evidence is silent on a supplication or seeking term directed against CHAR-5 in §3.D. No prayer-against formulation appears, unlike CHAR-2's Psa 19:13 ("keep back your servant from presumptuous sins"). The evidence for resistance to CHAR-5 is instructional (1Ti 6:17 — "charge them not to be haughty") rather than supplicatory.

**[CLUSTER]** E — CHAR-2 alone has a direct supplication term against the characteristic: Psa 19:13 (M08-B-VCG-02) — "keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me." This is the only prayer-against formulation in M08's entire vocabulary. CHAR-1, CHAR-3, CHAR-4, and CHAR-5 are all silent on supplication terms. The cluster-synthesis: the rarity of supplication vocabulary within M08 is analytically significant — the cluster is more extensively addressed through prohibition (do not boast; do not think of yourself more highly) and warning (pride goes before destruction) than through prayer-against forms. CHAR-2's Psa 19:13 is unique in naming the characteristic as something one prays against, recognising it as an inner force requiring divine restraint rather than merely human resolve.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The corpus does not directly evidence a specific vocabulary term for seeking submission from another. The authority-relationship is constituted by the command-and-response structure (the authority commands; the person submits) rather than by a supplication register. This absence is analytically significant: submission is evoked by command rather than sought through supplication.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The two-verse corpus does not include a specific vocabulary term for seeking contrition from another. The characteristic is described as a state the person is in rather than something sought or asked for. Broader canonical awareness (e.g., Psa51:17 — "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" — a nearby but outside-corpus verse) would add the seeking-of-acceptance dimension, but this is outside §3.B.
**[CHAR-4]** S — The corpus does not include a vocabulary term for seeking meekness or gentleness from another.
**[CHAR-5]** S — The corpus does not include vocabulary for seeking semnotēs from another.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes — Psa51:12 — "uphold me with a willing spirit" — is a supplication for the characteristic: the psalmist seeks and asks for the willing spirit from God. The supplication vocabulary is present within the term's usage — one of the five verses is precisely the act of seeking the characteristic from God. This is distinctive: CHAR-6 is the only M09 characteristic in this bundle for which the corpus includes a direct supplication for the characteristic itself.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The corpus does not directly evidence a distinct vocabulary term for seeking humility from another. The closest is the Phili4:12 "I have learned" (emathon — aorist of manthanō), suggesting the characteristic can be sought through learning and practice, but no specific supplication vocabulary targets humility as something sought from God or another person. This is a minor evidence gap — the characteristic is commanded and cultivated but seeking-vocabulary is not part of the attested terms.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Only Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6) includes explicit supplication vocabulary for the characteristic itself: Psa51:12 — "uphold me with a willing spirit" — the psalmist actively seeks and asks for the characteristic from God. This is the sole verse in the entire M09 corpus where any characteristic is the direct object of a supplication. The other five characteristics are addressed in imperative (commanded) or descriptive (stated as present states or person-types) forms — none are sought through supplication in their corpora. Cluster-level: the uniqueness of CHAR-6's supplication-vocabulary is analytically significant — it is the cluster's most explicitly divinely-dependent characteristic, the one that cannot be generated through willpower alone and must be sought from God, making it M09's most prayer-directed characteristic.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The corpus does not contain a dedicated seeking-term for wilful sinning itself (sinning is committed, not sought). However, the corpus evidences the seeking of the *remedy* for sinning through supplication: 1Ki 8:33/35/50 (Solomon's prayer as the seeking of forgiveness for sinning — the prayer is the supplication term for the forgiven state). Psa 41:4 ("O Lord, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you") uses the supplication form (chen + raph.ah) in the aftermath of sinning. The supplication operates at the post-sinning stage, not the sinning stage itself.

**[CHAR-10]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with any of the three mechanisms. The characteristic names sinful pathways; no seeking-of-these-mechanisms vocabulary appears.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Yes — the VCG-02 redemption register contains extensive supplication and seeking vocabulary associated with addressing the condition. Act 3:19 — "repent... and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out" — repentance is the seeking-response; Luk 11:4 — "forgive us our sins" — the prayer-petition for forgiveness names the supplication vocabulary; Act 22:16 — "calling on his name" — the calling-on is the seeking act that accompanies the washing of sins.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Yes — in the intercessory context. 1Jo 5:16 — "he shall ask, and God will give him life" (*erōtēsei, kai dōsei autō zōēn*) — the asking (*erōtēsei*) is an intercessory petition directed toward God for the sinning brother; the prayer is the seeking act that addresses the enslaving power's hold on the brother. This is the only explicit supplication vocabulary in the 9-verse corpus.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Yes — the forgiveness-petition vocabulary. Exo 10:17 — "forgive my sin, please" (*sĕʾ-nāʾ ḥaṭṭāṯî*); Exo 34:9 — "pardon our iniquity and our sin" (*wĕsālaḥtā laʿāwōnênû ûlĕḥaṭṭāʾṯênû*); Psa 25:7 — "remember not the sins of my youth" — the petitionary vocabulary of seeking record-erasure from God is extensive throughout the corpus. The supplication-seeking is directed toward the removal of the record rather than toward receiving a quality.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — Exo 32:30 — "perhaps I can make atonement for your sin" (*ûlây ăkappərâ bəʿad ḥaṭṭaṯkem*) — the "perhaps" (*ûlây*) is the seeking-term of uncertainty; Moses's going up to the Lord is the seeking-act itself. Act 2:38 — "repent" (*metanoeō*) — the NT seeking-term; Act 10:43 — "everyone who believes in him" (*pas ho pisteuōn eis auton*) — the believing is the faith-seeking act. The supplication vocabulary is embedded in the seeking-actions rather than in dedicated petition-terms.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — within the corporate confession context. 1Ki 8:47 — "repent (*nichāmû*) and plead (*hitchannĕnû*) with you" — the pleading (*hithchannēn* — to seek grace, to implore favour) is the supplication-term embedded in the seeking-movement toward God. The corporate pleading is the characteristic's seeking-posture: the community under the generational condition implores divine favour for the relief of the accumulated burden.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Yes — within the self-recognition texts. Luk 18:13 — "God, be merciful to me, a sinner" (*hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō*) — *hilasthēti* (be propitious/merciful) is the supplication-term; the sinner-identity is the explicit basis of the plea. The supplication is enabled by the self-recognition of the sinner-identity: "to me, the sinner" frames the identity as the ground of the appeal. Psa 25:8 — "he instructs sinners (*chat.ta.im*) in the way" — while not a supplication itself, implies that sinners are receptive to divine instruction when they accept the identity.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Yes — within the guilt-acknowledgment-seeking complex. Hos 5:15 — "until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me" — *bāqaš* (to seek) paired with *ḥālāh* (to earnestly seek/implore) are the supplication-seeking terms following guilt-acknowledgment. Ezr 9:6's prayer posture — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God" — is itself a supplication-posture though not using a specific supplication-term. The seeking that follows guilt-acknowledgment is the characteristic's embedded supplication-direction.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — within the iniquity-removal plea complex. Hos 14:2 — "take away all iniquity" (*śāʾ kol-ʿāwōn*) — the specific plea for iniquity-removal uses *śāʾ* (to lift, to take away); Psa 25:11 — "pardon my guilt" (*sālaḥtā laʿăwōnî* — "forgive my iniquity"); Exo 34:9 — "pardon our iniquity" — the supplication vocabulary for iniquity-removal consistently uses lifting/forgiving terms applied directly to a.von. The supplication is for removal of what CHAR-18 names.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes. Psa 51:1 — "blot out my transgressions" — the specific plea using *māḥāh* (to blot out, erase); Isa 43:25 — God's own use of the same term — "I blot out your transgressions for my own sake"; Psa 103:12 — "so far does he remove our transgressions from us" — *rāḥaq* (to remove far off) as the metaphor of spatial-relational distance. The supplication vocabulary for transgression-resolution is specifically erasure/blotting-out and removal — stronger than mere covering.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The offering-and-atonement language functions as the supplication register in CHAR-2. Num 15:27 ("he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering") — the bringing of the offering is the formal act of seeking atonement. Num 15:28 ("the priest shall make atonement before the Lord for the person who makes a mistake") — the priestly atonement is the intercession made before God. The seeking operates through institutional means (prescribed offering) rather than through verbal petition, though Lev 5:5's confession ("confesses the sin he has committed") carries a supplication dimension — the verbal acknowledgment before God as part of the seeking process.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — within the confession complex. Lev 26:40 — "if they confess (*hithwaddû*) their iniquity and... their treachery" — the Hithpael of *yadah* (to confess, to acknowledge) is the supplication-verb preceding the covenant-remembering; Ezr 10:2 — "we have broken faith with our God" — the verbal acknowledgment is the seeking-term. The seeking is not of abstract forgiveness but specifically of covenant-remembering: Lev 26:42 — "I will remember my covenant" — the confession of treachery seeks the reactivation of the divine covenant-memory.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — within the confession-prayer register. 1Ki 8:47 — "acting perversely... we have sinned" — the full confession-prayer including perversity-acknowledgment; Dan 9:5 — "we have sinned and done wrong" — Daniel's seeking-prayer names the perversity. The supplication is the naming of the perversity within prayer as the honest foundation of the God-turning. Psa 38:6's "bowed down and prostrate" is the bodily supplication-posture under the weight of perversion's consequences.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — within the victim's plea register. Job 6:29 — "please turn; let no injustice be done" — the direct plea that no injustice be enacted; Psa 43:1 — "vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me" — the plea for deliverance from the unjust as a seeking-term; Job 22:23 — "if you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents" — Eliphaz's condition framing removal of injustice as the human seeking-act.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The supplication dimension is evidenced in the post-confession plea. 2Sa 24:10 — "please take away (*na*) the iniquity of your servant" — *na* (please, I pray) is the supplication particle attached to the plea that follows confession. Num 21:7 — "pray (*hitpallel*) to the Lord that he take away the serpents" — the confession generates a petition for intercession. Dan 9:17–19 — extended supplication following confession: "O Lord, hear (*shema*); O Lord, forgive (*selach*); O Lord, pay attention and act." The supplication vocabulary (na, hitpallel, shema, selach) appears consistently after confession, confirming that confession's natural completion is petition — the confession opens the space for plea.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with conscience suppression. The conscience-suppressed person does not seek God through the suppression; the suppression is precisely the condition of not seeking. The absence of seeking-vocabulary is consistent with the characteristic's nature: the person who suppresses conscience does not know they need to seek anything — they believe all is well.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with refusal to repent. The characteristic is the condition of one who is not seeking God; the seeking-vocabulary belongs to its opposite (shuv — returning to God). The absence of seeking-vocabulary is consistent with the characteristic's nature: the person who refuses to repent is precisely the person who is not seeking the relational restoration that repentance would initiate.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Limited evidence. 1Ki 8:46's prayer context — "if they sin against you... and you give them to an enemy... if they repent... and pray to you in the land of their captivity" — contains the prayer-seeking vocabulary (*hitpallel* — to pray/intercede) as part of the restoration path Solomon envisions. The seeking term belongs to the restoration sequence that follows the recognition of habitual sinning, not to the habitual sinning itself. The sinner-type vocabulary (hachotet) contains no seeking dimension; seeking belongs to the exit from the habitual pattern.

**[CHAR-7]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with contagious sin. The characteristic is a leader's causing action; the seeking-vocabulary belongs to the restoration movement that counters contagious sin (1Ki 8:46's prayer context presupposes contagious sin's consequences but belongs to the broader restoration framework). No seeking-vocabulary appears in the 19-verse corpus itself.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with political revolt. Political revolt is a power-assertion act, not a seeking act. The characteristic has no seeking dimension within the corpus.
**[CHAR-9]** S — The corpus contains no supplication vocabulary in connection with sinful speech. The characteristic is a speech-act of harm; no seeking-of-sinful-speech vocabulary appears.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The vocabulary of this characteristic does not include a specific supplication term — a term for the act of seeking wickedness from another. This is expected: wickedness-as-settled-person-identity is not a characteristic one seeks from another as one might seek grace, wisdom, or peace. The relevant seeking vocabulary in the evidence belongs to the reversal direction: Ise 55:7 (VCG-07 — "let him return to the Lord, that he may have compassion on him") — the seeking vocabulary addresses the turn from wickedness toward God, not the seeking of wickedness itself. The absence of a supplication-seeking term is analytically coherent with the characteristic's nature.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The vocabulary does not include a term for seeking evil as constitutional inner nature from another. Mat 6:13 (vc=14415 — VCG-01): "deliver us from evil" contains a supplication term (deliver — rhyomai) but it is a supplication for protection from the characteristic rather than for the characteristic itself. The characteristic is not one sought from another — it is the constitutional baseline already present, from which deliverance is sought. The absence of a seeking term is analytically coherent with the characteristic's nature as a constitutional baseline condition rather than a received gift.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The vocabulary does not include a term for seeking or desiring abomination from another. Abomination is not a characteristic one seeks from another — it is a divine verdict applied to inner moral conditions. The one seeking-adjacent appearance is the call to turn from abominations (Eze 14:6 — VCG-04 — "repent and turn away from your abominations") which is a command away from the characteristic rather than a seeking toward it. No supplication-seeking term is present.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The vocabulary does not include a term for seeking idolatrous abomination from another. Idolatrous abomination is not a characteristic one seeks as a gift; it is entered through attraction to idol-objects and the will's choice. The evidence shows the characteristic as received through learning (Deu 20:18 — VCG-02), through relational entanglement (1Ki 11:5 — VCG-03), and through visual-desire feeding (Eze 20:7 — VCG-05) — none of these are supplication-seeking forms. The absence of a seeking term is analytically coherent: one does not seek idolatrous abomination as one seeks wisdom or grace.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The vocabulary does not include a term for seeking or desiring iniquity-as-scheming from another. Iniquity as active scheming is not sought as a gift; it is generated from within (VCG-02) or received through social formation (VCG-04 — association with evildoers). The absence of a seeking term is analytically coherent: one does not petition for the capacity to scheme evil; one cultivates it or drifts into it through volitional choices and relational influences. No supplication-seeking form is present.

**[CHAR-6]** S — The vocabulary does not include a term for seeking blasphemy or evil speech from another. The characteristic is not a gift that one seeks; it is generated from within the hardened will (VCG-01) or received as unwanted hostile speech (VCG-02/03). No supplication-seeking form is present. The absence is analytically coherent: no one petitions for the capacity to blaspheme or to be slandered.

**[CLUSTER]** S — No characteristic in the cluster includes vocabulary for seeking or petitioning for the inner evil it names. The cluster-level silence is analytically coherent: the M10b forms of inner evil are not gifts sought from another but conditions generated from within (Chars 1, 2, 5), divine-verdict responses triggered by inner conditions (Chars 3, 4), or speech-acts enacted from inner wickedness (Char 6). None of the six characteristics involves a form of inner evil that is received as a gift or sought from a source. This silence across all six is explicitly noted.

**[CHAR-1]** S — The defilement-state is not sought — it is incurred or declared. There is no supplication vocabulary for receiving the defilement-state from another. The seeking that does appear in the corpus is the seeking of remedy: Num 9:7 (M10c-A-VCG-07) — the men approach Moses to ask about provision for their defilement. This is a supplication for restoration, not for the characteristic itself. The vocabulary of seeking belongs to the M11 (Cleansing) domain, not to the defilement-state itself.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The 26-verse corpus does not include a supplication or seeking term for Characteristic 2. The defilement-state is not sought from another; the calls to cleansing (2Cor 7:1, VCG-03) are calls to active self-purification, not to petition of another for the characteristic. No seeking vocabulary is present.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The 83-verse corpus does not include a supplication or seeking term for the corporate/covenantal defilement-state. The characteristic is not sought; it is incurred through moral defection. The seeking that does appear is the seeking of divine inquiry (Eze 20:31 — "shall I be inquired of by you?" — the community seeking God while in the defilement-state, which God refuses). The seeking vocabulary relates to attempting to approach God while defiled, not to seeking the defilement itself.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — for the resolution, not for the condition. Mar 7:25 (VCG-01): "came and fell down at his feet" (prosepesen pros tous podas autou — prostrating in urgent supplication) — the mother's seeking of healing. Act 5:16 (VCG-02): "bringing the sick and those afflicted" — the verb "bringing" (pheron) captures the communal act of bringing the afflicted as a form of proxy supplication. The seeking vocabulary is oriented toward the resolution (seeking healing) rather than the condition itself.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's supplication vocabulary pattern is revealing: three of four characteristics are S on seeking-for-the-condition (defilement is not sought) and one (Char 4) has seeking vocabulary for the resolution. Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 show seeking only in the direction of remedy — Num 9:7 (Char 1 — men approaching Moses to ask about provision), 2Cor 7:1 (Char 2 — active self-cleansing as seeking holiness), Eze 20:31 (Char 3 — the community seeks God even while defiled, and is refused). Characteristic 4 has the most explicit seeking vocabulary for resolution: Mar 7:25 (prostrating in urgent supplication — the mother's proxy-seeking for her daughter's healing) and Act 5:16 (bringing the afflicted — communal proxy-seeking). The cluster pattern: defilement-states are never sought; resolution/healing is the direction of seeking. The seeking vocabulary belongs to the M11 (Cleansing/Restoration) cluster, not to M10c itself. Characteristic 4's explicit seeking vocabulary for healing is the most developed in the cluster because the affected person cannot seek for themselves — the proxy-seeking community bears the supplication vocabulary.

questions.question_text: What does the relationship between the OT Hebrew and NT Greek vocabulary show about continuity or development of the characteristic across the Testaments?
questions.review_note: Stage 1 rollup — GROUP BY verse_lexical.testament across every row sharing the term's root/family (via strong_related), counted per side.

findings.session_b_note:
The data package shows NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag for 98 terms — indicating that detailed lexical analysis (including LXX usage) has not been completed for the majority of the vocabulary. The flag count of 98 out of 97 total terms (more than the term count, suggesting some flags apply at the group level) indicates a significant lexical analysis gap across the registry.

**What the data does provide (partial):** Pass 1 includes brief observations on LXX-related terminology for specific terms:

- G4697 splanchnizō: "the verb appears in LXX and NT" (LSJ note, term 13 analysis). The term's presence in the LXX indicates continuity of the somatic-compassion vocabulary across the Testaments.
- G1654 eleēmosunē: Pass 1 term 20 traces the semantic development "classical Greek pity/mercy → LXX almsgiving/charitable giving → NT acts of generosity." This is the most developed cross-Testament lexical trajectory in the data — compassion arriving at its normative social form through the LXX period.
- G3356 metriopatheō: drawn from Stoic philosophical tradition; the LXX does not appear to be the primary carrier of this term's background.

**What is missing (P):** The systematic LXX analysis for the RACHAM and CHESED vocabulary — how ra.cham and chesed were rendered in the LXX (primarily as eleos/oiktirmos) and what that translation choice reveals about cross-Testament conceptual development — is not present in the data. The NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag is the indicator. This is a substantial lexical gap; no SD pointer captures it directly.

findings.session_b_note: The LXX connection is not directly addressed in the anchor verses, but inferrable evidence is present (SBF-067-Q097). Rom 3:12 cites Ps 14:3 LXX — confirming that chrēstotēs was used in the LXX to render a Hebrew moral-quality term in the goodness domain. This establishes lexical continuity: the LXX chrēstotēs bridges H2896A's moral register (OT) to the NT's chrēstotēs usage. G5543 (chrēstos — good/kind) and G5541 (chrēsteuomai — be kind) in the related-word set suggest a LXX-rooted word family inherited by the NT. For H2896A → Greek: the LXX renders tov primarily as agathos and kalos, providing the lexical bridge for the NT's agathos vocabulary. However, LSJ data was absent for both G0019 and G5544 (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags cover both — flagged in quality flags §7). The LXX analysis is therefore only partially supported by the available data. Genuine gap — NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms. (OBS-067-OBS-009, SBF-067-Q097)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-007: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two language…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two languages with distinct semantic ranges, a full root-family analysis, a NT coinage (agathōsunē), and a comprehensive vocabulary arc from phenomenological breadth (H2896A) to virtuous precision (agathōsunē) to relational precision (chrēstotēs — Q&A-177). The lexical evidence is rich. Literary: the primary anchor (Mic 6:8) uniquely combines revelatory and covenantal-obligation frames with an internal tri-fold structure that no other verse replicates (Q&A-183); the anchor corpus spans prophetic, wisdom, psalmic, and epistolary forms across multiple contextual settings (Q&A-181). Human science: virtue ethics is the closest parallel framework, with the critical divergence at the source of goodness (divine gift vs natural achievement — Q&A-186). Constraints: NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms limit the LXX analysis (Q&A-175); LSJ data is absent. The evidential foundation is strong at the lexical-semantic and verse-literary levels; it is constrained at the LXX-continuity and human-science elaboration levels. This asymmetry is itself an analytic finding — it identifies where future investigation would most strengthen the registry's evidential base.

findings.session_b_note: The key LXX observation from the data: the LXX translators used agapē/agapaō to translate both ahav and chesed, embedding the Hebrew covenantal sense of steadfast love into the Greek agapē vocabulary. This is historically significant — agapē in the NT carries the weight of the OT chesed through the LXX translation. When the NT says 'God so loved (ēgapēsen)' (Joh 3:16), it uses the term that the LXX used for God's chesed toward Israel. Continuity is established at the lexical level: the NT's agapē is not a new concept but the Hebrew chesed in Greek form. Gap: the NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag (142 instances, OBS-103-156) limits the depth of LXX-analysis available from the data package. Full LXX lexical analysis is not possible from the current data.

findings.session_b_note: The NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on several OWNER terms (67 in total for the registry) means structured LXX parse data is not available. From available evidence: the LXX renders dak.ka and related terms with Greek vocabulary for "broken," "humble," and "crushed" — the transfer maintains the inner-being register. The NT does not use the Hebrew contrition vocabulary's direct Greek equivalents in the same systematic way — NT penitential language uses different terms (*metanoia*, *penthos*, *tapeinophrosunē*). The cross-testament development is a genuine gap in the available data. OBS-030-007.

Classical koinōnia was a civic and philosophical term — shared life in the polis, business partnership, shared goods. The NT use retains the "holding-in-common" semantic core but extends it into vertical divine-human fellowship and redemptive suffering-participation — registers not present in classical usage. OBS-062-017.

findings.session_b_note: The LXX applied aphiēmi/afesis to render OT forgiveness vocabulary (H5545 → aphiēmi in the cultic passages), and the NT continues this rendering — extending it to commanded human practice. The cross-testament development is the use of the same Greek vocabulary for both divine and human forgiveness, which is not present in the Hebrew (where H5545 is exclusively divine). This lexical bridging is analytically significant: the NT does not create a new vocabulary for human forgiveness but applies the divine-forgiveness vocabulary to the commanded human act. OBS-064-006.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-064-007: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structura…
findings.finding_value: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structural theological claim. The cross-testament vocabulary development (LXX applying aphiēmi to render salach; NT extending aphiēmi to commanded human forgiveness) carries the programme's clearest lexical theological claim: human forgiveness is structurally shaped by divine forgiveness, named by the same vocabulary. The grammatical analysis (Niphal passive — "they shall be forgiven"; active Qal — God forgives) precisely encodes the act-structure: divine act → creaturely received status. The primary anchor trio (Jer 31:34, Psa 86:5, Luk 7:47) spans three literary forms (prophetic-eschatological, wisdom/psalm, Synoptic narrative) and three analytical registers (eschatological promise, divine character-statement, inner-being consequence). T7 synthesis: the forgiveness vocabulary is the most theologically structured in the current review set — its cross-testament development carries an explicit structural claim visible at the lexical level.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-013: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebr…
findings.finding_value: T1's definitional structure is encoded in the vocabulary's lexical and grammatical architecture (T7). T1's three Hebrew form-types (act, disposition, possession) correspond precisely to the three Hebrew terms (H5545 verb, H5546 adjective, H5547 noun). T1's four modes map onto the vocabulary's grammatical range (Niphal passive = covenantal-objective received status; Qal active = divine forgiving act; human commanded = G0863H in imperative/hortatory forms; seeking = H5545 imperative in intercessory prayer). T7's cross-testament development finding (NT applies divine-forgiveness vocabulary to commanded human forgiveness) is the lexical expression of T1's structural claim about the human horizontal mode being shaped by the divine model. T1 and T7 are mutually encoded — the vocabulary is structured to carry the definition.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-064-025: T4's relational directions map onto T7's literary forms. The God-to-human direction (T4.1 — dominant) is carried by the cultic-legal corpus (H5545 Niphal — God forgives, people receive), the prophetic…
findings.finding_value: T4's relational directions map onto T7's literary forms. The God-to-human direction (T4.1 — dominant) is carried by the cultic-legal corpus (H5545 Niphal — God forgives, people receive), the prophetic corpus (Jer 31:34 — divine forgiveness promise), and the apostolic letter corpus (Eph 1:7 — through his blood). The human-to-God direction (T4.2 — seeking) is carried by the penitential psalm corpus (Psa 130, Dan 9) and the Synoptic narrative (1Jo 1:9). The horizontal-giving direction (T4.3) is carried by the Synoptic parable corpus (Mat 18:23-35) and the apostolic command corpus (Eph 4:32; Luk 17:3-4). T7's literary forms are the evidential vehicles for T4's relational directions — each direction has a primary literary home.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-007: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: …
findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the v…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary architecture. The character-quality kind (ra.chum) is carried by the adjectival forms (H7349, G4835); the inner-event kind (splanchnizō) by the verbal forms (G4697, H7355); the externalised-act kind by the noun forms and compound forms (G1656, H2617B). T7's vocabulary arc (womb to almsgiving) is the lexical expression of T1's range from the most interior character quality to the most exterior externalised act — the same spectrum named by the definition is traversed by the vocabulary. The dual primary anchor (T7) maps onto T1's dimensional analysis: Hos 11:8 provides the evidence for the divine relational disposition; Luke 10:33 provides the evidence for the human relational disposition as moral norm.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-027: T5's finding that suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion is grounded in T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was …
findings.finding_value: T5's finding that suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion is grounded in T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient for the depth of compassion at the point of maximum permitted suffering) is the lexical expression of T5's most profound formation claim: suffering in the context of compassion-formation produces a depth of compassion that transcends ordinary vocabulary. T7's framework divergence at purposive suffering (Jas 5:11 — teleological frame required) is the analytical expression of T5.4's finding that suffering in the biblical frame produces compassion (as a formative outcome) rather than merely accompanying it. The dual primary anchor (Hos 11:8 and Luke 10:33) maps onto T5's dual-role finding: Hos 11:8 evidences compassion as the character being formed in God (which the human images); Luke 10:33 evidences compassion as the formed character in the human person (the moral norm).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-028: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural f…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural connections and T7's vocabulary analysis are mutually confirming at the most analytically significant points. The CHASAD root crossing two clusters (T6.4 — most unexpected structural finding) is confirmed and extended by T7's vocabulary analysis: the CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the root itself (T7.1 P5), not as an external antonym. This means the cluster-crossing T6 identifies is not an external structural anomaly but an internal semantic feature: the compassion vocabulary contains its own opposite at the root level. Exod 34:6 as the programme's most multiply-anchored verse (T6.6 — 6 registries) is also T7's most evidentially rich single text — the verse that carries the most structural connections is the same verse that is most analytically central to the vocabulary analysis. The love co-occurrence dominance (T6.1 — 196/351 verses) is confirmed by T7's vocabulary arc: the vocabulary's fullest range (womb to almsgiving) overlaps extensively with the love vocabulary's range, which is why they co-occur across more than half of all active verses.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-013: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verba…
findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. findings.session_b_note: The LXX translation of Hebrew berit as Greek diathēkē is the most significant lexical development in the covenant vocabulary's inter-Testament history. The choice of diathēkē rather than synthēkē (agreement, compact) for berit is deliberate and theologically loaded: diathēkē carries the testamentary meaning (will/testament) that synthēkē does not. The LXX translators, by choosing diathēkē, imported the inheritance-and-death dimension into covenant language. This choice — confirmed authoritative in the NT's explicit exploitation of the testamentary sense (Heb 9:16-17 — OBS-034-069) — reveals that the OT-to-NT development of the covenant vocabulary is not merely a translation but a semantic enrichment: the Greek term adds the legal dimension of inheritance through the testator's death to the Hebrew covenantal bond. The continuity: same relational bond (berit = diathēkē) with deepened semantic content (inheritance through death). The development: the NT reads this as anticipating the new covenant's enactment through Christ's death — the LXX translation itself participates in the typological movement from OT to NT.

**Cross-cluster finding 9 — OT implicit / NT explicit: a single God-dependency finding at two levels of resolution**
The OT and NT do not contain two different findings about God-dependency — they contain the same finding at two different levels of clarity. This is visible only when the full verse corpus is held in view across both testaments.

The OT names persons as righteous without always articulating the God-relation explicitly. Cases that appear to be purely moral descriptions — Noah (Gen 6:9), Job (Job 12:4), David (1Sa 24:17) — consistently reveal the God-relation on close reading: Noah is righteous "before me" (Gen 7:1, the same context); Job calls on God immediately before describing himself as righteous and blameless (Job 12:4a — "I call to God and he answers me"); David's greater righteousness is grounded explicitly in his fear of the Lord as the anointed (1Sa 24:6). The God-relation is present even when not foregrounded. The Ezekiel framework (Eze 18:9 — "walks in my statutes, and keeps my rules") confirms this: remove God's statutes and the standard against which righteousness is defined disappears entirely. The OT's God-dependency is structural and implicit.

The NT makes the same dependency explicit and categorical. Rom 3:10 — "none is righteous, no, not one" — removes the ambiguity. Rom 5:19 — "by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" — names Christ's work as the only path. Phili 3:9 — "the righteousness from God that depends on faith" contrasted with "a righteousness of my own that comes from the law" — states the two versions and names the genuine one by its source.

The analytical consequence for the programme: findings from the OT and NT on this question are not in tension and do not require harmonisation. They describe the same reality at different resolutions. OT close reading and NT categorical statement arrive at identical conclusions about the constitutive God-relation. The two testaments are reading at different focal lengths, not saying different things.

findings.finding_value: The relationship between the OT Hebrew and NT Greek wealth vocabulary reveals significant continuity and development. Continuity: the wealth-character relationship (M46-C), the wealth-trust relationship (M46-A's misplaced trust), and the rich/poor social-moral contrast (M46-B) all appear in both testaments. The OT wisdom tradition's engagement with wealth (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes) provides the conceptual framework that the NT applies and deepens. Development: the NT adds three elements absent from the OT: (1) the Christological poverty-for-enrichment pattern (2Cor 8:9 — entirely absent from the OT), (2) the ptōchos tō pneumati (poverty of spirit, Mat 5:3 — the inner-being extension of poverty vocabulary beyond the material), and (3) the autarkēs / autarkeia vocabulary (Phil 4:11 — the Stoic-adapted contentment concept that Paul christianises). The movement is from OT material-moral (wealth as the testing ground of character and trust) to NT inner-being (wealth as the domain where Christological patterns of poverty-for-enrichment and contentment are formed and expressed).

findings.finding_value:
[E] M01-A shows substantial **continuity** across Testaments. The Greek **fobeō / fobos** translates the Hebrew **ya.re / yir.ah** consistently across the Septuagint and NT. The NT picks up the same dispositional usage: Col 3:22 (fearing the Lord as governing orientation for conduct — identical to Lev 19:14 and M01-A-VCG-01 usage); Heb 12:28 (reverence and awe as the fitting disposition for approaching God in worship — identical to the Psalms worship corpus); 1Pe 1:17; 2:17 (fear as governing posture for conduct in exile — identical to Deu 6:2 and M01-A-VCG-02 usage). The NT does not introduce a new concept but extends and deepens the OT's reverential fear vocabulary into the new-covenant context.

---

[E] M01-A also shows **development** across Testaments. The NT introduces the tension between fear-as-slavery and fear-as-adoption: Rom 8:15 (the spirit of slavery associated with fear — the fear that adoption displaces is a different kind from the reverential awe that remains); 1Jo 4:18 (perfect love casting out the punishment-anticipatory fear — an eschatological-teleological development beyond the OT wisdom corpus's treatment of fear-of-God). The NT develops the inner discrimination between kinds of fear (servile vs. filial vs. reverential) more explicitly than the OT does.

M01-B shows development in the NT through the **christological intensification** of theophanic fear: the disciples' fear at Jesus's miracles, transfiguration, and resurrection appearances (M01-B-VCG-01 and 02) use the same vocabulary (fobeō, fobos) as OT theophanies but now applied to the incarnate Son. The development is christological — the OT's ya.re at divine theophanies becomes fobeō at Christ's acts and presence.

M01-G shows development: the **Greek evaluative vocabulary** (deilia, deiliaō, deilos) is a distinctively NT contribution. The OT does not have an exact equivalent evaluative person-type term for the coward; the closest is the "fearful and fainthearted" soldier of Deu 20:8 (ya.re — the same root as reverential fear) and the "fear of man" (cha.ra.dah) of Pro 29:25. The NT's deilia-family provides a dedicated evaluative-negative vocabulary for timidity that the OT addressed through contextual usage of shared roots.

The OT → NT trajectory across M01 shows: (1) **Continuity** — the same dispositional reverential fear (ya.re/yir.ah → fobeō/fobos) operates across both Testaments; (2) **Christological development** — NT theophanies are Christ-theophanies, concentrating the fear-encounter vocabulary around Jesus's identity; (3) **Discriminatory development** — the NT develops the inner taxonomy of fear (servile/adoption, punishment-anticipatory/love-perfected) more explicitly than the OT; (4) **Evaluative vocabulary addition** — the Greek deilia-family provides a dedicated negative-evaluative vocabulary that the OT lacked. Overall: strong continuity of concept, development of inner discrimination, and christological intensification.

The OT Hebrew vocabulary is richer, more varied, and more structurally organised than the NT Greek vocabulary for grief.
