The NT develops the OT's sin-as-predator into sin-as-constituted-master with the full slave-ownership vocabulary of the Greco-Roman world.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The vocabulary relationship reveals *continuity of the divine-record concept from OT to NT with eschatological resolution in the NT*. The OT develops the record through five term-groups (chat.tat, cha.ta.ah, chet, cha.ta verb, and the erasure vocabulary) across 203 of the 205 verses. The NT (Joh 1:29; Rom 3:25) deploys the equivalent Greek vocabulary (hamartia, hamartēma) to name the OT record's eschatological resolution: Joh 1:29 — "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" — the world's accumulated OT record is the burden the Lamb removes; Rom 3:25 — "former sins" passed over — the OT record's unresolved account is now addressed through Christ's propitiation.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The relationship reveals *progressive mechanism-clarification*: the OT vocabulary (kip.pu.rim — covering; chat.tat — sin-offering) describes the mechanism institutionally without naming its ultimate ground; the NT vocabulary (hamartia aphesis — forgiveness of sins; "through his blood" — Eph 1:7; "blood of the covenant" — Mat 26:28) names the mechanism's ground (Christ's blood) and the institution's fulfillment. The OT system points forward through its provisional character (Exo 30:10 — "once in the year throughout your generations"); the NT declares the once-for-all fulfillment (Mat 26:28 — poured out "for many"). The relationship is type-to-antitype: OT covering mechanism → NT blood-atonement fulfillment.

**[CHAR-15]** S — The 8-verse corpus contains no NT Greek vocabulary. The characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew (8 verses, all cha.ta). The absence of NT vocabulary in this specific corpus does not mean generational sin is absent from the NT but that the programme's Phase 9 corpus for CHAR-15 draws exclusively from OT Hebrew sources. The OT-only corpus is consistent with the characteristic's primary locus in the Israel-covenant framework where generational sin is most explicitly addressed through ancestral-lineage language.

**[CHAR-16]** E — The relationship reveals *continuity with expansion*. Chat.ta (H2400 — OT) is used primarily for extreme-type sinners (Gen 13:13; 1Sa 15:18; Amo 9:8/10) and collective characterisations (Psa 1:1/5; Isa 1:28/13:9/33:14). Hamartōlos (G0268 — NT) expands the range to include social category (Mat 9:10/11; Luk 7:37), self-recognised identity (Luk 5:8; Luk 18:13), and constituted federal status (Rom 5:19). The NT expansion adds: the social-stigma register (VCG-01 — 20+ NT verses in social settings), the self-aware sinner's plea (VCG-01 — Luk 5:8; Luk 18:13), and the Adamic-constitution register (VCG-02 — Rom 5:19). The OT establishes the extreme-type and collective categories; the NT adds the individual self-aware and constituted registers.

**[CHAR-17]** S — The 97-verse corpus contains no NT Greek vocabulary. The characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew. The guilt-realisation vocabulary (*ʾāšam* family) is distinctively OT in its priestly-ritual framing (Lev 4/5/6 sequences) and its communal accumulation language (Ezr 9:6/7/13/15). The NT equivalent vocabulary (conscience — *syneidēsis*; guilt-consciousness) does not appear in this corpus. The OT-only character reflects the characteristic's primary locus in the Levitical ritual framework and the historical-confessional tradition of the exilic period.

**[CHAR-18]** S — The corpus contains no NT Greek vocabulary. The characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew. The a.von H5771G crime-register does not directly correspond to a single NT Greek term; NT equivalents (anomia — lawlessness; adikia — unrighteousness; hamartia — sin) distribute the semantic field differently. The absence of NT vocabulary in this corpus reflects the OT nature of the iniquity-as-crime concept in its full development. The Isa 53:5/6/11 servant-bearing passages are the theological bridge toward NT soteriology but use OT a.von terminology exclusively.

**[CHAR-19]** E — The OT/NT relationship reveals *continuity with legal precision*. The OT pe.sha/pa.sha rebellion-vocabulary (relational, covenantal, political) is conceptually continuous with the NT parabasis-vocabulary (legal, boundary-specific). Rom 4:15 — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — makes the parabasis-definition explicit: what the OT pe.sha named relationally, the NT parabasis names legally. The OT term covers rebellion broadly (covenant, relationship, authority); the NT term specifies the law-known-boundary-crossing structure. The paraptōma (VCG-05) adds the stumbling-aside dimension that the OT terms do not directly name. The NT vocabulary clarifies and specifies what the OT vocabulary named more broadly.

**[CHAR-2]** S — The 18-verse CHAR-2 corpus is entirely from the OT (Hebrew Lev, Num, 1Sa, Exo, Eze). No NT Greek verses appear in the CHAR-2 corpus. The programme has not identified NT verses addressing unintentional sinning in the specific sense defined by CHAR-2. This absence itself is analytically noteworthy: the NT corpus does not carry the *bishgagah* (unintentional qualifier) vocabulary. The NT addresses sin broadly (hamartanō, hamartia) without the OT's systematic distinction between intentional and unintentional sinning through distinct remedial institutions. The relationship across Testaments is one of OT specification (CHAR-2 as a distinct category with a distinct remedy) and NT generalisation (sin addressed through Christ without the Levitical bifurcation).

**[CHAR-20]** S — The corpus contains no NT vocabulary. The characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew. The ma.al/ba.gad vocabulary for covenant-faithlessness does not have direct NT Greek equivalents within the programme's studied corpus; NT equivalents would fall into M13 (faithfulness) or M31 (faith/unbelief) territory rather than M10. The OT-only character reflects the specific covenantal-relational framework of the Levitical, Deuteronomic, and prophetic traditions in which faithlessness is most precisely named. The absence of NT vocabulary is analytically significant: CHAR-20 is the M10 characteristic whose conceptual framework is most thoroughly OT-covenantal.

**[CHAR-21]** E — The OT/NT relationship reveals *continuity with expansion into the cosmic and desire dimensions*. The OT terms (tah.pu.khah, a.vah, te.vel, sa.laph) address perversion primarily at the level of acts, speech, judgment, and specific category-violations. The NT ftheirō/fthora vocabulary expands this into: the desire as the active corruption-agent (Eph 4:22; 2Pe 1:4), the cosmic scope (Rom 8:21 — creation's bondage), the mind-specific depravity (1Ti 6:5), and the eschatological judgment (Rev 19:2). The NT adds the mechanistic precision (desire-driven) and the cosmic scope that the OT terms do not independently provide.

**[CHAR-22]** E — The OT/NT relationship reveals *conceptual continuity with legal-forensic precision in the NT*. The OT a.vel/av.lah vocabulary covers injustice broadly: judicial, commercial, violent, verbal. The NT adikos/adikēma vocabulary focuses on: the person-type (adikos — the unjust as a moral category) and the legal-actionable wrong (adikēma — the demonstrable crime). Rom 3:5 — "that God is unrighteous to inflict wrath" — uses adikos in a precisely theological-forensic argument. 1Pe 3:18 — "the righteous for the unrighteous" — deploys adikos in the Christological substitution context. The NT narrows and sharpens the OT's broader injustice vocabulary toward theological and forensic precision.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The OT-NT vocabulary relationship shows *continuity of structure, extension of scope*. Both Testaments use the sinning-vocabulary self-applied in the first person (*chatati* / *hēmarton*) as the confession form — no new confession-vocabulary is introduced in the NT. The extension: NT confessions include "against heaven" (Luk 15:18/21) — the cosmic dimension of sin named explicitly; and "by betraying innocent blood" (Mat 27:4) — specific act named with legal precision. The NT corpus is smaller within CHAR-3 (3 verses vs 31 OT) reflecting that the NT's confession theology is concentrated in its broader epistolary and narrative context rather than in the corpus's 34 verses. The shared form (*chatati*/*hēmarton*) across Testaments confirms that confession is not a NT innovation but a continuous theological practice.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Continuity of structure, development of context. Both Testaments use the sinning vocabulary in suppressed or denied mode: Jer 2:35 (OT — direct denial), 1Cor 15:34/Tit 3:11 (NT — ongoing suppression in community context). The OT instances show conscience suppression in the covenantal-prophetic confrontation mode: God speaks through the prophet to the denying people. The NT instances show it in the community-pastoral mode: Paul rebukes believers who continue sinning in spiritual stupor (1Cor 15:34) and describes the divisive person's deformed character (Tit 3:11). The development: the NT more explicitly describes the *cognitive* dimension ("no knowledge of God" — 1Cor 15:34) and the *character-deformation* consequence ("warped" — Tit 3:11) that the OT implies through narrative and prophetic confrontation.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The OT-NT vocabulary relationship shows continuity of concept with development of explicitness. The OT corpus expresses refusal to repent primarily through repeated narrative predication (did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam) — showing the characteristic through cumulative historical example. The NT corpus names the inner quality directly: Heb 10:26's *hekousiōs* (deliberately/willingly) and 1Ti 5:20's persistent-sinning present participle capture the volitional intensity of the refusal more explicitly than the OT's negated movement verbs. The development: OT shows the characteristic through recurring historical pattern; NT names the volitional quality (deliberate, persistent) that the OT implies.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The OT-NT relationship shows *continuity with NT intensification*. The OT establishes: the person-type (hachotet — Ecclesiastes), the universal baseline (1Ki 8:46; Ecc 7:20), the iterative pattern (Exo 9:34), and the historical persistence (Hos 10:9). The NT intensifies through: (1) the continuous-present participle (1Jo 3:6 — hamartanōn — "keeps on sinning"), which captures the ongoing-state dimension more precisely than the OT's participial person-type; (2) the relational-epistemic consequence (1Jo 3:6 — "never seen or known him") — a christological framing of the habitual sinning's relational meaning that the OT implies through covenant-language but does not name christologically.

**[CHAR-7]** S — The 19-verse corpus is entirely OT Hebrew. No NT Greek verses appear in CHAR-7. The characteristic is expressed exclusively through the Hiphil causative of the Hebrew cha.ta root — a grammatical form without a direct NT Greek equivalent in this corpus. The absence of NT vocabulary may reflect that the NT addresses the contagious sin dynamic through different conceptual frameworks (e.g. leadership accountability for communities — references to shepherds, elders) rather than through the Hiphil causative of the sinning verb specifically. The relationship reveals: CHAR-7 is a characteristically OT-Hebrew theological construct with its distinctive Hiphil grammatical expression; the NT may carry the same relational dynamic in different vocabulary.

**[CHAR-8]** S — The 9-verse corpus is entirely OT Hebrew; no NT Greek vocabulary appears. The political-revolt register of pa.sha (H6586) is a specifically OT Hebrew construct for breaking political submission. Whether the NT addresses the same political dynamic through different vocabulary (e.g. in political contexts) is outside the scope of this 9-verse corpus. The OT-NT relationship cannot be characterised from within this corpus.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The exclusively NT Greek corpus (no OT Hebrew vocabulary in the 22 verses) reveals that CHAR-9 as a conceptually unified characteristic is a distinctly NT formation. The OT does have verbal sin (e.g. Lev 24:11/16 — the blasphemer's stoning; 2Ki 19:6 — "blasphemed me" in the Assyrian context), but those OT instances use different Hebrew roots (gadaph, na.ats, na.aqab) and are not included in this corpus. The NT coheres around the single blasfēmia/blasfēmos word-family in a way the OT does not — the characteristic is thus more definitionally precise in NT Greek than its conceptual antecedents in OT Hebrew would allow.

**[CHAR-1]** E — For Characteristic 1, the OT Hebrew vocabulary (ra.sha, re.sha — 189 of 190 verses) overwhelmingly dominates; there is only 1 ro.a verse (1Sa 17:28) as a secondary Hebrew contribution. There are no NT Greek verses assigned to Characteristic 1. This vocabulary distribution reveals that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity is a primarily OT Hebrew anthropological category. The NT vocabulary for the equivalent domain is distributed across Characteristic 2 (M10b-B — ponēros, kakia — constitutional inner nature) and other characteristics. The OT-to-NT development appears to be: the OT concentrated the settled wicked-person analysis in the ra.sha vocabulary; the NT distributed that analysis across multiple Greek terms (ponēros for the evil person, kakia for entrenched inner badness, etc.) without a single dominant NT equivalent for ra.sha. This suggests a NT diversification of the OT person-type vocabulary.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The relationship reveals a significant developmental shift. CHAR-1 (wickedness as settled person-identity) is primarily OT Hebrew (ra.sha — 179V of 190 in CHAR-1) — the OT concentrated the evil-person analysis in the person-type vocabulary. CHAR-2 (evil as constitutional inner nature) is exclusively NT Greek (90V — no OT Hebrew verses assigned) — the NT developed a new analytical register for the constitutional dimension of human evil. The development reveals a deepening of the anthropological analysis: the OT named the wicked person as a type; the NT analysed the constitutional condition from which the wicked person-type emerges. The NT's distinctive contribution is the constitutional-depth analysis — "you who are evil" as a baseline statement about human nature (Mat 7:11; Luk 11:13 — VCG-02) is NT-specific and has no direct OT equivalent in this programme's evidence corpus.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The relationship reveals both continuity and intensification. Continuity: the content of what is abominable is consistent — the NT bdelugma passages address the same moral inner-being conditions as the OT to.e.vah moral sub-corpus: Luk 16:15 (vc=21 — VCG-02) names self-justifying pride as abomination before God, directly paralleling the OT heart-pride abominations (Pro 16:5 — VCG-02). Tit 1:16 (vc=27 — VCG-02) names the profession-works disconnect as abomination, extending the OT worship-integrity register (VCG-03). Intensification: the NT bdelugma/bdeluktos terms add the sensory-disgust dimension (stench-quality) that the Hebrew to.e.vah lacked at the root level. The NT also extends the category eschatologically: Rev 21:27 (VCG-05) — the final exclusion of the abominable from the holy city is an eschatological development of the OT's local exclusions from divine presence (Eze 44:13 — VCG-04).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The relationship reveals primarily continuity with NT extension to apocalyptic/eschatological deployment. Continuity: the OT's to.e.vah and shiq.quts identify idolatrous abomination as the category of divine revulsion at false devotion — this is consistent throughout OT. The NT's bdelugma (G0946 — Mat 24:15; Mar 13:14 — VCG-06) takes the same category and deploys it in the eschatological-apocalyptic register: the abomination of desolation as the culminating sacrilege event. The OT shiq.quts vocabulary (naming idol-objects as detestable — used 25V in CHAR-4) has no direct NT Greek equivalent in this corpus — the NT bdelugma verses are event-naming rather than object-naming. The NT development: from OT naming of specific idol-objects and practices as detestable to NT naming of an eschatological sacrilege event as the culminating abomination.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic is exclusively OT Hebrew in its evidence corpus: all 79 verses are OT, with no NT Greek terms appearing. This is a distinctive feature that requires analytical note. The absence of NT Greek evidence suggests either: (1) the NT addresses the same inner-being content through different vocabulary (ponēria/adikia/kakon — the CHAR-2 NT vocabulary in M10b-B); or (2) the characteristic's specific a.ven polysemy-field does not have a direct NT Greek equivalent that was extracted into this corpus. The exclusively OT character of the evidence confirms that CHAR-5 is a primarily OT-vocabulary characteristic. Cross-cluster NT engagement with the same content (active scheming of evil) would be located in the ponēros/ponēria word-family documented in CHAR-2's evidence. The relationship between the two testaments for this characteristic requires cross-cluster synthesis (Session D) rather than within-corpus analysis.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic is exclusively NT Greek in its evidence corpus — no OT Hebrew terms are extracted. This is a distinctive feature: the characteristic as defined (blasfēmeō, kakopoios, atopos) is specifically a NT-period vocabulary construction. The OT concept that corresponds most closely is the lashon hara (evil tongue) tradition and the Hebrew terms for curse (qalal), slander (rakhil), and false witness (ed shaqer) — but these are not present in this corpus. The exclusively NT character suggests that the specific conceptual formulation of blasphemy as the hardened will's speech-expression (VCG-01) and the false-accusation dynamic of the NT minority community (VCG-03) are NT-specific forms of a broader biblical concern. The OT-NT relationship would require cross-cluster analysis to address fully.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's OT-NT vocabulary relationship reveals a structural division within M10b itself. Chars 1 and 5 are exclusively OT Hebrew — they represent the OT tradition's characteristic vocabulary for wickedness (RSH root) and iniquity (a.ven/ro.a). Char 6 is exclusively NT Greek — it represents the NT's characteristic vocabulary for blasphemy and false accusation (blasfēmeō, kakopoios). Chars 3 and 4 span both testaments through the to.e.vah/bdelugma bridge — the most direct OT-NT vocabulary continuity within the cluster. Char 2 is primarily NT Greek (ponēros/kakia) but addresses content that overlaps with OT Hebrew ra.sha and re.sha vocabulary — the NT introduces more nuanced vocabulary for the constitutional-structure dimension that the OT addresses primarily through its person-type vocabulary. The cluster reveals: OT vocabulary addresses the wicked person-type and iniquity-scheming most precisely; NT vocabulary addresses the constitutional evil nature and its speech-expression most precisely; the abomination vocabulary bridges both.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Substantial continuity with a significant point of revision. Continuity: G0169 akathartos in the NT carries the same clean/unclean binary logic as H2931 ta.me in the OT — the categorical structure is preserved. The NT akathartos in the M10c-B-VCG-05 corpus (Act 10:14, 11:8) shows Peter operating with OT categorical logic fully intact. Revision: Act 10:28 shows the categorical system being authoritatively revised: "God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean." The divine speech act revises the OT categorical determination at the person-level. 1Cor 7:14 shows a further development: "unclean" is applied to a relational-covenantal status (children of unbelievers) rather than to bodily condition. The NT development moves from primarily bodily/ritual origin to including categorical-conscience and relational-covenantal origins.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The Hebrew-to-Greek vocabulary arc reveals a development from symbol-and-law to inner-reality. The Hebrew H2931 ta.me adj in Characteristic 2's VCG-01 corpus (Job 14:4, Isa 6:5, Isa 64:6, Hag 2:14) names the inner-moral uncleanness within a legal-ritual vocabulary that also governs Characteristic 1. The Hebrew prophetic use already makes the metaphorical-inner move (Isa 6:5 — "unclean lips" as a moral-inner recognition; Isa 64:6 — "all have become like the unclean") — the inner-moral move is already present in the OT. The NT Greek vocabulary (G0167 akatharsia, G3435 molunō, G3436 molusmos, G3394 miasmos) develops this inner-moral register explicitly and comprehensively, applying it to the conscience (1Cor 8:7), the will (Rom 6:19), the heart (Rom 1:24), and the body-and-spirit constitution (2Cor 7:1). The development is from occasional Hebrew prophetic inner-register to systematic NT moral-inner register.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Characteristic 3's 83-verse corpus is entirely OT Hebrew — no NT Greek verses appear. This is analytically significant in itself: the corporate/covenantal defilement-state is primarily an OT register, reflecting the specific covenantal structure of Israel-land-sanctuary-name that the OT context provides. The NT does not develop a direct corporate/covenantal defilement register using this vocabulary — Characteristic 3's concern (land, sanctuary, divine name as objects of defilement through corporate moral defection) is handled differently in the NT (through ecclesiology, the body of Christ as temple, the name of Jesus being profaned). The OT-only vocabulary confirms Characteristic 3 as the most distinctively OT of the four M10c characteristics, tied to the specific covenantal-sacral structures of Israel's life.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Characteristic 4 has no OT Hebrew vocabulary in its 21-verse corpus — it is entirely NT Greek. This is analytically significant: the unclean-spirit defilement register is a distinctly NT phenomenon in this programme's evidence base. The Hebrew ta.me root that carries Characteristics 1, 2, and 3 is absent from Characteristic 4's evidence. This OT-to-NT discontinuity reveals Characteristic 4 as the register that the NT gospel narrative introduces as its distinctive contribution to the defilement domain: the confrontation between Christ's authority and adversarial spiritual beings inhabiting and defiling persons.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's OT/NT vocabulary distribution reveals a striking pattern that maps onto the cluster's constitutional structure. Characteristic 3 is entirely OT Hebrew (83 verses, no NT terms) — the corporate/covenantal defilement register, tied to the specific covenantal-sacral structures of Israel's life (land, temple, divine name), is primarily an OT phenomenon. Characteristic 4 is entirely NT Greek (21 verses, no OT terms) — the unclean-spirit defilement register, constituted by the pneuma akatharton compound, is a NT phenomenon introducing the confrontation between Christ's authority and adversarial spiritual beings as the NT's distinctive contribution to the defilement domain. Characteristics 1 and 2 span both Testaments: Characteristic 1 has a substantial Hebrew corpus (133 verses) with an NT revision signal (Act 10:14/28 — the categorical system being authoritatively transformed); Characteristic 2 has a Hebrew prophetic foundation (VCG-01 — Job 14:4, Isa 6:5/64:6) and an extensive NT development (VCG-02/03/04/05 — the systematic moral-inner register). The cluster's OT/NT vocabulary arc: OT-only (Char 3 — corporate-covenantal) → OT-heavy with NT revision (Char 1 — ritual) → OT-foundation with NT development (Char 2 — moral-inner) → NT-only (Char 4 — external spiritual agency). This arc reveals the M10c cluster as a domain that both bridges and differentiates the Testaments.

C7 (Bitterness) is NT-pikria-only (G4088, 4 occ) by design. The OT bitterness-of-soul family (mar/marah — H4751, H4843, and the wider family) is owned and analysed in M03 (Grief). The English 'bitterness' is split by sense: NT pikria/pikros = resentment/anger-bitterness (M02/M28); OT mar nephesh = grief/anguish-bitterness (M03). C7 is therefore not expanded; the OT field remains in M03.

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — G4184 polusplanchnos (Jas 5:11) is a NT hapax legomenon — a term coined (or first attested in the NT) for this specific expression of divine compassion. Pass 1 term 18 analysis addresses this directly:

"The use of a compound hapax for this single statement signals that the writer needed a stronger term than the existing vocabulary supplied. Polusplanchnos — intensely, deeply compassionate — is coined for the moment when God's compassion needs to be named as something beyond the ordinary range of the word."

**What the coinage reveals:**

The coinage of polusplanchnos reveals two things:

**1. The existing vocabulary was insufficient for the theological claim being made.** The splanchnizō/splanchnon vocabulary was already in use; polusplanchnos intensifies it beyond its standard range. This signals that the compassion vocabulary was experiencing conceptual pressure — the claim about God's deep compassion in the context of Job's suffering required a stronger term than existed. The coinage is a lexical signal that the theological content was exceeding the available vocabulary.

**2. The coinage occurs at the point of maximum theological tension.** Jas 5:11 holds deep divine compassion (polusplanchnos) in direct proximity to divinely permitted suffering (Job's endurance). The new word is coined precisely for the moment where compassion and suffering are most acutely in tension. The term's uniqueness signals that this tension is not resolved in the existing vocabulary — a new word is required to hold both simultaneously. This is SD-014's finding: the most theologically complex and unresolved statement in the compassion data is the one that required a new word.

findings.session_b_note: G0019 (agathōsunē) is almost certainly a NT coinage — not attested in classical Greek or LXX (SBF-067-Q099). Its entire 4-verse NT corpus (Rom 15:14, Gal 5:22, Eph 5:9, 2Th 1:11) is Pauline and pneumatological. The coinage reveals: the NT needed a term for goodness as a named inner-being virtue distinct from the adjective agathos that applies broadly. Agathōsunē says: goodness is now a specific inner-being quality, not merely a predicate applied to things. The development from H2896A's ten-sub-sense breadth to agathōsunē's four-verse precision is pneumatological concentration: goodness in its fullest expression named as a Spirit-enabled virtue. The coinage represents the NT's sharpening of the concept from broad phenomenological range (Hebrew) to named Spirit-fruit virtue (NT). (OBS-067-OBS-009, SBF-067-Q099)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-018: T2's Spirit-level location finding (Q&A-037-039) — that genuine goodness requires Spirit-level intervention and is not naturally generated from within the person — is confirmed and enriched by T7's vo…
findings.finding_value: T2's Spirit-level location finding (Q&A-037-039) — that genuine goodness requires Spirit-level intervention and is not naturally generated from within the person — is confirmed and enriched by T7's vocabulary arc (Q&A-177). The NT coinage of agathōsunē (Q&A-176) as a Spirit-fruit term reflects precisely the T2 finding: the NT needed a new term to name goodness at the Spirit-production level because the existing vocabulary (H2896A, agathos) covered the full semantic range without isolating the Spirit-produced inner virtue. The coinage is the lexical response to a constitutional reality (Spirit-level goodness as distinct from natural goodness). T7's evidential strength in lexical analysis and T2's constitutional depth together explain why the NT created agathōsunē: to name a constitutional phenomenon (Spirit-produced inner virtue at the deepest level of the person) that the existing vocabulary did not isolate with sufficient precision.

findings.finding_value: T4 confirmed that the God-to-human direction of goodness is initiatory, generous, and sustaining (Q&A-101). T7 confirms that the primary literary form carrying divine goodness (prophetic covenantal address at Mic 6:8, doxological Psalm declarations, Pauline epistolary) all use forms that emphasise divine initiative and human receptivity. T7's literary analysis (Q&A-178-179) reveals that the literary forms carrying goodness are theologically intentional: the covenant lawsuit form (Mic 6:8) establishes divine initiative in defining the good; the invitation form ("taste and see" — Psa 34:8) establishes divine initiative in the encounter; the indicative-imperative structure of Col 3:12 (God has made you chosen → therefore put on kindness) establishes divine prior action before human response. T7's literary analysis confirms T4's relational architecture through the literary forms that carry them: the literature itself models the God-initiates-human-responds structure.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — agapē itself is effectively a NT-period coinage in its theological-central usage. The word exists rarely in classical Greek but carries no comparable weight; its meaning is constituted by its LXX/NT usage (OBS-103-016). The coinage-significance: the NT needed a word for love that was not pre-loaded with the Platonic eros tradition or the friendship-philia tradition — agapē fills this gap, its meaning entirely constituted by Scripture. This is analytically significant: agapē is the programme's strongest example of a characteristic whose vocabulary definition is wholly internal to the scriptural corpus. What agapē means cannot be determined by reference to classical Greek usage — it must be read from the LXX and NT contexts themselves.

findings.finding_value: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-covenantal (chesed), Spirit-produced self-giving (agapē), somatic-compassionate (racham), intense-erotic (ahavah/dod), and naturally affective (phileō). The vocabulary structure itself distinguishes disposition/act/condition, received/given, and quality/person-type — making it architecturally precise. The semantic range of the primary terms spans from divine ontology (God is love) to moral inversion (love of darkness) — the widest semantic arc in the programme. The primary anchor is Lam 3:22 — love's most definitive affirmation precisely at the moment of maximum empirical falsification: a theological confession rather than an empirical observation. The LXX connection is partially evidenced (agapē as chesed-translated); full LXX analysis is limited by NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags. The human science frameworks identified (attachment theory, virtue ethics) are named as Session D pointers but not elaborated — the instruction prohibits importing framework content not grounded in the data.

findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispositional), racham (somatic-compassionate), ahavah/dod (intense-erotic), phileō/agapē (affective-natural and willed-unconditional). The grammatical range analysis confirms the tripartite definition (Q&A-123): verb (act) + noun (disposition) + adjective-passive (condition). The semantic range analysis confirms the vocabulary arc (Q&A-124, Q&A-131). The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136, Q&A-137) confirms the definition's most counterintuitive feature: love at its most definitional is not evidenced by love's presence but confessed against its apparent absence. The definition says love is permanent, unwavering, faithful — and the evidential ground for this claim is a verse written in the context of Jerusalem's destruction. The evidential foundation is thus not primarily experiential but confessional — the definition's permanence-claim is a theological assertion, grounded in the character of God rather than in the consistency of human experience.

findings.finding_value: The structural relationship data and the evidential foundation are the most mutually confirming pair in the synthesis matrix. The co-occurrence breadth (T6.1) is directly explained by the vocabulary breadth (T7.1.10 — the widest semantic arc in the programme): a vocabulary that spans from divine being to love of darkness will co-occur with every other inner-being characteristic because it occupies every register of the inner-being vocabulary. The shared anchor density (48 verses — T6.6) is explained by the primary anchor's function (Lam 3:22 — T7.2.5/T7.2.6): the programme anchors the most significant cross-registry verses at love because love is the definitional centre from which adjacent characteristics derive their meaning. The vocabulary sharing ratio (0.701 — T6.4) is explained by the root-level connections (T7.1.2): the racham root connects love, compassion, and mercy; the ahav root connects love and desire; the tov root connects love and goodness. The structural relationship data is, at its core, the observable programme-level effect of the lexical architecture that the evidential foundation analysis reveals. Structural breadth and lexical breadth are the same reality at different levels of analysis.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. The NT coinage charitoō (T7.1 P9 — coined for standing-in-favour as completed, continuing state) is the lexical ground of T5.1's irreversibility finding: the perfect passive grammatical form encodes precisely the "transformation not reversed" character that T5.1 identifies. T7.2's argument structure analysis (Zec 12:10 — grace outpoured → recognition → mourning → supplication) is the textual grounding for T5.2's creaturely recognition response finding: the sequence is not an incidental narrative feature but an argued structural pattern. T7.3's framework divergence (human science frameworks assuming prior capacity; Scripture denying it at the point of maximum incapacity — Eph 2:1-5) is the methodological expression of T5.5's deepest formation finding: the person cannot initiate their own formation by grace. findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: G0802 (asunthetos — untrustworthy/covenant-breaker — OBS-034-018) appears to be a distinctive NT-period term for the covenant-breaking character quality. While the word's components are classical Greek, its appearance in Paul's vice-catalogue (Rom 1:31) as a moral character term within a NT theological context is the word's most prominent biblical use. It represents the NT's naming of covenant-faithlessness as a specific moral character defect — giving an explicit lexical label to what the OT described through narrative and prophetic denunciation. The other NT-specific development is not a newly coined term but a newly deployed term: diathēkē in its testamentary sense (Heb 9:16-17) exploits an existing Greek legal term for theological purposes — not a coinage but a semantic deployment that generates a new theological meaning-range for an existing word.

findings.session_b_note: Yes — G1517 eirēnopoieō (to make peace, Col 1:20) is attested primarily in the NT context and represents a verbal neologism: combining eirēnē (peace) with poieō (to make/do) to create a term for the specific act of cosmic peace-making. This term is thin (1 active verse in the corpus, Col 1:20) but carries maximum theological weight — it names what Christ accomplished at the cross as a unique act. G1518 eirēnopoios (peacemaker, Mat 5:9) similarly compounds the root to create a person-type term. The NT coinage of these compound terms reflects the NT's need to describe both the act (eirēnopoieō) and the agent (eirēnopoios) of peace-making — concepts that the OT vocabulary named differently (sha.lom as noun, baqash sha.lom as seeking-peace). The new terminology reflects new theological content: the specific Christological act of making peace through the cross.

**[CLUSTER]** E. Yes — several terms in M26 are NT-specific or extremely rare before the NT:
- **autokatakritos (G0843)** — self-condemned. This compound appears only in Tit 3:11 in the NT and has no Hebrew OT counterpart. The concept of the person who is self-condemned — whose own inner being pronounces them guilty — is the NT's unique contribution in the E-sub-group. No equivalent OT term or concept carries this reflexive-judicial nuance.
- **dikaiōsis (G1347)** — justification as the completed act. This rare noun appears in Rom 4:25 and Rom 5:18. It names the justification-event as a completed act (dikaiōsis = the act of justifying), distinct from dikaiosunē (the quality of righteousness) and dikaioō (the verb to justify). The specificity of this term suggests a NT theological development: the need to name the event of justification as a completed act is a NT-specific theological concern.
- **dikaiokrisia (G1341)** — righteous judgment (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001). A compound of dikaios (righteous) + krisis (judgment). While judicial language is OT-rich, this specific compound naming God's judgment as characteristically righteous is NT-specific.

What the coinages reveal: the NT needed new vocabulary to name experiences and realities that the OT vocabulary could not fully capture — specifically the reflexive-judicial reality of self-condemnation (autokatakritos), the completed event of justification as an act (dikaiōsis), and the characteristically righteous nature of divine judgment (dikaiokrisia). These coinages map the theological developments that the NT introduces into the righteousness domain.

G5428 fronēsis: practical wisdom/prudence in the NT (Luk 1:17 — "the wisdom of the righteous"; Eph 1:8 — "wisdom and insight"). Fronēsis is not entirely new (Aristotle) but its NT application to the wisdom of the righteous and to the Spirit's endowment reveals a distinctive NT development: practical wisdom as a Spirit-given capacity for godly living. Also: G4678 sophia applied to Christ personally (1Cor 1:24, 30 — "Christ the wisdom of God") — the personalisation of the abstract attribute as divine Person is a NT development building on Wisdom literature's personification.

findings.finding_value: G0050 agnoeō: to be ignorant (Act 17:30 — "times of ignorance God overlooked"). While agnoeō exists in classical Greek, its NT moral-theological loading (ignorance as culpable, as the condition that produces accountability rather than excusing it) is a distinctively NT development. Also: the gnōsis/epignōsis distinction in Paul (Col 1:9 — "knowledge [epignōsis] of his will") — epignōsis as full or thorough knowledge is a NT intensification of the knowing vocabulary applied to knowing God and his will.

findings.finding_value: G1252 diakrinō acquires a distinctive second NT meaning: doubt, self-division (Jas 1:6 — "ask in faith, with no doubting [diakrinō]"; Rom 4:20 — "he did not diakrinō with respect to the promise of God"). This is a significant NT development: the discrimination/evaluation root is turned inward to name the self-divided state of the one whose inner evaluative faculty is split between faith and doubt. This meaning does not appear in the LXX or classical usage.

findings.finding_value: G4307 pronoia in NT acquires moral-ethical loading: "make no provision [pronoia] for the flesh to gratify its desires" (Rom 13:14). In classical and LXX usage pronoia is primarily cognitive foresight (planning ahead). The NT application to the moral discipline of not planning for fleshly gratification is a NT development — foresight as a morally charged responsibility. Also: G1013 boulēma (Rom 9:19 — "who has resisted his boulēma?") — divine boulēma as irresistible divine will is given specific Pauline development.

findings.finding_value: G1760 enthumeomai: to ponder within (Matt 1:20 — Joseph's pondering before angelic disclosure; Matt 9:4 — Jesus perceiving the scribes' inner thoughts). The en + thumos compound root is NT-period usage: the emphasis on reflective activity within the deep inner movement (thumos) is a distinctive NT emphasis on the reflective-affective depth of inner deliberation. Not an entirely new coinage but a NT-specific deployment.

findings.finding_value: G3540 noēma: the mind's formed content (2Cor 4:4; 2Cor 10:5 — "taking every noēma captive"). While noēma exists in classical Greek (Plato uses it for the mind's grasp), its NT deployment in a spiritual warfare context (adversarial blinding, taking captive) is a distinctively Pauline theological development. The noēma as contested inner cognitive territory — simultaneously the object of adversarial attack and of volitional governance — is a NT development of the term.

findings.finding_value: G3056 logos as divine Person (Jn 1:1 — "in the beginning was the logos, and the logos was with God, and the logos was God"). This is the most theologically radical NT development in the cluster and arguably in the NT. The word-as-divine-Person transcends all classical or LXX uses: the logos is no longer merely the rational principle (Stoic), the divine word (OT prophetic tradition), or the wisdom-as-agent (Wisdom literature) — it is the pre-existent divine Person who becomes flesh (Jn 1:14). This coinage reveals that M15-H's characteristic is grounded in a Person, not merely in a principle or phenomenon.

It was coined to name "the act of bestowing grace as a completed, continuing state" — a concept that existing vocabulary could not carry. findings.finding_value: Autarkēs (G0842 — self-sufficient/content) and autarkeia (G0841 — self-sufficiency/contentment) are Stoic philosophical terms adopted and adapted by Paul. They are not found in the OT Hebrew tradition. The coinage (or adoption) reveals that the NT's theological account of contentment in the wealth domain draws on the best philosophical vocabulary available (Stoic self-sufficiency) while entirely reframing its ground: Paul's autarkeia is not grounded in Stoic rational self-mastery but in "him who strengthens me" (Phil 4:13). The term is borrowed; the foundation is transformed.

findings.finding_value: The NT's Greek compound intensifiers represent vocabulary newly coined or specifically deployed for the fear register in NT contexts: **ekthambeo (G1568), ekthambos (G1569), ekfobos (G1630)** — these ek- prefixed compound forms intensify the base fear-terms and appear specifically in the gospel literature describing reactions to Jesus's acts and presence. The ekthambeo root in particular appears to be used distinctively for the awe-shock produced by Jesus's supernatural acts (Mar 9:15 anchor: the crowd's amazement at seeing Jesus; Mar 14:33: Jesus himself ekthambeo in Gethsemane). The coinage of these intensified compound forms in the NT context reveals that the encounters with Jesus produced an intensity of awe-shock that the existing vocabulary of fobeō/fobos did not fully capture — a new vocabulary was deployed to describe what it was like to encounter the incarnate Son of God directly.

The **deilia / deiliaō / deilos** vocabulary, while existing in classical Greek, is newly deployed in a theological-moral context in the NT. 2Ti 1:7's use of deilia as a named spirit-level disposition not from God, and Rev 21:8's use of deilos as the heading term for the condemned, represents a theological appropriation of the classical Greek ethical vocabulary into the NT's moral-spiritual framework. The coinage reveals that the NT treats timidity as a moral-theological category equivalent in seriousness to idolatry — an evaluation that goes beyond the classical Greek understanding.

The NT's distinctive coinages in M01 are: the ekthambeo / ekfobos compound-intensifiers (for christological encounter-fear) and the theological appropriation of deilia / deilos (for the evaluative-moral category of cowardly apostasy). Both reveal that the NT needed new or newly-deployed vocabulary to describe the intensity of the christological encounters and the seriousness of the failure of courage under pressure.

Yes. *Parorgizō* (G3949 / M02-D-VCG-02) is a NT compound — "to anger alongside/intensely" — with no direct Hebrew antecedent as a compound; it intensifies the basic orgē with the para- prefix. *Logomachia* (G3055 / M02-F-VCG-01 / 1Ti 6:4) — word-quarrels — is a NT coinage that names a specific form of contentious dispute that arises in early Christian community debates. *Filoneikos* (G5380 / 1Cor 11:16) — dispute-loving — is a compound coinage naming the dispositional quarrel-lover. These NT coinages reveal a development: the early church was confronted with a specific form of anger-expression (verbal theological disputes) for which new terminology was needed. The NT coinage of logomachia and filoneikos reveals that the community's primary anger-expressions shifted from physical violence and covenantal-idolatry-provocation (OT dominant) to verbal-theological contention (NT dominant).
