findings.finding_value:
[E] In Pro 1:7 (anchor M01-A-VCG-02): "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction." The term yir.ah (fear of the Lord) functions as the **subject and predicate nominative** of the main clause — it IS the beginning of knowledge. The grammatical function is definitional and constitutive: the verse does not say fear leads to knowledge but that fear IS the beginning. This elevates fear from a precondition to a constitutive element. The contrast clause ("fools despise") makes the argument by antithesis: the absence of fear = despising wisdom = foolishness. The argument is: right inner orientation (fear) = knowledge; its absence = folly.

---

[E] In Lev 19:14 (anchor M01-A-VCG-01): "You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God: I am the Lord." The term ya.re (fear your God) functions as the **grounding imperative** — the theological basis for the ethical prohibitions. The argument structure is: prohibition (do not exploit the vulnerable) + grounding command (fear your God) + divine identity (I am the Lord). The fear-term grounds the ethics in the divine reality rather than in consequentialist or social reasoning.

In Mar 4:41 (anchor M01-B-VCG-02): "And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, 'Who then is this?'" The term fobos functions as the **content of their inner state** that produces the christological question. The fear functions argumentatively as the evidence that what they have witnessed exceeds natural categories — it is the inner-being sign that points toward Jesus's identity.

In Dan 5:6 (anchor M01-D-VCG-03): "Then the king's color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together." The term be.hal (alarmed/dismayed) functions as the **verbal expression of the inner event** from which all somatic consequences flow — the be.hal of his thoughts produces the color change, the limb-failure, the knocking knees. The term is causal in the argument's logic.

In 2Ti 1:7 (anchor M01-G-VCG-01): "For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control." The term deilia (fear/timidity) functions as the **named negative** in a contrast structure — God gave NOT this but THAT. The argument structure is: what God gives (positive triple) defined by contrast with what he does not give (deilia). The term carries the full evaluative weight of the sentence.

The primary terms function in their anchor verses as: subject/predicate nominative (constitutive definition — Pro 1:7), grounding imperative (theological basis for ethics — Lev 19:14), inner state pointing outward (christological evidence — Mar 4:41), causal inner event (producing somatic collapse — Dan 5:6), and contrast-term defining what God does not give (evaluative negation — 2Ti 1:7). The diversity of grammatical functions across anchor verses reflects the cluster's diversity of phenomenological registers.

**Anchor focus: A-VCG-01 anchor: Heb 3:11 / orgē:** In Heb 3:11, orgē (wrath) functions as the affective ground of the oath: "as I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest." The term is predicative — it names the inner state within which the divine oath was made, making the inner state legally constitutive of the oath's binding force. Grammatically, wrath is the prepositional object ("in my wrath") — the inner state is the context in which the consequential act (oath-swearing) occurred. The function is to name the moral-emotional foundation of a legal-covenantal act.

For the primary distress term tsar (H6862B), in the primary distress VCG anchor Psa 18:6: "In my distress I cried to the Lord..." — tsar functions as the subject-condition that motivates the verbal act of crying out. It is the inner state that initiates the entire verse's action. The function is motivational-causal: tsar names the condition that causes the psalmist to act. For ba.khah at 2Sa 18:33 (M03-A-VCG-01 anchor): ba.khah names the act ("the king wept") that reveals the totality of his grief — the verb is the primary revelatory action of the verse. For perilupos at Mat 26:38 (M03-C-VCG-03 anchor): perilupos is a predicate adjective modifying Jesus's soul — its function is descriptive-definitional, naming the condition of Jesus's inner being at maximum depth.

**[CHAR-1]** E — In Psa 35:9 ("my soul will rejoice in the Lord, exulting in his salvation"), the primary term (gil_verb — "rejoice" / su.s — "exulting") functions as the **main predicate** of the soul — it names what the soul will do as the culmination of the psalmist's hope and expectation. The terms are the syntactic and semantic peak of the verse: the soul as subject + rejoice/exult as predicate + "in the Lord" / "in his salvation" as the governed prepositional objects. The terms carry the full weight of the verse's inner-being claim.

**[CHAR-2]** E — In Deu 16:11 ("And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God"), sa.mach functions as the **main predicate of a second-person command** — it is the central imperative of the verse, making Joy the required inner act of covenant participation before God. The "before the Lord your God" prepositional phrase gives the term its constitutive object and direction. The grammatical weight of the term as command-predicate across the Deuteronomic feast-corpus shows Joy as the defining inner act that covenant worship requires.

In Phili 4:4 ("Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice") — chairo functions as a repeated imperative with the unique intensification of double repetition ("I will say it again") — showing Joy's commanded standing as so fundamental that it requires insistence.

**[CHAR-7]** E — In 1Pe 1:8 ("though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice [agalliate] with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory"), **agalliao** functions as the **main predicate of the faith-community** — it names the primary defining act of the community in its unseen-Christ faith context. The term is qualified by two superlatives: "inexpressible" and "filled with glory" — both modifiers emphasising the quality's transcendence of ordinary affective categories. The term's function as the main predicate confirms Suffering-Joy as the defining inner-being act of the community under this characteristic: this is what they DO in faith, even amid trial (v.6).

**[CHAR-3]** E — In Mic 6:8 ("He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?"), **tov** functions as the **object of divine declaration** — "what is good" names the content God has revealed. The term is the syntactic and semantic centre around which the verse's three requirements cluster as its definition. God's declaration establishes the good as a known, revealed reality — not a matter of human invention or preference — and the human person's task is to recognise it (evaluative Gladness) and live it (conscientiousness). The term's function as the object of divine declaration confirms Gladness's cognitive-receptive character: goodness is first known, then lived.

**[CHAR-4]** E — In Psa 37:4 ("delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart"), **a.nog** (hitpael — reflexive: "delight yourself") functions as the **commanded reflexive volitional act** — the psalmist is commanded to direct the luxuriating delight faculty toward the Lord. The hitpael form is theologically significant: it names a self-directed action of the inner being — the person is to actively orient themselves toward God as the object of a.nog. The second clause ("he will give you the desires of your heart") shows the consequential divine response: Delight in God restructures the heart's desires in alignment with what God gives. The primary term functions as the pivotal inner-being act on which the whole verse's promise turns.

**[CHAR-5]** E — In Psa 27:4 ("one thing have I asked of the Lord… to gaze upon the beauty [no.am] of the Lord"), **no.am** functions as the **object of the supreme desire** — the pleasantness/beauty of the Lord is what the psalmist most deeply wants to behold. The term names the quality of God that makes dwelling in his presence the soul's supreme pursuit. No.am here is not merely aesthetic — it is the totality of God's agreeable, beautiful, life-giving character that the soul seeks to gaze upon. The term's function as the object of the supreme petition reveals Pleasure in God as the highest form of the characteristic's operation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — In Psa 118:23 ("this is the Lord's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes"), **pa.la** (niphal — "it is marvellous") functions as the **community's perceptive-evaluative declaration**: the niphal passive form names what is marvellous not as an objective quality claimed by God but as what is experienced as marvellous by the worshipping community ("in our eyes"). The verse structure: "this is the Lord's doing" (attribution) + "it is marvellous in our eyes" (inner perceptive response). The term's function confirms Wonder as a relational-perceptive response — something seen (perceptive) and recognised as extraordinary (evaluative) by the inner being of those who observe it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The comparative analysis of primary-term function across the seven characteristics reveals that each characteristic's primary term functions differently within its anchor verse — confirming the phenomenological distinctiveness of the seven: (1) Exultation (Char 1) — primary term as soul's main predicate: the soul acts (Psa 35:9); (2) Joy (Char 2) — primary term as commanded predicate (Phili 4:4; Deu 16:11) — the most command-weighted; (3) Gladness (Char 3) — primary term as object of divine declaration: "what is good" (Mic 6:8) — the most cognitively-received; (4) Delight (Char 4) — primary term as pivotal commanded reflexive act: "delight yourself" (Psa 37:4 hitpael) — the most volitionally-constituted; (5) Pleasure (Char 5) — primary term as object of supreme desire: God's no.am as what is most deeply sought (Psa 27:4) — the most aspirationally-directed; (6) Wonder (Char 6) — primary term as communal perceptive-evaluative declaration: "marvellous in our eyes" (Psa 118:23 niphal) — the most communally-located; (7) Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — primary term as main predicate of the faith-community: "you rejoice" (1Pe 1:8) — the most community-definitional. The seven grammatical functions together confirm the cluster's diversity: command, aspiration, declaration, reflexive act, perceptive-communal assertion, community-definition — these are genuinely distinct modes of inner-being expression.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Taking Psa 44:15 (vc=37310) as a representative primary verse: "all day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face" — *bo.shet* functions as the subject of "has covered my face" — shame is the agent that covers. This is a significant grammatical observation: shame is not merely a quality the person has; it is described as a covering-agent acting on the person. The person is covered by shame; the relationship is one of passive reception. This grammatical function (shame as agent, person as recipient) confirms the condition-character of CHAR-1 across its primary vocabulary.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Taking 2Sa 10:5 (vc=38517) for VCG-01: ka.lam functions as a stative verb ("the men were greatly ashamed/humiliated") — the men are in a state produced by what was done to them. The stative confirms CHAR-2's received-condition character: shame here is what they are in, not what they do.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary literary forms: parable (Luk 18:2-4 — the unjust judge); epistle (Rom 2:23; 2Cor 6:8; Jam 2:6; 1Cor 11:4-5); narrative (Joh 8:49). The parable form (Luk 18) uses the character of the dishonoring judge as a contrast-figure — his absent-regard makes the point precisely by its absence. Primary anchor: Joh 8:49 (vc=35000) — "I honor my Father, and you dishonor me" — the most compressed, relational, and personally directed expression of CHAR-3 in the corpus, revealing worth-denial as a relational act directed at a specific person in a specific exchange. This verse uniquely reveals worth-denial as a personal relational act within a face-to-face exchange, where the standard (honouring the Father) and the violation (dishonoring the Son) are simultaneously named.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Taking Eph 5:12 (vc=34985) as the primary anchor: aischros functions as a predicate adjective ("it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret") — shame is a quality attributed to both speaking about and doing certain deeds. The predicate use confirms CHAR-4's quality-character: shamefulness is being predicated of conduct, not attributed to a person's experience.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Taking Luk 18:9 (vc=54639) as the primary VCG-01 anchor: exoutheneō functions as a participial verb in a relative clause ("who treated others with contempt") — it characterises the inner habit of those who trust in themselves. The participial form confirms CHAR-5's dispositional character in VCG-01: contempt-producing-shame is not an isolated act but the expression of a habituated inner disposition.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Taking Gen 20:5 (vc=22817) as the primary anchor: niq.qa.von functions as a noun in a prepositional phrase ("in the innocence of my hands") — innocence is the medium or condition in which the hands acted. The prepositional construction ("in the innocence") confirms CHAR-6's condition-character: the hands acted within the condition of innocence, meaning the moral condition enveloped and characterised the action. No guilt-stain is present to contaminate the action or bar the approach.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's primary terms function across two grammatical modes that mirror the cluster's characteristic diversity. Stative verbs (bosh — "they were ashamed," Psa 44:9; sha.phel — "he is brought low," Isa 2:9) name the condition the person is in — the being-in-a-state of shame or abasement. Transitive verbs (atimazō — "you dishonour me," Joh 8:49; exoutheneō — "treated others with contempt," Luk 18:9) name what one person actively does to another. The stative/transitive grammatical distinction mirrors the received/enacted analytical distinction: shame is received statically (conditions fall upon the person); dishonour and contempt are enacted transitively (one person acts upon another). Char 6's niq.qa.von operates nominally ("in the innocence of my hands," Gen 20:5) — naming a quality of the hands that is claimed rather than performed, a condition possessed rather than enacted.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Taking rum (H7311A) in Deu 8:14 (vc=34223, M08-A1-VCG-01) as the primary verse: "then your heart will be lifted up [rum], and you will forget the Lord your God." Rum functions here as the passive/reflexive verbal pivot in the conditional-consequence sentence structure: prosperity received (preceding context: eating and being full — Deu 8:12–13) → heart lifted up [rum] → God forgotten (the consequence). The grammatical function is causal-transitional: rum names the inner movement that is the pivot between the before-state (material satisfaction received) and the after-state (spiritual forgetfulness). The sentence argument is: conditions of blessing, when they activate CHAR-1 (heart lifted up), produce the specific downstream consequence of divine forgetfulness. Rum therefore bears the entire analytical weight of the verse's argument at the causal hinge-point. Without rum, the sentence has no mechanism for the connection between prosperity and forgetfulness — rum is what makes the connection intelligible.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Taking zid in Deu 18:20 (vc=34119, M08-B-VCG-01): "the prophet who presumes [zid] to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die." Zid functions as the participial qualifier of "the prophet" — naming the defining inner quality of the transgression (presumptuousness) as what constitutes the capital offence. The grammatical function is definitional-qualificatory: zid distinguishes this prophet's speech from legitimate prophecy not by the form of the speech but by the inner quality of the speaker's self-authorising will. The verse's argument rests on zid as the diagnostic criterion: it is the inner presumptuous claim to speak God's word that God did not command that constitutes the transgression, not merely the content of the speech.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Taking kauchaomai in 1Cor 1:31 (vc=33878, M08-C-VCG-03): "let the one who boasts [kauchaomai], boast in the Lord." The verb functions here as a commanded act — not a prohibition but an imperative redirection. The grammatical function is command/commission: Paul redirects the boasting-impulse rather than eliminating it. The theological argument of 1Cor 1:26–31 rests on this: since God has chosen the weak and foolish to shame the strong (1Cor 1:27), the proper response is not silence (the boasting-capacity suppressed) but God-directed boasting (the boasting-capacity redirected). Kauchaomai carries the entire transformational logic: the same verb that names VCG-01's condemned boasting (1Cor 1:29: "no human being might boast") is the verb that commands VCG-03's God-directed exultation (1Cor 1:31: "let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord").

**[CHAR-4]** E — Taking fusioō in 1Cor 8:1 (vc=33935, M08-D-VCG-01): "knowledge puffs up [fusioō], but love builds up [oikodomeō]." Fusioō functions as the main verbal predicate of a structural antithesis: knowledge → fusioō (inflate) vs love → oikodomeō (build up). The grammatical function is contrastive-evaluative: the two actions are placed in direct antithesis. Fusioō's specific function is to name the characteristic outcome of knowledge when received without love — not that all knowledge inflates, but that knowledge-without-love inflates. The verse's argument rests on fusioō as the diagnostic term: it names what happens to the inner person when cognitive goods are processed without the relational anchor of love.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Taking a.din in Isa 47:8 (vc=9563, M08-E-VCG-02) as the primary verse: "you who love pleasures [a.din], who sit securely, who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children.'" A.din functions as the participial characteriser of the addressee — "you who love pleasures" identifies the affective ground of CHAR-5 before the verse states its cognitive-declarative climax. The grammatical function is characterising-prior-to-indicting: the verse first characterises the inner affective orientation (pleasure-love/ease) that generates CHAR-5, then names the inner declaration it produces ("I am, and there is no one besides me"). A.din provides the causal affective ground from which the self-declaration emerges — it is the generating-ground term for what the verse then names as the declaration of self-completeness.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The primary-verse comparison across the five reveals that each characteristic's primary term functions as the analytical pivot of the verse's argument. CHAR-1's rum in Deu 8:14 (M08-A1-VCG-01): the causal hinge between prosperity received and God forgotten. CHAR-2's zid in Deu 18:20 (M08-B-VCG-01): the qualificatory term distinguishing the transgressive prophet from the legitimate one. CHAR-3's kauchaomai in 1Cor 1:31 (M08-C-VCG-03): the commanded redirect — preserving the boasting-impulse while directing it to God. CHAR-4's fusioō in 1Cor 8:1 (M08-D-VCG-01): the pivot in the knowledge/love contrast. CHAR-5's a.din in Isa 47:8 (M08-E-VCG-02): the affective-ground term preceding the ontological self-declaration. The cluster-synthesis: M08's primary terms consistently function as analytical pivots — they do not merely describe but explain the causal or structural logic of their verse's argument.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The Phase 7 anchor of M09-C-VCG-01 is vc_id 61397 (Rom6:17 — "obedient from the heart"). In this verse, hupakouō (implied by "obedient") functions as the *predicate complement* — it defines what the Roman believers have become through the transformation from sin's slavery: they have become "obedient from the heart." The term's function is to name the constitutional quality that the transformation has produced — not an act being described but a character-state that now defines the person. The phrase "from the heart" is the qualifying locative that distinguishes this genuine submission from mere compliance — placing it constitutionally in the inner person rather than at the behavioural surface.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The Phase 7 anchor of M09-E-VCG-01 is vc_id 62969 (Isa57:15). In this verse, dak.ka functions as an *adjectival qualifier of spirit* within a relative clause: "with him who is of a contrite [dak.ka] and lowly spirit." The term qualifies the spirit, making the condition of the spirit the criteria for God's dwelling. The function is constitutive: dak.ka names the specific inner-being condition that qualifies the person for God's dwelling-with. In the sentence's argument, dak.ka is the defining inner-being criterion paired with lowly (shpal) that specifies who receives the divine indwelling alongside the divine transcendent dwelling. Without dak.ka, the criteria for God's relational nearness would be incomplete.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The Phase 7 anchor of M09-F-VCG-01 is vc_id 6225 (Heb5:2). Metriopatheō functions as an *infinitive complement* to the modal verb "can" (dunatai): "he can deal gently" — naming the capacity that the high priest possesses and deploys in his mediating role. The function in the argument is causal-enabling: the high priest's metriopatheō capacity is grounded in his shared weakness, making him fit for his priestly function. The term is the key to the argument's claim about priestly fitness — without the capacity named by metriopatheō, the high priest would be constitutionally unfit for his role. The term thus functions as the name of the priestly qualification.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The Phase 7 anchor of M09-G-VCG-01 is vc_id 12081 (1Ti2:2). Semnotēs functions as part of a *compound descriptor of the desired manner of life*: "godly and dignified in every way" — the adverbial phrase "in every way" gives the comprehensive scope, while semnotēs names one of the two qualities (alongside godliness) that characterise this life. The function is *characterological qualification* of the desired manner of Christian existence in the civic sphere — semnotēs names the manner-quality alongside the content-quality (godliness). In the argument (prayer for rulers enabling a peaceful quiet life), semnotēs is the manner-quality that makes such a life genuinely honourable rather than merely comfortable.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The Phase 7 anchor of M09-H-VCG-01 is vc_id 43495 (Exo35:5). Na.div (as nadiv — willing, generous) functions as an *adjectival qualifier of lev (heart)* within a conditional relative clause: "whoever is of a generous/willing heart [lev nadiv], let him bring." The function is *defining the inner condition for the outward act* — the na.div quality of the heart is the constitutional criterion for the bringing. In the argument (Moses instructing the community on contributions for the tabernacle), the term functions as the discriminating criterion: not all are to bring equally, but only those whose hearts are genuinely willing — the inner condition defines who the appropriate giver is. The term thus identifies the character-type (willing-hearted person) whose offering is the kind God seeks.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary anchor verse of the characteristic, based on the Phase 7 designation, is 2Ch7:14 (vc_id 60903 — anchor of M09-A-VCG-01). The function of ka.na ("humble themselves") in the sentence: it is the first in a conditional sequence — "if my people… humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear." Ka.na is the syntactically first and logically foundational act in the conditional clause: it initiates the series of acts that together constitute the full movement of return to God. Without the humbling, the subsequent acts (prayer, seeking, turning) do not have their inner-being foundation. The term functions as the *initiating condition* of the conditional structure — the first inner act without which the promised divine response ("I will hear, forgive, heal") cannot proceed.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The primary term's grammatical function in the anchor verse maps precisely onto the characteristic's operational profile. Humility (CHAR-1, anchor 2Ch7:14 — ka.na): initiating-condition function — the first act in the conditional sequence whose fulfilment opens the divine response; without the humbling, the subsequent acts lack their inner-being foundation. Submission (CHAR-2, anchor Rom6:17 — obedient from the heart): predicate-complement function — names the constitutional quality that divine transformation has produced; the heart-location modifier distinguishes genuine submission from surface compliance. Contrition (CHAR-3, anchor Isa57:15 — dak.ka): qualifying-criterion function — names the specific inner-being condition that qualifies the person for God's dwelling-with. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4, anchor Heb5:2 — metriopatheō): priestly-capacity-naming function — names the qualifying capacity that makes the high priest adequate to their mediating role. Dignity (CHAR-5, anchor 1Ti2:2 — semnotēs): characterological-qualification function — names the manner-quality alongside godliness that characterises the whole desired Christian existence. Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6, anchor Exo35:5 — na.div): discriminating-criterion function — the inner condition that identifies who the appropriate worship-contributor is. Cluster-level: each primary term functions at a different syntactic position in its anchor verse, reflecting each characteristic's operational role — initiating (CHAR-1), qualifying-outcome (CHAR-2), criterial (CHAR-3), capacity-naming (CHAR-4), manner-qualification (CHAR-5), and discriminating-criterion (CHAR-6).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary anchor verse is Psa 51:4: "Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight." Cha.ta functions here as the confessional predicate — the act that David names as the fundamental moral reality of his situation. The term functions syntactically as the verb of confession ("I have sinned"), semantically as the identifier of the act's relational target ("against you, you only"), and theologically as the premise of the entire psalm's petition for forgiveness. It locates the entire moral reality — adultery, murder, deception — within the single relational frame of sinning against God. The function is definitional: cha.ta names what all David's wrongs ultimately are in their deepest character.

**[CHAR-10]** E — The primary anchor verse is Jam 1:14: "But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire." Deleazō (in its two passive forms — "lured" and "enticed") functions as: (1) *the mechanism-naming term* — two near-synonymous terms for the enticement process, naming the progressive stages (lured first, then enticed — escalating engagement); (2) *the responsibility-locating term* — "his own desire" — the possessive confirms that the mechanism operates through the person's own inner faculty, not through purely external forces; (3) *the universalising anchor* — "each person" — the subject makes the mechanism applicable to all moral subjects. The term functions as the entry-point definition of the enticement mechanism.

**[CHAR-11]** E — The primary anchor verse is Rom 3:23: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." *Hamartanō* (verb — "have sinned") functions as the universalising past-tense verb that encompasses all moral subjects in a single completed-act framing: "all have sinned" is the conclusion of the universal-sinning indictment that begins in Rom 1. The complementary phrase "fall short of the glory of God" adds the definitional framework: the universality (all) + the act (have sinned) + the deficiency (fall short of) + the standard (glory of God) together constitute the most precise and comprehensive statement of the universal sin-condition in the entire 112-verse corpus.

**[CHAR-12]** E — The primary anchor verse is Joh 8:34: "everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin." Hamartia in the genitive (*tēs hamartias* — of sin) functions as the *owner-name*: "a slave of sin" — sin is named in the genitive as the master in whose possession the slave stands. The genitive of possession/ownership is the grammatical expression of the enslaving relationship: the person is sin's property. The subject (*pas ho poiōn tēn hamartian* — everyone who is making sin) names the universal scope of the mechanism: every practising sinner is sin's property.

**[CHAR-13]** E — The primary anchor is Jer 17:1: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars." *Cha.ta.ah* (H2403A/H2401 — "the sin of Judah") functions as the subject of the writing metaphor: sin is the content being inscribed. The double-instrument metaphor (iron pen + diamond point) functions as an intensifier of permanence: the record is inscribed with the hardest possible writing tools, implying the inscription cannot be self-erased. The dual location (heart tablet + altar horns) functions to name the record's internal (heart — private inner register) and external (altars — public institutional register) locations simultaneously.

**[CHAR-14]** E — The primary anchor is Mat 26:28: "for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." The primary terms function as: (1) *"blood of the covenant"* (*to haima mou tēs diathēkēs*) — the covenant-blood functions as the ground of forgiveness; the possessive ("my blood") identifies Christ as the one whose blood establishes the mechanism; (2) *"poured out for many"* (*to peri pollōn ekchunoumenon*) — the pouring-out (present passive participle) names the act of self-offering as the forgiveness-mechanism; (3) *"for the forgiveness of sins"* (*eis aphesin hamartiōn*) — the purpose clause names the telos: all of this is for the releasing of sins. The terms function together: mechanism (blood) + act (poured out) + scope (for many) + purpose (forgiveness).

**[CHAR-15]** E — The primary anchor is Isa 43:27: "Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me." Cha.ta (*chāṭaʾ* — Qal perfect, third person masculine singular) functions as the *founding-attribution verb*: it attributes the first father's sinning as the origin-event of the present community's condition. The grammar is significant: the Qal perfect names a completed past act whose consequences are still operative ("your first father sinned" — the sinning is past and complete, but "your" indicates the present community still stands in the resulting condition). The parallel with "your mediators transgressed against me" establishes a two-stage chain: foundational ancestor + institutional reinforcers = the generational pattern.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Two primary anchors. (1) *Rom 5:19* — "by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners (*hamartōloi katestathēsan*)" — *hamartōloi* functions as the predicate-complement of *katestathēsan* (were constituted/appointed); the passive voice names the sinner-identity as received rather than achieved; the aorist passive confirms a completed past constitution-event. (2) *Gen 13:13* — "the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners (*chat.ta.im gĕdōlîm*) against the Lord" — *chat.ta.im gĕdōlîm* functions as the predicate characterisation: the agent-noun plural with the intensifier "great" describes the extreme extent of the totalised sinner-character.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Two primary anchors. (1) *Ezr 9:6* — "I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt (*ash.mah*) has mounted up to the heavens" — ash.mah functions as the subject of the mounting metaphor; the guilt-condition is named as the entity that has risen and accumulated; the verb "mounted up" (*gāḏlāh*) measures its quantity. The mounting metaphor names the accumulation dynamic of VCG-02 precisely. (2) *Lev 5:5* — "when he realizes his guilt (*yʾāšam*) in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed" — a.sham (Qal imperfect) functions as the guilt-recognition verb; its activation is the trigger for the confession that follows; the verb names the conscience's engagement event.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Three primary anchors. (1) *Gen 15:16* — "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" — a.von functions as the subject of the measurability statement; the iniquity is the entity being measured toward its threshold; the "not yet complete" (*lōʾ šālēm*) establishes the accumulation-toward-threshold mechanism. (2) *Eze 18:20* — "the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself" — a.von functions as the personal-attachment predicate; the iniquity is what adheres to the responsible individual. (3) *Isa 53:6* — "the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" — a.von functions as the object of divine placement; the collective human iniquity is the content transferred to the servant.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Three primary anchors. (1) *Psa 36:1* — "transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes" — pe.sha functions as the speaking-subject; transgression is personified as an inner voice that has taken up residence in the heart; the verse's key move is locating transgression as an internal counselling presence; (2) *Rom 4:15* — "where there is no law there is no transgression" — parabasis functions as the predicate of the conditional: law is the necessary precondition; the definitional structure reveals the law-boundary-crossing nature; (3) *Amos 1:3* — "for three transgressions of Damascus, and for four" — pe.sha functions as the counted moral-crimes of a nation; the counting formula reveals the threshold-measurement structure.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The primary anchor verse is Lev 4:2: "If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the Lord's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them." Cha.ta + bishgagah functions here as the *conditional predicate* — defining the condition under which the entire sin-offering system's individual-person provisions apply. The term governs the entire Lev 4–5 case-law structure: the "if" + the sinning-unintentionally condition opens the legal gate through which the remedial provisions flow. The term is definitional and structural: it establishes the precise inner-quality criterion (inadvertence) that triggers this specific regulatory path rather than the high-handed path (Num 15:30).

**[CHAR-20]** E — Three primary anchors. (1) *1Ch 10:13* — "Saul died for his breach of faith (*māʿal*). He broke faith (*māʿal*) with the Lord in that he did not keep the command of the Lord" — ma.al functions as both the verdict-noun ("for his breach of faith") and the accusation-verb ("He broke faith") in the same verse; the double use names the faithlessness as both the cause of death (juridical function) and the specific act (evidential function); (2) *Mal 2:14* — "though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" and "to whom you have been faithless (*bāgadtāh*)" — ba.gad functions as the predicate naming the faithlessness within the most intimate covenantal relationship; (3) *Isa 48:8* — "I knew that you would surely deal treacherously (*bāgôd tibgôd*)" — the infinitive absolute + finite verb construction (*bāgôd tibgôd*) intensifies the certainty and totality of the foreknown treachery; the doubling is the Hebrew grammar of absolute certainty.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Two primary anchors. (1) *Pro 6:14* — "with perverted heart (*tahpukôt*) devises evil, continually sowing discord" — tah.pu.khah functions as the qualifying adjective for the heart; the perverseness characterises the heart's operative condition from which the evil-devising proceeds; the heart's perverted state is the grammatical subject's inner characterisation; (2) *Eph 4:22* — "old self which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt (*phtheiromenos*) through deceitful desires" — ftheirō in the present passive participle ("being corrupted") functions as the active ongoing condition of the old self; the present tense confirms the progressive nature; the passive voice names the old self as the entity being acted upon by deceitful desires.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Three primary anchors. (1) *Psa 58:2* — "in your hearts you devise wrongs (*av.lah*); your hands deal out violence on earth" — av.lah functions as the object of the devising: it is what the heart schemes; its position as the scheming's content names it as the substance of the planned wrongdoing; (2) *Luk 16:10* — "one who is dishonest (*adikos*) in a very little is also dishonest (*adikos*) in much" — adikos functions as the character-predicate; its repetition in both clauses names dishonesty/injustice as the consistent character-property; (3) *Deu 32:4* — "without iniquity (*av.lah*), just and upright is he" — av.lah functions as the negated quality; its explicit negation establishes injustice as the standard-opposite of God's character.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The primary anchor verse is 2Sa 24:10: "But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the Lord, 'I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O Lord, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly.'" *Chatati* ("I have sinned") functions as the *confessional predicate* — the moral verdict David applies to his own act. Within the sentence, it functions as the main verb of self-accusation, followed by two supporting characterisations ("greatly in what I have done," "done very foolishly") that specify the moral quality of the named sin. The term functions as both the legal confession (naming the act as culpable) and the relational acknowledgment (naming the act against the background of David's relationship with God).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The primary anchor verse is Jer 2:35: "you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'" The term *lo chatati* ("I have not sinned") functions as: (1) *the quoted speech-act* that God declares will be judged — it is the specific verbal act that constitutes the false innocence claim; (2) *the defining inversion of confession* — the term is the exact grammatical form of the confessional chatati (*I have sinned*), negated; (3) *the grounds of judgment* — the verse makes the speaking of this negation the specific basis for the announced judgment. The term functions simultaneously as speech-act, moral verdict, and the ground of divine accountability.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The primary anchor verse is 2Ki 3:3: "Nevertheless, he clung to the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin; he did not depart from it." The term *davaq* ("clung to") functions as: (1) the *predicate of attachment* — it names the volitional relationship between Jehoram and the sinful course as an active bonding; (2) *the intensifier* — "clung to" is stronger than the standard "did not depart from," signalling an advanced stage of the refusal; (3) *the structural contrast* within the verse — "nevertheless... clung" — despite the context of other reforms (Jehoram had removed the Baal pillar — 2Ki 3:2), the clinging persists; the contrast makes the refusal more visible.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The primary anchor verse is Hos 8:11: "Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they have become to him altars for sinning." The primary term *cha.ta* (sinning — appearing twice in the verse) functions as: (1) the *purpose-marker* of the altars ("altars for sinning" — the sinning is the declared purpose of the multiplied altars, naming the habitual defection's institutional form); (2) the *productive-outcome* of the altars ("they have become to him altars for sinning" — the second occurrence names what the altars produce: more sinning). The term functions in a causal self-reinforcing structure: the sinning produces altars that produce sinning. The double appearance of the term in a single verse is unique in the corpus and evidences the self-reinforcing logic of habitual defection.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The primary anchor verse is 1Ki 16:2: "Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins." The Hiphil causative *wayaḥṭē* ("made... to sin") functions as: (1) *the specific indictment term* — the precise charge God lays against the king is the causative sinning, not merely the personal sinning; (2) *the relational qualifier* — "my people" combined with the Hiphil shows God's continuing relational claim over the community the leader has corrupted; (3) *the causal chain marker* — "made... to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins" — the Hiphil is the causal link between the leader's action and God's provocation.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The primary anchor verse is 2Ch 21:10: "So Edom revolted from the rule of Judah to this day. At that time Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had forsaken the Lord, the God of his fathers." Pa.sha functions as: (1) *the act-term naming the decisive political defection* ("revolted from the rule of"); (2) *the condition-term marking the permanent consequence* ("to this day" — the revolt is still in effect); (3) *the first element in a compound causal-consequential statement* — the revolt is named first, then its theological ground ("because he had forsaken the Lord") is given. The term thus functions as both the act-name and the consequence-marker within a theologically framed causal argument.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The primary anchor verse is Mat 15:19: "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, *slander*." Blasfēmia functions as: (1) *the final named member* of the heart-generated evil list — placed at the end, giving it climactic weight; (2) *the speech-act representative* of the entire list — while murder, adultery, and theft are acts, slander is specifically the speech-act, confirming that sinful speech carries the same moral weight as the gravest acts; (3) *the diagnostic term* — slander's presence in the list confirms that the heart's corruption reaches all the way to the mouth, making speech the diagnostic site of inner moral condition.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Taking Psa 36:1 (vc=42567 — M10b-A-VCG-02 anchor) as the primary verse: "Transgression speaks to the wicked (ra.sha) deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes." Here ra.sha functions as a dative-relational noun naming the addressee of transgression's inner speech — it is not an active subject but the characterised recipient of an inner-voice event. The function is descriptive-classifying: the verse uses ra.sha to identify the type of person to whom this inner dynamic pertains. This classifying function of ra.sha — naming the type of person for whom this is the inner condition — is representative of its dominant function across the corpus. In the Proverbs antithetical couplets (Pro 10:6, 10:11, etc.), ra.sha functions as the negative comparison-term in a moral-quality pair.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Taking Mat 7:11 (vc=14438 — VCG-02: "you who are evil, know how to give good gifts") as the primary verse for ponēros: the term functions as a predicative adjective in the second-person address ("you who are evil" — hypers ponēroi ontes) — it functions as a constitutional description of the human addressees, not a moral accusation about specific acts. The grammatical form (present participle — "being evil") is particularly significant: it is continuous, describing a state that is ongoing, not episodic. The function is diagnostic and constitutive — it identifies the constitutional state of the human hearers as the given context within which the argument about God's better giving operates. The verse's logic is a fortiori: if the evil-constitutioned humans can still give good gifts, how much more can God. ponēros here functions as the term that names the baseline anthropological condition from which the argument proceeds.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Taking Pro 3:32 (vc=1686 — VCG-02) as the primary anchor candidate: "for the devious person is an abomination to the Lord, but the upright are in his confidence." to.e.vah functions here as the predicate noun in a comparative antithetical statement — it names the relational status of the devious person before God as abomination-status. The function is diagnostic and relational: the term does not merely describe a moral quality but names the relational position of the person in relation to God. The antithetical parallel ("the upright are in his confidence") reinforces the relational nature of the term by contrasting it with the opposite relational status (intimate confidence). The function of to.e.vah in this primary verse is therefore: relational verdict (naming the status of the devious before God), diagnostic (identifying the specific inner condition that triggers the verdict — devious/crooked inner way), and antithetical (defining by contrast with its opposite).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Taking Eze 11:21 (vc=1631 — VCG-05) as the primary anchor: "those whose heart goes after their detestable things (shiq.quts) and their abominations (to.e.vah), I will bring their deeds upon their own heads." Here shiq.quts functions as the direct object of the heart's going-after — naming the idol-objects as the specific destinations of the misdirected devotional movement. to.e.vah functions as an associated category expanding on what the shiq.quts involves (they are not just detestable objects but abominations in the full divine-verdict sense). The grammatical function is object-of-devotion (shiq.quts) and verdict-category (to.e.vah) combined in a single verse. The verse's overall argument: the heart's directional faculty going after abominable objects → the deeds that result → divine judgment bringing those deeds back on the person. The terms function as the diagnostic statement of the inner condition that triggers judgment.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Taking Psa 36:4 (vc=38235 — VCG-02) as the primary anchor candidate: "He plots trouble [a.ven] while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil." Here a.ven functions as the direct object of "plots" (verbalised) — naming what is planned and produced through the scheming process. The function is: named content of the scheming act. a.ven is what the inner person is plotting; it names both the content of the plot (iniquity/trouble) and the harmful quality of the planned output. The verse's structure — plotting a.ven (inner) → setting himself in a wrong way (directional orientation) → not rejecting evil (volitional refusal) — shows a.ven at the productive heart of a three-part inner-being description. The term functions as the generative target of the cognitive-volitional scheming act.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Taking Rev 16:9 (vc=14352 — VCG-01) as the primary anchor candidate: "They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed [blasfēmeō] the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory." Here blasfēmeō functions as the main verb of the subject's active response — naming the specific verbal act (cursing God's name) that is the primary content of the sentence. The term carries the full weight of the verse's analytical disclosure: it names what the hardened will does in the moment of judgment. The function is primary-verb disclosure: the term is not background or incidental but the central predicate that defines the verse's inner-being content. The name of God as the object of the verb shows what specifically is targeted — God's name-reputation-honour is the thing the term harms.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The six primary anchors' primary terms serve six distinct grammatical-functional roles, one per characteristic: (1) Char 1 — ra.sha as descriptive-classifying dative noun in Psa 36:1 ("transgression speaks to the wicked") — the term classifies the person to whom the inner dynamic pertains; (2) Char 2 — ponēros as predicative constitutional adjective in Mat 7:11 ("you who are evil") — the term names the baseline constitutional state; (3) Char 3 — to.e.vah as predicate noun naming relational status in Pro 3:32 ("the devious person is an abomination to the Lord") — the term names the divine-relational verdict; (4) Char 4 — shiq.quts as direct object of devotional movement in Eze 11:21 ("heart goes after their detestable things") — the term names the objects of misdirected devotion; (5) Char 5 — a.ven as direct object of scheming in Psa 36:4 ("plots trouble") — the term names the content of the inner cognitive-volitional scheming act; (6) Char 6 — blasfēmeō as primary verb naming the enacted response in Rev 16:9 ("they cursed the name of God") — the term names the speech-act itself. At cluster scope: the six terms function as classifier, constitutional-state-descriptor, relational-verdict-name, devotion-object-name, scheming-content-name, and speech-act-name — collectively covering the full range of grammatical functions through which inner evil is named in Scripture.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary anchor verse for Characteristic 1 is Num 19:11 (vc_id 21481, M10c-A-VCG-07): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days." In this sentence, the ta.me adjective (H2931, "shall be unclean") functions as the predicate — the main assertion of the verse. The sentence structure is: universal subject ("whoever") + condition trigger ("touches the dead body of any person") + predicate-condition ("shall be unclean") + duration ("seven days"). The term is the primary claim of the sentence: this is what the contact produces. The argument function: it establishes death-contact as the most severe triggering event, producing the longest standard defilement duration.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The primary anchor verse for Characteristic 2 (identified at T7.2.5 below) is 2Cor 7:1 (vc_id 9329, G3436 molusmos): "let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God." Within this sentence, molusmos (defilement) functions as the object of the cleansing imperative — it is what must be removed ("from every defilement"). The term names the comprehensive condition (body and spirit) from which the person must actively cleanse themselves. The grammatical function is: object of the preposition apo (from) — the defilement is what is being moved away from in the cleansing action.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The primary anchor verse for Characteristic 3 is Eze 5:11 (vc_id 21497, H2930A, VCG-03): "therefore, as I live, declares the Lord God, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things and with all your abominations, therefore I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity." Within this sentence, ta.me (you have defiled, piel perfect) functions as the ground of the divine consequence — it is the stated reason for divine withdrawal. The grammatical function: causal premise (because you have defiled → therefore I will withdraw). The term names the completed act of defiling the sanctuary as the decisive moral event that triggers the divine response.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The primary anchor verse for Characteristic 4 is Luk 8:29 (vc_id 21297, G0169, VCG-01): "For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)" Within this verse, akathartos (in "unclean spirit") functions as the identifier of the entity being commanded out — the subject of the commanding; the spirit is named as "unclean" to establish its character as the defiling agent from which the man must be freed. The term functions as a character-qualifier justifying the command.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four primary anchors' term-functions reveal the cluster's internal grammatical logic. Characteristic 1 (Num 19:11/Lev 15:31): ta.me (H2931 adj) functions as predicate — "shall be unclean" — naming the direct consequence of the triggering event. The term is the main assertion: this is what the contact produces. Characteristic 2 (2Cor 7:1): molusmos (G3436) functions as the object of the cleansing imperative — "from every defilement" — naming what must be removed. The term is the starting-point of the movement: the condition to be left behind. Characteristic 3 (Eze 5:11): ta.me (H2930A verb) functions as the causal ground of divine consequence — "because you have defiled" — the completed act is the premise from which "therefore I will withdraw" follows. The term names the decisive moral event triggering divine response. Characteristic 4 (Luk 8:29): akathartos functions as a character-qualifier justifying the command — "he had commanded the unclean spirit" — the term identifies the entity and establishes why the command is appropriate (it is unclean). The cluster's grammatical role spectrum: predicate of consequence (Char 1) → object of cleansing (Char 2) → ground of divine response (Char 3) → character-qualifier of the commanded entity (Char 4).

questions.question_text: What literary form carries the primary verse evidence (narrative, psalm, wisdom, prophecy, epistle, apocalyptic), and what does that form require for responsible interpretation?

findings.session_b_note:
The forgiveness corpus is distributed across multiple literary forms, each requiring distinct interpretive attention:

**Narrative (Gospels — primary weight):** Luk 7:47, Mat 18:35, Mar 2:5, Mar 3:29, Mat 5:24. Narrative form requires attention to: (1) the speaker (Jesus in most cases — authoritative declaration), (2) the occasion (who is present, what has happened), (3) the narrative arc (the story is making a point beyond the individual verse). The parable of Mat 18 is embedded narrative within narrative — requiring attention to both the story-world (the characters) and the real-world application (Jesus's teaching point).

**Psalm (Psa 86:5; Psa 130:4):** Poetic and devotional form. Requires attention to: (1) the genre's address — psalms are addressed to God or about God; (2) the emotional register — psalms name inner-being states with directness; (3) the absence of systematic prose logic — meaning is carried through image and juxtaposition, not argument. The counterintuitive observation of Psa 130:4 (forgiveness → fear, not presumption) is characteristic of the Psalm form's capacity for unexpected insight.

**Prophecy (Jer 31:34):** Prophetic declaration — requires attention to: (1) the covenantal context (new covenant promise); (2) the divine-speech register ("declares the Lord"); (3) the future orientation (promise, not description of present reality). The declarative force of the verse carries the eschatological quality noted in T5.6.

**Epistle (Eph 1:7; 1Jo 1:9):** Theological argument and instruction — requires attention to: (1) the argumentative structure (Eph 1:3-14 is a single extended blessing); (2) the community context (the epistle addresses a community, not individuals); (3) the doctrinal precision (epistles systematise what narrative presents).

**Levitical law (Lev 4:20):** Legal/cultic instruction — requires attention to: (1) the procedural register (this is prescriptive, not descriptive); (2) the covenantal framework (the ritual operates within the Sinai covenant); (3) the absence of inner-being language (the cultic text does not narrate inner experience).

Narrative form requires attention to: (1) the speaker (Jesus in most cases — authoritative declaration), (2) the occasion (who is present, what has happened), (3) the narrative arc (the story is making a point beyond the individual verse). **Psalm (Psa 86:5; Psa 130:4):** Poetic and devotional form. Requires attention to: (1) the genre's address — psalms are addressed to God or about God; (2) the emotional register — psalms name inner-being states with directness; (3) the absence of systematic prose logic — meaning is carried through image and juxtaposition, not argument. The counterintuitive observation of Psa 130:4 (forgiveness → fear, not presumption) is characteristic of the Psalm form's capacity for unexpected insight.

**Prophecy (Jer 31:34):** Prophetic declaration — requires attention to: (1) the covenantal context (new covenant promise); (2) the divine-speech register ("declares the Lord"); (3) the future orientation (promise, not description of present reality). The declarative force of the verse carries the eschatological quality noted in T5.6.

**Epistle (Eph 1:7; 1Jo 1:9):** Theological argument and instruction — requires attention to: (1) the argumentative structure (Eph 1:3-14 is a single extended blessing); (2) the community context (the epistle addresses a community, not individuals); (3) the doctrinal precision (epistles systematise what narrative presents).

**Levitical law (Lev 4:20):** Legal/cultic instruction — requires attention to: (1) the procedural register (this is prescriptive, not descriptive); (2) the covenantal framework (the ritual operates within the Sinai covenant); (3) the absence of inner-being language (the cultic text does not narrate inner experience).

findings.session_b_note:
The compassion evidence spans multiple literary forms, each requiring different interpretive care:

**Gospel narrative (splanchnizō — Matt 9:36; Mark 1:41; Luke 7:13):** The primary splanchnizō evidence is narrative — biographical accounts of Jesus's inner life and actions. Narrative requires attention to: what the narrator is reporting (inner state named explicitly — unusual in ancient narrative), what follows the inner state (action — always), and what the narrative context frames as the interpretive meaning. The narrator's access to Jesus's inner state (splanchnizō) is a theological claim, not merely a psychological observation. Responsible interpretation reads the narrative's theological intent.

**Parable (Luke 10:33; 15:20; Matt 18:27):** The parable form carries splanchnizō in didactic contexts — the compassion-movement is named in parables to instruct on the nature of the kingdom, neighbourly love, and divine mercy. Parables require attention to the point of comparison: not every detail carries weight, but the splanchnizō verb in each parable is structurally central to the teaching. Luke 10:33 — the compassion is the moral criterion of the whole parable.

**Prophetic poetry (Hos 11:8; Isa 46:3; 54:8):** The primary Hebrew compassion evidence is in prophetic poetry — lyrical, imagistic, affectively charged. Prophetic poetry requires attention to: the images being deployed (womb, warmth, momentary anger vs everlasting love), the speaker (God in first person — unusually direct), and the rhetorical context (judgment about to be pronounced, then withdrawn or reframed). The visceral language of prophetic poetry is not hyperbole — it is the form most suited to conveying inner-being reality precisely because it does not reduce to propositional statement.

**Wisdom and covenant formula (Exod 34:6; Mic 6:8; Hos 6:6):** The formulaic covenant declarations and wisdom sayings carry the structural-definitional claims. These require attention to: the canonical function of the formula (Exod 34:6 cited across the canon), the imperative form of the wisdom saying (Mic 6:8 — "what does the LORD require?"), and the polemical function of Hos 6:6 (chesed over sacrifice). The formula carries more definitional weight than any single narrative instance.

findings.session_b_note:
The primary verse evidence is carried overwhelmingly by **psalmic poetry** — specifically lament psalms and wisdom psalms:

- **Lament psalms** (penitential and individual): Psa 34:18, Psa 38:8, Psa 51:17, Psa 143:3 — the contrite condition expressed and appealed to God from within the genre of individual lament. The lament form structures contrition: confession of crushed condition → appeal to God → expectation of divine response.
- **Penitential psalms**: Psa 51 is the great penitential psalm — the defining literary context for the penitential-relational mode of contrition.
- **Corporate lament**: Psa 44:19 — the community's crushed condition addressed to God.
- **Prophetic oracle**: Isa 53:5, Isa 57:15, Isa 66:2, Jer 44:10, Jer 46:5 — prophetic declarations that embed contrition-vocabulary in proclamations about God's character and Israel's condition.

The literary context reveals that contrition is pre-eminently a **psalmic/liturgical condition** — the inner posture characteristic of Israel's worship life, specifically its lament and penitential tradition. This is not a philosophical concept but a lived inner-being reality expressed in the poetry of prayer and encounter with God.

findings.session_b_note:
The fellowship evidence is carried across multiple literary forms:

**Epistle (1Jo 1:3, 2Cor 6:14, Phili 3:10, 2Pe 1:4):** The majority of the koinōnia evidence is in epistolary form — letters written to specific communities addressing their particular circumstances. Responsible interpretation requires attention to the communal context: these are not abstract theological propositions but pastoral directives for actual communities.

**Psalm (Psa 119:63, Psa 58:5):** Wisdom-devotional poetry. The companionship language of Psa 119:63 is part of an acrostic psalm of sustained devotion. Responsible interpretation attends to the cumulative, repetitive character of the psalm — it is not making a single logical claim but rehearsing sustained commitment.

**Wisdom literature (Ecc 4:10, Ecc 9:4, Pro 20:30, Job 16:4):** Observational wisdom form. These verses are empirical observations about how life works, not direct theological propositions. Responsible interpretation recognises the observational character: *this is how it goes* rather than *this is the theological definition*.

**Prophecy (Isa 53:5, Isa 1:23, Isa 47:9, Hos 4:17, Eze 37:19, Jer 13:23, Mal 2:14):** Prophetic address — often accusation, lament, or promise. Responsible interpretation attends to the prophetic *direction* of each verse (accusation, comfort, promise) and does not flatten them into neutral descriptive statements.

**Narrative-argument (Mat 23:30):** Controversy dialogue. The Pharisees' claim is part of a complex rhetorical exchange. Responsible interpretation reads the claim in its polemical context.

findings.session_b_note: The anchor verse corpus spans multiple literary forms, each with distinct interpretive requirements: (1) Prophetic address (Mic 6:8; Eze 36:31): legal covenant-speech, including divine accusation and requirement. Mic 6:8 functions as the verdict of a covenant lawsuit (rib) — God's requirement is stated as the standard against which Israel's failure is measured. Requires: attention to covenantal frame; the "requirement" is not a new imposition but a restoration of what was always known. (2) Wisdom sayings (Pro 15:16; 16:32): comparative instruction for individual moral formation. Requires: attention to the rhetorical purpose of persuasion toward wise living; the better-than structure is pedagogical. (3) Psalms of lament and praise (Psa 34:8; 73:28; 34:8 — crisis context; Psa 119:68 — torah psalm): personal address and corporate declaration. Requires: attention to the experiential context from which the declaration arises. (4) NT epistolary (Rom 2:4; 11:22; Gal 5:22; Col 3:12): doctrinal instruction and paraenesis. Requires: attention to the theological argument in which the verse is embedded. (OBS-067-OBS-027, OBS-067-OBS-042, SBF-067-Q042)

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-007: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two language…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two languages with distinct semantic ranges, a full root-family analysis, a NT coinage (agathōsunē), and a comprehensive vocabulary arc from phenomenological breadth (H2896A) to virtuous precision (agathōsunē) to relational precision (chrēstotēs — Q&A-177). The lexical evidence is rich. Literary: the primary anchor (Mic 6:8) uniquely combines revelatory and covenantal-obligation frames with an internal tri-fold structure that no other verse replicates (Q&A-183); the anchor corpus spans prophetic, wisdom, psalmic, and epistolary forms across multiple contextual settings (Q&A-181). Human science: virtue ethics is the closest parallel framework, with the critical divergence at the source of goodness (divine gift vs natural achievement — Q&A-186). Constraints: NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms limit the LXX analysis (Q&A-175); LSJ data is absent. The evidential foundation is strong at the lexical-semantic and verse-literary levels; it is constrained at the LXX-continuity and human-science elaboration levels. This asymmetry is itself an analytic finding — it identifies where future investigation would most strengthen the registry's evidential base.

findings.session_b_note: Love's evidence base spans every major literary form: (a) **Wisdom/Proverb** (Pro 10:12, 27:6): requires attention to the comparative and aphoristic structure — proverbs describe patterns, not absolutes; (b) **Psalm** (Psa 63:3, 16:11, 97:10): requires reading as first-person prayer/meditation — the psalmist's inner orientation, not universal dogma; (c) **Prophetic oracle** (Jer 31:3, Eze 16:8, Isa 49:15): the love-language is covenantal and often metaphorical (marital imagery); responsible reading holds the metaphorical dimension; (d) **Epistle** (1Cor 13, 1Jo 4, Rom 5): the most theologically discursive form — allows propositional claims about love's nature; (e) **Gospel narrative** (Joh 3:16, Luk 7:38, Joh 15:13): love embedded in narrative events requiring attention to the narrative's argument; (f) **Song/Poem** (Song of Songs): erotic love in a canonical wisdom-poem; the allegorical interpretive tradition and the literal reading must both be held. No single form dominates — love's evidence is multi-formal.

findings.finding_value: T7 reveals that the fellowship vocabulary has the widest semantic arc of any characteristic in the programme: from tabernacle seam (physical construction) through wound (somatic joining) through companionship (relational) through moral complicity (evaluative) through ontological divine nature participation. This breadth is encoded in the root-level architecture (chavar — the joining logic applied universally). The two primary anchor verses (2Pe 1:4 and 1Jo 1:3) are complementary in perspective: 2Pe 1:4 is the vertical-ontological statement (human participating in divine nature); 1Jo 1:3 is the relational-structural statement (horizontal derived from vertical). The LSJ gap (T7.1.8) is an acknowledged data limitation — the classical background of koinōnia is unavailable from this registry's data, which means the NT's transformation of a Hellenistic civic-philosophical term into a theological term cannot be traced from this evidence base.

findings.finding_value: T7 reveals a vocabulary architecture that is unique in the programme: two distinct lexical domains (H5545 salach — divine exclusive; G0863 aphiēmi — shared divine-human) that together make a structural theological claim. The cross-testament vocabulary development (LXX applying aphiēmi to render salach; NT extending aphiēmi to commanded human forgiveness) carries the programme's clearest lexical theological claim: human forgiveness is structurally shaped by divine forgiveness, named by the same vocabulary. The grammatical analysis (Niphal passive — "they shall be forgiven"; active Qal — God forgives) precisely encodes the act-structure: divine act → creaturely received status. The primary anchor trio (Jer 31:34, Psa 86:5, Luk 7:47) spans three literary forms (prophetic-eschatological, wisdom/psalm, Synoptic narrative) and three analytical registers (eschatological promise, divine character-statement, inner-being consequence). T7 synthesis: the forgiveness vocabulary is the most theologically structured in the current review set — its cross-testament development carries an explicit structural claim visible at the lexical level.

findings.finding_value: T4's relational directions map onto T7's literary forms. The God-to-human direction (T4.1 — dominant) is carried by the cultic-legal corpus (H5545 Niphal — God forgives, people receive), the prophetic corpus (Jer 31:34 — divine forgiveness promise), and the apostolic letter corpus (Eph 1:7 — through his blood). The human-to-God direction (T4.2 — seeking) is carried by the penitential psalm corpus (Psa 130, Dan 9) and the Synoptic narrative (1Jo 1:9). findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.finding_value: T3's perceptive-trigger and affect-mechanism findings are grounded in T7's primary anchor evidence. The Synoptic pattern of splanchnizō — always triggered by sight, always preceding action — is the textual ground for T3.1's finding (compassion is perceptively dependent) and T3.4's finding (affect is the mechanism of movement). T7's argument structure finding (Matt 9:36 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response) is the evangelist's literary expression of T3.10's analytical claim (compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action). T7's framework divergences (human science frameworks failing at sovereignty, cross-boundary extension, and purposive suffering) correspond to the three areas where T3's faculty analysis finds its most distinctive results: the sovereign freedom of divine compassion exceeds the natural automaticity of empathic response; the cross-boundary extension exceeds natural empathic scope; the purposive suffering (T5.4/T5.5) requires the teleological frame that T7.3 identifies.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-025: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-le…
findings.finding_value: T4's most analytically distinctive finding (the vocabulary encodes the two-sided grace-circuit in a single root: chen/chanan for giving; tachanum/techinah for seeking) is T7's most significant root-level finding. T7.1 confirms: the chen root family embeds both the giving side (chen — favour, chanan — to be gracious) and the receiving-seeking side (tachanum, techinah — supplication) in a single etymological family. This is unique in the programme's vocabulary data: no other characteristic has the giving-side and receiving-side vocabulary built from the same root. T4's relational architecture and T7's lexical analysis are the relational and lexical descriptions of the same structural reality — that grace is constitutively a two-sided circuit whose two sides are inseparable at the root level.

findings.session_b_note: The covenant vocabulary spans four primary literary forms in the data: (1) Legal/contractual narrative (Torah — Exo 24, Deu 7, Gen 9): the covenant is made in narrative context with formulaic legal-treaty elements (terms, signs, witnesses, sanctions). Responsible interpretation requires attention to the ancient Near Eastern treaty context and the formal elements of covenant-making, not merely the spiritual meaning. (2) Prophetic oracle (Jer 31:31-34; Isa 54; 59): the new covenant promise is in the form of divine oracle — first-person divine declaration. Requires treating these as authoritative divine speech-acts, not merely poetic expressions. (3) Epistle and theological argument (Heb, Gal, 2 Cor): the NT covenant material is embedded in theological argumentation. Hebrews especially builds a sustained typological argument from OT texts. Responsible interpretation requires following the logical-theological argument, not proof-texting individual verses. (4) Liturgical (1 Cor 11:25; Mat 26:28): the Eucharistic institution narrative is liturgical-formular. Responsible interpretation requires reading within the covenant-meal tradition, not as isolated doctrine.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-034-025: T4 establishes that covenant's relational interfaces are carried through specific acts — oath-taking, blood-shedding, covenant-meal participation, circumcision. T7 establishes that these acts are carr…
findings.finding_value: T4 establishes that covenant's relational interfaces are carried through specific acts — oath-taking, blood-shedding, covenant-meal participation, circumcision. T7 establishes that these acts are carried by specific literary forms — legal-narrative (covenant-making), prophetic oracle (new covenant promise), liturgical (Eucharist), and epistle-argument (Hebrews). The T4 × T7 synthesis: the relational acts of covenant (T4) are embedded in and shaped by their literary contexts (T7). The covenantal meal (T4 receiving — Q&A-113) is not merely a relational act but a liturgical-formular act (T7). The prophetic oracle of the new covenant (Jer 31:31-34) is not merely a T4 divine-to-human act of declaration but is embedded in the prophetic genre's authority structures (T7). The literary form analysis (T7) provides the interpretive framework within which the relational interface data (T4) must be read. Responsible interpretation of the covenantal acts requires attention to their literary embedding.

findings.session_b_note: (P1 — contextual settings) Psalmic lament and praise (dominant for chesed); narrative of covenant relationships (Ruth, Genesis, Samuel-Kings); prophetic indictment (Hos 6:6, Mic 6:8); NT epistolary instruction (Eph 4:32, Col 3:12, Rom 2:4). This verse asserts the permanence and inexhaustibility of divine kindness in the context of maximum suffering and loss. It reveals what no other verse reveals: chesed is not contingent on circumstances or human faithfulness — it persists when everything else has failed. Every other kindness statement in the evidence is a specific expression of this; Lam 3:22 is the structural foundation.

findings.session_b_note: The anchor verse corpus spans four literary forms. (1) Narrative (Gen 12:7, Gen 15:18, Gen 29:33, Job 1:21): responsible interpretation requires attention to plot and character — the giving is embedded in a specific relational and historical moment. (2) Prophecy (Isa 61:3, Isa 50:6, Hos 11:8, Hos 13:11, Jer 12:7, Jer 13:16): responsible interpretation requires attention to rhetorical address and the distinction between divine speech and prophetic interpretation. The first-person divine speeches ("I gave," "How can I give you up") require particular care about the nature of divine inner-being language. (3) Wisdom/divine speech (Job 38:36, Job 1:21): responsible interpretation requires attention to the dramatic frame — Job's blessing is within a frame where Satan has made a claim, and God's question from the whirlwind is within a legal disputation. (4) Liturgical/prayer (Neh 9:20): responsible interpretation requires attention to the retrospective narrative form — this is communal confession of divine faithfulness, not direct reportage. The diversity of literary forms means no single interpretive lens covers the whole corpus.

Five forms: legal text (Lev 19:17, Deu 19:4, 19:11, Num 35:20), narrative (Gen 37:4-8, Gen 27:41, 2Sa 13:15), Psalm/lament (Psa 25:19, 69:4, 109:3-5, 139:21-22), wisdom (Pro 10:12, 10:18, 26:24-26, 8:13), and prophetic (Isa 1:14, Amos 5:10-15, Hos 9:7-8). Each form requires distinct interpretive discipline: legal precision (the term operates as a legal criterion), narrative tracking (hatred develops through plot), lament (first-person testimony of receiving hatred), wisdom (aphoristic compression of observed patterns), and prophetic (divine address in covenantal context).
