(1) Distress-prayer argument (M03-D-VCG-01): Premise — I am in distress; Premise — God is a present help in distress; Conclusion — I will call on God; Counter-evidence — God hears and delivers. This is a consequential argument: the distress's reality implies prayer's necessity; the covenantal relationship implies God's responsiveness. (2) Godly grief argument (M03-C-VCG-02): Premise — grief caused by truth about sin; Premise — grief of this quality is godly; Conclusion — godly grief produces repentance and moral reformation. This is a qualitative argument distinguishing worldly grief (leads to death) from godly grief (leads to salvation — 2Cor 7:10).

**[CHAR-1]** E — The dominant logical structure is: **Because God has done X → therefore exult in him.** Psa 48:11 — "Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments" (causal: judgments → exultation). Joe 2:23 — "Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God, for he has given the early rain" (causal: God's gift → commanded exultation). Isa 25:9 — "we have waited for him, that he might save us... let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation" (inference: salvation received → exultation follows). The characteristic is evidence-based in its argument: exultation is called for by the facts of God's acts, not as an arbitrary emotional demand.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Several key argument structures: (1) **Because God has done X, therefore rejoice** — Deu 16:11 (because God has blessed you); Psa 126:3 (because God has done great things for us → we are glad); Joe 2:23 (because God has given rain → rejoice); (2) **Rejoice because your reward is eschatological, not present** — Mat 5:12 (rejoice under persecution because your reward is great in heaven — the Joy is grounded in an eschatological reality, not the present circumstances); (3) **Joy is the goal of divine action** — Psa 85:6 (revive us → that your people may rejoice in you — Joy as the telos of revival); (4) **My joy is your joy** — Joh 15:11; 17:13 — the argument that Christ's own Joy is intended to be fully in the disciples; (5) **Count trials as Joy** — Jas 1:2 — the argument that trials, when rightly evaluated, yield Joy (through the tested faith → endurance → completeness chain).

**[CHAR-7]** E — (1) **Jas 1:2–4**: Command (count trials as joy) → grounds (faith-testing → steadfastness → completeness); (2) **1Pe 1:6–8**: State (you rejoice) ↔ parallel (though grieved) → purpose (tested faith → proved genuine → praise/glory/honour at Christ's revelation); (3) **Mat 5:12**: Command (rejoice and be glad) → grounds (great reward in heaven; the prophets were persecuted similarly); (4) **1Pe 4:13**: Conditional command (rejoice insofar as sharing Christ's sufferings) → purpose (that you may also rejoice at glory's revelation); (5) **Heb 12:2**: Example (Christ endured the cross) → mechanism (for the joy set before him) → result (seated at the right hand). The dominant argument structure across all five is: **command or description → eschatological grounds → eschatological goal**.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Key argument structures: (1) **Because God is good, therefore praise** — ki-tov formula (Psa 100:5; 106:1; 136:1) — the logical structure is character → commanded response; (2) **A is better than B because A has quality X** — wisdom-comparative form (Pro 16:8 — a little with righteousness better than great revenue with injustice; Pro 8:11 — wisdom better than jewels) — the argument evaluates competing goods against a standard of genuine value; (3) **This conduct is not good, therefore it is condemned** — the lo-tov verdicts (Pro 17:26; 18:5 etc.) — the standard of goodness is the premise; the falling-short is the condemnation; (4) **God's good promises have not failed, therefore trust** — Jos 21:45 — the historical evidence of promise-fulfilment grounds present and future trust; (5) **Blessedness is declared to the one who has faith counted as righteousness** — makarismos argument (Rom 4:6–9) — declarative logic: status is assigned by divine declaration, not achieved.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Key argument structures: (1) **Delight condition → divine response** — Psa 37:4 (delight yourself in the Lord → he will give you desires); Num 14:8 (if the Lord delights in us → he will bring us to the land); Isa 58:14 (call the Sabbath a delight → you shall take delight in the Lord → God exalts); (2) **God's inner character → God's action** — Jer 9:24 (I delight in these things → understand and know me); Mic 7:18 (delights in steadfast love → pardon iniquity); Eze 18:23 (no pleasure in death → so turn and live); (3) **Isa 53:10 — divine delight as atonement mechanism**: it was the Lord's will to crush him → his soul makes an offering → he sees offspring → the will of the Lord prospers; (4) **Negated Delight → judgment** — Isa 65:12; 66:4 (chose what I did not delight in → sword); Heb 10:38 (if he shrinks back → my soul has no pleasure); (5) **Law-Delight → formation** — Psa 1:2 (delight → meditation → like a tree planted by water).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Key argument structures: (1) **Wisdom → Pleasure** — Pro 2:10 (wisdom enters heart → knowledge pleasant to soul); Pro 3:17 (wisdom's ways = pleasantness — definitional equivalence); (2) **Correct worship → divine Pleasure** — Gen 8:21 (offering → God smells → God resolves); Lev 1:9 (entrails washed, fully burned → pleasing aroma to Lord); the logical structure is: proper action → produced quality → divine receptive state; (3) **Better-than evaluation** — M04-K-VCG-03's comparatives: X (modest moral quality) > Y (abundant material goods) — the argument structure of wisdom's evaluative logic applied to Pleasure; (4) **Covenant faithfulness → pleasantness of years** — Job 36:11 (listen and serve God → complete days in prosperity → years in pleasantness).

**[CHAR-6]** E — Key argument structures: (1) **Incomparability → Wonder** — Exo 15:11 ("who is like you… doing wonders?") — incomparability as the logical ground for Wonder; (2) **Remembering → not forgetting → faithfulness** — Neh 9:17 and Psa 78 provide the reverse argument: not-remembering wonders → rebellion; therefore remembering wonders → faithfulness (implied); (3) **Wondrous acts → therefore my soul keeps them** — Psa 119:129 (the wonderfulness of testimonies as the logical ground for the soul's obedience); (4) **Nothing too hard for the Lord → therefore pray** — Gen 18:14; Jer 32:17, 27 — God's unlimited wonder-capacity as the logical ground for petitionary prayer; (5) **Wonder upon wonder → wisdom of the wise shall perish** — Isa 29:14 — escalating wonder as the logical consequence of human wisdom's inadequacy.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Three dominant argument structures span the cluster: (1) **"Because God has done X → therefore respond with characteristic Y"** — the causal-responsive structure for Exultation (Joe 2:23), Joy (Deu 16:11), Gladness (ki-tov formula), and Wonder (Psa 107's refrain); (2) **"Characteristic X → produces consequence Y"** — the formative-production structure for Delight (Psa 37:4; 1:2), Suffering-Joy (Jas 1:2–4), and Wonder (Psa 119:129 — "therefore my soul keeps them"); (3) **"X is better than Y"** — the wisdom-comparative structure for Gladness (M04-L-VCG-03) and Pleasure (M04-K-VCG-03). The most theologically significant argument structure: **Isa 53:10's cha.phets** — "it was the will of the Lord to crush him" — where divine Delight is the operative logical principle of the atonement. No other single verse in the cluster places the cluster's characteristics in as central a logical role in the mechanics of salvation as Isa 53:10 places divine Delight.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Several logical structures recur. (1) **Trust → protection from shame** (Psa 22:5; 31:1; Rom 5:5; 9:33; 10:11): the argument form is: *because one trusts/believes, shame will not overtake*. The logical structure is conditional: trust is the condition; shame-protection is the consequence. (2) **Sin → shame as judgment** (M07-B-VCG-03: Pro 3:35; 6:33; Jer 2:26): the argument form is: *because one has sinned/acted foolishly, shame follows*. The logical structure is moral-consequence: failure is the antecedent; disgrace is the consequent. (3) **Shame → gateway to knowledge** (Eze 43:10-11): the argument form is: *if Israel is ashamed, then the design will be disclosed*. The logical structure is conditional gateway: shame is the necessary condition for the disclosure.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Dominant argument form in VCG-03: if pride (inner disposition of self-exaltation), then disgrace (enforced downward movement) — this is divine law. Pro 11:2 is the compressed form. The Isa 2 series expands it: the Lord's day targets all proud and lofty, bringing them low, so the Lord alone is exalted. Logical structure: moral necessity — the proud over-reach of standing inevitably attracts the corrective action of the one who alone has absolute standing.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary literary forms: parable (Luk 18:2-4 — the unjust judge); epistle (Rom 2:23; 2Cor 6:8; Jam 2:6; 1Cor 11:4-5); narrative (Joh 8:49). The parable form (Luk 18) uses the character of the dishonoring judge as a contrast-figure — his absent-regard makes the point precisely by its absence. Primary anchor: Joh 8:49 (vc=35000) — "I honor my Father, and you dishonor me" — the most compressed, relational, and personally directed expression of CHAR-3 in the corpus, revealing worth-denial as a relational act directed at a specific person in a specific exchange. This verse uniquely reveals worth-denial as a personal relational act within a face-to-face exchange, where the standard (honouring the Father) and the violation (dishonoring the Son) are simultaneously named.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Dominant argument form: if conduct violates the moral standard (as confirmed by God's sight or created order), then it is shameful — and its shamefulness is itself a reason for renouncing it. 2Cor 4:2's argument: we renounce disgraceful ways -> we commend ourselves to everyone's conscience in the sight of God. The logic is moral-calibration: shameful = cannot bear God's sight -> therefore renounce.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The dominant argument form in VCG-01: if one despises a fellow believer, one despises one whom God has welcomed (Rom 14:3 — "God has welcomed him"). The logic is worth-grounding in divine acceptance: the worth that contempt denies is the worth God has already assigned. For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God (Rom 14:10) — the eschatological accountability reverses the contempt-er's assumption of superiority.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The dominant argument form: if innocence is present (heart-integrity + hand-cleanness), then approach to God is appropriate and enabled. Gen 20:5-6: Abimelech claims innocence -> God confirms it. Psa 26:6: innocence claimed through hand-washing -> approach to altar enabled. The inverse argument: if innocence-capacity is absent (Hos 8:5), then approach to God is blocked. The logic is moral prerequisite: innocence is the condition that the covenant relationship with God requires of the person.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's dominant argument forms correspond to three primary logical structures. (1) Trust produces shame-protection: the Psalm supplication pattern and its NT echo ("the one who trusts will not be put to shame" — Rom 9:33; 10:11) names God's protective commitment toward those who rely on him (Chars 1, 5). (2) Pride produces disgrace: "when pride comes, then comes disgrace" (Pro 11:2; Char 2) and the Isa 2 series name the moral law connecting inner pride to enforced abasement. (3) Innocence enables approach: "I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar" (Psa 26:6; Char 6) names the inner moral condition that makes relational access to God possible. These three argument-forms together constitute M07's core theological logic: the shame-field is governed by a moral-relational order in which trust in God protects, pride invites correction, and innocence enables approach.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Four argument structures are evidenced. First, causal-conditional (Deu 8:14, vc=34223, M08-A1-VCG-01): premise — prosperity is received; mechanism — heart is lifted up; conclusion — God is forgotten. The argument presupposes that CHAR-1 is the inner mechanism that converts received blessing into spiritual displacement of God. Second, structural wisdom law (Pro 16:18, vc=34073, M08-A1-VCG-03): premise — CHAR-1 (haughty spirit/pride) is present; conclusion — destruction/fall follows necessarily. The argument is a structural observation stated as an invariant pattern with no exception clause. Third, divine-prerogative declaration (Psa 75:6–7, vc=34301, vc=34230, M08-A4-VCG-05): premise — lifting up does not originate from east, west, or wilderness (i.e., from any human direction); conclusion — God alone executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another. The argument makes CHAR-1 structurally impossible as a legitimate act: if exaltation is exclusively God's prerogative, then self-exaltation is a prerogative-usurpation with no valid basis. Fourth, structural opposition (Jam 4:6, vc=33931, M08-A4-VCG-01): premise — God opposes the proud; premise — God gives grace to the humble; conclusion — arrogance and humility produce structurally opposite divine responses. The argument frames CHAR-1 as determinative of the divine relational response.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Three argument structures are evidenced. First, conditional-judicial (Deu 17:12, vc=34110, M08-B-VCG-02): if-condition — the man presumes to disobey the appointed judge; consequence — he shall die; purpose — "so you shall purge the evil from Israel." The argument combines diagnostic criterion + consequence + social-purification purpose. Second, structural wisdom law (Pro 11:2, vc=34109; Pro 13:10, vc=34113, M08-B-VCG-02): premise — CHAR-2 is present; invariant conclusion — disgrace follows (Pro 11:2) / strife comes (Pro 13:10). Third, intercessory prayer (Psa 19:13, vc=34095, M08-B-VCG-02): premise — presumptuous sins seek dominion over the will; request — divine restraint ("keep back your servant"); goal — blamelessness. The argument reveals CHAR-2 as an inner dominating force requiring external (divine) restraint.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three argument structures. First, received-goods argument (1Cor 4:7, vc=33871, M08-C-VCG-01): premise — everything you have was received; conclusion — boasting as if it were self-generated is logically false. This is the most formally tight argument against CHAR-3: it grounds the condemnation in ontological fact (all goods are received) rather than merely in moral prohibition. Second, elective-design argument (1Cor 1:27–31, vc=33877/33878, M08-C-VCG-01/03): God chose the weak to shame the strong in order to eliminate human boasting and redirect it to the Lord. Third, boundary argument (2Cor 10:13, vc=33888, M08-C-VCG-02): Paul limits his boasting to the sphere God assigned him — the argument is that legitimate self-commendation has God-defined boundaries that the self must not exceed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Three argument structures. First, contrastive structural law (1Cor 8:1, vc=33935, M08-D-VCG-01): premise — knowledge without love; conclusion — inflation (CHAR-4) results; alternative — love produces building-up. The argument implies a structural law: cognitive goods processed without love inevitably inflate; with love they build. Second, qualification-conditional (1Ti 3:6, vc=33924, M08-D-VCG-02): if a new convert is given leadership → he may become conceited → and fall into the devil's condemnation. The qualification ("recent convert") is the diagnostic criterion — the argument uses formation-status as the risk variable. Third, God-measure standard (Rom 12:3, vc=60866, M08-D-VCG-02): premise — God has assigned each person a measure of faith; command — do not exceed that measure in cognitive self-assessment; alternative — think soberly according to that measure.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Three argument structures. First, covenantal conditional (Lev 26:19, vc=33982, M08-E-VCG-01): if-condition — Israel walks contrary to God; consequence — "I will break the pride of your power." The argument grounds God's breaking of CHAR-5 in covenantal violation — power-pride is the inner symptom of the violation; breaking it is the covenantal consequence. Second, prophetic reversal argument (Eze 30:6, vc=33996; Jer 49:16, vc=34167; Obd 3, vc=65674): premise — the nation holds structural height/power; declaration — God will bring it down. The argument rests on the contrast between present structural height and its coming reversal — the very structural goods that generate CHAR-5 will be removed. Third, pastoral charge (1Ti 6:17, vc=60878, M08-E-VCG-02): premise — God richly provides everything; command — do not be haughty; alternative — be generous and ready to share. The argument grounds the anti-CHAR-5 command in God's role as the actual provider of all structural goods.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison reveals four dominant argument structures across M08. First, structural wisdom law (Pro 16:18: "pride goes before destruction" — CHAR-1/CHAR-2): premise → invariant causal consequence. Second, received-goods argument (1Cor 4:7: "what do you have that you did not receive?" — CHAR-3/CHAR-4): ontological premise (all goods are received) → the boasting or inflation is logically false. Third, divine-prerogative declaration (Psa 75:6–7: "it is God who executes judgment, putting down and lifting up" — CHAR-1; Rom 12:3: "each according to the measure God has assigned" — CHAR-4): God's role as the only legitimate exalter or measure-giver → pride is a prerogative-usurpation. Fourth, prophetic reversal (Lev 26:19; Eze 30:6; Jer 49:16 — CHAR-5; Mal 4:1 — CHAR-2): present pride → divinely-enacted reversal. The cluster-synthesis: M08's primary argument types are the causal-consequence law, the received-goods ontological argument, the divine-prerogative declaration, and the prophetic reversal — four structurally distinct but theologically convergent forms of establishing that pride is disordered.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Three key logical structures are evidenced. (1) Rom 1:24 (VCG-02) — consequential logic: because they suppressed truth and rejected God (premise) → therefore God gave them up to impurity (conclusion). The premise is prior human moral defection; the conclusion is judicial release into deepened defilement. (2) Rom 6:19 (VCG-02) — analogical-imperative logic: just as you once were slaves to impurity (prior state) → so now present yourselves as slaves to righteousness (new calling). The argument uses the prior condition as the rhetorical measure for understanding the new calling. (3) 2Cor 7:1 (VCG-03) — promissory-imperative logic: since we have these promises (premise: divine promise of dwelling) → let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement (imperative: the appropriate response). The divine promise grounds and motivates the purification call. (4) Eph 5:5 (VCG-04) — definitional logic: everyone who is impure is an idolater (definition) → has no inheritance in the kingdom (consequence). The impure inner state is definitionally equivalent to idolatry, producing the consequence of exclusion.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three key logical structures. (1) Eze 5:11 (VCG-03) — causal consequence: because you have defiled my sanctuary (premise) → therefore I will withdraw (consequence). The corporate act of defilement produces the divine response as a logical-covenantal consequence. (2) Eze 20:43 (VCG-02) — temporal-eschatological sequence: in that place (the future restoration) → you shall remember (temporal trigger) → you shall loathe yourselves (consequence). The memory produces the affect. (3) Zec 13:1 (VCG-05) — promissory: on that day (eschatological marker) → a fountain shall be opened (divine provision) → to cleanse from sin and uncleanness (result). The divine eschatological act addresses the accumulated corporate defilement.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Three key logical structures. (1) Mar 1:27 (VCG-03) — indicative-amazement: "he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him" — the spirits' obedience (premise) from which the community infers superior authority (conclusion). (2) Mat 10:1 (VCG-03) — commission-authority: Jesus gave them authority (premise) → to cast out unclean spirits and heal (commissioned action) — authority precedes and enables action. (3) Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 (VCG-02) — consequential warning: when the spirit is expelled (condition) → it seeks re-entry → if it returns and finds the house empty (condition) → the final state is worse (conclusion) — warning that expulsion without positive filling produces a worse outcome.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four characteristics' key argument structures reveal the cluster's logical range. Characteristic 1: casuistic conditional (if X contact → then Y condition → for Z duration → must undergo R remedy; or: if unclean + refuses remedy → cut off from assembly). The logic is case-based: specific condition triggers specific consequence. Characteristic 2: consequential (Rom 1:24 — prior sin → God gives up to impurity); analogical-imperative (Rom 6:19 — prior slavery to impurity :: new calling to righteousness); promissory-imperative (2Cor 7:1 — divine promise grounds cleansing call); definitional (Eph 5:5 — impure = idolater → excluded from inheritance). Characteristic 3: causal-consequence (Eze 5:11 — because defiled sanctuary → therefore divine withdrawal); temporal-eschatological (Eze 20:43 — in the future → you shall remember → you shall loathe); promissory (Zec 13:1 — on that day → fountain opened → to cleanse). Characteristic 4: indicative-amazement (Mar 1:27 — spirits obey → community infers authority); commission-authority (Mat 10:1 — authority given → casting out enabled); consequential-warning (Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 — spirit expelled → seeks re-entry → worse final state). The cluster's logical range: casuistic (Char 1) → consequential/definitional (Char 2) → causal and promissory (Char 3) → indicative and commissional (Char 4). The defilement domain employs the full logical toolkit of biblical argumentation.

questions.question_text: What contextual setting carries the primary verse evidence (judicial, liturgical, covenantal, communal, eschatological), and what does that setting show?

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence is distributed across multiple contextual settings:

**Judicial (Mar 2:5-7; Mat 18:21-35; Mar 3:29):** Forgiveness operates in a legal-moral framework — debts, guilt, penalty. The judicial setting reveals forgiveness as a legal act: the cancellation of a legitimate charge. The authority question (Mar 2:7 — "who can forgive sins but God alone?") is explicitly judicial.

**Liturgical (Lev 4:20; Num 15:25; group 5379-001):** The OT atonement context is liturgical — the prescribed ritual produces forgiveness as its outcome. The liturgical setting reveals forgiveness as covenantally mediated — it comes through the prescribed form of worship, not outside it.

**Covenantal (Jer 31:34; group 5379-003):** The new covenant promise is the covenantal setting. Forgiveness is embedded in the structure of the covenant relationship — it is what God promises to his covenant people as the foundation of the new arrangement. The covenantal setting reveals forgiveness as structurally foundational, not episodic.

**Communal (Mat 18:21-35; Luk 17:3-4; Mar 11:25):** The horizontal forgiveness commands operate in community — "your brother," repeated offence within a community, prayer as a communal practice. The communal setting reveals forgiveness as the relational glue of community life — without it, community breaks down under the weight of accumulated offence.

**Eschatological (Jer 31:34; Mar 3:29):** The new covenant promise and the permanent outer limit both carry eschatological register. The covenantal setting becomes eschatological when the permanence and finality of the declaration are at issue.

findings.session_b_note:
The primary verse evidence is distributed across four major contextual settings:

**Covenantal-crisis setting (Hos 11:8; Isa 54:8; Lam 3:22; Joel 2:13):** The deepest Hebrew compassion evidence arises in contexts of covenantal breach and exile — the moment of maximum relational rupture between God and Israel. The setting reveals that compassion operates most powerfully and is most clearly defined at the point of relationship's greatest strain. Divine compassion is not primarily experienced in stable covenantal peace but in the moment of judgment, exile, and potential abandonment. This contextual setting gives the compassion vocabulary its extraordinary theological depth: it is forged in crisis.

**Healing and restoration setting (Mark 1:41; Matt 20:34; Luke 7:13; Matt 9:36):** The primary Synoptic evidence arises in encounters between Jesus and those in acute physical, spiritual, or material need. The setting reveals that compassion is the characteristic most directly responsive to human need and suffering as it presents itself in ordinary encounter. This is not the compassion of crisis-and-exile but of immediate, perceptive response to the person in front of the compassionate person.

**Parable and didactic setting (Luke 10:33; 15:20; Matt 18:27):** Compassion appears in parable to instruct on the nature of divine action (prodigal father), moral duty (Good Samaritan), and eschatological warning (unforgiving servant). The didactic setting reveals that compassion is not merely a natural emotional response but a moral norm — it is what is taught, modelled, and required.

**Community and epistle setting (1 Pet 3:8; Heb 4:15; 1 Cor 12:26; Heb 10:34):** The NT epistle evidence carries compassion in the context of community formation and Christological grounding. The setting reveals that compassion is a community-constituting virtue and a Christological reality — not merely a private feeling but a shared inner quality that shapes the community's corporate inner life.

findings.session_b_note:
The dominant contextual setting is **liturgical and covenantal**:

- **Liturgical**: Psa 51:17 explicitly displaces ritual sacrifice — the liturgical system is the frame against which contrition is defined. The broken heart replaces the burnt offering as the acceptable liturgical offering. The context is the worship encounter between the person and God.
- **Covenantal**: All penitential-relational instances occur within the Israel-God covenant framework (Psa 34, 51, Jer 44:10 — covenant failure). The contrite condition is the inner-being expression of covenant faithfulness or its restoration after failure.
- **Judicial**: Jer 44:10 has judicial overtones — the people have not observed God's law (a judicial framing of covenant). The context of Isa 57:15 and 66:2 is prophetic pronouncement carrying authoritative (quasi-judicial) weight.
- **Communal**: Psa 44:19 is corporate; Isa 53:5 produces communal outcomes (peace and healing for the community).

The primary setting is liturgical-covenantal. Contrition is the inner-being condition proper to covenantal worship — the posture in which the covenant member approaches the covenant God.

findings.session_b_note:
The fellowship evidence spans multiple contextual settings:

**Covenantal:** Mal 2:14 (marriage covenant), 1Jo 1:3 (new covenant community), 873-001 (fellowship with Father and Son), Ecc 4:10 (covenantal partnership imagery). The covenantal setting reveals that fellowship's deepest operations are covenantal — they happen within the framework of binding relational commitments.

**Communal:** Psa 119:63, 873-002 (horizontal fellowship among believers), Eze 37:19 (restoration of divided community). The communal setting reveals that fellowship is not a private inner experience but an inherently social reality.

**Moral-accusatory:** Mat 23:30, Isa 1:23, Hos 4:17, Job 34:8. The moral-accusatory setting reveals that fellowship vocabulary is frequently deployed where moral culpability is at stake — who someone is joined to has legal and moral implications.

**Suffering/redemptive:** Isa 53:5, Pro 20:30, Phili 3:10. The suffering-redemptive setting reveals that fellowship's deepest transformative operations occur in contexts of pain, wounding, and death — not in comfort.

findings.session_b_note: The anchor verse corpus spans a notably broad contextual range: (1) Covenantal-judicial setting (Mic 6:8 — covenant lawsuit; Jos 23:14 — covenant farewell address): the primary human moral goodness verse is set in a judicial-covenantal frame — goodness is the standard of covenant obligation. (2) Liturgical-doxological setting (Psa 34:8; 119:68; doxological refrain): corporate worship and individual prayer as the context for declaring and encountering divine goodness. (3) Wisdom-instructional setting (Pro 15:16; 16:32): educational and formational context for human moral development. (4) Prophetic-restorative setting (Eze 36:31): post-exilic restoration context where goodness is encountered through recognition of its absence. (5) Pauline-pneumatological setting (Gal 5:22; Col 3:12): community formation in the new covenant context. The breadth of contextual settings confirms that goodness is not restricted to a single register of life — it operates across judicial, liturgical, instructional, prophetic, and community contexts. (OBS-067-OBS-027, OBS-067-OBS-042, SBF-067-Q042)

findings.session_b_note: Three dominant contextual settings: (a) **Covenantal** — the OT love vocabulary (chesed, ahavah, racham) is carried primarily in covenantal contexts (Sinai formula, Deuteronomy love-command, prophetic covenant-marriage imagery). This reveals love as the inner disposition of covenant — it is what the covenant relationship requires and produces at the inner-being level. (b) **Communal/ecclesial** — the NT love vocabulary (agapē in Paul and John) is carried in the context of the believing community (1Cor 13 in worship-chaos context; Joh 13:34 at the Last Supper; 1Th 3:12 in community growth prayer). This reveals love as the community's constitutive practice. (c) **Lament/petition** — Lamentations, Psalms of lament: love's permanence is specifically evidenced under conditions of suffering and judgment. This reveals that love's most definitive testimony is given precisely when circumstances deny it — chesed is most powerfully stated when experience is most desolate (Lam 3:22).

findings.finding_value: The relational tier (T4) shows the divine-to-human and human-to-God directions of contrition; the evidential tier (T7) identifies the primary literary contexts (penitential psalm = human-to-God; prophetic address = God-to-human). The literary forms in T7 directly correspond to the relational directions in T4: the psalm form is the human-to-God literary vehicle; the prophetic form is the God-to-human literary vehicle. The two primary anchor verses confirm this: Psa 51:17 (psalm — human addressing God in contrition) and Isa 57:15 (prophecy — God addressing the community with the promise of dwelling with the contrite). T7's literary analysis explains why T4 finds two distinct relational directions: they are embedded in two distinct literary genres.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-007: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: …
findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-025: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidence…
findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-022: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of che…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of chen (SD041), Zec 12:10's grace-produced vision, and SD012's hearing-receptivity pattern. T7's argument structure for Zec 12:10 (grace outpoured → "when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced") confirms T3.1 precisely: the grace-event produces and requires the inner sight that recognises what grace has cost. T3.6's agency-constituting paradox (1Cor 15:10) is T7.3's most significant framework-divergence point: at the moment of constitutional incapacity, all human science frameworks assume the person has some prior agency; the biblical account holds the paradox of grace-constituted agency that is genuinely human while grace-originated. This is the methodological divergence T7.3 identifies and T3.6 establishes as the operative finding.

findings.session_b_note: The primary covenant verse evidence is overwhelmingly covenantal-cultic in its contextual setting — which is to say, the verse evidence is typically embedded within the explicit covenantal life of the worshipping community. The primary settings: (1) Covenantal — the covenant renewals, covenant-making ceremonies, and covenant oracles are the primary covenantal-formal context (Exo 24; Deu 29; Neh 9-10; Jer 31; Heb 8). (2) Judicial — Dan 9:11 (the covenant curse activated by moral failure); Heb 10:29 (the judgment for profaning the covenant blood). The covenant operates within a judicial framework that enforces its sanctions. (3) Liturgical — 1 Cor 11:25; Mat 26:28 (the Eucharistic words of institution). The covenant is enacted and recalled within the worshipping community's ritual. (4) Eschatological — Rev 11:19 (the ark in the heavenly temple); Rev 21:1-5 (new creation). What this combination of settings reveals: covenant is not abstract theology but embedded in the concrete practices of worship, law, and community life.

findings.session_b_note: (P1 — contextual settings) Psalmic lament and praise (dominant for chesed); narrative of covenant relationships (Ruth, Genesis, Samuel-Kings); prophetic indictment (Hos 6:6, Mic 6:8); NT epistolary instruction (Eph 4:32, Col 3:12, Rom 2:4). (P5 — primary anchor verse) Lam 3:22: "The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end." This verse asserts the permanence and inexhaustibility of divine kindness in the context of maximum suffering and loss. It reveals what no other verse reveals: chesed is not contingent on circumstances or human faithfulness — it persists when everything else has failed. Every other kindness statement in the evidence is a specific expression of this; Lam 3:22 is the structural foundation.

findings.session_b_note: The anchor verses are distributed across four contextual settings. (1) Covenantal: Gen 12:7, Gen 15:18, Mal 2:5, Neh 9:8 — formal covenant-establishment or covenantal renewal contexts. These settings require the giving to be read as covenantally binding, not merely generous. (2) Prophetic-judicial: Jer 12:7, Hos 13:11, Isa 42:8, Isa 47:6 — prophetic contexts of divine judgement and address to Israel. These require the giving to be read as morally consistent with the divine character, not arbitrary. (3) Eschatological-prophetic: Isa 61:3, Hos 2:15, Isa 35:2 — contexts of divine restoration announcement. These require the giving to be read as new-creation initiative, not mere restoration to prior state. (4) Narrative-individual: Gen 29:33, Job 1:21, Job 38:36 — individual persons encountering divine giving. These require attention to the specific relational situation of the individual. The diversity of settings confirms that inner-being giving is not a specialised sub-category of divine action but a pervasive mode present across the full range of biblical contexts.

findings.finding_value: M01-A's evidence is carried across multiple contextual settings: (1) **covenantal** — Mal 2:5 (fear as the covenant's defining substance with Levi); Deu 6:2 (fear governing the covenant life); (2) **judicial** — Lev 19:14; 25:17; 2Ch 19:7-9 (fear as the inner judge in judicial settings); (3) **liturgical** — Psa 5:7; Heb 12:28 (fear as the posture of worship); (4) **communal** — Mal 3:16; Psa 119:63; Act 9:31 (fear as community-forming and sustaining); (5) **eschatological** — Rev 11:18; 14:7; 19:5 (fear as the defining posture of the redeemed at the consummation). The spread across all five settings reveals that M01-A is not restricted to one domain of life but governs the whole person's life in every setting.

M01-B's evidence is carried across: **narrative encounter settings** (OT military crisis, NT miracle events, resurrection appearances), **pastoral settings** (Paul's "do not fear" commands, Jesus's commands throughout the gospels), and **eschatological settings** (Luk 21:26 — cosmic fear at the end). The narrative encounter setting is dominant.

M01-G's evidence is carried across: **epistolary pastoral** (2Ti 1:7 — letter to a pastor in threatened community), **parabolic wisdom** (Mat 25:25 — the talent parable), and **eschatological judgment** (Rev 21:8). The eschatological setting reveals the ultimate stakes of the characteristic — timidity is not a minor personality trait but a disposition whose ultimate consequence is judgment.

The cluster's contextual settings span the entire range of Scripture's life-settings. M01-A governs all settings (judicial, liturgical, covenantal, communal, eschatological). The eschatological setting is particularly significant: multiple sub-groups have their climactic statements in eschatological contexts (M01-A: Rev corpus; M01-G: Rev 21:8; M01-F: Heb 10:27; M01-B: Luk 21:26), confirming that fear is a characteristic whose fullest significance is eschatological.

Multiple contextual settings are evidenced: (1) Judicial/legal: Heb 3:11 (oath of exclusion from rest); Rom 4:15 (law exposing transgression triggering wrath); Num 5:14 (jealousy as judicially actionable inner state). (2) Covenantal: Deu 29:28 (wrath driving exile); Num 25:3 (covenant betrayal kindling anger). (3) Liturgical: Num 1:53 (priestly guard protecting against wrath at the tabernacle); Lev 10:6 (ritual propriety holding corporate anger at bay). (4) Communal: Neh 5:6 (anger at economic oppression within community); Gal 5:20 (strife as communal flesh-work). (5) Eschatological: Rev 6:16–17; 14:10; 19:15 (final day of wrath). The setting reveals that anger is not culturally or contextually peripheral — it is operative in every major life-setting evidenced in Scripture.

The M03 corpus spans four primary contextual settings. Covenantal (M03-D-VCG-01/03): distress within the covenant relationship between God and Israel, where God's covenant faithfulness is the basis for the prayer that distress activates. Communal (M03-A-VCG-03, M03-B-VCG-02): communal mourning as the social expression of shared grief within the community of Israel or another nation. Personal/relational (M03-A-VCG-01, M03-C-VCG-01): grief within personal relational bonds — family, friendship, pastoral. Eschatological (M03-A-VCG-05, M03-B-VCG-04, M03-E-VCG-02): grief as the condition of the not-yet, oriented toward the fullness.

Heb 10:26's eschatological-sacrificial context is the most theologically dense.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Four contextual settings. (1) *Wisdom-reflective* (Ecclesiastes and Proverbs passages): the sinner-type as an observed reality in wisdom's view of human moral life. (2) *Prophetic-covenantal* (Hosea; 2Ki 17:7): habitual defection as the covenantal failure of Israel addressed by the prophetic word. (3) *Liturgical-petitionary* (1Ki 8:46): the temple prayer as the context for realistic acknowledgment of habitual sinning and appeal for divine provision. (4) *NT community-doctrinal* (1Jo 3:6; Heb 3:17): habitual sinning addressed as a theological-existential question within the NT community of faith.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Three settings. (1) *Monarchic-covenantal* (Kings corpus — dominant): contagious sin addressed within the context of Israel and Judah's monarchic history under the Davidic covenant — the theological evaluation of each king's reign. (2) *Legal-preventive* (Exo 23:33; Deu 20:18): contagious sin addressed within the Mosaic law's boundary regulations — the covenantal boundary-setting before entry into Canaan. (3) *Prophetic-judicial* (Jer 32:35; 1Ki 16:2; 21:22): contagious sin addressed through direct prophetic word, naming specific leaders and specific acts.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Two contextual settings. (1) *Monarchic-covenantal* (dominant): the Kings and Chronicles corpus addresses political revolts within the context of Israel and Judah's monarchic governance under the Davidic covenant. The revolt is always against a king or kingdom within the covenant-historical framework. (2) *Political-military* (2Ki 3:7): the revolt becomes the occasion for military alliance-seeking — the political revolt is the context for covenant-level political diplomacy and military response.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Four settings. (1) *Didactic-discipleship* (Mat 15:19 — Jesus teaching the crowd and disciples about inner purity): heart-origin teaching in a purity-debate context. (2) *Judicial-christological* (VCG-02 — the blasphemy-charge scenes): sinful speech as a formal legal charge in the trial of Jesus. (3) *Community formation* (Eph 4:31; Col 3:8 — community paraenesis): sinful speech addressed within the practical moral formation of the NT community. (4) *Eschatological-cosmic* (Rev 13:1/5/6; 17:3): sinful speech as the defining feature of the eschatological anti-God power.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Three primary contextual settings: (1) Judicial/forensic — the wicked as the legally guilty party (VCG-01, 5V: Exo 23:7; Deu 25:1-2; 1Ki 8:32; 2Ch 6:23). The INTEGRATION_NOTE carry-forward is most relevant here: these forensic uses are the cross-register with M10. (2) Covenantal/prophetic — the wicked as those who have broken covenant relationship with God and face prophetic call to turn (VCG-07, VCG-02, VCG-05 — concentrated in Ezekiel and the Psalms of divine address). (3) Wisdom/communal — the wicked as a human moral type observed within social life, whose patterns of inner character and consequence are documented for instruction (Proverbs — VCGs 06, 08, 09). The contextual diversity across judicial, covenantal, and wisdom settings shows the characteristic is not confined to a single institutional setting but is a general moral-anthropological category operative across all three.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Three primary contextual settings: (1) Communal/ecclesial formation — the largest body of evidence (Pauline letters, VCGs 05/06) addresses believers in community — the constitutional inner evil is named in the context of ongoing formation imperatives within established churches. The communal setting reveals the characteristic as a pastoral concern within the covenant community, not merely an external moral category. (2) Apocalyptic/eschatological — the separation of evil from righteous at the end of age (Mat 13:49 — VCG-04), the cosmic evil-one's dominion (1Jo 5:19 — VCG-01), and the progressive deterioration of evil people (2Ti 3:13 — VCG-06) all carry eschatological-frame settings. (3) Conflict/challenge — Jesus addressing the Pharisees (Mat 12:34-35; Luk 11:39 — VCG-03/05), the entrapment attempts (Mat 22:18 — VCG-05), and the community expulsion of the evil person (1Cor 5:13 — VCG-04) all carry conflict-context settings.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Three primary contextual settings. (1) Wisdom-communal instruction (Proverbs — VCGs 01, 02, 03): the commercial market (false weights — Deu 25:16; Pro 11:1; Pro 20:10; 20:23 — VCG-01), the judicial court (Pro 17:15 — VCG-01 — perverted judgment), and the worship/ritual context (Pro 15:8; 21:27; 28:9; Isa 1:13 — VCG-03). These settings reveal the characteristic as operative across all the practical domains of daily life (commerce, justice, worship), not confined to religious or ritual contexts. (2) Covenantal-prophetic address (Jeremiah, Ezekiel — VCG-04): the covenant community's communal moral state addressed by the prophets — the conscience of Israel collectively is the concern. (3) Eschatological/cosmic (Revelation — VCG-05): the final-judgment exclusion context. The breadth of contextual settings (commerce to court to worship to covenant community to eschatological) confirms the characteristic as operating across all levels of human moral-relational life.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Three primary contextual settings. (1) Covenantal-legal (Leviticus, Deuteronomy — VCGs 01, 02): the boundary-law context of divine statutes defining Israel's holy distinctness from surrounding nations. The covenantal setting reveals the characteristic as a specifically covenantal-betrayal category. (2) Royal-historical (reform narratives — VCG-03): the political context of kings whose wills shape national covenant fidelity or infidelity. The royal-historical setting reveals the characteristic as having an institutional-political dimension — it is embedded in political structures as much as in individual inner lives. (3) Prophetic-judicial (Jeremiah, Ezekiel — VCGs 04, 05): the prophetic confrontation context where accumulated idolatrous abominations reach the threshold requiring divine declaration and judgment. The prophetic-judicial setting reveals the characteristic as the subject of the divine legal case against the covenant community.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Four primary settings. (1) Judicial-divine (Psalms of complaint/imprecation — VCG-03): the divine court is the setting in which evildoers are brought before God and their iniquity judged — Psa 94:23 (VCG-03): divine bringing-back of iniquity; Psa 5:5 (VCG-03): God's court before which evildoers cannot stand. (2) Wisdom-instructional (Job, Proverbs — VCGs 02, 04): the classroom and counsel setting where iniquity is named and warned against — Job 4:8; 11:14; 36:10/21 (VCG-04). (3) Prophetic-confrontational (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah — VCGs 01, 02, 05): the prophetic oracle setting in which specific communities or rulers are confronted with their iniquity. (4) Personal prayer/lament (Psalms — VCGs 01, 03, 04): the prayer setting where the righteous pray for protection from and release from the influence of evildoers.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Three primary contextual settings. (1) Eschatological judgment setting (Revelation VCG-01): the end-time context of divine plagues falling on an unrepentant humanity under cosmic judgment. This setting reveals the characteristic at maximum intensity — the most extreme possible divine pressure producing the most extreme possible defiant speech. (2) Community-conduct setting (Pauline VCG-02; Petrine VCG-03): the NT church community living as a minority within Gentile society, managing the social testimony of their conduct and the false accusations of hostile neighbours. This setting reveals the characteristic in its social-communal dimension. (3) Judicial-legal setting (VCG-03: Joh 18:30; Act 25:5): formal trial proceedings where false charges are formally delivered. This setting reveals the characteristic's institutional dimension — evil speech institutionalised through legal process.

**[CLUSTER]** E — Five primary contextual settings carry the cluster's evidence. (1) Wisdom-instructional (Chars 1, 3, 5 — Proverbs/Job): the classroom and counsel context where the wicked person is identified, warned against, and contrasted with the wise/righteous. (2) Judicial-divine (Chars 1, 3, 5, 6 — Psalms of lament and imprecation; Rev 16): the divine court where the inner evil is brought before God and judged. (3) Prophetic-confrontational (Chars 4, 5, 3 — Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Micah): the prophetic oracle confronting specific communities with their inner evil and demanding response. (4) Community-conduct (Char 6 — Pauline and Petrine epistles): the NT community living in hostile social environments, managing testimony through honourable conduct against false accusation. (5) Eschatological-cosmic (Chars 2, 4, 6 — Revelation, Daniel, NT eschatological): the end-time context where the inner evil reaches its peak expression and faces final judgment. The cluster's contextual range mirrors its literary breadth — M10b is not a narrow specialist category but addresses inner evil in every major social and theological context.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The primary contextual setting is liturgical-covenantal: the Levitical legislation operates in the context of the divine presence dwelling in the tabernacle among Israel (Lev 15:31 — "defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst"). The clean/unclean system is the boundary management system for a community in which the holy God dwells. The Num 9 and Num 19 material operates in the wilderness-camp setting — Israel as a covenant community travelling with the divine presence. The M10c-B leprosy corpus (Lev 13-14) operates in a diagnostic/judicial setting — priestly examination as authoritative verdict. The NT akathartos material (Act 10-11) operates in a narrative-revelatory setting — divine vision overturning established categorical conviction. The settings reveal the characteristic as a condition managed within structured institutional contexts (tabernacle, priestly authority, apostolic revelation).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The contextual settings vary by literary form. Communal-pastoral: 2Cor 7:1, 12:21 (VCG-03/02) — Paul addressing the Corinthian community's moral state and calling to cleansing. Covenantal-ethical: Eph 4:19, 5:3, 5:5 (VCG-02/04) — Paul framing the Gentile moral condition in contrast to the new-covenant community's calling. Theological-doctrinal: Rom 1:24, 6:19 (VCG-02) — systematic theological exposition of the defilement-state and its resolution in the gospel. Prophetic-confessional: Isa 6:5, 64:6, Hag 2:14 (VCG-01) — prophetic setting of divine encounter and communal confession before God. Wisdom-existential: Job 14:4 (VCG-01) — existential-wisdom setting of the human condition before God. Eschatological: Rev 3:4, 14:4, 16:13, 17:4, 18:2 (VCG-05/04) — apocalyptic eschatological revelation context. The diversity of settings reveals the characteristic as operating across the full range of biblical literary and communal contexts.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The contextual settings vary by literary form. Covenantal-judicial: the Levitical legal code (VCG-01 — Lev 18, Num 5, Deu 21/24) addresses the covenant community as bound by Mosaic law. Prophetic-accusatory: Ezekiel's pre-exilic judgment oracles (VCG-02 — Eze 20/22/23; VCG-03 — Eze 5/9/23/43) address the corporate defilement as the reason for the coming judgment. Exilic-lament: Lamentations (VCG-05 — Lam 1:17/4:15) addresses the post-destruction reality of Jerusalem's defilement and expulsion. Eschatological-promissory: the VCG-05 restoration texts (Eze 37:23, Isa 52:1, Zec 13:1) address the future community in the context of the coming divine restoration. The dominant setting is prophetic-covenantal: the characteristic's primary arena is the covenant community's relationship with its sacred environment in the context of covenantal accountability.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The primary contextual setting is the public communal context of Jesus's Galilean ministry: synagogue gatherings (Mar 1:23, Luk 4:33), public healing sessions (Luk 6:18 — "who came to hear him"; Act 5:16 — gathering from surrounding towns), and specific encounter narratives (Mar 5:2 — among the tombs; Mar 7:25 — a woman coming; Luk 9:42 — "while he was coming"). Secondary setting: the apostolic mission context (Act 5:16, Act 8:7 — Philip's ministry in Samaria). The dominant setting is public-communal encounter with divine authority in the context of Jesus's kingdom mission.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four contextual settings reveal the M10c cluster's institutional range. Characteristic 1: liturgical-covenantal — the tabernacle-community in the wilderness, governed by priestly authority; the clean/unclean system is the boundary management system for a community in which the holy God dwells (Lev 15:31). Characteristic 2: the settings span communal-pastoral (Paul addressing Corinthian and Ephesian communities), theological-doctrinal (Romans' systematic exposition), prophetic-confessional (Isaiah's divine encounter), wisdom-existential (Job's reflection), and eschatological-apocalyptic (Revelation). The characteristic operates in every institutional and literary context of the NT. Characteristic 3: prophetic-covenantal (Ezekiel's pre-exilic judgment oracles addressed to Israel), exilic-lament (Lamentations' post-destruction testimony), eschatological-promissory (the restoration texts of Eze 37, Isa 52, Zec 13). The characteristic's dominant institutional arena is the covenant community's relationship with its sacred environment under prophetic accountability. Characteristic 4: public-communal encounter with divine authority in the context of Jesus's kingdom mission (synagogue, public healing sessions, specific encounter narratives). The cluster's institutional range: tabernacle-covenantal (Char 1) → every NT literary setting (Char 2) → prophetic-covenantal and lament (Char 3) → kingdom-mission public encounter (Char 4).

questions.question_text: Does any verse function as the primary anchor — the one most fully and directly expressing the characteristic's essential character? Record it, or none.

findings.session_b_note:
The data identifies two verses as candidates for primary anchor status, with different claims:

**Luk 7:47 — highest inner-being density:** Q043 answer — "highest inner-being density: forgiveness received, love produced, quantity-proportional relationship, implied guilt-state resolved. The verse names: (1) the act of forgiving; (2) the inner state of the recipient; (3) the causal relationship; (4) the comparative case. Four inner-being elements in one clause."

**Jer 31:34 — highest theological centrality:** Q042 answer — "the most theologically central verse: it joins divine forgiveness with the new covenant, direct knowledge of God, and cognitive cessation of the guilt-claim. This verse establishes forgiveness as the covenantal-structural foundation of the new human-divine relationship."

**The tension:** Luk 7:47 is the primary anchor for inner-being analysis (the characteristic's operation in a specific person); Jer 31:34 is the primary anchor for theological-structural analysis (the characteristic's covenantal significance). The programme's human-centred focus (human being as unit of study) arguably gives Luk 7:47 priority — it names what forgiveness does in the inner being of the person most explicitly.

findings.session_b_note:
Two candidates emerge from the data, each capturing a different dimension of the essential character:

**Candidate 1 — Hos 11:8 (for divine compassion at its deepest):** "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender." This verse names divine compassion with the greatest constitutional specificity in the data: it locates compassion in the heart, names its felt quality (warmth, tenderness), shows its deliberative character (competing with judgment), and demonstrates its outcome (restoration rather than abandonment). No other verse in the data so fully and directly describes the inner-being reality of compassion at its constitutional depth.

**Candidate 2 — Luke 10:33 (for human compassion at its fullest expression):** "But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion (splanchnizō)." This verse names human compassion at its fullest: cross-boundary, perception-triggered, fully acted-upon, morally normative, and the answer to the question of what love of neighbour looks like. It also connects splanchnizō to the Good Samaritan's complete investment — the fullest chain from inner-movement to outer action in the data.

**Assessment:** Neither alone captures the full essential character — Hos 11:8 is the definitive statement of compassion as divine inner-being; Luke 10:33 is the definitive statement of compassion as human moral norm. Together they form the essential character's two faces: the divine originating reality and its human instantiation.

findings.session_b_note:
**Psa 51:17** is the primary anchor for the penitential-relational mode: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise." It is the most comprehensive single-verse statement: it names the constitutional loci (spirit and heart), the condition (broken and contrite), the relational frame (before God), and the divine response (non-despising = acceptance). It also locates contrition within the worship/sacrifice framework.

**Isa 57:15** is the primary anchor for the divine-response dimension: it names who God is (holy, transcendent), the person God dwells with (contrite and lowly), and what God does (revives spirit and heart). It is the most complete statement of the divine attentiveness to the contrite.

Taken together, Psa 51:17 and Isa 57:15 function as the two complementary primary anchors: one from the human side (the broken heart as sacrifice), one from the divine side (the holy God dwelling with the contrite to revive).

findings.session_b_note:
**1Jo 1:3** functions as the primary anchor for fellowship's essential character: it encodes both the vertical axis (fellowship with the Father and his Son) and the horizontal axis (fellowship with us), the extension mechanism (proclamation), the ground of extension (prior witness), and the telos (that you too may have fellowship). It is the most structurally complete expression of what fellowship is.

**2Pe 1:4** functions as the primary anchor for fellowship's ontological depth: divine nature participation as the highest register of what fellowship enables.

No single verse captures all six modes of operation. If a single anchor must be named, **1Jo 1:3** is the most complete.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-007: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two language…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two languages with distinct semantic ranges, a full root-family analysis, a NT coinage (agathōsunē), and a comprehensive vocabulary arc from phenomenological breadth (H2896A) to virtuous precision (agathōsunē) to relational precision (chrēstotēs — Q&A-177). The lexical evidence is rich. Literary: the primary anchor (Mic 6:8) uniquely combines revelatory and covenantal-obligation frames with an internal tri-fold structure that no other verse replicates (Q&A-183); the anchor corpus spans prophetic, wisdom, psalmic, and epistolary forms across multiple contextual settings (Q&A-181). Human science: virtue ethics is the closest parallel framework, with the critical divergence at the source of goodness (divine gift vs natural achievement — Q&A-186). Constraints: NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms limit the LXX analysis (Q&A-175); LSJ data is absent. The evidential foundation is strong at the lexical-semantic and verse-literary levels; it is constrained at the LXX-continuity and human-science elaboration levels. This asymmetry is itself an analytic finding — it identifies where future investigation would most strengthen the registry's evidential base.

findings.session_b_note: Two verses function together as the primary definitional anchor for love in the data: (a) **Lam 3:22**: 'The steadfast love (chesed) of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end' — the OT's most concentrated statement of love's permanence under maximum adverse conditions. The theological claim is absolute: love does not cease. (b) **Joh 15:13**: 'Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends' — the NT's primary definition of love by its maximum expression. Together they bracket the love vocabulary: Lam 3:22 defines love by its permanence (it never stops); Joh 15:13 defines love by its cost (it gives everything). If only one is chosen: Lam 3:22 is the more foundational — it states what love ultimately is (permanent, reliable, the ground of hope in desolation); Joh 15:13 states what love ultimately does.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-103-007: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-cove…
findings.finding_value: Love's evidential foundation is the most comprehensive in the programme. The primary terms (chesed, agapē/agapaō, racham/rachamim, ahavah, dod, phileō) cover the full constitutional range: willed-covenantal (chesed), Spirit-produced self-giving (agapē), somatic-compassionate (racham), intense-erotic (ahavah/dod), and naturally affective (phileō). The vocabulary structure itself distinguishes disposition/act/condition, received/given, and quality/person-type — making it architecturally precise. The semantic range of the primary terms spans from divine ontology (God is love) to moral inversion (love of darkness) — the widest semantic arc in the programme. The primary anchor is Lam 3:22 — love's most definitive affirmation precisely at the moment of maximum empirical falsification: a theological confession rather than an empirical observation. The LXX connection is partially evidenced (agapē as chesed-translated); full LXX analysis is limited by NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags. The human science frameworks identified (attachment theory, virtue ethics) are named as Session D pointers but not elaborated — the instruction prohibits importing framework content not grounded in the data.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-006: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispos…
findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation confirms and specifies the definition at every point. The vocabulary analysis confirms the four-mode structure of the definition (Q&A-122, Q&A-123): chesed (covenantal-dispositional), racham (somatic-compassionate), ahavah/dod (intense-erotic), phileō/agapē (affective-natural and willed-unconditional). The grammatical range analysis confirms the tripartite definition (Q&A-123): verb (act) + noun (disposition) + adjective-passive (condition). The semantic range analysis confirms the vocabulary arc (Q&A-124, Q&A-131). The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136, Q&A-137) confirms the definition's most counterintuitive feature: love at its most definitional is not evidenced by love's presence but confessed against its apparent absence. The definition says love is permanent, unwavering, faithful — and the evidential ground for this claim is a verse written in the context of Jerusalem's destruction. The evidential foundation is thus not primarily experiential but confessional — the definition's permanence-claim is a theological assertion, grounded in the character of God rather than in the consistency of human experience.

HUMAN→GOD axis — Psa 63:3 (chesed above life), Mat 22:37 (total inner mobilisation), Joh 14:15 (love producing obedience); these are carried by the agapaō-love-of-God group (571-001) and the chesed-human group (536-002). HUMAN→HUMAN axis — Lev 19:18 (neighbour-love commandment), Mat 5:44 (enemy-love), Joh 13:34 (new commandment), Joh 13:35 (community identity); these span the rea-group (173 active), the agapaō-mutual group (571-004, 53 relevant), and the filadelfia group (558-001). findings.finding_value: The evidential foundation grounds the formation claims at the lexical level. The growth-capacity finding (Q&A-092) is grounded in the verbal form agapaō and the noun-verb movement: chesed as noun (stable quality) requires formation before it functions as such; the transition from occasional loving acts (verb) to stable covenantal character (noun-quality) is the formation process in lexical form. The reversibility asymmetry (divine love irreversible; human love redirectable — Q&A-094) is grounded in the vocabulary's own structure: the divine forms of chesed and agapē carry permanence qualifiers (olam — everlasting; Lam 3:22 — never ceasing) that the human love forms do not. The primary anchor (Lam 3:22 — Q&A-136) is itself a formation text: the confession of love's permanence in extremity is a formation of the inner person toward trust in what cannot be seen. The formation process produces the person capable of making the Lam 3:22 confession — the developmental trajectory toward love's perfection includes the formation of the inner person's capacity to confess love against empirical evidence.

The T7 synthesis: mercy's evidential base is wide and cross-genre (liturgical, prophetic, sapiential, narrative, epistolary) — this breadth confirms that mercy is not a sectional or contextual biblical theme but a structural reality appearing in every major literary context.

The cross-testament gap (T7.1.8–9) is the methodological limitation — without LXX analysis the vocabulary arc from OT to NT cannot be closed from this registry's data. Human science frameworks confirm rather than challenge the biblical account, with the theocentric causality as the point of genuine divergence.

T5's formative account is not speculative but exegetically derived: T7 provides the textual ground; T5 provides the formative interpretation. The highest-evidenced formative movement (the crushing-to-reviving sequence) is precisely the movement most clearly encoded in the primary anchor verses.

The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.
