findings.finding_value: T1's four-kind structure is encoded in T7's vocabulary with structural completeness. The disposition kind (chen, charis as noun) has dedicated terms. The act kind (chanan, charizō) has dedicated verbal forms. The completed-state kind (charitoō — NT coinage, G5487) required a new word because existing vocabulary could not carry the concept of standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state. The character-quality kind (chen in conduct and speech — 889-003) is carried by chen's adjectival and behavioural register. The vocabulary is structurally complete for the four kinds — each kind has a corresponding lexical form. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō) is the lexical evidence that T1's four-kind analysis is correct: the fourth kind (standing as completed state) required new vocabulary because it was conceptually unique.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-018: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The spirit-reception level (T2.1) is carried by the perfect passive form of charitoō (kecharitōmenē — the completed act of b…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional levels are carried by specific grammatical forms in T7. The soul-standing level (T2.2) is carried by charis as noun (the inhabited state of favour) and chen as the relational standing-in-favour term. The character-expression level is carried by chen in its conduct/speech register (889-003) and charizō in its human-forgiving mode. T7's NT coinage finding (charitoō invented to carry the standing-in-favour concept) is the lexical evidence that T2's spirit-level reception was conceptually unprecedented — no prior vocabulary could name what happened constitutionally when grace-as-standing arrived.

T7's argument structure for Zec 12:10 (grace outpoured → "when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced") confirms T3.1 precisely: the grace-event produces and requires the inner sight that recognises what grace has cost. T3.6's agency-constituting paradox (1Cor 15:10) is T7.3's most significant framework-divergence point: at the moment of constitutional incapacity, all human science frameworks assume the person has some prior agency; the biblical account holds the paradox of grace-constituted agency that is genuinely human while grace-originated. This is the methodological divergence T7.3 identifies and T3.6 establishes as the operative finding.

The NT coinage charitoō (T7.1 P9 — coined for standing-in-favour as completed, continuing state) is the lexical ground of T5.1's irreversibility finding: the perfect passive grammatical form encodes precisely the "transformation not reversed" character that T5.1 identifies. T7.2's argument structure analysis (Zec 12:10 — grace outpoured → recognition → mourning → supplication) is the textual grounding for T5.2's creaturely recognition response finding: the sequence is not an incidental narrative feature but an argued structural pattern. T7.3's framework divergence (human science frameworks assuming prior capacity; Scripture denying it at the point of maximum incapacity — Eph 2:1-5) is the methodological expression of T5.5's deepest formation finding: the person cannot initiate their own formation by grace. T5 and T7 describe the same formation reality from narrative and lexical angles.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-028: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimens…
findings.finding_value: T6's structural uniqueness (grace is not produced by any inner-being characteristic — categorically the originating point of the causal chain) and T7's vocabulary structural completeness (every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term, including the structural negative acharistos) confirm and explain each other. T6 establishes that grace stands outside the characteristic-production network; T7 establishes that the vocabulary encodes this structural position with unique completeness — including the negative (acharistos) and the NT coinage (charitoō) as markers of grace's conceptual uniqueness. The shared anchor verses (T6.6) are also T7's most evidentially rich texts: Eph 2:8 (which anchors multiple co-occurring registries) carries the most complete single-verse expression of grace's structural position (sovereign gift, not of works, producing faith). T6 and T7 mutually confirm that grace's structural uniqueness in the programme landscape corresponds to a lexical uniqueness in the vocabulary — both point to the same underlying analytical claim: grace is categorically distinct from every other inner-being characteristic.

findings.session_b_note: Jer 31:33 / Heb 8:10 reveals uniquely that God's covenantal action targets the inner constitutional organs (mind and heart) directly — that the new covenant is not a new external legal code but a new mode of inner operation where God himself inscribes his law on the person's inner organs. No other verse in the registry states this constitutional claim as directly: it names the specific organs (mind, heart), the specific action (writing, inscribing), the specific content (God's laws), and the specific agent (God himself). The verse also uniquely links the constitutional inscription to the relational formula ("I will be their God and they shall be my people") and to the cognitive outcome ("they shall all know me"). The sequence — inscription → belonging → knowing — is stated explicitly only here. This makes Jer 31:33 / Heb 8:10 the irreplaceable anchor verse for the entire inner-being analysis of covenant: no other verse carries all four elements simultaneously (constitutional site, divine action, relational outcome, cognitive product).

findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals that the covenant vocabulary is one of the most lexically rich and methodologically demanding in the programme. The full vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) shows seven simultaneous semantic dimensions (relational, bodily, oral, legal, moral, transformative, eschatological) that require the complete term inventory to see — no single term carries all seven. The LXX translation choice (diathēkē over synthēkē — Q&A-177) is a theological-methodological decision that imports the testamentary/death dimension into covenant language and is directly exploited by the NT. The primary anchor verse (Jer 31:33 / Heb 8:10 — Q&A-185) is uniquely comprehensive — it states simultaneously the constitutional site, the divine action, the relational outcome, and the cognitive product. The human science frameworks (Q&A-186, Q&A-187) illuminate specific dimensions (attachment, covenant-vs-contract) but diverge from the biblical material at the point of covenant's theological uniqueness — God's unilateral initiative, constitutional transformation, and eschatological scope are not captured by any human science framework. T7 confirms that the analysis rests on solid evidential and methodological ground, while acknowledging the inherent limitations of the 9% G1242 verse coverage and the legacy-VC status of all 15 OWNER terms.

The T1 × T7 synthesis: the working description (T1) is grounded in and accountable to the lexical evidence (T7). The four-modal composite structure named in T1 (disposition, act, quality, condition) corresponds to the seven vocabulary-arc dimensions named in T7 (relational, bodily, oral, legal, moral, transformative, eschatological). The working description is not imposed on the data but emerges from it — T7 confirms T1's accountability to the vocabulary.

findings.finding_value: T3 shows that memory is one of the most structurally prominent inner faculties in covenant — divine memory of covenant is the guarantee of its continuing operation; human memory is the activating condition for faithfulness (Q&A-074, Q&A-076). T7 shows that the primary verse evidence spans four literary forms (legal-narrative, prophetic oracle, epistle-argument, liturgical — Q&A-181), all of which are forms that require and shape memory. The T3 × T7 synthesis: the memory-faculty centrality (T3) and the literary form analysis (T7) converge on the same insight: covenant is constitutively a narrative and liturgical reality — it is held active through storytelling, declaration, and ritual re-enactment. The Eucharistic "do this in remembrance of me" (Q&A-075) is the liturgical instantiation of memory's role in covenant (T3), and it is carried by the liturgical literary form (T7). Memory and liturgy are co-constituting — covenant is kept alive through the practice of remembering performed in narrative and liturgical forms.

T7 establishes that the full vocabulary arc includes an eschatological dimension (Q&A-179) and that the primary anchor verse (Jer 31:33 / Heb 8:10 — Q&A-185) contains the covenant's telos within its text (the knowing of God — Jer 31:34). The eschatological dimension is not imposed on the data but is resident in the vocabulary arc and primary anchor verse.

findings.session_b_note: (P1 — contextual settings) Psalmic lament and praise (dominant for chesed); narrative of covenant relationships (Ruth, Genesis, Samuel-Kings); prophetic indictment (Hos 6:6, Mic 6:8); NT epistolary instruction (Eph 4:32, Col 3:12, Rom 2:4). (P2 — literary forms) Lament, praise, narrative, instruction, argument — kindness appears across all major literary forms; not genre-specific. (P5 — primary anchor verse) Lam 3:22: "The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end." This verse asserts the permanence and inexhaustibility of divine kindness in the context of maximum suffering and loss. It reveals what no other verse reveals: chesed is not contingent on circumstances or human faithfulness — it persists when everything else has failed. Every other kindness statement in the evidence is a specific expression of this; Lam 3:22 is the structural foundation.

findings.session_b_note: Isa 26:3 uniquely: the doubled shalom (shalom shalom) — no other verse uses this superlative form; the combination of cognitive direction (mind stayed on God), trust, and the doubled-shalom outcome in one verse is unique. It establishes that perfect peace is not a goal to be achieved independently but a condition God actively maintains ("you keep him") in the person whose mind is properly directed. The subject-object relationship is: God keeps; the person's mind is the instrument; trust is the ground; shalom shalom is the outcome. No other verse combines all four elements so economically. Eph 2:14 uniquely: the ontological identification of a person with peace (he himself IS our peace) — no other verse in any biblical corpus makes this claim. "He IS peace" (not "he gives peace" or "he makes peace" — though both also appear) is the unique claim. The dual primary anchors together cover the experiential and the ontological dimensions of peace — neither alone is sufficient.

The vocabulary arc culminates in two primary anchors that jointly constitute the definitive biblical statement: Isa 26:3 (perfect peace for the trust-directed mind — experiential) and Eph 2:14 (he himself IS our peace — ontological). findings.session_b_note: Taking Hos 11:8 as primary (Q&A-184): what it reveals that no other verse reveals is the divine inner-being conflict between judicial consistency and compassionate love — and its resolution. The verse discloses that faithfulness-as-giving is not mechanically determined by covenant rules; it is determined by the interaction of divine inner-being qualities (justice and compassion) at the level of the heart (leb). No other anchor verse shows this internal divine deliberation. Gen 15:18 shows the covenantal giving but not its inner deliberation. Isa 61:3 shows the outcome of transformative giving but not the inner-being movement that produces it. Jer 12:7 shows love coexisting with judicial giving but not the mechanism of their relationship. Hos 11:8 alone shows: (1) the competing inner-being logics in the divine person; (2) the faculty (leb/rahamim) where resolution occurs; (3) that faithfulness is not determined by moral logic alone but by the primacy of compassion within the divine character. This makes Hos 11:8 irreplaceable.

findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals the evidential and methodological shape of this registry's analysis. The vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) is the governing finding: two poles — na.tan (enacted) and emunah/hesed/pistis (constituted) — are both necessary and neither alone is sufficient. The grammatical gap (verb vs. nominal) maps directly onto the analytical distinction between the two poles. The literary diversity of the anchor corpus (narrative, prophecy, wisdom, liturgy) means no single interpretive lens covers the full evidence base. The primary analytical anchor (Hos 11:8) is identified for its unique revelation of the divine inner-being decision structure. The human science frameworks (virtue ethics, attachment theory) illuminate the characteristic while also diverging at critical points — the divergences are themselves analytically productive: biblical faithfulness requires both a virtue-ethical foundation (the character basis of giving) and something that virtue ethics cannot supply (the constitutive primacy of received divine giving as the ground of human virtue). What T7 reveals as a whole: the evidential base of this characteristic is rich, methodologically complex, and internally consistent. The two main methodological challenges — the registry label/OWNER term gap, and the legacy-VC status of all classified verses — are acknowledged and do not undermine the analysis but do qualify its certainty.

findings.finding_value: The disposition-in-action definition (T1) is confirmed and grounded by the vocabulary arc (T7). The grammatical structure of na.tan (exclusively verbal) is precisely the lexical form of the disposition-in-action structure: a verb cannot be possessed without being enacted. The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10) — enacted pole (na.tan) + constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) — maps directly onto the T1 finding that the registry captures the enacted dimension while the XREF vocabulary carries the dispositional. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) confirms the T1 finding that the characteristic's most analytically revealing expression is the one that shows the inner-being decision mechanism — precisely because that is where disposition and act are most visibly integrated. What this pair reveals: the lexical evidence independently confirms the definitional analysis. The characteristic is verbally grounded because faithfulness as enacted commitment is inherently event-shaped — it happens at a moment, from an inner state, toward a recipient. It cannot be abstracted from this event structure.

findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — hearing precedes giving, memory is narrative-temporal, affect is at source and target, conscientiousness is the apex) and the methodological-evidential analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, attachment theory illuminates, both diverge at critical points) converge in an analytically productive way. Virtue ethics (T7.3) addresses the same faculties that T3 identifies: moral evaluation, volition, agency, conscientiousness are the virtue-ethics faculties. The virtue-ethics framework illuminates T3 findings precisely because both are addressing the same inner-being territory. The divergence (T7.3.3 — virtue ethics cannot account for the constitutive primacy of received divine giving) maps onto the T3 finding that cognition is constituted by endowing giving (Q&A-071) rather than generated by the person. Attachment theory illuminates the hearing-precedes-giving pattern (T3.1 — God hears inner suffering) and the restoration of relational responsiveness (T3.11 — relational capacity restored). What this pair reveals: the human-science frameworks are useful precisely because they address the same inner-being faculties, and limited precisely where they diverge from the biblical account of those faculties' grounding.

findings.finding_value: The relational interface analysis (T4 — six of seven groups are God-to-human; the divine disposition ranges from covenantal to compassionate to formative to moral-consequential) and the primary anchor identification (T7 — Hos 11:8 as the verse that uniquely reveals the divine inner-being decision structure) converge. Hos 11:8 is the primary anchor precisely because it holds the full complexity of T4 in a single verse: it shows the God-to-human relational direction (the giving is addressed at Ephraim/Israel), the multiple bases of divine giving (deserved-judgement vs. compassionate restraint), and the divine disposition (heart recoiling, compassion warming). The full vocabulary arc (T7.1.10 — enacted + constituted poles) maps onto the two directions of T4: the enacted pole (na.tan) is the God-to-human and human-to-God relational act; the constituted pole (emunah/hesed/pistis) is the dispositional quality that makes the relational giving faithful rather than merely generous. What this pair reveals: the relational architecture and the vocabulary architecture are the same structure described at two levels of abstraction.

findings.finding_value:
[E] Pro 1:7 reveals uniquely that reverential fear of God is not merely a virtue alongside wisdom but is **constitutively prior to wisdom as its beginning**. No other verse makes this definitional claim as directly: it is not that wisdom leads to fear or that wisdom and fear coexist — it is that fear IS wisdom's beginning. The verse establishes a hierarchical relationship (fear → wisdom, not wisdom → fear) that no other single verse in M01 establishes as explicitly.

---

[E] Lev 19:14 reveals uniquely that reverential fear of God is the **operative inner moral standard in situations of power asymmetry where no human accountability exists**. The specific pairing with the deaf and blind (who cannot see or report exploitation) shows that fear of God fills the accountability gap left by the absence of human witnesses. No other verse makes this specific function so explicit.

Mar 4:41 reveals uniquely that acute fear before Jesus's supernatural power is not the endpoint but the **epistemological entry-point for christological recognition**. The disciples' fear immediately produces "who then is this?" — no other verse so precisely captures the cognitive-question-generating function of encounter-fear in the NT's christological argument.

Isa 66:2 reveals uniquely that **God himself describes and evaluates a specific human inner posture of trembling — located in the spirit — as the posture he looks for**. No other verse establishes that God actively attends to and values this specific spirit-level somatic response to his word.

2Ti 1:7 reveals uniquely that timidity is **explicitly not from God** — it is a spirit-level disposition God has not implanted. No other verse makes this negative divine-origin claim for the characteristic. The verse establishes both the spirit-level location and the non-divine origin of timidity in a single assertion.

[E] **Anchor focus: A-VCG-01 anchor: Heb 3:11:** Heb 3:11 reveals uniquely that divine wrath is the constitutive inner state of an oath — not an emotion that preceded a legal act but the very ground of the oath's binding force. No other verse makes this specific connection between wrath and sworn covenantal exclusion with such explicitness. The revelation is that wrath can function as legal ground — it is sufficiently objective and weightful to be the foundation of an irrevocable oath.

---

[E] **Anchor focus: A-VCG-05 anchor: Joh 3:36:** Joh 3:36 reveals uniquely that wrath can be an abiding, present existential condition — not a future event, not an episodic reaction, but a current sustained state contrasted with eternal life. No other verse presents wrath as an alternative to eternal life, naming it as the permanent state of those who disobey the Son. This positions anger/wrath as a constitutional relational condition, not merely an emotional experience.

Psa 18:6 (M03-D-VCG-01 anchor) reveals the structural mechanism of the distress → prayer → divine answer pattern with maximum clarity: the psalmist names his distress, names the act of crying out, and names God's response from his temple — all in one verse. No other verse narrates all three stages of this central M03 pattern so compactly. Mat 26:38 (M03-C-VCG-03 anchor) reveals the soul as the constitutional site of maximum grief — the soul-location is explicit ("my soul") and the depth is named ("even to death"). No other verse so precisely names grief at the soul level at its maximum depth. 2Sa 18:33 (M03-A-VCG-01 anchor) reveals grief as a total, overwhelming relational-loss experience without reservation or restraint — "he would rather have died himself." No other verse names the totality of grief in the face of irreversible loss so completely.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Psa 35:9 reveals that exultation is **the soul's own act toward God** — not a body-function, not a communal event, not an external performance, but the soul itself as the exulting agent directed toward the Lord. The soul as the explicit grammatical subject of both "rejoice" and "exult" makes this the most direct constitutional-location statement in the corpus. Zep 3:17 uniquely reveals the **mutuality and tender intensity of divine exultation** — the pairing of "exult with loud singing" and "quiet you by his love" in the same verse shows that God's exultation over his people is not triumphalist but tenderly relational — the loud singing is the overflow of the same love that also quiets.

**[CHAR-2]** E — **Phili 4:4** uniquely reveals: (1) Joy as a standing, unconditional commanded posture — "always" removes any circumstantial qualification; (2) The double-command structure — "again I will say, rejoice" signals that this is the characteristic most needing insistence; Joy is the inner-being state most at risk of being conditional, so it requires the most emphatic command; (3) The Lord as the constitutive object — "in the Lord" is not circumstantially dependent; the command is to rejoice *in* God regardless of what is happening outside. **Psa 16:11** uniquely reveals that Joy reaches its maximum not in circumstances but in God's presence itself — "fullness of joy" is a statement about Joy's maximum capacity, which is found only in the direct encounter with God. No other verse names Joy's ceiling as unambiguously: the fullness of Joy is God's presence.

**[CHAR-7]** E — **1Pe 1:8** uniquely reveals: (1) The **faith-without-sight** structure of the characteristic — "though you do not now see him, you believe and rejoice" — Suffering-Joy is the form of joy that is specifically fitted to the period of not-yet-seeing; no other verse captures this so clearly; (2) The **inexpressible** quality — the agalliao is beyond the capacity of words to capture, revealing that Suffering-Joy at its fullest transcends ordinary affective categories and requires a category larger than human language; (3) **"Filled with glory"** — the present exultation already participates in the quality that belongs to the eschatological age; no other verse names this present-eschatological quality of the joy so directly.

**[CHAR-3]** E — **Mic 6:8** uniquely reveals that Gladness in its evaluative face is not a human construction or preference but **divinely declared content** — "he has told you what is good." The good is known because God has spoken it; the human evaluative faculty's proper operation is not autonomous but responsive to divine declaration. No other verse states so explicitly that the content of genuine goodness is known because God has declared it. **Gen 1:31** uniquely reveals that Gladness originates in a divine inner-being act (God's evaluative delight in his own creation) that precedes and grounds all human evaluative-gladness — the "very good" at creation is the ontological baseline from which all departures (the "not good" verdicts) and all returns (the ki-tov praise declarations) are measured.

**[CHAR-4]** E — **Psa 37:4** uniquely reveals that Delight in God is the precondition for the proper operation of the heart's desires: the verse does not say "give up your desires and delight in God instead" but "delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart" — Delight in God restructures desire rather than eliminating it. No other verse makes so explicit that the correction to disordered desire is not desire-elimination but desire-reorientation through Delight in the right object. **Rom 7:22** uniquely reveals the constitutional depth of Delight: the "inner being" (esō anthrōpos) as the deepest layer of the self that genuinely delights in God's law even while the flesh operates against it — this is the only verse locating Delight at the deepest constitutional layer and distinguishing it explicitly from the flesh's contrary operation. **Mat 3:17** uniquely reveals the trinitarian basis: divine Delight is first the Father's declared pleasure in the Son before it is God's pleasure in any human person; the divine inner life of Delight precedes and grounds all human participation in it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — **Psa 27:4** uniquely reveals that Pleasure's highest expression is directed toward God's own character-beauty (no.am) as the supreme object of the soul's aspiration — not pleasure in created things, not pleasure in material ease, but the beauty of God himself as the soul's supreme desired pleasantness. No other verse makes so clear that genuine Pleasure at its fullest is specifically the experience of God's own agreeable, beautiful character. **Pro 16:24** uniquely reveals Pleasure's constitutional holism: the honey simile is the only verse in the corpus that explicitly names both soul AND body as recipients of the same instance of Pleasure from the same source (gracious words). No other verse demonstrates the full soul-to-body range of Pleasure's constitutional scope in a single sentence.

**[CHAR-6]** E — **Psa 118:23** uniquely reveals Wonder as simultaneously perceptive ("in our eyes"), communal ("our"), and theologically certain ("this is the Lord's doing"). No other verse names all three simultaneously: the perceptive faculty, the communal nature of genuine Wonder, and the theological attribution of the marvellous to God as its exclusive source. **Job 42:3** uniquely reveals the epistemological register of Wonder that no other verse states so plainly: the person in genuine Wonder recognises they have exceeded their own comprehension — Wonder is not only astonishment at the external but is simultaneously a revelation about oneself (the limits of one's own knowledge and speech).

**[CLUSTER]** E — Each anchor's unique contribution to the cluster: (1) **Psa 118:23** — uniquely reveals the communal, perceptive, and christologically certain nature of Wonder simultaneously; (2) **Isa 53:10** — uniquely reveals that divine Delight (cha.phets) is the operative theological mechanism of atonement — no other verse in the cluster places a positive inner-being state so directly at the centre of the mechanics of salvation; (3) **Heb 12:2** — uniquely reveals that the cluster's two most forward-leaning characteristics (Joy Char 2 and Suffering-Joy Char 7) converge in Christ's own inner-being at the cross: his Joy enabled his Suffering-Joy; both characteristics are in operation simultaneously in the most costly saving act; this confirms the cluster's christological fullness — not one characteristic but two simultaneously operative in the atonement's inner life.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Ezr 9:6 (vc=65495) uniquely reveals the simultaneity of shame's dimensions: the *felt* shame ("I am ashamed"), the *bodily* expression ("blush to lift my face"), the *relational direction* ("to you, my God"), the *moral cause* ("our iniquities"), and the *scale* ("risen higher than our heads, mounted up to the heavens"). No other single verse in the corpus simultaneously names all five dimensions. What Ezr 9:6 reveals beyond all others is that shame is the constitutive experience of the guilty person standing before the holy God — not one experience among many, but the defining inner state of that encounter. The impossibility of lifting the face is not merely a posture but the full inner reality of the person before God in that moment: they cannot stand before what they face.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Isa 2:11 uniquely reveals the three-dimensional structure of CHAR-2: mechanism (haughty looks and lofty pride brought low), target (inner orientations of self-exaltation), and eschatological purpose (God alone exalted in that day). No other verse simultaneously names all three. The verse makes explicit that CHAR-2's divine-abasement mode is teleological — it serves the goal of God's proper exaltation over against all human pride-structures.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primary literary forms: parable (Luk 18:2-4 — the unjust judge); epistle (Rom 2:23; 2Cor 6:8; Jam 2:6; 1Cor 11:4-5); narrative (Joh 8:49). The parable form (Luk 18) uses the character of the dishonoring judge as a contrast-figure — his absent-regard makes the point precisely by its absence. Primary anchor: Joh 8:49 (vc=35000) — "I honor my Father, and you dishonor me" — the most compressed, relational, and personally directed expression of CHAR-3 in the corpus, revealing worth-denial as a relational act directed at a specific person in a specific exchange. This verse uniquely reveals worth-denial as a personal relational act within a face-to-face exchange, where the standard (honouring the Father) and the violation (dishonoring the Son) are simultaneously named.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Eph 5:12 uniquely reveals that CHAR-4 has a threshold: the conscience's evaluative operation does not merely grade conduct on a scale of shameful-to-honourable but identifies certain conduct as so degraded that it cannot be named. This reveals the conscience as having a built-in censor that exceeds simple moral assessment — some conduct falls outside the range of what moral discourse can legitimately handle. No other verse in the CHAR-4 corpus establishes this threshold-quality with the same explicitness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Act 4:11 uniquely reveals the eschatological structure of CHAR-5: the rejected stone — the one subjected to the builders' contempt-verdict — is the very one God has made the cornerstone. No other verse simultaneously names both the contempt-rejection (the human verdict) and the divine reversal (God's counter-verdict) with such compression. The verse reveals that CHAR-5's shame is not divinely endorsed: God acts specifically against the contempt-verdict by making the rejected one the foundation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Gen 20:5 uniquely reveals the two-dimensional structure of CHAR-6: the inner will (integrity of heart) and the outer action (innocence of hands) together constituting the moral condition. No other verse in the corpus names both dimensions simultaneously. The verse also reveals CHAR-6's functional character as an appeal before God — it is not merely a psychological state but a claim made before the divine audience, which God then confirms (Gen 20:6). This confirms CHAR-6 as a relational moral characteristic: it is constituted in the encounter between the person's moral condition and God's assessment of it.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's primary anchors collectively reveal what no single characteristic's anchor reveals alone: the shame-field is governed by a single overarching theological logic — the person's inner moral condition (innocent or guilty, conscience functioning or seared) determines their relationship to the shame-field (approach-enabled or approach-blocked), and God's sovereign action (abasing the proud, vindicating the humble, overturning contempt-verdicts) determines the ultimate resolution. The four anchor-verses that together state this logic most completely: Ezr 9:6 (the condition of guilt-shame), Gen 20:5 (the condition of innocence), Act 4:11 (the divine reversal of contempt), Isa 2:11 (the divine correction of pride). These four verses constitute M07's complete theological logic in compressed form.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Pro 16:5 (vc=12083, M08-A1-VCG-03) reveals four things that no other single verse in the corpus does simultaneously: (a) Universality without exception — "everyone who is arrogant in heart": the universal quantifier makes CHAR-1's divine assessment invariant across person, situation, and covenant status; no other verse states this scope so explicitly for CHAR-1. (b) The deepest divine evaluation language — "an abomination to the Lord" (tōʿăbat yhwh): this is the language used for the most offensive violations of the divine-human order; no other CHAR-1 verse applies this specific evaluative term to CHAR-1 in its heart-form. Job 14:4 (VCG-01) names constitutional uncleanness but not body-and-spirit specifically. Rom 6:19 (VCG-02) names the will and bodily members but not the spirit. The body-and-spirit formulation of 2Cor 7:1 reveals the characteristic as penetrating to the deepest constitutional level (spirit) while simultaneously inhabiting the most external constitutional level (body) — making it the most constitutionally comprehensive statement of the characteristic in the corpus. It also uniquely grounds the cleansing call in the fear of God, revealing that the motive for resolution is not self-improvement but theocentric orientation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Eze 5:11 (VCG-03) uniquely reveals the covenantal consequence of the characteristic's operation: divine withdrawal of compassion. "I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity." No other verse in the 83-verse corpus is as direct in naming the consequence of the corporate/covenantal defilement-state at the level of the God-community covenantal bond: when the community defiles the sanctuary, the compassion that sustains the covenant relationship is withdrawn. This withdrawal — God's eye that no longer sees with pity — is the covenantal severance that makes the characteristic most theologically significant. Every other verse in the corpus describes the condition, its causes, and its consequences; Eze 5:11 names the covenantal rupture at its most interior point: the withdrawal of divine compassionate attention.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Luk 8:29 (VCG-01) uniquely reveals the futility of all human remedies: "kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds." No other verse in the 21-verse corpus names the specific human attempts at containing the characteristic and their failure. This reveals the characteristic as beyond human management — the chains and shackles comprehensively ineffective. This failure distinguishes Characteristic 4 from all other M10c characteristics: Characteristic 1 has a prescribed remedy system; Characteristic 2 has a path through repentance; Characteristic 3 has a path through prophetic confrontation and divine cleansing. Characteristic 4's only effective remedy is the direct divine command.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The four anchor verses' unique contributions together form the cluster's most important theological statements. Characteristic 1 (Lev 15:31): uniquely reveals the existential stakes — the defilement-state, left unmanaged, threatens death and the loss of divine habitation. No other verse makes the stakes as explicit: defilement is not a compliance matter but a life-or-death boundary condition for a community whose God dwells among them. Characteristic 2 (2Cor 7:1): uniquely reveals the bi-constitutional scope — defilement inhabits both body and spirit simultaneously, making it the most constitutionally comprehensive verse in the corpus; no other verse locates the moral-inner defilement-state at both constitutional extremes. Characteristic 3 (Eze 5:11): uniquely reveals the covenantal severance — divine withdrawal of compassion ("my eye will not spare, and I will have no pity") is named as the direct consequence of sanctuary-defilement; no other verse names the practical covenantal consequence at the level of divine compassionate attention. Characteristic 4 (Luk 8:29): uniquely reveals the futility of all human remedies — "bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds" — no other verse names specific human attempts at containing the characteristic and their comprehensive failure. The four anchor verses together form the cluster's most concise theological summary: defilement is life-threatening (Char 1), constitutionally pervasive (Char 2), covenantally severing (Char 3), and beyond all human remedy (Char 4).

questions.question_text: Which human-science framework (psychology, moral philosophy, developmental psychology, sociology, anthropology, or other) serves as the most useful interpretive lens for this characteristic?

findings.session_b_note:
The data does not address human science frameworks directly. No finding, observation, or SD pointer invokes psychological, philosophical, or social science frameworks as interpretive lenses.

From the evidence available, two frameworks are most relevant as potential lenses:

**Clinical/depth psychology:** The forgiveness corpus maps closely onto several domains of contemporary forgiveness psychology — the distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation, the cost of withholding (rumination, the "poisoned inner life"), the relationship between received forgiveness and the capacity to extend it, the role of empathy/compassion in enabling the act. The Luk 7:47 proportionality (forgiven much → loved much) has parallels in clinical observations about the relationship between the experience of grace and the capacity for relational generosity.

**Moral philosophy:** The corpus engages the moral philosophy of forgiveness — the legitimacy of the claim, the cost of absorbing rather than exacting payment, the distinction between forgiveness and condonation (the wrong is acknowledged, not minimised), the conditions under which forgiveness is appropriate (Luk 17:3-4 — conditional on repentance, vs. the unconditional divine model). These are live questions in moral philosophy of forgiveness.

*New finding:* The most immediately useful framework is likely **clinical/depth psychology of forgiveness** — it provides the most direct parallel to the inner-being dynamics the corpus names. This has not been examined in the data and is a gap.

findings.session_b_note:
Three frameworks are relevant, each addressing a different dimension of the compassion data:

**1. Affective neuroscience / embodied cognition psychology (most relevant for the somatic vocabulary):** The splanchnizō/ra.cham vocabulary's insistence on the body's interior as the seat of compassion aligns with contemporary affective neuroscience's understanding of emotion as fundamentally embodied — arising from interoceptive signals in the body's interior (particularly the gut and heart). The research on gut-brain connection and the role of the vagus nerve in empathic response provides a contemporary framework that illuminates what the ancient vocabulary was naming. The somatic reality the biblical vocabulary targets has a contemporary neurological correlate.

**2. Moral philosophy — virtue ethics (most relevant for the character-quality vocabulary):** The chesed/rachum/sumpathēs vocabulary names compassion as a virtue — a stable character disposition (hexis) that defines what kind of person one is and enables characteristic action. Aristotelian virtue ethics provides the most coherent framework for understanding the relationship between the character-quality vocabulary and the action-generating vocabulary: virtue is the stable disposition from which characteristic action arises naturally. The Good Samaritan as the paradigmatic compassionate person maps directly onto the virtue-ethics model of the person whose actions flow from formed character rather than from deliberated calculation.

**3. Developmental psychology — attachment theory (most relevant for the womb and formative vocabulary):** The RACHAM root's womb-grounding and the eusplanchnos (tender heart) pre-condition vocabulary align with attachment theory's understanding of primary relational bonds as constitutional in their effect. The capacity for compassion-based connection may be constitutively shaped in earliest developmental stages (before conscious memory — the "from the womb" language of Psa 22:10). Attachment security as the constitutional ground of the capacity for compassion-giving is a productive framework for understanding how early relational formation shapes later compassionate character.

findings.session_b_note:
The most relevant human science framework is **moral psychology**, specifically research on guilt, shame, and moral self-conscious emotions. The registry description explicitly distinguishes contrition from shame — a distinction that is well-developed in psychological research (Tangney & Dearing's guilt-shame distinction: guilt is behaviour-focused and oriented toward repair; shame is self-focused and oriented toward self-protection/withdrawal). Contrition in the biblical vocabulary aligns closely with psychological guilt-as-repair-motivator rather than shame-as-self-protection.

Secondary frameworks:
- **Developmental/character formation psychology**: the formative arc of contrition over the life — how the contrite orientation is cultivated or deepened — is a developmental question.
- **Affect theory**: the affective dimensions of contrition (grief, groaning, anguish as genuine emotional responses to moral failure) are well-addressed by affect research on negative self-conscious emotions.
- **Existential psychology**: the encountering-of-one's-limits dimension of contrition (the inner being confronted with its creaturely condition) connects to existential accounts of limit-situations and authenticity.

**Most relevant frameworks (by inference from the verse evidence):**

**Social psychology — Attachment Theory (Bowlby, Ainsworth):** Fellowship's verse evidence emphasises the constitutional need for genuine relational joining, the consequences of isolation (Ecc 4:10), and the effects of wrong attachment (idolatrous joining). Attachment theory addresses the constitutional need for secure relational bonds and the inner-being consequences of insecure, avoidant, or disorganised attachment. The fit with fellowship's moral-relational spectrum is strong.

**Social psychology — Social Identity Theory (Tajfel, Turner):** Fellowship's moral-alignment dimension (companionship with the fear-of-God community, moral complicity through fellowship with evildoers) maps onto social identity theory's account of how group membership shapes inner-being identity and moral self-assessment.

**Developmental psychology — Formation through relationship:** The character-conformity finding (062-CHAR-001) aligns with developmental psychology's understanding that character is formed through relational participation — persons become like those they are relationally attached to.

**Gap:** The data contains no Human Science framework analysis. All framework identification in this prompt is inference from the characteristic's structure, not from programme-conducted analysis.

findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals a characteristic whose evidential foundation is both exceptionally strong in some dimensions and genuinely constrained in others. Lexically: three OWNER terms across two languages with distinct semantic ranges, a full root-family analysis, a NT coinage (agathōsunē), and a comprehensive vocabulary arc from phenomenological breadth (H2896A) to virtuous precision (agathōsunē) to relational precision (chrēstotēs — Q&A-177). The lexical evidence is rich. Literary: the primary anchor (Mic 6:8) uniquely combines revelatory and covenantal-obligation frames with an internal tri-fold structure that no other verse replicates (Q&A-183); the anchor corpus spans prophetic, wisdom, psalmic, and epistolary forms across multiple contextual settings (Q&A-181). Human science: virtue ethics is the closest parallel framework, with the critical divergence at the source of goodness (divine gift vs natural achievement — Q&A-186). Constraints: NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flags on both Greek OWNER terms limit the LXX analysis (Q&A-175); LSJ data is absent. The evidential foundation is strong at the lexical-semantic and verse-literary levels; it is constrained at the LXX-continuity and human-science elaboration levels. This asymmetry is itself an analytic finding — it identifies where future investigation would most strengthen the registry's evidential base.

findings.finding_value: Reading T7 as a whole reveals the evidential foundation as both rich and gapped. The lexical foundation is comprehensive: mercy has terms for all grammatical roles (noun, verb, adjective, person-type), all operational aspects (disposition, act, seeking, structural opposite), and all major dimensions (compassion, covering, grace, propitiation, supplication). The vocabulary arc is itself a theological narrative (Q&A-180). The primary anchor verse is Psa 78:38 — the verse that most fully encodes the complete mercy-event structure (Q&A-185). The gaps are structural: LXX analysis and NT coinage data are unavailable (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag, 67 terms). Human science engagement identifies three relevant frameworks (moral psychology, attachment theory, shame theory) with the key divergence that the biblical model grounds mercy in prior reception rather than autonomous moral development (Q&A-189). The T7 synthesis: mercy's evidential base is wide and cross-genre (liturgical, prophetic, sapiential, narrative, epistolary) — this breadth confirms that mercy is not a sectional or contextual biblical theme but a structural reality appearing in every major literary context.

findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals that the contrition vocabulary has a high degree of internal coherence and a sophisticated grammatical apparatus (distinguishing process, settled state, active/passive/volitional voice) that the English word "contrition" cannot render. The primary anchor verses (Isa 57:15, Psa 51:17) are architecturally complementary: Isa 57:15 provides the complete relational frame (divine character → divine dwelling → divine reviving); Psa 51:17 provides the inner-being substance (broken spirit, contrite heart as the acceptable sacrifice). The literary context (psalm and prophecy) requires reading the same characteristic in two modes: as human address to God (penitential psalm) and as divine address to the community (prophetic promise). The cross-testament gap (T7.1.8–9) is the methodological limitation — without LXX analysis the vocabulary arc from OT to NT cannot be closed from this registry's data. Human science frameworks confirm rather than challenge the biblical account, with the theocentric causality as the point of genuine divergence.

findings.finding_value: The faculty tier (T3) shows that contrition deepens conscience, moral evaluation, and cognition; the evidential tier (T7) identifies the primary literary form as penitential psalm and prophetic address — both forms that are constitutively about honest self-knowledge before God. The Psa 51 genre (penitential psalm — T7.2) is the literary vehicle for contrition in the conscience-and-cognition registers (T3.8, T3.9): the psalm form presupposes accurate self-assessment and directed it to God. The prophetic form (Isa 57:15, 66:2 — T7.2) is the vehicle for contrition in the volitional and relational registers (T3.6, T3.11). T7's literary analysis explains why T3 finds that different faculties are engaged in different evidential contexts.

findings.finding_value: T7 produces the most vocabulary-analytically significant findings in the registry. The full vocabulary arc (from womb — most intimate — to almsgiving — most institutional) is unique in the programme: no other characteristic traverses this complete arc with equivalent lexical clarity. The CHASAD root includes shame as the negative semantic pole embedded within the compassion vocabulary itself — not an external antonym but an internal semantic component of the root family. The dual primary anchor finding (Hos 11:8 for divine compassion at constitutional depth; Luke 10:33 for human compassion as moral norm) establishes the two poles of the characteristic's evidential range. Three key argument structures: compassion-mission logic (Matt 9:36-10:1 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response), divine compassion-repentance ground (Joel 2:13 — divine character as the ground of human response-posture), Good Samaritan's moral logic (Luke 10:25-37 — compassion as the answer to "who is my neighbour?"). Three human science frameworks illuminate the vocabulary with genuine alignment (affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, attachment theory) and all three diverge from the biblical account at specific points (sovereignty vs automaticity; cross-boundary extension exceeding natural empathic scope; purposive suffering in Jas 5:11 requiring teleological frame). The LXX systematic analysis gap (NO_WORD_ANALYSIS flag on 98 terms) is the most significant methodological limitation — a new gap for the programme.

The Synoptic pattern of splanchnizō — always triggered by sight, always preceding action — is the textual ground for T3.1's finding (compassion is perceptively dependent) and T3.4's finding (affect is the mechanism of movement). T7's argument structure finding (Matt 9:36 — compassion as the theological engine of missional response) is the evangelist's literary expression of T3.10's analytical claim (compassion converts moral knowledge into motivated action). T7's framework divergences (human science frameworks failing at sovereignty, cross-boundary extension, and purposive suffering) correspond to the three areas where T3's faculty analysis finds its most distinctive results: the sovereign freedom of divine compassion exceeds the natural automaticity of empathic response; the cross-boundary extension exceeds natural empathic scope; the purposive suffering (T5.4/T5.5) requires the teleological frame that T7.3 identifies.

findings.finding_value: T4's three bases of divine compassion (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) are each grounded in specific textual evidence from T7. The sovereignly-free basis is evidenced in Rom 9:15 (T7's argument structure analysis — divine compassion as sovereign determination). The covenantally-grounded basis is evidenced in Exod 34:6 (T7's most multiply-anchored verse — the divine self-declaration in the covenant context). The situationally-responsive basis is evidenced in the Synoptic splanchnizō pattern (T7.2 — the sight-event structure of the Gospels). T7's framework divergences (sovereignty vs automaticity) map directly onto T4's relational analysis: the framework correctly identifies that divine compassion's sovereign freedom (T4.1) is what exceeds the natural empathic automaticity that human science frameworks describe.

findings.finding_value: T5's finding that suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion is grounded in T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The polusplanchnos hapax (T7 — coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient for the depth of compassion at the point of maximum permitted suffering) is the lexical expression of T5's most profound formation claim: suffering in the context of compassion-formation produces a depth of compassion that transcends ordinary vocabulary. T7's framework divergence at purposive suffering (Jas 5:11 — teleological frame required) is the analytical expression of T5.4's finding that suffering in the biblical frame produces compassion (as a formative outcome) rather than merely accompanying it. The dual primary anchor (Hos 11:8 and Luke 10:33) maps onto T5's dual-role finding: Hos 11:8 evidences compassion as the character being formed in God (which the human images); Luke 10:33 evidences compassion as the formed character in the human person (the moral norm).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-007: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun),…
findings.finding_value: T7 produces three analytically distinctive findings. First, the vocabulary is structurally complete: every dimension of grace's operation has a corresponding term — disposition (chen, charis as noun), act (chanan, charizō), completed state (charitoō — G5487, NT coinage), receiving-side posture (tachanum, techinah), structural negative (acharistos — built from the same root with alpha-privative). No other characteristic in the review set has equivalent lexical completeness. Second, the NT coinage (charitoō, G5487) is analytically significant: coined because existing vocabulary was insufficient to name "standing-in-favour as a completed, continuing state." The perfect passive kecharitōmenē (Luk 1:28) encodes completed act with continuing state — a grammatical form that no prior vocabulary could carry. Third, the human-science/Scripture divergence is the most significant methodological finding in the review set: at the point of constitutional incapacity (the person cannot respond to grace without grace — SD026, SD008), every human science framework diverges from the biblical account. Affective neuroscience, virtue ethics, and cultural anthropology all assume the person has some prior capacity for response; the biblical account denies this at the point of maximum need (the constitutionally dead of Eph 2:1-5). The LXX analysis gap (T7.1 P8) is confirmed as a methodological limitation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-068-022: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of che…
findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are grounded in and confirmed by T7's primary anchor evidence. The perceptive-faculty finding (T3.1 — grace requires and enables perception) is grounded in the eye-formula of chen (SD041), Zec 12:10's grace-produced vision, and SD012's hearing-receptivity pattern. T7's argument structure for Zec 12:10 (grace outpoured → "when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced") confirms T3.1 precisely: the grace-event produces and requires the inner sight that recognises what grace has cost. T3.6's agency-constituting paradox (1Cor 15:10) is T7.3's most significant framework-divergence point: at the moment of constitutional incapacity, all human science frameworks assume the person has some prior agency; the biblical account holds the paradox of grace-constituted agency that is genuinely human while grace-originated. This is the methodological divergence T7.3 identifies and T3.6 establishes as the operative finding.

findings.finding_value: T5's most distinctive formation finding (five mechanisms, creaturely recognition response as consistent transitional state, grace inhabiting rather than resolving suffering) is grounded in and confirmed by T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The NT coinage charitoō (T7.1 P9 — coined for standing-in-favour as completed, continuing state) is the lexical ground of T5.1's irreversibility finding: the perfect passive grammatical form encodes precisely the "transformation not reversed" character that T5.1 identifies. T7.2's argument structure analysis (Zec 12:10 — grace outpoured → recognition → mourning → supplication) is the textual grounding for T5.2's creaturely recognition response finding: the sequence is not an incidental narrative feature but an argued structural pattern. T7.3's framework divergence (human science frameworks assuming prior capacity; Scripture denying it at the point of maximum incapacity — Eph 2:1-5) is the methodological expression of T5.5's deepest formation finding: the person cannot initiate their own formation by grace. T5 and T7 describe the same formation reality from narrative and lexical angles.

findings.session_b_note: Two frameworks are most useful, addressing different dimensions of covenant. (1) Attachment theory (developmental psychology / relational psychology): covenant is structurally analogous to what attachment theory describes as a secure attachment bond — a stable, reliable relational connection that provides the inner-being conditions for exploration, formation, and flourishing. The covenant's constituting of belonging ("I will be their God") and the conditions it creates for inner hope, identity, and knowing (Jer 31:34) map closely onto what attachment theory identifies as the effects of secure attachment. This framework illuminates the relational-psychological dimension of covenant's inner-being function. (2) Contract and covenant theory (social philosophy / political philosophy / legal theory): the distinction between contract (exchange of equal obligations between independent parties) and covenant (bond of committed loyalty that constitutes a relationship, typically with asymmetric parties) is directly relevant to covenant's inner-being structure. The biblical covenant is explicitly not a contract (OBS-034-002 — "not a contract between equals"). Covenant theory illuminates the structural asymmetry (God initiates, human responds), the constitutive (not merely regulative) character of the bond, and the role of obligation within relationship.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-034-007: T7 as a whole reveals that the covenant vocabulary is one of the most lexically rich and methodologically demanding in the programme. The full vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) shows seven simultaneous semanti…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals that the covenant vocabulary is one of the most lexically rich and methodologically demanding in the programme. The full vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) shows seven simultaneous semantic dimensions (relational, bodily, oral, legal, moral, transformative, eschatological) that require the complete term inventory to see — no single term carries all seven. The LXX translation choice (diathēkē over synthēkē — Q&A-177) is a theological-methodological decision that imports the testamentary/death dimension into covenant language and is directly exploited by the NT. The primary anchor verse (Jer 31:33 / Heb 8:10 — Q&A-185) is uniquely comprehensive — it states simultaneously the constitutional site, the divine action, the relational outcome, and the cognitive product. The human science frameworks (Q&A-186, Q&A-187) illuminate specific dimensions (attachment, covenant-vs-contract) but diverge from the biblical material at the point of covenant's theological uniqueness — God's unilateral initiative, constitutional transformation, and eschatological scope are not captured by any human science framework. T7 confirms that the analysis rests on solid evidential and methodological ground, while acknowledging the inherent limitations of the 9% G1242 verse coverage and the legacy-VC status of all 15 OWNER terms.

findings.session_b_note: (P1 — most useful framework) Moral philosophy and developmental psychology. Moral philosophy: kindness as other-oriented virtue — but chesed exceeds Aristotelian beneficence: it is covenantally obligated and divinely grounded, not merely virtuous. Developmental psychology: the chasid formation arc describes a developmental trajectory — character formed over time through relational encounters and deliberate practice [XREG: H2623, OBS-099-094]. (P2 — illumination) Attachment theory illuminates the chesed relationship: God's chesed as secure attachment base (Psa 23:4 — "you are with me" as the secure base from which the person faces the valley of death [OBS-099-066]). The chasid is the person with secure attachment to God, expressed in relational capacity toward others. Makes the evidence more coherent. (P3 — divergence) Biblical chesed exceeds psychological attachment: it is not merely emotional security but covenantal obligation and moral formation. Psychology can describe the attachment function; it cannot account for the covenantal structure. (P4 — gaps) Evidence does not address formation of kindness in early development or parental kindness shaping child's capacity for chesed. A genuine gap requiring further verse investigation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-099-007: T7 reveals that the evidential foundation for kindness is now strong following cross-registry supplementation, but with a residual gap at the LXX/semantic-history level. The primary lexical finding: c…
findings.finding_value: T7 reveals that the evidential foundation for kindness is now strong following cross-registry supplementation, but with a residual gap at the LXX/semantic-history level. The primary lexical finding: chesed's semantic range (goodness/kindness/faithfulness as a single integrated concept) does not map onto English "kindness" without loss — every English translation must choose between the loyalty dimension and the warmth dimension of chesed; neither alone captures the whole. This translation complexity is not a peripheral philological problem but a structural one for understanding what kindness is — if you translate chesed as "love" (as many English Bibles do), you lose the specifically loyal-relational character; if you translate it as "kindness," you lose the covenant-faithfulness dimension. The LXX gap (chesed → eleos/mercy) is analytically significant: the Greek-speaking world's reception of the Hebrew chesed concept emphasised its compassion/mercy dimension over its faithfulness dimension — which may partly explain why chrēstos/chrēstotēs in the NT emphasises benign goodness over covenantal loyalty. The primary anchor verse finding is secure: Lam 3:22 is the structural foundation — it asserts what no other verse asserts: that divine kindness is unconditional in its permanence even when everything else has failed. The most useful human science framework is developmental psychology (attachment theory illuminating the chesed relationship as secure-base attachment), but the biblical chesed exceeds it in covenantal obligation and moral transformation. T7's most significant intra-tier finding: the translation complexity of chesed is not merely a translation problem but a definitional one — the programme's use of "kindness" as the registry name captures only part of what chesed names; the full concept requires "loyal kindness" or "covenant faithfulness" as a corrective.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-022: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quali…
findings.finding_value: T3's finding that taste is the primary perceptive faculty for kindness (1Pet 2:3 — "tasted that the Lord is good / chrēstos") is grounded in T7's lexical finding that chrēstos itself carries the quality of agreeable goodness — something that can be tasted and found to be of a certain quality. The word chrēstos, which names the characteristic, contains an implicit sensory metaphor: it is the kind of characteristic that one encounters through experience (taste) before grasping conceptually. T7's lexical finding that chesed's semantic range includes goodness/faithfulness — not merely kindness — maps onto T3's cognition finding (T3.2 — Hos 6:6 pairing chesed with knowledge of God): genuine chesed requires a cognitive grasp of who God is, which is consistent with chesed carrying a knowledge-dimension in its semantic range. T7's most useful human science framework (developmental psychology/attachment theory) connects with T3's relational capacity finding: attachment theory explains the faculty-level mechanism by which the "secure base" of divine chesed enables the human person to exercise relational capacity toward others.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-099-027: T5's formation findings are directly grounded in T7's lexical evidence in a specific way: the three formation mechanisms (Spirit-formation, inscription, encounter) each correspond to a specific textua…
findings.finding_value: T5's formation findings are directly grounded in T7's lexical evidence in a specific way: the three formation mechanisms (Spirit-formation, inscription, encounter) each correspond to a specific textual cluster in the chesed corpus. Spirit-formation is the NT Greek evidence (Gal 5:22 — chrēstotēs as fruit of the Spirit); inscription is Pro 3:3 (chesed written on the heart — the clearest constitutional formation text); encounter is the Psalms lament/praise corpus (the psalmist encountering God's chesed in distress and being transformed). T7's literary finding that kindness appears across all major literary forms (lament, praise, narrative, instruction, argument) is the T5 formation diversity mapped onto literary genre — the formation occurs in all contexts and genres, not only in instructional texts. T7's most useful human science framework (developmental psychology / attachment theory) illuminates T5's formation arc: the chasid formation trajectory maps onto attachment theory's "secure attachment → exploration → resilience" pattern — the person who has received divine chesed as secure attachment base (Psa 23:4) is equipped to explore and sustain relational kindness toward others (T4 giving) and to withstand suffering without losing kindness (T5 suffering finding).

findings.session_b_note: Two frameworks are most directly relevant: (1) Positive psychology / wellbeing science: the concept of eudaimonia (flourishing/wellbeing) in Aristotle's ethics, and its contemporary development in positive psychology (Seligman's PERMA model — Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment), maps most closely onto the shalom vocabulary. Shalom as comprehensive welfare and flourishing overlaps substantially with eudaimonia — both name the condition of the whole person thriving rather than merely experiencing pleasure; (2) Attachment theory (psychology): the Bowlby/Ainsworth framework of secure attachment producing a "safe base" from which the person can operate with confidence — this maps directly onto the peace-trust relationship (Psa 4:8 — resting in God's sole keeping; Isa 26:3 — mind stayed on God produces perfect peace). Secure attachment to God as the constitutional basis of inner peace is the closest psychological equivalent to the biblical structure. Neither framework is identical to the biblical concept — both illuminate without capturing it fully.

findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are validated and illuminated by T7's methodological analysis. T3's attachment-theory insight (Psa 131:2 — weaned child posture as attachment security) is the human science framework most appropriate to the relational capacity faculty (T3.11) and the soul's quiet (T2.2). T3's conscience-gateway finding (Psa 32:3-5) is the verse that T7.2.3 classifies as exhibiting the conditional-causal argument structure: the logical structure (suppressed conscience → deterioration → confession → peace) is both a faculty engagement pattern (T3.9) and a coherent causal argument (T7.2.3). The faculty map and the lexical-literary analysis describe the same biblical reality through different analytical lenses.

findings.session_b_note: Two frameworks are relevant at different levels. (1) Moral philosophy (virtue ethics): the characteristic as analysed engages moral character (the primary dimension), voluntary action, the relationship between inner disposition and outer act, and the formation of stable character over time — all central concerns of virtue ethics (Aristotle, MacIntyre). Virtue ethics provides a framework for understanding how faithfulness-as-giving constitutes character rather than merely performing actions. (2) Attachment theory (developmental psychology/relational psychology): the responsive-giving mode (872-002) and the eschatological-restoration mode (872-007) engage attachment dynamics — attentiveness to the inner condition of the attached person, the protective withholding of harm (Hos 11:8), the restoration of relational responsiveness (Hos 2:15). Attachment theory illuminates the relational-dispositional dimension of the characteristic. Moral philosophy is the most useful for the overall characteristic; attachment theory is most useful for the compassionate-responsive mode.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-007: T7 as a whole reveals the evidential and methodological shape of this registry's analysis. The vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) is the governing finding: two poles — na.tan (enacted) and emunah/hesed/pistis (…
findings.finding_value: T7 as a whole reveals the evidential and methodological shape of this registry's analysis. The vocabulary arc (Q&A-179) is the governing finding: two poles — na.tan (enacted) and emunah/hesed/pistis (constituted) — are both necessary and neither alone is sufficient. The grammatical gap (verb vs. nominal) maps directly onto the analytical distinction between the two poles. The literary diversity of the anchor corpus (narrative, prophecy, wisdom, liturgy) means no single interpretive lens covers the full evidence base. The primary analytical anchor (Hos 11:8) is identified for its unique revelation of the divine inner-being decision structure. The human science frameworks (virtue ethics, attachment theory) illuminate the characteristic while also diverging at critical points — the divergences are themselves analytically productive: biblical faithfulness requires both a virtue-ethical foundation (the character basis of giving) and something that virtue ethics cannot supply (the constitutive primacy of received divine giving as the ground of human virtue). What T7 reveals as a whole: the evidential base of this characteristic is rich, methodologically complex, and internally consistent. The two main methodological challenges — the registry label/OWNER term gap, and the legacy-VC status of all classified verses — are acknowledged and do not undermine the analysis but do qualify its certainty.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-015: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — hearing precedes giving, memory is narrative-temporal, affect is at source and target, conscientiousness is the apex) and the methodological-evidential analysis (T…
findings.finding_value: The faculty engagement pattern (T3 — hearing precedes giving, memory is narrative-temporal, affect is at source and target, conscientiousness is the apex) and the methodological-evidential analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, attachment theory illuminates, both diverge at critical points) converge in an analytically productive way. Virtue ethics (T7.3) addresses the same faculties that T3 identifies: moral evaluation, volition, agency, conscientiousness are the virtue-ethics faculties. The virtue-ethics framework illuminates T3 findings precisely because both are addressing the same inner-being territory. The divergence (T7.3.3 — virtue ethics cannot account for the constitutive primacy of received divine giving) maps onto the T3 finding that cognition is constituted by endowing giving (Q&A-071) rather than generated by the person. Attachment theory illuminates the hearing-precedes-giving pattern (T3.1 — God hears inner suffering) and the restoration of relational responsiveness (T3.11 — relational capacity restored). What this pair reveals: the human-science frameworks are useful precisely because they address the same inner-being faculties, and limited precisely where they diverge from the biblical account of those faculties' grounding.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-020: The formation arc (T5 — developmental, eschatologically oriented, suffering-tested) and the methodological analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, diverges on received-constitutive character; Hos 11…
findings.finding_value: The formation arc (T5 — developmental, eschatologically oriented, suffering-tested) and the methodological analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, diverges on received-constitutive character; Hos 11:8 as primary anchor) produce a pointed finding. The virtue ethics framework (T7.3.2) illuminates the formation arc well — disposition formed through repeated enacted commitment toward stable character — but diverges at the key point: virtue ethics assumes the person generates virtue through practice, while the biblical account places constitutive divine giving (Spirit, wisdom) as the prior condition of formative capacity (T5.5, T2.1). The divergence maps exactly onto the T5 finding that formation is constitutively dependent on received divine giving. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) is also the key verse for the formation arc: divine compassion overriding judicial logic is itself a formative act — it preserves the relational context within which human formation can continue. What this pair reveals: the evidential and methodological analysis (T7) independently identifies the same structural priority that the formation analysis (T5) finds: the constitutive primacy of divine giving as the ground of human formation.

findings.finding_value: Attachment theory (Bowlby, Ainsworth) — the directed attachment structure of love maps closely to attachment research. Positive psychology's work on love and connection (Sternberg's triangular theory). Divergence: love is commanded (enemy-love); attachment theory does not include volitional extension of attachment toward those who are hostile.

Empathy and affective response research (Preston and de Waal's "perception-action model" of empathy); somatic empathy research. Divergence: compassion's womb-root and the directional asymmetry (never flows upward to God) have no psychological structural equivalent.

Restorative justice and forgiveness psychology (Worthington, McCullough). Divergence: the sovereignty of mercy (Rom 9:15-16 — Group 1628 — cannot be coerced) has no psychological equivalent; psychological forgiveness is a human choice, not a sovereign act.

Virtue ethics (Aristotle — goodness as acquired stable disposition); character strengths research (VIA Character Strengths — Peterson, Seligman). Divergence: goodness as derivative from divine source (Mar 10:18 — Group 1096) has no equivalent in virtue ethics, which treats character as human self-acquisition.

Emotional regulation psychology (Gross); non-violent communication (Rosenberg); distress tolerance research. Divergence: the eschatological grounding of epieikēs (Phili 4:5 — Group 1103 — "the Lord is at hand") produces a non-anxious relational presence for which no psychological framework has a structural equivalent.

Grief psychology (Kübler-Ross, Worden); post-traumatic growth research (Tedeschi, Calhoun — comforter-capacity emerging from processed suffering corresponds to PTG's compassion-toward-similar-sufferers finding). Social support research. Divergence: the divine comforter as primary source and the eschatological comfort (eternal comfort — 2Th 2:16 — Group 3074) have no psychological equivalents.

Social psychology of belonging (Baumeister and Leary — "need to belong"); reconciliation psychology (Tutu, Gobodo-Madikizela); community of practice theory (Wenger, Lave). Divergence: the Trinitarian fellowship as the ground of koinōnia (2Cor 13:14 — Group 1055) and participation in the divine nature (2Pe 1:4 — Group 1057) have no structural psychological equivalents.

The cluster's characteristics converge with human science frameworks at the phenomenological level — the observable inner-being dynamics correspond to documented psychological phenomena. The most consistent divergences are: (1) the divine origination of all characteristics (no framework treats virtues as divinely sourced and Spirit-produced); (2) the eschatological orientation (no framework orients present virtue toward an eschatological completion); (3) the sovereign/unconditional dimension (particularly in mercy and love — these characteristics are exercised without regard for merit in their divine form, which no psychological account of motivation accommodates).

**[CLUSTER]** E. Three frameworks are engaged by M26's verse evidence, per the external reference document (WA-M26-righteousness-external-reference-v1_0-20260510.md):

1. **Virtue ethics (moral philosophy, Aristotle)** — the most structurally aligned. Aristotle's *dikaiosunē* uses the same Greek word as the NT's primary righteousness term. His treatment of virtue as a stable inner state (*hexis*) evidenced by conduct — never directly observable — parallels the cluster's finding that righteousness is a governing state (A2 condition) evidenced by righteous acts (A2-012, practiced righteousness). His requirement for a *telos* (an external reference point for what the good is) parallels the programme's finding that human righteousness requires God as its constitutive reference point.

2. **Moral psychology (Haidt, Kohlberg)** — useful for the formation and developmental dimensions (T5). Kohlberg's highest stage of moral reasoning (appeal to universal principles regarded as binding independent of preference) structurally parallels the programme's finding that righteousness requires submission to a standard the person did not create. The moral-foundations research (universal moral intuitions) is relevant to the cross-cultural presence of righteousness-cognates.

3. **Developmental psychology (conscience formation)** — useful for T3.9 (conscience) and T5.2 (sequence of inner states). The developmental arc from external moral constraint to internalized moral identity parallels the biblical arc from law as external standard to law written on the heart (Jer 31:33, VSG M26-A2-005).

findings.finding_value: Clinical psychology — anxiety research (Beck, Emery, Borkovec, Dugas). The cognitive model of anxiety (threat appraisal + insufficient coping resources) maps directly onto M20-A's profile: the person perceives threat and does not appraise their own resources (or God's provision) as sufficient. Borkovec's verbal-cognitive characterisation of worry maps onto merimnaō's ruminative-attentional dimension.

findings.finding_value: Cognitive psychology — ambivalence and decision research (Festinger, Priester and Petty, Kahneman). Festinger's cognitive dissonance maps onto dipsuchos: holding two incompatible commitments (God and world) produces the psychological discomfort named as double-mindedness. Priester and Petty's ambivalence research (simultaneous positive and negative evaluation of the same object producing instability) maps precisely onto the double-minded person whose evaluation of God and the world is simultaneously positive in both directions.

findings.finding_value: Per the science extract (Section 1): positive psychology — gratitude and wellbeing research (Emmons, McCullough, Mauss). The gratitude research (Emmons's *Thanks!*, 2007; McCullough's three-component model: benefit received + attribution to intentional benefactor + recognition that benefit exceeded what was owed) maps with precision onto the theological structure of grace-reception: grace is received, it is attributed to God as intentional benefactor, and it exceeds any claim the recipient could make. Mauss's gift theory (*The Gift*, 1925) addresses the structure of pure gift — a gift without obligation — which is the sociological form of grace.
